### Siren
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/siren-1cc2) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/B2JK-Industry/Upgrade-Siren-ETHPrague2026) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://upgrade-siren.vercel.app) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHPrague%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethprague2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-4-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Siren turns public evidence into trust signals.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![OpenZeppelin](https://img.shields.io/badge/OpenZeppelin-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Vercel](https://img.shields.io/badge/Vercel-333333?style=flat-square) ![alchemy](https://img.shields.io/badge/alchemy-333333?style=flat-square) ![sepolia](https://img.shields.io/badge/sepolia-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

**The problem.** Today, deciding whether to trust an ENS-named agent, contract, or team means manually checking Sourcify, GitHub, Etherscan, and ENS records — separately, with no shared standard for discounting unverified claims, and no way to prove later that a report ever existed. Token holders approve proxy upgrades blind. Investors back agents on screenshots. Hackathon judges have no way to score a project's verifiability fast.

**Siren turns any .eth name into an on-chain trust certificate.**

Every Bench verdict can be minted as an EAS attestation (Sepolia + mainnet schemas registered) — an EIP-712-signed certificate that binds the full report payload (subject, namehash, score, tier, computedAt, reportHash, reportUri) to the wallet that published it. The certificate is shareable as an EAS Explorer URL, decodeable by any third party, and the next time someone runs Siren on the same subject, the live verdict can be DIFFED against the previous certificate — surfacing score regressions, tier downgrades, and identity rotations as ALERT-level signals.

**What you can use Siren for**

- **Mint your project's trust certificate on-chain.** /b/<ens> gives you a 0–100 benchmark across four data sources (Sourcify, GitHub, on-chain activity, ENS-internal records). One click → Publish to EAS → permanent receipt. Try it on sbo3lagent.eth — the certificate already lives at sepolia.easscan.org/attestation/view/0xa5b4e5a48e23127a0b9284c7c1128028cc84a06d2fe973092f2dc494e83775ff.

- **Approve a proxy upgrade safely.** /r/<ens> gives a 5-second SAFE / REVIEW / SIREN verdict backed by Sourcify-verified bytecode. No source, no upgrade.

- **Diff a previous certificate against the live verdict.** Paste an EAS Explorer URL on the homepage, click "Open live verdict" — instant diff banner with severity-coded changes (UNCHANGED / CHANGED / ALERT). Identity rotation, score regression, revocation — all surfaced automatically. This is chain-of-custody for reputation.

- **Apply to Umia's Tailored Auctions** (sponsor track). Siren signs EIP-712 ServerPermits that gate Umia's UmiaValidationHook on Bench tier. Founders avoid running their own gating server; bidders embed Siren's hookData blob in their bid. First verifier-as-a-service for Umia, no new key custody.

- **Export a draft Umia application.** The verdict page also generates a schema-validated umia venture apply payload (canonical Community Track schema), prefilled from ENS records, locked when sourced from public evidence, JSON-download-only.

**Why the certificate is structurally trustworthy**

1. **Full-payload EIP-712 binding.** The signature covers subject, namehash, score, tier, timestamp, reportHash AND reportUri — verifier rejects on any field mismatch. Score-only signing left subject-spoofing wide open; we explicitly closed that hole.

2. **ECDSA-recovered, not field-claimed.** The off-chain verifier doesn't trust the "signer" string in the JSON envelope — it recovers the address from the EIP-712 signature via viem.recoverTypedDataAddress and rejects on mismatch.

3. **Trust-discounted source weights.** Unverified GitHub claims contribute at ×0.6 — never hidden, never inflated. The math the certificate carries is honest about what's verified.

4. **Re-derivable.** /api/bench/<ens> returns the raw evidence the certificate was minted from. Anyone can recompute the score themselves; no black box behind the signature.

5. **ENS-anchored.** Every certificate is bound to a human-readable .eth name via namehash. No opaque IDs, no URL shortlinks to phish.

6. **Honest ceiling.** Tier S is reserved for v2 (verified GitHub cross-sign). v1 doesn't pretend to mint a certificate at a tier the math can't reach.

**The 30-second story**

Type sbo3lagent.eth — see live tier B verdict pulled from Sourcify, GitHub, on-chain, and ENS-internal sources — click Publish to EAS — receive your on-chain certificate (Sepolia EAS UID). Tomorrow, paste that UID back into Siren — diff banner says UNCHANGED. Type a fresh agent — see tier U with "no data, no score" — fix your ENS records — re-run — tier C — mint a new certificate. Reputation that compounds, on-chain.

**Challenges we ran into**

**Making the on-chain certificate actually trustworthy, not just a signed JSON blob.** The first version of the EAS attestation flow did three things wrong at once: (1) the on-chain bytes field was the eas-sdk JSON envelope serialized, not the ABI-encoded BenchAttestationPayload — so on-chain decoders returned garbage instead of score/tier; (2) the off-chain verifier compared the "signer" field claim against expected, but never recovered the address from the EIP-712 signature — an attacker could write any signer into the JSON and we'd accept it; (3) the verifier checked reportHash only — leaving subject-spoofing wide open. Fix in one batch: re-encode via encodeBenchPayload before submit, recover via viem.recoverTypedDataAddress against eas-sdk-provided sig.domain/types/message, and verify all material fields (subject, namehash, reportHash, reportUri, score, tier, computedAt, recipient). An audit caught all three the day of the deadline.

**The publish flow was broken end-to-end and the broken state had been live for hours.** record-publish required an off-chain row in Turso before accepting the on-chain attestation, but saveOffchainAttestation had zero callers — every publish attempt failed with no_offchain_record. Fix: when no row exists, derive the bundle from the on-chain decoded payload itself and INSERT a fresh row, then record the publication. Now the certificate flow works whether or not the off-chain build endpoint ran first.

**Multi-chain ENS routing without exploding the page deadline.** Production defaulted to Sepolia (DEFAULT_BENCH_CHAIN_ID=11155111) so the curated demo agent on Sepolia would resolve, but real mainnet names like sbo3lagent.eth then routed through Sepolia first, hit "no resolver" rpc errors, retried on mainnet, and consistently blew the 12s page deadline. Fixed via name-suffix routing (only *.upgrade-siren-demo.eth go to Sepolia) plus per-source timeout budgets so one slow source can't wedge the whole orchestrator.

**Identity rotation false positives in the diff layer.** The compare-with-previous-certificate flow flagged "primaryAddress changed" ALERT every time a Sepolia attestation was diffed against a mainnet ENS resolution — because each chain holds its own resolver state. Solution: read attestation.network → chainId, only flag rotation when same chain; cross-chain compares get an INFO note explaining why addresses are not directly comparable.

**Tier ladder math contradiction visible to judges.** Engine thresholds were S>=65 / A>=50 after axis rebalance, but the UI legend still said S>=90 / A>=75 from a prior version. A score of 59 landed in A by the engine but the legend said A>=75. Caught by audit. Fix touched ScoreBanner, the new TierLadder component, the homepage tier-range table, and four demo booth tile labels — all of which had been tuned for the old ladder.

**Vercel "Sensitive" environment variables don't export.** We needed local scripts to query the prod ENS subgraph and Alchemy RPC, but vercel env pull returned empty strings for any var marked Sensitive. Workaround: ship a dedicated /api/ens/debug/<name> route that runs server-side with the real prod env, hit it from the browser to enumerate text records and coinType slots without ever pulling secrets to disk.

**Network Economy**

Siren Bench turns reputation into an economic primitive. Today, agents and onchain ventures can enter markets, raise capital, join auctions, or ask for trust mostly through social proof, private judgment, or opaque platform scoring. 

Siren replaces that with a public, verifiable benchmark: an ENS-named agent or project is scored from real evidence across Sourcify-verified contracts, GitHub activity, onchain history, ENS records, attestations, and signed reports. Every score is inspectable, every source is visible, and unverified claims are discounted instead of blindly trusted. 

For the Network Economy track, we take this one step further: the benchmark is not just shown in a report, it can control economic access. A founder can require a minimum Siren Bench tier for a Tailored Auction step, and a bidder who controls the subject ENS can mint a signed permit that is checked by an onchain validation hook. 

This makes reputation portable, transparent, and programmable across markets. Siren is building the trust layer that lets agentic economies decide not just who looks credible, but who is actually allowed to participate.

**Future Society**

Siren Bench is public due diligence for autonomous agents and onchain projects.

Today, agents and ventures can ask for funding, access, or trust with very little public evidence. A polished website and a GitHub link can look convincing, but communities need a way to see what is verified, what is unverified, and what is missing.

Siren Bench makes that process transparent. It turns ENS, Sourcify, GitHub, and onchain data into an inspectable report. Every score has a breakdown. Every source has a trust label. Unverified claims are discounted instead of being treated as truth.

This helps communities allocate attention, capital, and governance support more fairly.

**Sourcify Bounty**

**Sourcify is the part of Siren's trust math that proves your code does what your source says it does.** Siren reads four public sources for every ENS-named subject: Sourcify-verified bytecode, on-chain activity, ENS-internal records, and GitHub. Three of them — Sourcify, on-chain, ENS-internal — are weighted at full trust (×1.0) because they're structurally unfakeable: you can't lie about your nonce, you can't fake an ENS registration date, and Sourcify cryptographically anchors source code to the deployed bytecode hash. GitHub is the one source weighted at ×0.6, because a "com.github" claim in an ENS text record is just a claim — anyone can write it, no one verifies it.

**But Sourcify is special among the three full-trust sources, because only Sourcify links the source code to what's actually running on-chain.** On-chain activity proves the wallet exists and has been used. ENS-internal proves the name was registered. Neither tells you whether the smart contract behind that wallet does what its source claims. Only Sourcify does. That's why Sourcify gates the single-contract verdict (no Sourcify-verified source for a new proxy implementation → automatic SIREN, "no source, no upgrade") and why the Bench score collapses for any subject whose declared contracts aren't on Sourcify.

**When you mint a Siren report on-chain (EAS attestation), Sourcify proof flows into the certificate.** The signed payload embeds a hash over the full evidence record, including Sourcify match-levels and the verified source set. If the same subject is re-attested next month and Sourcify has gained a new verified deployment in the meantime, our diff banner lights up automatically. Sourcify's verification status becomes a reputation primitive that shows up in every certificate, every comparison, every governance vote based on a Siren report.

**Siren creates a structural incentive to verify on Sourcify.** Every page surfaces explicit "Verify on Sourcify" and "Submit to Sourcify" CTAs whenever a contract is unverified or only verified on Etherscan. Etherscan-only contracts are deliberately scored at half weight, and the panel says so out loud — telling the user exactly what they need to do to lift their tier. Agents, protocols, and projects that want a higher Siren benchmark are pushed toward Sourcify, not away from it.

**Reviewers can confirm the integration is live, not theatre.** A real-time "Sourcify · live · ~250ms" status indicator in the homepage hero pings Sourcify's v2 server on every poll. Click any verified contract entry on a bench page and you land on Sourcify's actual repo URL — same bytes, same hashes. The deep evidence panel shows compiler version, EVM target, optimizer settings, OpenZeppelin pattern detection (Pausable, Ownable, UUPS, AccessControl), proxy implementations, and the full storage layout slot-by-slot. None of it is mocked; the JSON behind it (/api/bench/<ens>) returns the raw evidence so reviewers can recompute the score themselves.

**Try it on sbo3lagent.eth** (live mainnet ENS with a published EAS certificate at sepolia.easscan.org/attestation/view/0xa5b4...) **or siren-agent-demo.upgrade-siren-demo.eth** (curated agent with a full four-source verdict). One click into either page shows Sourcify doing the load-bearing work the score talks about.

**Best Agentic Venture**

Siren tells Umia which agents have proof, not just promises.

The product. Type any ENS-named subject — agent, team, or project — into /b/[name] and Siren reads its public evidence in parallel: Sourcify-verified contracts (storage-layout history, license, compiler version, proxy resolution), GitHub repositories (top-20, README, LICENSE, test directory presence), on-chain history (first transaction via binary-search on historical nonce, contracts deployed via Sourcify deployer crosswalk, recent activity), and ENS-internal records (registration date, subname count, text-record count, last TextChanged block). Every signal carries a trust factor: 1.0 for verified sources (Sourcify, RPC, ENS subgraph), 0.6 for unverified GitHub claims. The score is a deterministic function of those contributions, locked in packages/evidence/src/score/weights.ts, and rendered to every user as a full breakdown — weight × value × trust = contribution per row. No black box.

The Umia integration. We deployed UmiaValidationHookMock on Sepolia and shipped packages/umia-permit, a workspace package that issues EIP-712 ServerPermit signatures from the Siren operator key. POST /api/umia/permit returns a permit encoding the subject's Bench tier, score, and signed report URI. The hook recovers the signer in-contract and gates the launch action. Without the hook there is no venture-launch surface to gate — Umia is the actual programmatic consumer of Bench, not a logo on a slide.

Reviewer outcomes. Bench routes subjects into clear lanes: fast-track (high seniority + relevance + verifiability), emerging review (relevant, not yet senior), evidence required (claim-heavy, low verifiability), reject (low relevance), or security audit (contract SIREN).
No data, no score.

**Best ENS Integration for AI Agents**

Siren Bench uses ENS as the public identity root for AI agents.

Each agent is represented by an ENS name. From that name, the product resolves a live benchmark manifest, owner information, metadata, public endpoints, contracts, GitHub identity, and onchain address. The benchmark is built from the agent’s ENS identity outward.

Removing ENS would break the product. The agent would lose its public discovery surface, ownership anchor, and evidence registry. ENS is not a decorative username here; it is how the agent is found, identified, and evaluated.

For the demo, we show multiple prepared AI agents with ENS identities. A judge can enter an agent’s ENS name and immediately see its score, seniority, relevance, source grid, trust discount, and evidence drawers.

**Most Creative Use of ENS**

Siren uses ENS for more than name-to-address resolution. We use ENS as a public evidence router.

An ENS name can represent a protocol, an AI agent, a team, or an onchain project. From that single name, Siren resolves the subject’s evidence map: contracts, source verification, ownership, report endpoints, benchmark manifests, public metadata, and signed report references.

This creates a new ENS pattern: name-to-evidence. Instead of treating an ENS name as a profile or wallet alias, Siren turns it into an inspectable trust surface. A user can type an ENS name and see what is verified, what is unverified, what is missing, and how each signal affects the final score.

The creative part is that ENS becomes the routing layer for public due diligence. One name opens a full report across Sourcify, GitHub, onchain history, ENS records, and attestations.

### Wallexa
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/wallexa-ecc1) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/admpr/eth-prague-2) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/isin8x664CE) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHPrague%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethprague2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-4-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Agentic Hardware Wallet

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![C](https://img.shields.io/badge/C-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![EF: Account Abstraction](https://img.shields.io/badge/EF:%20Account%20Abstraction-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

initial commits: [FE](https://github.com/admpr/eth-prague-2/commit/9460e20f5767d15eea1a170bdb87d2db47c4ec98), [contracts](https://github.com/admpr/eth-prague-contracts/commit/b8c20656c2a91f3314ea8fff581c0e10b17d280b), [agent-showcase](https://github.com/admpr/eth-prague-agent/commit/5d949f62535eae2f817cab183af4b11454a6d622)

**Wallexa** makes AI agents safer to use onchain by turning a regular hardware-wallet into a modular smart wallet with scoped agent access.

Today, giving an AI agent blockchain access usually means handing it a private key with full control, or creating a separate wallet that must be constantly funded and often lacks the permissions, reputation, or app history of the main wallet. Wallexa solves this by keeping the hardware wallet as the root authority while using **EIP-7702**, **ERC-4337**, and **ERC-7579** modular account infrastructure to issue limited agent keys.

Agents can transact from the user’s real wallet address, but only within boundaries enforced onchain: token spend limits, ETH budgets, contract allowlists, function-level permissions, time windows, and revocation. Example roles include stablecoin payment assistants, DeFi rebalancers, rewards claimers, treasury payers, gas runners, governance voters, and many more.

Users no longer need to expose their main private key or constantly refill separate agent wallets. The wallet owner can sleep calmly knowing their agents can keep working from the secure hardware-wallet, but cannot bypass the rules set for them.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the biggest challenges was that the idea started from the hardware itself. The Idea was born at the hackathon when we received a small hardware wallet with open-source firmware, but the firmware did not support signing the new **EIP-7702 authorization** needed to delegate an EOA and turn it into a smart account. To make Wallexa possible, we had to fork the wallet firmware and add custom support for signing EIP-7702 authorization lists directly from the hardware wallet.

Another major hurdle was the permission system. We could not find an existing **ERC-7579 validator module** that matched the exact access-control model we needed for AI agents: token spending limits, native ETH budgets, contract allowlists, function-level restrictions, time windows, and revocation. So we built and deployed our own Solidity ERC-7579 validator module that enforces these boundaries onchain.

The final challenge was proving that the system actually works with real agents. We built a small agent demo repo where agents can be initialized with the generated access keys and attempt transactions from the user’s wallet address. This let us demonstrate both sides: transactions inside the agent’s permissions succeed, while transactions outside its boundaries fail, even if the agent is instructed to perform them. Most importantly, the successful transactions are still made from the hardware wallet’s address, showing that the agent can operate through the user’s real wallet without ever receiving full control over it.

**Ethereum Core**

Wallexa is built directly on Ethereum account abstraction primitives and explores a practical use case for the next generation of wallets.

The project uses **EIP-7702** to delegate an existing hardware-wallet EOA into smart account logic while preserving the same address. It also uses **ERC-4337** execution patterns and an **ERC-7579-compatible validator module** to support modular, scoped agent permissions.

We also built a custom Solidity validator module because existing modules did not provide the exact permission model needed for AI agents, such as token spending limits, native ETH budgets, contract allowlists, function-level restrictions, time windows, and revocation.

Wallexa demonstrates how Ethereum accounts can evolve from single-key wallets into programmable, modular, safer accounts without forcing users to abandon their existing address.

**Network Economy**

Wallexa fits the Network Economy track because it improves how users safely participate in autonomous onchain economic activity.

AI agents increasingly need to make payments, interact with protocols, claim rewards, manage balances, or pay for services on behalf of users. Today this usually requires giving the agent full wallet control or creating a separate wallet that must be manually funded. Both options create friction and risk.

Wallexa keeps the user’s hardware wallet as the root authority while allowing agents to operate from the user’s real wallet address under onchain-enforced permissions. The owner can define token budgets, ETH limits, contract allowlists, function restrictions, expiration windows, and revocation.

This creates a safer model for agent-driven economic activity: agents can participate in markets, services, and protocols, but users remain in control of the wallet and its risk boundaries.

**Best Agentic Venture**

Wallexa is designed for the agentic economy: AI agents that can safely act onchain for users.

The core problem is that agents need wallet access to be useful, but traditional wallets are controlled by a single private key. Giving that key to an agent gives it full control over funds, permissions, and account history. Wallexa solves this by letting users create scoped access keys for agents while keeping the hardware wallet as the root authority.

Agents can transact from the user’s real wallet address, but only within boundaries enforced onchain: token budgets, ETH limits, contract allowlists, function permissions, time windows, and revocation.

This enables practical agent roles such as payment assistants, DeFi rebalancers, rewards claimers, treasury payers, gas runners, governance voters, and paid-data agents, without giving those agents unlimited wallet power.

**Apify Bounty**

Wallexa fits the Apify bounty through an agent workflow where an AI agent uses Apify as an external data/tool provider and pays for it safely with a scoped wallet key.

In our demo, the wallet owner creates an access key for an Apify-enabled agent with a strict **$5/day spending limit**. When the agent needs external data, such as Instagram data, it calls an Apify scraper. If that service requires payment through an **x402 payment flow**, the agent uses its Wallexa signing key to pay for the service.

This demonstrates a safer model for autonomous agents consuming paid web services. The agent can fetch data and pay for tools when needed, but it cannot exceed the wallet owner’s programmed spending limit or bypass the permissions enforced by Wallexa while still keep making transaction from main wallet and without never ending top up balance to wallet.

### OffPay
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/offpay-03c3) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/ayushsaklani-min/offline-pay) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/j5fesI0yR4g) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-NMIT%20HACKS%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://nmithacks26.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-4-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Tap Now, Chain Later — Offline USDC Payments

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![Android](https://img.shields.io/badge/Android-333333?style=flat-square) ![Kotlin](https://img.shields.io/badge/Kotlin-333333?style=flat-square) ![NFC](https://img.shields.io/badge/NFC-333333?style=flat-square) ![ESP32](https://img.shields.io/badge/ESP32-333333?style=flat-square) ![Web3](https://img.shields.io/badge/Web3-333333?style=flat-square) ![Polygon](https://img.shields.io/badge/Polygon-333333?style=flat-square) ![Bluetooth](https://img.shields.io/badge/Bluetooth-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Digital payments fail without internet — UPI, mobile wallets, and crypto all need connectivity. In rural markets, crowded festivals, and underground transit, millions can't transact during outages.

**OffPay enables fully offline USDC payments via NFC tap-to-pay.** Lock USDC into an on-chain vault on Polygon, pre-sign bearer vouchers, and pay by tapping phones — no internet on either side. Settlement auto-triggers when connectivity returns.

### How it works

1. **Lock funds** — Deposit USDC into OfflineVault on Polygon
2. **Pre-sign vouchers** — Android app signs bearer vouchers using device's secp256k1 key
3. **Tap to pay** — NFC HCE transfers signed voucher instantly to receiver phone or ESP32 reader
4. **Verify locally** — Receiver verifies ECDSA signature + nonce + digest offline
5. **Auto-settle** — Pending vouchers batch-settle on-chain via `settleBearerBatch`

### Key features

- **Unified Android wallet** — sender + receiver in one app, NFC HCE tap-to-pay
- **ESP32 POS terminal** — RC522 NFC + Bluetooth bridge to merchant phone
- **P2P mesh replication** — Google Nearby Connections gossips vouchers for redundancy
- **On-chain settlement** — double-spend protection via `usedVouchers` mapping
- **Sybil-resistant handshake** — ECDSA challenge-response for mesh peer auth
- **Key backup** — PBKDF2 + AES-GCM encrypted backup with server-side pepper

**Challenges we ran into**

### Voucher digest byte-identity across 5 platforms

The keccak256 hash must be identical in Solidity, JavaScript, Kotlin (sender), Kotlin (verifier), and C++ (ESP32). A single byte mismatch breaks signature recovery. We matched ABI encoding, EIP-191 prefix, and Keccak-256 (NOT NIST SHA3) across all five.

### ESP32 Keccak-256 vs SHA3-256

mbedtls on ESP32 only provides NIST SHA3 (different padding from Ethereum's Keccak). We shipped a standalone Keccak-256 implementation — using the library's `sha3` would silently break all signatures.

### Offline double-spend prevention

Without a blockchain at tap-time, we combine:
- Per-payer monotonic nonces (client-side + on-chain)
- Pre-flight locked balance checks before settlement
- On-chain `usedVouchers` mapping as safety net
- Mesh `claimAndWait` so two backups don't settle the same voucher

### Unified app architecture

Consolidated separate customer and merchant apps into one wallet handling NFC HCE send, NFC reader receive, ESP32 Bluetooth bridge, and mesh replication — single APK, single cryptographic identity.

### NFC payload constraints

Android HCE APDU frames have strict size limits. Voucher JSON had to be carefully serialized to fit single-tap exchanges while preserving all cryptographic fields.

**Internet of Things**

OffPay bridges **physical and digital worlds** through a custom ESP32-based NFC reader terminal:

- **ESP32** with on-device secp256k1 key generation and Keccak-256 hashing
- **RC522 NFC module** reading vouchers from phones via ISO 14443A
- **Bluetooth Classic SPP** bridge to merchant's Android phone
- **Cryptographic pairing** — phone signs ESP32's challenge, ESP32 verifies and stores owner in NVS flash

The reader operates as a standalone POS terminal. Combined with **P2P mesh** (Google Nearby Connections) for voucher replication, this is a full IoT payment ecosystem without cloud dependency.

**Blockchain / Cybersecurity**

OffPay is a **blockchain-native offline payment system** on Polygon. It uses an `OfflineVault` smart contract to lock USDC, issue cryptographically signed bearer vouchers, and settle on-chain with double-spend protection via `usedVouchers` mapping and monotonic nonce enforcement.

The voucher lifecycle is secured by **ECDSA over secp256k1** with EIP-191 signing. The ESP32 firmware implements Keccak-256 for Ethereum-compatible verification. The mesh layer uses a **Sybil-resistant challenge-response handshake** to prevent fake peers.

This brings stablecoin payments to environments without internet — extending crypto's reach beyond always-online users.

**The problem it solves**

**The Problem It Solves**

Modern honeypots are largely passive systems - they log attacker activity but treat every intruder the same. Security teams are left with raw logs and no clear way to distinguish whether they are dealing with a human attacker, an automated botnet, or an emerging AI-driven agent.

This distinction is critical. Each type of attacker requires a different response strategy:

Human attackers may indicate targeted intrusion attempts
Botnets suggest large-scale automated exploitation
AI agents represent a new class of adaptive, intelligent threats

Misclassification leads to wasted time, delayed response, or unnecessary escalation, weakening overall security posture.

**⚡ Our Solution: SPECTRE Lite**

SPECTRE Lite transforms the traditional honeypot into an intelligent threat analysis system.

It operates as a deceptive SSH server that not only attracts attackers but actively analyzes and classifies them in real time.

**Key Capabilities**

- Behavioral Fingerprinting
- Uses advanced signals such as:
- Keystroke timing
- Command entropy
- Command diversity and clustering
- AI Trap Mechanism
- A cognitive trap designed to specifically identify AI-driven attackers — something traditional systems cannot detect.
- Real-Time Classification

Every attacker is categorized within seconds as:

- Human
- Automated Bot
- AI Agent
- Actionable Intelligence, Not Raw Logs
- Instead of overwhelming logs, the system provides:
- Instant alerts (e.g., Discord)
- MITRE ATT&CK mapping of attacker techniques
- AI-generated incident summaries via Gemini API

**Impact**

SPECTRE Lite converts a traditionally reactive security tool into a proactive intelligence system.

What used to take hours of manual log analysis is now delivered instantly as clear, actionable threat intelligence.

This enables security teams to:

- Respond faster and more accurately
- Prioritize threats effectively
- Detect next-generation AI-driven attacks early

**Challenges we ran into**

**Challenges I Ran Into**

The biggest challenge was integrating the **AI report generator using the Gemini API.** Even with correct setup, all requests failed with a 403 permission error due to the Google Cloud project being flagged. To handle this, I built a fallback system that generates structured, professional incident reports without relying on the API, ensuring the demo remains reliable.

Another challenge was making attacker detection robust. Simple timing-based methods were easily bypassed by bots adding random delays. I solved this by combining multiple behavioral signals like entropy, command variation, and timing patterns, making evasion significantly harder.

Additional hurdles included:

*Debugging environment/setup issues* during deployment on Amazon EC2
Ensuring the honeypot environment looked realistic to avoid detection
Balancing real-time detection with performance (using background processing)

**Cybersecurity + Artificial Intelligence**

**How My Project Fits into “Cybersecurity + Artificial Intelligence”**

*SPECTRE Lite* sits at the intersection of cybersecurity and AI by combining a traditional honeypot with intelligent, real-time analysis.

From a cybersecurity perspective, it functions as a deceptive SSH honeypot (built using Cowrie) that attracts and captures attacker activity in a controlled environment. It monitors commands, tracks behavior, and maps actions to frameworks like MITRE ATT&CK.

From an AI perspective, the system goes beyond logging by using:

Behavioral analysis (entropy, timing, command patterns)
AI-powered interpretation via Gemini API

This allows the system to:

Classify attackers as human, automated, or AI-driven
Understand attacker intent (reconnaissance, exploitation, etc.)
Generate intelligent incident summaries in real time

**Why This Matters**

Traditional cybersecurity tools are mostly reactive and rule-based. SPECTRE Lite introduces AI-driven decision-making, enabling faster, smarter, and more adaptive threat detection — especially against emerging AI-powered cyber attacks.

**The problem it solves**

### **The Problem Aptum Solves**

1. **Fragmented digital growth**

   * Creators, developers, and small projects struggle to grow audiences across multiple platforms. Each social channel has its own discovery mechanics, requiring constant attention, experimentation, and content generation. There’s no automated way to consistently identify opportunities or engage effectively at scale.

2. **Limited access to autonomous capabilities**

   * Current tools are either static analytics dashboards, simple bots, or manual marketing processes. They do not act autonomously to discover, create, and engage on behalf of the user. This creates a bottleneck for solo builders or small teams who want to maximize reach and impact without hiring full marketing or growth teams.

3. **Unsustainable monetization approaches**

   * Many tools or agents in the market focus on extractive monetization, incentivizing spammy engagement or short-term gains. There is no solution that allows creators to capture revenue opportunities sustainably while growing an ecosystem, building long-term value rather than chasing fleeting metrics.

4. **Chain-specific and siloed ecosystems**

   * On-chain projects and Web3 communities are often isolated per chain or platform. There’s no chain-agnostic agent that can bridge social growth with on-chain capabilities, modularly expanding its utility across multiple ecosystems.

5. **High technical barrier to entry**

   * Building autonomous agents capable of growth, content generation, and engagement is technically complex. Non-technical creators and small teams cannot deploy or scale these capabilities themselves without significant investment in time, money, or engineering expertise.

---

**In short:**
The digital creator and Web3 ecosystem suffers from **fragmented growth, limited automation, unsustainable monetization, siloed platforms, and high technical barriers**. Aptum solves this by being a **modular, autonomous, chain-agnostic agent that discovers, creates, engages, and monetizes opportunities sustainably**, enabling creators and projects to scale without requiring a full team or manual effort.

**The problem it solves**

## 💸 The Problem

Crypto and real money don't talk to each other — and that's a billion-dollar gap.

| Pain Point | Reality Today |
|-----------|--------------|
| 🔁 **Cross-currency transfers** | Require CEX accounts, KYC, and 1–3 day settlement |
| 📭 **Receiver compatibility** | Receiver must also have a crypto wallet |
| 🔐 **Wallet addresses** | 42-character hex strings — error-prone, unusable for everyday people |
| 💸 **On-ramp friction** | Converting crypto → INR requires exchange fees + bank delays |
| 🚫 **No UPI bridge** | India's ₹20 lakh crore/month UPI economy is completely siloed from crypto |

---

## ✅ What SwyftPay Solves

**SwyftPay lets anyone pay with crypto while the receiver gets INR — instantly, securely, with just a QR scan.**

### Who uses it?

| User | How SwyftPay helps |
|------|-------------------|
| 👨‍💻 **Crypto holder** | Spend AMOY for real-world payments without selling on an exchange |
| 🏪 **Merchant / Freelancer** | Accept crypto from global clients, receive INR in their UPI account |
| 👨‍👩‍👧 **Everyday user** | Receive payments without needing a wallet — just a SwyftPay account |
| 🌍 **Remittance sender** | Send value cross-border in seconds vs. SWIFT's 3–5 days |

### How it makes things easier

- **One QR code** replaces wallet addresses — scan and pay in seconds
- **No exchange account needed** — receiver gets INR directly via Razorpay
- **Escrow-backed** — funds are locked in a smart contract, no partial execution risk
- **< 2 second settlement** — on-chain event detected and INR credited instantly
- **Non-custodial** — SwyftPay never holds your private keys or your funds

### How it makes things safer

- 🛡️ Smart contract escrow — rate locked at initiation, no slippage attacks
- 🔏 HMAC-SHA256 signature verification on every Razorpay withdrawal
- 🔑 One wallet per account — enforced at the database level
- 🍪 BetterAuth sessions with HTTP-only cookies — no token leakage

---

SwyftPay bridges India's ₹20 lakh crore UPI economy with the global crypto ecosystem — making cross-currency payments as simple as showing a QR code.

**Challenges we ran into**

## ⚔️ Challenges We Ran Into

### 1. 📸 The QR Scanner Was Completely Fake

**The bug:** Our initial "Scan QR" page was a CSS-animated box with a fake scanning line — it had zero actual camera access. Judges would have immediately seen through it.

**The fix:** We ripped it out entirely and rebuilt it using the browser's native **`BarcodeDetector` API** — which actually reads QR codes frame-by-frame from a live `getUserMedia` camera feed. We added **`jsQR`** as a canvas-based fallback for Firefox/Safari where `BarcodeDetector` isn't supported. The result: a real, working QR scanner with live camera feed.

---

### 2. 💸 Razorpay Payouts API Was Locked Behind Business Verification

**The bug:** Our original plan was for the admin's account to automatically push INR directly to the receiver's UPI ID using **Razorpay Payouts API**. We built it — then hit a wall. Payouts require a fully KYC-verified Razorpay business account, which can't be activated instantly.

**The fix:** We pivoted to **Razorpay Checkout** — the receiver initiates their own withdrawal, the Razorpay payment popup opens with their UPI pre-filled, and our backend verifies the transaction using **HMAC-SHA256 signature verification** before releasing the balance. This is actually *more secure* than the original plan — the user authenticates the payout themselves, and our server validates cryptographic proof of payment.

---

### 3. ⛓️ Settlement Watcher Missing On-Chain Events

**The bug:** Our initial settlement watcher polled the blockchain but used a fixed block number — meaning if the server restarted mid-event, the transaction would be silently lost and the receiver would never get credited.

**The fix:** We rebuilt the watcher to use **`eth_getLogs` with a rolling block range** — it tracks the last processed block in memory and resumes exactly where it left off. Every `OrderCreated` event is caught even across restarts, guaranteeing no missed settlements.

---

### 4. 🔧 Next.js Edge Runtime vs Razorpay Node.js SDK

**The bug:** We tried using the official `razorpay` npm SDK in our API route — it instantly crashed. Next.js API routes using the Edge runtime don't support Node.js built-ins like `crypto.createHmac` natively, and the SDK depends on them.

**The fix:** We switched the API routes to the **Node.js runtime** (`export const runtime = "nodejs"`) and used the **Razorpay REST API directly** via [fetch](cci:1://file:///home/sushovan/Hackathon/swiftpay/SwyftPay/web/src/app/inventory/page.tsx:256:2-270:4) for order creation, keeping the SDK only where needed and implementing HMAC verification manually using the built-in `crypto` module.

---

### 5. 🤳 Chrome Detecting Camera but Page Showing Black

**The bug:** Even though the browser confirmed camera access, the `<video>` element on the scan page displayed a completely black frame.

**The fix:** The `srcObject` assignment on the video element was happening *before* the element mounted in the DOM, causing a race condition. We moved the `getUserMedia` call into a `useEffect` with a `ref` to the video element, ensuring the stream is only attached after the DOM node exists.

---

| # | Challenge | How We Solved It |
|---|-----------|-----------------|
| 1 | Fake QR scanner | Native `BarcodeDetector` API + `jsQR` canvas fallback |
| 2 | Razorpay Payouts locked | Pivot to Checkout + HMAC-SHA256 server-side verification |
| 3 | Missed blockchain events | `eth_getLogs` rolling-block watcher with restart recovery |
| 4 | Edge runtime crash | Switched to Node.js runtime + raw REST API calls |
| 5 | Black camera feed race condition | `useEffect` + `useRef` to gate `srcObject` assignment |

> Stripe for MCP, settled on Solana

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Solana Blockchain](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solana%20Blockchain-333333?style=flat-square) ![solana/web3.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/solana/web3.js-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

# The Problem It Solves

MCP (Model Context Protocol) lets AI agents like Claude access real-world tools — fetching data, running searches, triggering actions. Thousands of developers are building MCP servers. But right now, there's no way to charge for them. Every MCP tool is either free or locked behind a manual API-key billing system that wasn't designed for AI agents.

This creates two compounding problems. First, developers can't monetize the tools they build, so the incentive to build high-quality MCP servers is weak. Second, AI agents have no native way to pay for services — they can't hold credit cards, can't sign up for SaaS plans, and can't navigate billing portals. The result: the emerging MCP ecosystem is stuck at "hobby project" scale.

What's needed is a payment layer that AI agents can use natively — instant, frictionless, and programmable — with a discovery layer so users can find monetized tools in the first place.

# What People Use It For

Doorman is a three-part system: a payment middleware for MCP server developers, a payment proxy for end users, and a public registry for discovery.

## For MCP Server Developers

Add one line of x402 middleware to any Express-based MCP server and it instantly becomes monetizable. Every `tools/call` request triggers a `$0.001 USDC` payment requirement. The server only processes the call after the payment is verified on Solana — no accounts, no invoices, no billing dashboards. Revenue flows directly to the developer's wallet in ~400ms per call.

## For End Users (AI Agent Users)

Run Doorman's local payment proxy, point Claude Desktop at it, and every tool call to a paid MCP server is handled automatically. The proxy intercepts the HTTP `402` response, signs a Solana USDC transaction, and forwards the result to Claude — invisible to the user. Built-in spend limits (`$0.01/call`, `$5/day` default) prevent runaway spend.

## For the Ecosystem

The Doorman Registry is a public directory of paid MCP servers — like an App Store for AI tools. Developers list their servers with pricing, tool schemas, and wallet addresses. Users browse, click "Add to Claude Desktop," and get a ready-to-paste config. No manual setup, no digging through GitHub READMEs.

**Challenges we ran into**

# Challenges We Ran Into

The most complex issue was bridging Claude Desktop's stdio JSON-RPC transport with our HTTP-based MCP server — intercepting `402` responses mid-stream, signing a Solana transaction, and retrying without dropping messages required careful async handling.

We also had to account for the external x402 facilitator service going down mid-development, which produced errors indistinguishable from bad payment signatures in our own code, so we added a backup facilitator URL to keep things stable.

Finally, the demo's 9 concurrent exchange API calls triggered rate limits across Binance, Coinbase, and even our CoinGecko fallback, which took a few rounds of caching and retry logic to get running reliably end to end.

**Best Use of Solana**

Doorman is built for the "Agentic Commerce, Identity, Payments & Stablecoins" track — and it couldn't exist on any other chain.

Speed is load-bearing. AI agents work in real time. A tool call that takes 5 seconds waiting for payment confirmation breaks the UX. Solana's ~400ms finality means the payment verification step is nearly imperceptible — Doorman's merchant server processes the signed authorization and returns the tool result in under a second. On Ethereum, the same payment would take 12–30 seconds and cost dollars in gas. The math doesn't work anywhere else.

Cost makes micro-payments viable. At $0.001 USDC per tool call, Solana transaction fees (~$0.00025) are less than 25% of the payment value. On any EVM chain, L1 gas would dwarf the payment itself, making per-call billing economically impossible. Doorman's pricing model exists only because Solana's fee structure allows it.

The x402 standard is Solana-native. Doorman uses @x402/svm — the Solana Virtual Machine implementation of the HTTP 402 payment protocol. This is the same primitive highlighted in the track brief. Doorman is a direct production application of x402 on Solana, applied to the fastest-growing category in AI tooling.

USDC composability unlocks the economy. By settling in USDC (SPL token), developer revenue is immediately composable with the rest of DeFi — earnable, swappable, and deployable without off-ramp friction. A developer earning $50/day in tool-call revenue could automatically route that into a Meteora yield vault, all on-chain.

> Structured Predictions

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Prediction markets are just yes or no bets. You're right or you're out. That works for degens but it's not how you build a portfolio.

We built Senthos to fix that.

Constellations are baskets of 100+ correlated prediction market legs bundled into one token. One leg goes wrong, who cares. You're spread across the whole theme.

Tranches split a basket's payout into senior, mezz, and junior slices. Want safety? Sit at the top. Want yield? Take the bottom. Same basket, different risk shapes.

Principal Protected Notes pair your basket position with a USDC yield sleeve that grows your deposit back to par by maturity. Your principal is guaranteed. The upside is still live.
TradFi has been doing this with mortgage pools and structured credit forever. We just built it for prediction markets on Solana, with live Polymarket data, real on-chain yield, and an ML model deciding which baskets qualify for which products.

**Challenges we ran into**

**Training the ML model**

We built a model to automatically cluster prediction markets into baskets. Getting it to produce groupings that actually made sense took a lot of iteration. This took awhile, but eventually we got it working

**PPN and tranche math**

The PPN split has to guarantee you get your principal back across different APYs and maturities but it kept glitching and we weren't sure why so we derived the math on our own.

**AI portfolio analysis**

Getting the AI portfolio commentary working across the full stack was tricky. The backend needs the right position data, the frontend needs to stay in sync, and doing inference in the middle without killing performance required more work than we expected.

**Demo state bugs**

We had a one issue where our hardcoded demo data kept showing up even after a full reset. Took a while to track down where the stale data was hiding and make sure the sandbox cleared properly every time.

**Best Use of Solana**

Senthos is a DeFi and prediction markets project.

Prediction markets on Solana are already fast and cheap, but the products are flat. You get a binary outcome and nothing else. We used Solana's speed and low fees to build structured financial products on top of those markets, something that would be too slow and too expensive on any other chain.

We also use USDC vaults on Solana for stablecoin yield powering our PPNs, deployed our basket and tranche programs on Solana devnet, and wired live market data, on-chain yield, and structured payoffs into one product. The whole thing is wrapped in a clean UI so anyone can structure a position

Fast settlement, sub-cent fees, and composable DeFi primitives are what make this possible. That's why it's on Solana.

**The problem it solves**

Most companies are permanently one step behind attackers.
Security teams run penetration tests once a year: **expensive, manual, and instantly outdated the moment a new CVE drops**. When a vulnerability is found, a human has to read the report, understand the context, find the right patch, test it, and deploy it. That process **takes days**. Sometimes **weeks**. Attackers need minutes.

Yuddha is built for the teams who cannot afford to wait.

Security engineers get a **continuous red team running 24/7** against a live digital twin of their stack; no scheduling, no vendor calls, no waiting for a quarterly report
Developers get **auto-generated**, sandbox-verified pull requests the moment a vulnerability is found, review the diff, merge, done
CISOs and compliance teams get every patch automatically tagged to the **relevant DPDP Act 2023 clause**, with a breach cost estimate in INR audit-ready without manual documentation
Small and mid-size businesses that **cannot afford** a dedicated **security team** get enterprise-grade continuous pen testing at open-source cost

The core shift Yuddha makes: security tools today alert humans and wait. **Yuddha closes the loop: detect, isolate, patch, verify, commit autonomously, in minutes.**

**Challenges we ran into**

### 1. LangGraph State Lost on Container Restart
Mid-cycle, if the ARES or KAVACH container crashed, the entire agent graph state was wiped. This was particularly painful during long attack cycles where ARES had already completed recon and was mid-exploit — a crash meant starting from zero.

**Fix:** Graph state now persists in Redis, so a restarted container picks up exactly where it left off.

---

### 2. Out-of-Memory Crashes in the Akhara
The root cause was that running nmap, ZAP, sqlmap, and the LangGraph agent simultaneously inside the same network was hammering RAM, causing Docker to OOM-kill containers mid-cycle.

**Fix:** Added Docker healthchecks to every service and built **watchdog** a background script that monitors container health every 15 seconds and automatically restarts anything that goes unhealthy.

---

### 3. Mostly False Positives from the Anomaly Detector
The Isolation Forest model was flagging almost everything as anomalous in early runs, essentially useless signal. The problem was we were training it on too little baseline data before the attack cycle started.

**Fix:** Added a 60-second baseline collection window before each cycle starts, giving the model enough normal traffic patterns to actually distinguish attack behaviour. Combined Isolation Forest with Suricata's rule-based IDS as a second layer so both need to agree before KAVACH acts.

---

### 4. All LangGraph Nodes Using Mistral Large
Early builds routed every single agent node through mistral-large. This made every cycle painfully slow and burned through API credits fast.

**Fix:** Built a model selector. Simple classification and labelling nodes now use mistral-small. Only patch generation and attack planning use the large model. Cycle time dropped significantly.

---

### 5. ARES and the Database on the Same Network
Early in Phase 1 we realised ARES could theoretically reach Postgres and Redis directly, meaning it could read its own findings queue or accidentally write to the DB. This would have made the whole red vs blue separation meaningless.

**Fix:** Split into two isolated Docker networks: attack-net for ARES and targets, backend-net for KAVACH and the data layer. Only the FastAPI container bridges both, acting as the controlled gateway.

**The problem it solves**

Sales, marketing, and HR teams live and die by consistency but manual outreach doesn't scale. Crafting personalized messages, deciding the right channel, following up at the right time, and tracking every touchpoint across hundreds of leads is overwhelming and error-prone.
We automate the entire outreach lifecycle. The system pulls leads from existing databases or accepts leads directly from the user, then takes over from there deciding where to reach out (email, LinkedIn, etc.), what to say, what tone to strike based on the prospect's profile, and when to send for maximum impact.
It doesn't stop at the first message either. The system automatically follows up with non-responders, adjusts its approach based on engagement signals, and maintains a full progress tracker so your team always knows exactly where every lead stands, without lifting a finger.
The result: the consistency of a seasoned sales team, running at the scale of an automation engine.

**Challenges we ran into**

Since this was an open innovation hackathon, the first hurdle was simply deciding what to build, with no constraints on the problem space, narrowing down to a meaningful, feasible idea took significant time and iteration.
Once the concept was locked in, the next challenge was choosing the right tech stack specifically weighing LangChain vs. Mastra for the agentic layer. Both had trade-offs in terms of flexibility, abstraction level, and ecosystem maturity, and picking the wrong one early would've been costly to undo.
Integrating broker/exchange APIs for order execution was another pain point, documentation inconsistencies, rate limits, and sandbox quirks made reliable trade execution harder than expected.
Finally, prompt engineering for personalized responses proved to be an ongoing challenge. Getting the LLM to factor in a user's risk profile, portfolio context, and preferences rather than giving generic answers, required careful system prompt design, structured user context injection, and multiple rounds of tuning

![x402](https://img.shields.io/badge/x402-333333?style=flat-square) ![OpenClaw](https://img.shields.io/badge/OpenClaw-333333?style=flat-square) ![X8004](https://img.shields.io/badge/X8004-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

DCT Protocol lets people delegate AI agent actions safely by giving each agent only the exact permissions it needs, with limits on tools, spending, depth, and time, plus revocation and on-chain enforcement. It makes multi-agent workflows, external HTTP actions, and blockchain execution easier to control and audit, so teams can use agents for research, payments, coordination, and demos without handing over unrestricted access or relying on trust alone.

**Challenges we ran into**

The team ran into a few core integration challenges while building the demo and protocol stack.
1. TLS integration was the hardest part, especially making the browser extension, server-side prover, verifier, and on-chain attestation format work together reliably.
2. Trust score calculation was tricky because the off-chain algorithm had to stay consistent with what the on-chain contracts recorded, so the scoring logic and contract state had to align.
3. OpenClaw integration with the chain needed careful wiring so agent workflows could be triggered, tracked, and connected to on-chain actions without breaking the demo flow.
4. Setting up the OpenClaw agents themselves was also a challenge because each agent needed the right tunnel URL, bearer token, model config, and workflow order to run correctly.

In short, most of the complexity came from making several moving pieces line up cleanly: TLS proofs, trust scoring, on-chain enforcement, and multi-agent OpenClaw workflows.

> Neutral trust on Aptos—hash, anchor, verify proof

![Cryptography](https://img.shields.io/badge/Cryptography-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Firebase Authentication](https://img.shields.io/badge/Firebase%20Authentication-333333?style=flat-square) ![Github Actions](https://img.shields.io/badge/Github%20Actions-333333?style=flat-square) ![Vite](https://img.shields.io/badge/Vite-333333?style=flat-square) ![aptos](https://img.shields.io/badge/aptos-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Teams in security, compliance, and AI operations often need to show which file or bundle existed at what time: policy packs, IOC exports, incident artifacts, dataset snapshots, or model outputs. When proof lives only in email, shared drives, or a vendor database, disputes are easier, tampering is harder to detect, and third parties must trust whoever runs the server.

QuantAnchor makes integrity checks neutral and verifiable: you hash the artifact off-chain (content does not go on-chain), anchor the commitment on Aptos with a Move module, and verify later by recomputing the hash and comparing to chain state, backed by explorer events and a read API. Optional flows support wallet-free public verify, custody and handoff style timelines, supersede lineage, multi-party approvals, Merkle bundles for many files at once, and declared AI-related digests for governance-style metadata. Those AI fields are declared hashes, not a claim of cryptographic proof of model inference.

Who can use it: SOC and IR for anchored exports and incident bundles; GRC and audit for policy and evidence versions; AppSec and platform for release baselines tied to CI; AI and MLOps for dataset or output fingerprints with declared lineage fields.

In short: a practical receipt, lifecycle, and integration path (UI, API, CLI, GitHub Actions), framed as git-for-evidence rather than reinventing hashing.

**Challenges we ran into**

Keeping dev config consistent: the web app and read API each need the published module address and network settings; mismatches caused confusing commitment-not-found or failed wallet transactions. We aligned on copying both env examples and checking addresses character for character before demos.

Chain versus product surface area: we wanted explorer-visible events, clear views for verification, and a state machine on-chain without putting file bytes on-chain. That took several passes on Move entry functions and on matching the Hono read API to on-chain semantics.

Verification without a wallet: external verifiers should not need a wallet to sanity-check a hash. Public verify plus read endpoints that return consistent JSON, including responses that work for timelines, needed extra care.

Automation path: wiring the anchor CLI and the release-integrity GitHub Action to the same signing model as local runs meant getting secrets, network, and metadata strings right end to end.

**The problem it solves**

# Mecha Pay: The Problem of the "Locked" Crypto Economy

## Executive Summary

In India, a massive market of **1 million cryptocurrency earners** is currently "locked" out of the digital economy. While these users earn significant income in USDC, they face a **60% loss in purchasing power** due to tax friction and a fragmented blockchain landscape.

Mecha Pay identifies and solves this multi-billion dollar market failure by leveraging **Circle's Programmable Wallets** and **Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol (CCTP)** to create a compliant, frictionless payment layer that treats USDC as a unified, native asset across all major ecosystems.

---

## 1. The User Problem: The "Forced-Exit" Economic Trap

Blockchain-native companies—including Web3 SaaS platforms, NFT marketplaces, and decentralized education providers—operate globally but hit a brick wall in the Indian market due to a **“Forced-Exit” Economic Trap** that destroys up to **60% of user purchasing power**.

Over **1 million Indian developers and creators** earn significant income in native USDC. However, they are effectively **locked out of participating in this global economy**.

### The Core Issue

To spend their earnings, users must:

- Off-ramp USDC to INR  
- Trigger a **30% flat tax + 1% TDS**  
- Incur additional slippage and fees  

### Compounding Frictions

#### 🔹 Chain Fragmentation
- Liquidity is spread across multiple chains (Polygon, Ethereum, etc.)  
- Users cannot seamlessly pay merchants across chains  

#### 🔹 The "Zero-State" Wall
Users must:
- Acquire native gas tokens (ETH, MATIC, etc.)  
- Set up wallets  
- Navigate bridges and swaps  

### Result

> Users are forced to hoard USDC as a stagnant asset rather than spend it  

This creates a massive inefficiency:

> **$5B–$10B in annual revenue is left unrealized**

---

## 2. The Merchant Problem: The "INR Gap"

Blockchain-native companies, including:

- Web3 SaaS platforms  
- NFT marketplaces  
- Decentralized education providers  

operate globally but struggle to penetrate the Indian market.

These businesses rely on **USDC-native infrastructure** and lack integrations with traditional fiat processors like Stripe or Razorpay.

### The Core Issue: The “INR Gap”

Even when users are willing to pay in USDC, merchants face critical limitations:

- Cannot easily convert USDC into INR  
- Cannot pay local employees and vendors  

### Result

- Revenue generated in India becomes **operationally unusable**  
- Market expansion is stalled  

> **$5B–$10B in annual revenue remains untapped**

### Structural Limitation

There is currently:

> **No automated, compliant bridge between on-chain liquidity and the Indian banking system**

---

## 3. The Fragmentation Problem: The Multi-Chain Mess

USDC liquidity is fragmented across multiple blockchains, including:

- Ethereum  
- Polygon  
- Arbitrum  
- Base  
- Optimism  
- Avalanche  

### The Problem: Liquidity Silos

A user might:
- Earn on one chain  
- Need to pay on another  

### Challenges

#### ❌ Wrapped Asset Risk
- Bridged tokens (e.g., USDC.e) are IOUs  
- Issued by third-party bridges  
- Vulnerable to exploits  

#### ❌ Complex Cross-Chain Swaps
- Requires DEX usage  
- Managing gas fees  
- Handling slippage  
- Waiting for confirmations  

#### ❌ Security Risks
- Reliance on lock-and-mint bridges  
- Frequent multi-million dollar exploits  

#### ❌ High Gas Fees
- $10–$50 per transaction on some chains  
- Makes micro-payments infeasible  

---

## 4. Technical Gaps in Existing Solutions

### Heavy State Storage

- Contracts store:
  - Transaction histories  
  - User balances  

- Expensive operations (`SSTORE`)  
- Costs exceed **20,000 gas per slot**  

➡️ Not viable for high-volume micro-payments  

---

### Zero-State Hurdles

- Smart contract wallets require:
  - Deployment transactions  
  - Native gas tokens  

➡️ Creates onboarding friction  

---

### MPC Silos

- Wallets are:
  - Isolated  
  - Hard to integrate across apps/devices  

➡️ Poor composability and UX  

---

## 5. Mecha Pay's Solution: Zero-State & Event-Driven Architecture

### 🔹 Minimizing On-Chain Footprint

- Store only essential data on-chain  
- Use **events (logs)** instead of storage  

**Benefits:**
- ~90% reduction in gas costs  
- Scalable for high-volume transactions  
- Immutable yet queryable  

---

### 🔹 Native-to-Native Interoperability

- Powered by **Circle CCTP**  

Enables:
- Burning USDC on source chain  
- Minting native USDC on destination chain  

**Result:**
- True 1:1 transfers  
- No wrapped assets  
- No liquidity risk  

---

### 🔹 Gasless Onboarding

- Built with **Circle Programmable Wallets**  

Users can:
- Receive USDC without gas  
- Send transactions without holding native tokens  

➡️ Eliminates the Zero-State problem  

---

## 6. Developer Platform: SDKs & Public APIs

Mecha Pay is not just a payment layer—it is a **developer-first platform** designed for rapid integration across Web3 and Web2 applications.

#

**Challenges we ran into**

The primary challenge I encountered was managing the "Zero-State" initialization and asynchronous transaction signing within Circle's Multi-Party Computation (MPC) architecture. Because Circle Programmable Wallets are smart-contract-based, they don't technically exist on a new network like the Arc Testnet until a deployment transaction is triggered; I solved this by implementing Circle’s Paymaster to sponsor the initial gas, making the "cold start" invisible to the user. Additionally, I had to re-architect the transaction flow into a state machine to handle the challengeId and user PIN signatures asynchronously. By utilizing Webhook Listeners and EIP-3009 (Transfer with Authorization), I was able to bypass the need for native gas tokens entirely, allowing the smart contracts on the Arc Testnet to "pull" USDC and execute logic natively, ensuring a seamless, gasless cross-chain swap experience.

**Ethereum Track**

This project fits into the Ethereum and EVM Ecosystem track as a high-performance payment middleware that solves the "L2 Fragmentation" crisis. By implementing Account Abstraction (ERC-4337) principles via Circle Programmable Wallets, it removes the requirement for users to hold native ETH for gas, enabling a completely "seedless" and "gasless" onboarding experience.The core technical innovation lies in the seamless cross-chain swaps between established EVM chains and custom smart contracts deployed on the Arc Testnet. Since the Arc Testnet is fully EVM-compatible, Mecha Pay utilizes a Zero-State Event-Driven architecture to minimize expensive on-chain storage (SSTORE). Instead, it leverages immutable logs to handle transaction data, making the system highly scalable and cost-efficient. By using Circle’s CCTP for native 1:1 USDC transfers, the project unifies liquidity across the entire Ethereum ecosystem—including Base, Polygon, and Arbitrum—and bridges it directly to the specialized environment of the Arc Testnet, creating a frictionless economy for the next million crypto earners.

**Blockchain & Decentralized Applications**

Mecha Pay fits into the blockchain track as a high-scalability payment middleware that solves the "UX-Security Paradox" using Circle’s advanced Web3 infrastructure. By implementing Circle Programmable Wallets for gasless, MPC-secured onboarding and CCTP for native 1:1 transfers across 15+ chains, the project eliminates the risks of third-party bridges and the complexity of fragmented liquidity. Technically, it stands out through a Zero-State Event-Driven Architecture, which avoids costly on-chain storage by leveraging blockchain logs instead of persistent state variables. This makes the system highly scalable and cost-efficient, transforming USDC from a stagnant asset into a fluid, spendable currency that bypasses traditional tax friction and technical hurdles for the next million crypto earners.

### NoMoreBrainRot

> Reclaim your attention. Mine your focus.

![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Expo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Expo-333333?style=flat-square) ![Smart Contract](https://img.shields.io/badge/Smart%20Contract-333333?style=flat-square) ![Artificial Intelligence](https://img.shields.io/badge/Artificial%20Intelligence-333333?style=flat-square) ![React Native](https://img.shields.io/badge/React%20Native-333333?style=flat-square) ![Web3](https://img.shields.io/badge/Web3-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

## The Attention Extraction Economy

Modern digital platforms are built to **capture and monetize attention**.  
Recommendation algorithms, infinite feeds, and short-form content loops are designed to maximize engagement — not focus.

The result is a global **attention crisis**.

- It takes **~23 minutes** to regain deep focus after a single interruption.
- Platforms are engineered to keep users scrolling rather than thinking.
- Average human attention span has fallen from **12 seconds in 2000 to ~8 seconds today**.

Existing solutions fail because they rely on **self-control alone**.  
Most productivity blockers are simply walls that users can bypass with one click.

In a world where billion-dollar algorithms are competing against human willpower, **willpower is not enough**.

---

## Our Solution: The NoMoreBrainRot Protocol

**NoMoreBrainRot** is a decentralized **Attention Protocol** that transforms focus into a measurable, valuable digital asset.

Instead of merely blocking distractions, the protocol **re-engineers the incentives of attention** using AI guidance, social accountability, and Web3 infrastructure.

The system detects distraction loops, intervenes intelligently, and rewards sustained focus — turning deep work into a verifiable and incentivized activity.

---

## Overview of the Platform

### AI Cognitive Intervention Engine
When the system detects a potential distraction loop, an AI assistant initiates a reflective intervention.  
Rather than blocking access immediately, the AI prompts the user to explain their intent and encourages deliberate decision-making.  
This shifts users from **impulsive behavior to conscious engagement**.

### Proof-of-Focus
The platform logs deep work sessions as **attention metadata**.  
Users earn tokens for sustained focus, effectively turning productive time into a **mineable resource**.

### Study Squads (Social Accountability Layer)
Users can join collaborative focus sessions with peers.  
If one member breaks the focus protocol by switching to distracting apps or sites, the block lifts for the entire group.  
This creates a **shared accountability mechanism inspired by multi-signature consensus systems**.

### Tokenized Knowledge Forum
Users can ask and answer questions within the platform’s knowledge forum.  
High-quality answers earn token rewards, aligning incentives around **valuable knowledge sharing instead of content spam**.

### On-Chain Achievements
Focus milestones such as streaks and completed deep work sessions are minted as **non-transferable identity assets**.  
These form a verifiable record of discipline and productivity.

### Ephemeral Mental Space
Before starting a focus session, users can offload distracting thoughts into a **private, encrypted space**.  
Once the session begins, these entries are automatically deleted, allowing users to start work with a clear mental state.

---

## Impact

NoMoreBrainRot shifts the digital economy of attention.

Focus becomes **measurable, rewarded, and socially reinforced**, while distraction carries real cost.  
The platform transforms productivity from an isolated struggle into a **structured, incentivized system for sustained deep work**.

**Challenges we ran into**

### Platform-Level Intervention Limitations

One of the biggest hurdles we encountered was **how to actually intervene when a user starts doomscrolling**.

True intervention requires the system to **detect and control app usage in real time** — for example detecting when a user opens Instagram, YouTube Shorts, or other distracting apps and triggering an AI intervention.

However, this level of control is **only possible through a native mobile application with system permissions**. A website cannot reliably detect or block other apps running on a user's device.

To implement real intervention, the app needs permissions such as:
- Usage statistics access
- Foreground app monitoring
- Notification access

Because of these requirements, the most effective implementation is through an **Android application distributed as an APK**.

### Distribution Challenge

Publishing an app with deep system-level monitoring permissions through traditional app stores can be complicated and time-consuming due to strict platform policies.

Since our goal during the hackathon was to **demonstrate the protocol and product concept quickly**, we chose not to go through the full publishing process.

### Our Solution

To overcome this, we built **two versions of the platform**:

**1. Mobile App (APK Prototype)**  
This version demonstrates how the real system works:
- Detecting distraction loops
- Triggering AI interventions
- Running focus sessions with monitoring

**2. Web Platform (Concept Demonstration)**  
Since most judges and users cannot install APKs easily during a demo, we also built a **web interface** that showcases the core protocol features such as:
- Proof-of-Focus sessions
- Study Squads
- Token incentives
- AI interaction flows

The website allows users to understand and interact with the system , while the mobile app represents the full intervention layer required for real-world deployment.

This dual-platform approach allowed us to demonstrate both the concept and the technical feasibility of the NoMoreBrainRot protocol within the limited time of the hackathon.

**The problem it solves**

GAME V3 is a Web3 gaming platform we built to connect gaming with real-world impact. In the game, players defeat enemies and earn gear that can be minted as NFTs, giving them true ownership of the items they collect. These NFTs can then be traded in a decentralized marketplace, and when a trade happens, a large portion of the payment automatically goes to a charity wallet. This means that something as simple as playing a game or trading an item can contribute to a meaningful cause.

One thing we really care about in GAME V3 is transparency. Because the donations happen through blockchain transactions, every contribution is recorded and can be publicly verified. Players can actually see the impact of their actions, which makes the experience feel much more meaningful than a typical game.

We also added guilds so players can form communities and compete on donation leaderboards, making it a shared effort rather than something done individually. On top of that, creators can stream their gameplay and receive crypto tips directly from viewers. Overall, with GAME V3 we wanted to create something fun but purposeful, where gaming, community, and social good come together in one ecosystem.

**Challenges we ran into**

While developing GAME V3, our team faced several challenges that helped us learn and improve both technically and as a team. Since the project combines gaming, Web3, and a full web platform, integrating everything smoothly required effort and continuous problem-solving. Some of the key challenges we faced include:

1)Learning blockchain concepts:
Understanding smart contracts, NFTs, wallet connections, and blockchain transactions was initially challenging and required a lot of research and experimentation.

2)Integrating different modules:
Each team member worked on separate parts such as the game, frontend, and smart contracts, so combining these components and ensuring they worked together smoothly required careful coordination.

3)Connecting the game with Web3 features:
Linking gameplay events with blockchain actions like NFT minting and wallet interactions was technically complex and needed multiple tests.

4)Making the platform user-friendly:
We had to repeatedly modify the interface and navigation to ensure the website remained simple and accessible even for users unfamiliar with Web3.

5)Debugging and handling updates:
As features were added or modified, new bugs and compatibility issues appeared, requiring continuous debugging and improvements.

6)Managing time and feature priorities:
With multiple systems such as the marketplace, guilds, and streaming features, deciding what to focus on first while staying within the development timeline was a challenge.

### AnonFund
