> Anonymous Quadratic Funding Platform

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![ethers.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/ethers.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Hardhat](https://img.shields.io/badge/Hardhat-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

**AnonFund — Fund What Your Community Actually Wants**

Most communities have a problem. A small group of wealthy people ends up deciding where the money goes. Everyone else just watches.

AnonFund changes that.

**Everyone Gets a Fair Voice**

AnonFund uses a smart system called quadratic funding. The basic idea is simple — if a lot of people support something, even with small amounts, that project wins over one backed by a single rich donor.

So a thousand regular people can beat one big wallet. That means the community — not the money — makes the call.

You can use it to fund things like open-source tools, local events, research, educational projects, or public infrastructure. Basically, anything a community cares about.

**Your Vote Stays Private**

Nobody wants to be watched when they vote. In most systems, your wallet, your identity, and your choices are all visible. That makes people nervous — or worse, it gets them targeted.

With AnonFund, you vote anonymously. Nobody can see who you are or how you voted. The system just knows you're a real person — and that's enough.

**No Fake Accounts**

One common trick in online voting is creating many fake accounts to game the results. AnonFund blocks this using a verification system called Anon Aadhaar. It checks that you're a real, unique person — without ever exposing your personal details.

One person, one vote. No tricks.

**Easy for Builders Too**

If you're building something and need funding, AnonFund keeps it simple. Post your project, share what you're working on, and let the community decide. No long applications. No gatekeepers. No need to know the right people.

**Less Spam, Better Projects**

To keep things clean, anyone submitting a project has to put down a small deposit. If your project gets approved, you get it back. If it gets rejected, you lose it. This keeps spam out and makes sure only serious builders show up.

**Open and Honest**

Even though votes are private, everything else is open. Anyone can see which projects are running, how much support they've received, and how funds are being used. Private votes, public results.

**Who Is It For?**

AnonFund works for DAOs, open-source groups, local communities, research teams, and Web3 ecosystems — really anyone trying to fund good work in a fair way.

It's a simple idea: let the people decide, keep it honest, and protect everyone's privacy while doing it.

**Challenges we ran into**

**A Big Problem We Hit While Building AnonFund**
Building AnonFund wasn't smooth sailing. At one point, we ran into a wall — and it took us a while to figure our way out.

**What Was the Problem?**
AnonFund uses a tool called Anon Aadhaar to confirm that each voter is a real person. This stops people from creating multiple fake accounts to cheat the voting system.

But when we tried to connect this with our smart contracts, things got complicated.

Anon Aadhaar gives each verified user something called a nullifier. Think of it like a secret stamp — it proves you went through verification, but it doesn't tell anyone who you are. Our contract uses this stamp to make sure the same person can't register twice.

The tricky part? We had to find the right balance. Store too much information, and someone could figure out who voted for what. Store too little, and people could sneak in duplicate accounts.
We needed to hit all four of these at once:

- Stop the same person from registering more than once
- Never store anything that could identify a user
- Make sure votes can't be traced back to anyone
- Keep things fast and light enough to run on-chain

**Where We Went Wrong**
In our first version, most of the checking happened on the frontend — the part of the app users interact with. The smart contract itself didn't do much of the heavy lifting.

This worked on the surface. But it had a quiet flaw. If someone bypassed the frontend — which isn't hard for a technical person — the contract wouldn't stop them from registering twice.

That's a real problem.

**How We Fixed It**
We moved the responsibility into the smart contract itself.
The contract now keeps a record of every nullifier that's been used:

mapping(uint256 => bool) public nullifiers;


Every time someone tries to register, the contract checks — has this stamp been used before?


require(!nullifiers[nullifier], "Nullifier already used");
nullifiers[nullifier] = true;


If yes, it blocks them. If no, it lets them through and marks the stamp as used.
Simple. Clean. And it can't be bypassed.

The best part is that the nullifier itself reveals nothing about the person. So we got the security we needed without giving up any privacy.

**What We Took Away From This**
The biggest lesson here: never trust the frontend alone to protect your system.
The UI can be skipped. The contract can't.

In decentralized systems, the smart contract is the real rulebook. Everything else is just a nice interface on top of it. Once we treated it that way, things clicked into place.

The result was a stronger, more honest system — one that keeps bad actors out while keeping every voter completely anonymous.

> Own Your Achievements as NFTs.

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![MetaMask](https://img.shields.io/badge/MetaMask-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![MongoDB](https://img.shields.io/badge/MongoDB-333333?style=flat-square) ![NFT](https://img.shields.io/badge/NFT-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Certificates and academic credentials are still mostly issued as PDFs or physical documents, which can be easily forged, modified, or lost. Employers and institutions often have no simple way to verify whether a certificate is genuine, which leads to fraud, manual verification processes, and delays.

CertChain solves this problem by turning certificates into blockchain-verified NFTs. Each certificate is securely stored on IPFS and minted as a unique NFT on the blockchain. This ensures that the credential is tamper-proof, permanently verifiable, and owned by the recipient’s wallet.

With CertChain:

Educational institutions can issue certificates instantly and securely.

Students receive a verifiable digital credential stored in their wallet.

Employers can verify authenticity in seconds using a certificate ID or transaction hash.

All records are immutable and publicly verifiable on the blockchain.

By combining IPFS for decentralized storage and smart contracts for secure issuance, CertChain eliminates certificate fraud and provides a trustless verification system for academic and professional achievements.

**Challenges we ran into**

Building CertChain involved integrating multiple technologies including blockchain, decentralized storage, and a traditional backend. One of the main challenges was correctly connecting the smart contract events with the backend server. Extracting the NFT tokenId from blockchain transaction logs required debugging the event logs and ensuring the server correctly parsed ERC-721 Transfer events.

Another challenge was handling IPFS uploads through Pinata while sending certificate files from the frontend. Managing multipart file uploads, generating metadata for the NFT, and ensuring the metadata correctly referenced the IPFS file required careful debugging.

I also encountered issues with local blockchain resets when using Hardhat. Each restart cleared previous transactions, which caused verification failures when testing certificate validation by transaction hash.

Finally, connecting MetaMask, the backend API, and the smart contract smoothly required handling asynchronous blockchain calls and ensuring the correct wallet addresses and network configuration were used.

These challenges helped improve my understanding of smart contract events, Web3 integration, decentralized storage, and backend–blockchain communication.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Hardhat](https://img.shields.io/badge/Hardhat-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Seed2Shelf  is a blockchain-based agricultural supply chain transparency platform for India. It tracks produce from farmer to consumer, recording every handoff, price, and quality check permanently on the Ethereum blockchain.

**The Problem**
A farmer sells tomatoes at ₹8/kg. The consumer buys them at ₹60/kg. Nobody in between is accountable for where that ₹52 went. Farmers have no visibility into what happens after they sell, payments are delayed 30–60 days with no recourse, weight and grade fraud happens silently at every node, and consumers have no way to verify origin or price fairness.

**How Seed2Shelf Fixes This**
Every handoff is signed on-chain by both parties. Price mismatches are auto-detected by smart contracts. Farmer payments are held in escrow and released on confirmation. Consumers scan a QR code to see the full farm-to-shelf journey.

**Who It's For**
Farmers get fair pricing, on-time payment, and on-chain proof if exploited. Processors and distributors get transparent records and fewer disputes. Retailers get verified provenance via QR code a trust advantage over competitors. Consumers finally know where their food came from and what the farmer actually earned.

**Challenges we ran into**

**Smart Contract Logic**
Working with Solidity's integer-only arithmetic took adjustment
 no floats means storing prices in paise to avoid precision loss.

**Dynamic Routing**
Getting the QR code to correctly link to /trace/[batchId]
and handling role-based redirects after login required
careful state management.

**Mock Data Design**
Structuring mock data to mirror real smart contract responses
so switching to live blockchain reads later needs minimal rework.

> Skills Face the Fire and Truth Emerges Immutable.

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![MetaMask](https://img.shields.io/badge/MetaMask-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Judge0 API](https://img.shields.io/badge/Judge0%20API-333333?style=flat-square) ![ethers.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/ethers.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS3](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS3-333333?style=flat-square) ![Express.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Express.js-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

## The Problem It Solves

In today's tech hiring ecosystem, **resumes and certificates do not reliably represent real technical skills**. Developers can list programming languages, frameworks, and achievements on their resumes, but recruiters often struggle to verify whether those claims truly reflect a candidate's ability.

At the same time, talented developers—especially students and self-taught programmers—face difficulty proving their real capabilities beyond traditional resumes or college grades.

This leads to several problems:

- **Skill verification gap** – Recruiters cannot easily validate real coding ability.
- **Resume inflation** – Developers may list skills they are not truly proficient in.
- **Lack of trust** – Companies spend significant time conducting multiple interview rounds just to validate basic skills.
- **No permanent proof of achievements** – Coding platform scores and certificates can be modified or lost.

## Our Solution

**AGNI PARIKSHA** solves this problem by combining a **coding challenge platform with blockchain-based credential verification**.

Developers solve coding problems on the platform, and when they successfully complete challenges, their **skills and scores are permanently recorded on the blockchain**.

This creates **tamper-proof, verifiable skill credentials** that recruiters can trust.

## How It Helps

- **Developers** can prove their real skills through blockchain-backed achievements.
- **Recruiters** can instantly verify a candidate's coding capability.
- **Hiring becomes faster and more trustworthy**.
- **Achievements become permanent and immutable**, eliminating fake claims.

By leveraging blockchain, AGNI PARIKSHA ensures that **skill verification becomes transparent, trustworthy, and globally accessible.**

**Challenges we ran into**

## Challenges I Ran Into

Building **AGNI PARIKSHA**, a blockchain-based coding verification platform, required integrating multiple systems including **React, Node.js, MongoDB, Ethereum smart contracts, and the Judge0 code execution engine**. While developing the project, we faced several technical challenges.

### 1. Real-Time Code Execution Integration

One of the biggest challenges was integrating the **Judge0 API** to execute user-submitted code safely. Handling different programming languages, managing execution responses, and properly displaying outputs in the UI required careful backend handling.

**Solution:**  
We implemented a backend service that sends user code submissions to the **Judge0 code execution API**, waits for the result, and then returns the output to the frontend. Proper error handling and response parsing were added to ensure the platform behaves reliably even when code execution fails.

### 2. Blockchain Connection Errors

Initially, the backend attempted to connect to a local Ethereum RPC endpoint (`127.0.0.1:8545`), which caused connection errors when no local node was running.

**Solution:**  
We switched to a **Sepolia testnet RPC endpoint** and stored the configuration securely in environment variables. This ensured stable communication between the backend and the blockchain network.

### 3. Smart Contract Interaction

Calling smart contract functions using **ethers.js** required proper configuration of the ABI, wallet private key, and contract address. Incorrect configuration initially caused transaction failures.

**Solution:**  
We implemented a dedicated blockchain controller that handles contract interactions, verifies parameters, and confirms transactions before storing the credential hash.

### 4. MongoDB Authentication Issues

While connecting the backend to MongoDB Atlas, we encountered authentication errors due to incorrect credentials and database access settings.

**Solution:**  
We corrected the connection string, verified database user credentials, and configured proper network access permissions in MongoDB Atlas.

### 5. Frontend–Backend Synchronization

Another challenge was ensuring that the frontend coding platform correctly interacts with the backend APIs for submitting solutions, executing code through Judge0, and storing verified results on the blockchain.

**Solution:**  
We designed a structured API flow where:

1. User submits code  
2. Backend sends code to **Judge0** for execution  
3. If the output is correct, a **credential is issued on the blockchain**

This ensured that only **valid solutions receive blockchain credentials**.

- **Building blockchain-backed credential systems**
- **Smart contract interactions using ethers.js**

**The problem it solves**

## THE PROBLEM IT SOLVES

Today, if you want an AI agent to manage your DeFi — find yield, analyze your portfolio, execute a trade — you have to **trust a centralized platform** with your wallet, your strategy, and your data. No escrow. No accountability. No privacy. The platform sees everything, the agent has no skin in the game, and if it screws up — no recourse.

**Obscura fixes this with three primitives:**

**Trustless Agent Commerce (ERC-8183)** — Users post DeFi jobs on-chain with USDC escrowed in a smart contract. The agent only gets paid if a deterministic evaluator approves the work. Bad work = user gets refunded. No middleman. ERC-8183 was proposed 3 weeks ago by the Ethereum Foundation's dAI team and Virtuals Protocol. We built the first implementation.

**On-Chain Reputation (ERC-8004)** — Every completed job generates a reputation score on the same registry backed by researchers from Google, Coinbase, and MetaMask. Better agents earn more jobs. Bad agents get filtered out.

**Privacy-First Execution** — Reports are AES-256-GCM encrypted with per-job keys derived from your wallet signature. Only you can decrypt. Your DeFi preferences (risk tolerance, allowed assets, kill switch) live as ENS text records and agents enforce them on every job. Your EOA never needs to touch a DEX directly.

**What can you do with it?**

- "Find me the best yield for USDC on Base" — Scout queries DeFiLlama and x402 APIs, writes an encrypted report with real APY data
- "Analyze my wallet on Base" — Analyst audits your portfolio, produces an encrypted risk assessment
- "Deep analysis of Aerodrome Finance" — Scout pulls protocol TVL, yield data, and web research into an encrypted report

Every job follows the same flow: USDC escrowed, agent executes, Sentinel scores 0-100, on-chain settlement, ERC-8004 reputation recorded.

This isn't a wrapper around ChatGPT. It's an on-chain economic system where AI agents earn reputation, get paid in USDC, and are held accountable by smart contracts. Built on standards that didn't exist a month ago.

**Challenges we ran into**

## CHALLENGES I RAN INTO

**x402 Protocol Version Mismatch** — The x402 payment servers had upgraded to v2, sending payment requirements in an HTTP header as base64 JSON with eip155:8453 network IDs. The client library expected the old format in the response body. Every paid API call failed silently. We built a custom Axios interceptor that decodes the v2 header, transforms eip155:8453 to "base", flattens the nested resource object, and bridges the two formats.

**LLM Tool Calling Failures (3 Providers in 42 Hours)** — Groq Llama 3.3 70B intermittently generated malformed function call syntax that Groq's own parser rejected. Llama 4 Scout 17B had reliable tool calling but produced shallow one-liner reports. Gemini 2.5 Flash worked great but hit rate limits mid-demo. We rewrote the Scout agent as a hybrid pipeline — tools called programmatically in our code, LLM only generates the report text. Zero tool calling means zero parsing failures.

**ERC-8004 ABI Was Completely Wrong** — We wrote the reputation ABI based on assumptions. Every giveFeedback call reverted. The deployed contract uses int128 not int64, string tags not bytes32, and a different return tuple ordering. Function selectors didn't match at all. We extracted selectors from the deployed bytecode, cross-referenced with the official erc-8004-contracts repo, and rewrote the entire ABI. Also discovered our agent IDs (1-4) belonged to other people on the shared registry — had to register new agents (IDs 1843-1846) from separate wallets to avoid the "self-feedback not allowed" restriction.

**Parallel Tool Calling = Garbage Reports** — Llama 3.3 called all tools simultaneously, including writeEncryptedReport, before research data came back. Reports contained placeholder text. We added a content validation guard that rejects reports under 150 characters or containing placeholder text, forcing the LLM to gather data first.

**Nonce Collisions on Rapid Transactions** — Sentinel sends complete and reputation write in quick succession. The second tx failed with "nonce too low." We added explicit nonce fetching before each tx with a retry mechanism for nonce-related errors.

**ENS V3 Registration** — Registering obscuratester.eth on Sepolia required the new V3 Registration struct tuple format. Took multiple attempts with cast send to get the ABI encoding right.

**DeFi**

First implementation of ERC-8183 (Agentic Commerce) — proposed 3 weeks ago by the Ethereum Foundation's dAI team and Virtuals Protocol. Users escrow USDC in a smart contract, AI agents execute DeFi research (live yield data from DeFiLlama, protocol analysis, x402-paid web search), and a deterministic evaluator settles on-chain. USDC flows to the agent on approval or back to the user on rejection. Reputation is recorded on the ERC-8004 registry — the same standard authored by researchers from Google, Coinbase, and MetaMask. Novel DeFi primitive: a trustless job marketplace where agents are accountable service providers, not black boxes.

**AI**

Obscura runs 4 autonomous AI agents (Scout, Analyst, Ghost, Sentinel) that execute DeFi jobs independently. Agents use Gemini 2.5 Flash for reasoning,
  call real APIs via x402 micropayments (paying USDC per request), and produce encrypted research reports. Sentinel is a fully deterministic evaluator — no LLM — that scores agent output on deliverable quality, tool usage, timeliness, and risk compliance (0-100). Agents hold their own wallets, earn USDC from completed jobs, and build on-chain reputation via ERC-8004. This is AI with real economic identity on-chain — not a chatbot wrapper.

**Best creative use of ENS**

### ENS as the Agent Control Layer

ENS isn't cosmetic in Obscura — it's the **governance layer** that controls how every AI agent behaves.

### Custom DeFi Text Records

Demo user: **obscuratester.eth** (Ethereum Sepolia)

We defined 6 custom ENS text record keys that agents read and enforce on every job:

| Text Record Key | Example Value | What It Controls |
|----------------|---------------|-----------------|
| defi.risk | conservative | Agent risk tolerance — conservative agents avoid high-risk protocols |
| defi.assets | ETH,USDC,WBTC | Asset whitelist — agents can only recommend/trade these |
| defi.maxTrade | 500 | Maximum trade size in USD — hard limit on agent execution |
| defi.protocols | aave,compound | Protocol whitelist — agents restricted to approved protocols |
| agent.killswitch | false | Emergency halt — set to true and ALL agents stop immediately |
| agent.preferred | scout.eth | Preferred agent for auto-routing jobs |

### How It Works In Practice

1. User connects wallet — ENS name resolves via useEnsName wagmi hook on chain ID 11155111 (Sepolia)
2. Orchestrator calls getEnsText() for all 6 keys via viem on Ethereum Sepolia
3. Preferences are passed to every agent as part of the job context
4. Sentinel evaluator uses defi.risk to score risk compliance (25% of total score)
5. Kill switch is checked in BaseAgent before every job execution — if true, agent halts immediately with a killswitch event

The activity feed shows ENS loading in real-time:

> ENS policy loaded from obscuratester.eth: risk=moderate, assets=ETH,USDC, maxTrade=500

### ENSIP-25 Agent Verification

Each agent (scout.eth, analyst.eth, ghost.eth, sentinel.eth) implements ENSIP-25 agent verification. The useEnsAgentVerification hook reads agent.address, agent.verified, agent.role, and agent.capabilities text records to verify agent identity on-chain. Verified agents show a checkmark badge on their marketplace card.

### Key Code Paths

**ENS text record reader** — apps/web/src/lib/integrations/ens.ts contains getUserPreferences() and checkKillSwitch()

**Wagmi hooks** — apps/web/src/hooks/useEnsIdentity.ts contains useEnsIdentity(), useEnsPreferences(), and useEnsAgentVerification()

**Kill switch enforcement** — apps/web/src/lib/agents/base-agent.ts checks kill switch before every agent execution

**Privacy page** — apps/web/src/components/privacy/ens-control.tsx reads ENS records live and links to the ENS app for editing

### Why This Is Creative

ENS text records are typically used for avatars and social links. We turned them into a **programmable policy engine for autonomous AI agents**. Change your risk tolerance on ENS and every agent respects it on the next job. Flip the kill switch and all agents halt. Your ENS name is your master key to an autonomous DeFi system.

No hard-coded values. No centralized config. Just ENS.

**Pool prize**

**Build What Big Tech Won't**

## Build What Big Tech Won't

### How We Use Fileverse

Every AI agent in Obscura produces a research report — yield analysis, portfolio audits, protocol deep dives. These reports contain your DeFi strategy. With a centralized platform, the operator can read everything. With Obscura, **nobody can read your report except you**.

### The Encryption Flow

1. User signs a message with their wallet when posting a job
2. That signature + the job ID are hashed to derive a unique AES-256-GCM encryption key
3. The agent writes its research findings as markdown
4. The report is encrypted client-side before it ever leaves the server
5. The encrypted ciphertext is stored on Fileverse via the Agents SDK (IPFS + Pimlico gasless operations on Gnosis)
6. On-chain, only a keccak256 hash of the deliverable is posted — no content visible
7. When the user wants to read the report, they sign the same message, recreate the key, and decrypt

**Even we can't read the reports. Even Fileverse can't read the reports. Only the user's wallet can.**

### Fileverse Integration Details

**Primary: Fileverse REST API (ddocs.new)**

We integrated the new Fileverse REST API for document creation and retrieval. Agent reports are sent as encrypted content to POST /api/ddocs with the user's API key. Documents are stored with a ddoc: prefix file ID for retrieval.

**Fallback: @fileverse/agents SDK v2.0.1**

If the REST API server isn't running, we fall back to the Fileverse Agents SDK which stores content on IPFS via Pinata with Pimlico gasless transactions on Gnosis chain.

**Fallback: Local encrypted storage (Upstash Redis)**

If both Fileverse paths fail, reports are encrypted locally and stored in Upstash Redis with a local: prefix. The encryption is identical — AES-256-GCM with the same signature-derived key. Only the storage layer changes.

### What Gets Stored on Fileverse

- **Scout reports** — DeFi yield research, protocol analysis, market sentiment
- **Analyst reports** — wallet audits, portfolio breakdowns, P&L analysis
- **Ghost reports** — trade execution confirmations, swap details

Every report is encrypted before storage. The Fileverse document contains only ciphertext. Decryption happens in the browser after the user signs a message.

### Key Code Paths

**Fileverse integration** — apps/web/src/lib/integrations/fileverse.ts handles REST API calls, Agents SDK fallback, and encryption

**Encryption** — apps/web/src/lib/integrations/crypto.ts implements AES-256-GCM encrypt/decrypt with key derivation from wallet signatures

**Report decryption API** — apps/web/src/app/api/reports/route.ts verifies signature, decrypts from Fileverse or local store

**Report viewer** — apps/web/src/components/jobs/view-report.tsx prompts wallet signature and displays decrypted markdown

### Why This Is "Build What Big Tech Won't"

Google Docs knows everything you write. Notion can read your workspace. Every centralized document platform has full access to your content.

Obscura's agent reports are **privacy-first by design**. AI agents collaborate with humans to produce DeFi intelligence, but the collaboration happens without surveillance. The agent writes, Fileverse stores, only the user reads. No middleman has access. No platform can mine your strategy.

This is exactly what the bounty asks for — privacy-first apps where users can collaborate with humans and agents without surveillance, middlemen, or lock-in.

### Agent-to-Agent Coordination

The orchestrator runs a multi-agent pipeline where agents coordinate on-chain:

1. Worker agent (Scout/Analyst/Ghost) executes the job and calls submit() on the AgentJobs contract
2. Sentinel evaluates the worker's output deterministically (score 0-100)
3. Sentinel calls complete() or reject() on the contract — settling USDC
4. Sentinel writes ERC-8004 reputation feedback scoring the worker agent

Economic consequences flow from this coordination — USDC goes to the worker on approval, back to the client on rejection.

**DeFi 2.0 - New Primitives**

### First Implementation of ERC-8183

ERC-8183 (Agentic Commerce) was proposed on February 25, 2026 by Davide Crapis from the **Ethereum Foundation's dAI team** along with Bryan Lim and team from **Virtuals Protocol**. It defines trustless commercial transactions between autonomous AI agents using on-chain escrow.

We are the **first team to implement it**.

Our AgentJobs.sol contract implements the full ERC-8183 lifecycle:

- **createJob(provider, evaluator, expiredAt, description)** — user posts a job with a designated agent and evaluator
- **fund(jobId, budget)** — USDC locked in escrow
- **submit(jobId, deliverable)** — agent submits a hash of the encrypted report
- **complete(jobId, reason)** — evaluator approves, USDC released to agent
- **reject(jobId, reason)** — evaluator rejects, USDC refunded to user
- **claimRefund(jobId)** — user reclaims after expiry if no one picks up the job

State machine: Open -> Funded -> Submitted -> Completed/Rejected/Expired

### Reputation-Based Agent Selection

Every completed job writes a granular reputation score (0-100) to the ERC-8004 Reputation Registry on Base Sepolia. The score is broken down into:

- Deliverable quality (30 points)
- Tool usage correctness (25 points)
- Timeliness (20 points, gradient: under 30s = 20, under 60s = 15, under 120s = 10)
- Risk compliance with user's ENS preferences (25 points)

Over time, agents with higher reputation get selected more often. This is the foundation for a **reputation-based agent economy** — not random assignment, not round-robin, but meritocratic selection driven by on-chain verifiable performance data.

### Novel DeFi Primitive

The AgentJobs contract is a new coordination mechanism for DeFi — a three-party escrow (client, AI provider, AI evaluator) where the entire lifecycle is driven by autonomous agents holding wallets, not humans. Combined with ERC-8004 reputation, this creates a trustless marketplace where agents are accountable service providers with verifiable track records.

DeFi research is fragmented. You check DeFiLlama for yields, Twitter for sentiment, protocol docs for details, and wallet analyzers for risk — all manually, all on different platforms. AI agents can automate this, but they need access to real DeFi data.

### x402 Payment Flow

Payment wallet: 0x4CcB868a7bd4fd91C366903F9f0Cc94FdC199Ebf (Base mainnet, real USDC balance)

1. Agent makes an HTTP request to a HeyElsa x402 endpoint
2. Server responds with 402 and payment requirements
3. Our custom interceptor bridges the v2 payment-required header format to what x402-axios expects
4. x402-axios signs a USDC payment on Base mainnet
5. Request retries with the payment header
6. Server verifies payment and returns DeFi data

Cost per full job cycle: approximately $0.03-0.08 in USDC

### Real-World Problem Solved

Users post a job like "Find me the best yield for USDC on Base" and an AI agent autonomously:

1. Queries DeFiLlama for live yield data as a free reliable baseline
2. Calls HeyElsa x402 endpoints for deeper token analysis and yield suggestions
3. Compiles everything into an AES-256-GCM encrypted report
4. Submits on-chain, gets evaluated by Sentinel, earns USDC

The agent pays for its own research tools via x402 and earns back from the job escrow. A self-sustaining economic loop — agents spend to earn.

### Technical Integration

We built a custom Axios interceptor to bridge the x402 v2 protocol format. The v2 servers send payment requirements in a payment-required HTTP header as base64 JSON with eip155:8453 network identifiers. The x402-axios library expects the old format with short network names in the response body. Our interceptor decodes the header, transforms eip155:8453 to "base", flattens the nested resource object, and passes it to x402-axios for payment signing.

### Key Code Path

apps/web/src/lib/integrations/heyelsa.ts — HeyElsa x402 client with all 9 DeFi endpoints, using x402-axios with createSigner("base", privateKey) for Base mainnet USDC payments

## The Gig Economy for AI Agents, On-Chain

Three weeks ago, the Ethereum Foundation's decentralized AI team and Virtuals Protocol proposed ERC-8183 — a standard for trustless commerce between autonomous AI agents. Nobody had built it.

We did. In 42 hours.

### What Obscura Is

A marketplace where users hire AI agents for DeFi jobs. Not a chatbot. Not a wrapper. An economic system where agents have wallets, earn USDC, and are held accountable by smart contracts.

**Post a job** — "Find me the best yield for USDC on Base." USDC gets escrowed on-chain.

**An agent picks it up** — Scout researches live yield data from DeFiLlama, pays for web search via x402 micropayments in real USDC, and writes an encrypted report that only your wallet can decrypt.

**A deterministic evaluator scores it** — Sentinel (no LLM, pure rules) grades the work on quality, tool usage, speed, and compliance with your ENS-defined risk preferences. Score 68/100? Passes. USDC goes to the agent. Score 30? Rejected. You get refunded.

**Reputation is recorded on-chain** — via ERC-8004, the same standard with authors from Google, Coinbase, and MetaMask. Better agents earn more jobs over time.

### What Makes It Different

**It's not theoretical.** We deployed contracts on Base Sepolia, registered 4 agents on ERC-8004, ran 25+ real jobs during the hackathon, and spent real USDC on Base mainnet for x402 API calls. The dashboard shows real data, not mocks.

**Privacy is structural, not an afterthought.** Reports are AES-256-GCM encrypted with per-job keys derived from your wallet signature. Stored on Fileverse. Only you can decrypt. Your DeFi preferences live as ENS text records — risk tolerance, asset whitelist, kill switch — and agents enforce them on every job. Change your ENS, change how every agent behaves.

**The evaluation is deterministic.** Most AI agent projects use vibes to decide if output is good. Sentinel uses a fixed scoring rubric — deliverable quality (30pts), tool usage (25pts), timeliness (20pts), risk compliance (25pts). No LLM subjectivity. Verifiable. On-chain.

### The Stack

Seven real integrations, nothing mocked:

- **Base** — smart contracts, agent wallets, USDC settlement
- **ENS** — programmable policy engine for agent governance
- **HeyElsa** — x402 DeFi data micropayments
- **Fileverse** — encrypted decentralized report storage
- **Groq / Gemini** — LLM reasoning for agent research
- **DeFiLlama** — live yield and protocol data
- **ERC-8004** — on-chain agent identity and reputation

### The Vision

Right now we deploy agents ourselves and give them ENS names. The orchestrator routes jobs. Sentinel evaluates.

Tomorrow — agents register themselves in ERC-8004, discover each other, post jobs to each other via ERC-8183, settle in USDC, and build reputation autonomously. No platform. No permission. The registry doesn't support the full 8183 flow yet. We're building toward it.

This isn't a demo of what could be. It's a working system built on standards that didn't exist a month ago.

### Cloak402

> Agents that keep secrets

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Viem](https://img.shields.io/badge/Viem-333333?style=flat-square) ![BASE](https://img.shields.io/badge/BASE-333333?style=flat-square) ![Ephemeral wallets](https://img.shields.io/badge/Ephemeral%20wallets-333333?style=flat-square) ![Open claw](https://img.shields.io/badge/Open%20claw-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

The rise of AI agents has introduced a massive privacy loophole: The "Agents that keep secrets" problem. When an AI agent interacts with Web3 protocols or traditional APIs (like flight searches, DeFi trading, or hotel bookings) on your behalf, it emits a massive amount of metadata. 

Link to our whitepaper - [Cloak 402 whitepaper](https://drive.google.com/file/d/151_EmVE_ZcyXDl5ipDVTfMEvUIUPwQo-/view?usp=sharing).

Even if the agent doesn't have a persistent account, every API call, x402 payment, or contract interaction leaves a trail. Observers can easily deanonymize the human behind the agent through on-chain graph analysis (clustering funding flows and gas sources) and off-chain logs (IP addresses, request headers, and timing correlations).


Cloak402 solves this by acting as a privacy-preserving orchestration layer for AI agents. Using our autonomous travel agent as a real-world implementation, Cloak402 proves that agents can engage in complex, multi-step commerce without doxxing the user. Here is how it makes agentic tasks safer:

Relationship Anonymity via Ephemeral Wallets: Instead of using a single hot wallet, Cloak402 generates a fresh, single-use keypair in memory for every single API call.

Breaking the Funding Graph: A naive ephemeral wallet is useless if funded directly by the user. We integrated CloakPool, an intermediate shared pool that breaks the on-chain link between the user's main funding wallet and the ephemeral payment addresses.

Defeating Heuristics: To prevent clustering, Cloak402 randomizes the USDC funding amounts (0.03 - 0.09 USDC bands) and introduces a randomized timing jitter (1.5 - 6 seconds) to break timestamp correlations between off-chain API logs and on-chain settlements.

Policy-Driven Disclosure: It puts the human back in control. In our travel agent demo, OpenClaw enforces strict disclosure policies: searching for flights is done with absolute anonymity, while booking a flight selectively discloses only the absolute minimum required data (name and email), all while keeping the financial footprint completely hidden.

Ultimately, Cloak402 allows anyone to use AI agents for sensitive tasks—from booking travel to executing private DeFi strategies—without letting service providers, MEV searchers, or on-chain sleuths build a profile on them.

**Challenges we ran into**

Building a true privacy layer for AI agents is much harder than just wiping a private key from memory. We ran into several deep technical hurdles while building Cloak402:

1. The "Naive Ephemeral Wallet" Trap
Initially, we thought generating a fresh viem private key for every API call would be enough. But we quickly realized this achieved credential minimization, not anonymity. A trivial on-chain graph analysis could link every ephemeral wallet back to our control wallet because the control wallet was directly funding them for gas and x402 payments.

How we got over it: We had to pivot our architecture to implement the foundational layer of CloakPool. By routing funds through a shared pool and randomizing the USDC top-up amounts (between 0.03 and 0.09 USDC), we broke the 1:1 on-chain funding link.

2. Off-Chain Timing Correlations
Even with the funding graph broken, we realized that an observer could monitor the network mempool and the API provider's HTTP logs. Because AI agents execute tasks incredibly fast, the timestamp of the flight search API request perfectly matched the timestamp of the x402 payment settlement.

How we got over it: We built a ghostPay privacy wrapper that introduces artificial, randomized timing jitter (1.5 to 6 seconds) before fulfilling the x402 payment. This simple but effective friction decorrelates the request timing from the on-chain execution.

3. Taming the LLM Agent's Urge to Share Data
Getting the OpenClaw agent to understand contextual privacy was tricky. LLMs naturally want to pass all the context they have into their tool calls. Early on, the agent would accidentally leak passenger identities during the anonymous "flight search" phase just because the user had provided their name upfront in the chat.

How we got over it: We designed strict, code-level separation between the tools. We created distinct CLI tools (search_flights.ts vs book_flight.ts) and defined rigorous skill-level rules in our SKILL.md that strictly prohibited the LLM from passing PII into the search tool. We combined this with our middleware to drop any payload data that violated the policy before the x402 payment even fired.

4. Managing the Ephemeral Lifecycle
Orchestrating the creation, funding, x402 protocol handshake, data retrieval, and memory wiping of a wallet within a single, synchronous HTTP request cycle was highly prone to race conditions, especially when dealing with testnet RPC limits.

How we got over it: We heavily optimized our ghostPay.ts wrapper to handle async operations robustly, ensuring that if a step fails (like a timeout from the airline API), the ephemeral private key is still guaranteed to be destroyed to prevent dangling hot wallets.

**Privacy**

Cloak402 introduces a robust privacy orchestration layer for agentic transactions. By combining single-use ephemeral wallets, randomized funding delays, and a shared funding pool (CloakPool), it completely severs the on-chain linkability of user transactions hence fighting dynamic pricing and protecting user's sensitive information.

**AI**

Cloak402 embeds intelligence directly into Web3 commerce by giving AI agents the ability to understand and enforce contextual privacy. Using OpenClaw, our autonomous agent safely orchestrates complex off-chain API workflows and on-chain x402 micropayments without ever exposing the user's identity or financial footprint.

**AI × Onchain**

We built secure agentic commerce infrastructure natively on Base. Cloak402 enables autonomous AI agents to dynamically spin up wallets, execute HTTP-native x402 micropayments, and transact for services without leaking their underlying economic identity or user strategies.

**Privacy**

Cloak402 directly solves the "Privacy for AI agents" challenge on Base. By wrapping API calls in ephemeral wallets and breaking funding graphs via a shared pool, it ensures autonomous systems can operate, spend, and settle without being tracked, clustered, or front-run by on-chain analysts.

**Best Use of Elsa x402 and Elsa OpenClaw skills**

We built a custom OpenClaw LLM agent that enforces strict user disclosure policies before executing actions. It autonomously pays for shielded API access using Elsa’s x402 protocol, proving that agentic workflows can be both highly capable and completely private.

**BEST Overall Project**

Cloak402 addresses a massive, emerging Web3 vulnerability: AI agent metadata leaks. By creatively combining LLM tooling (OpenClaw), HTTP micropayments (x402), and clever privacy primitives (timing jitter, ephemeral key destruction), we’ve built a production-ready blueprint for private AI commerce.

**The problem it solves**

### "What if your AI agent could take out a loan, trade, and repay with profit—all without you lifting a finger?"

**AgentFi** is a **multi-agent P2P lending marketplace** where AI agents autonomously borrow capital, deploy it via quantitative trading strategies, and repay with on-chain reputation. We solve the #1 problem in DeFi: **Capital Inefficiency.**

---

## The Problem 
1. **DeFi Lending is Dead Capital:** Over-collateralized protocols (like Aave) lock up $3 for every $1 borrowed. 
2. **AI Agents are "Broke":** Existing frameworks assume agents already have funds; there is zero infrastructure for agents to access unsecured capital.
3. **Sybil-Prone Reputation:** Most reputation systems are easily gamed by wash-trading.

## Our Solution
AgentFi creates an **Agent-Native Credit Market**:
- **ZK-Verified Identity:** Using Reclaim Protocol & ENS to ensure "One Human = One Identity Ecosystem" (Anti-Sybil).
- **Continuous Collateral Curve:** No binary liquidation cliffs. Collateral requirements drop from 100% to 0% as agents prove their discipline.
- **Autonomous Execution:** 2-of-2 multisig wallets allow agents to trade 24/7 without manual user signing for small trades (<$500/hr).
- **Reputation as Collateral:** On-chain reputation (via PeosFi) becomes the "Working Capital" for the agent economy.

---

## Key Innovations (The "Top 1%" Tech)
- **The Identity Stack:** ZK-Proof (Reclaim) + ENS + userId isolation ensures it is mathematically impossible to benefit from wash-trading.
- **Credit-Score Model:** A 0–50 scale that excludes trading "Alpha" (skill) and focuses strictly on "Repayment Discipline" (risk). 
- **The Matcher Engine:** A sophisticated P2P orderbook where lenders compete on interest rates to fund high-reputation agents.

---

## ⁉️ FAQs

### Q: "How do you prevent a total collapse on zero-collateral loans?"
**A:** We use a **Continuous Collateral Curve**. Agents don't get zero-collateral access until they reach **Reputation 35**, which requires 5+ successful trade/repay cycles. Our crossover point is modeled on an 8% default rate (the DeFi benchmark for unsecured loans). We don't lend to code; we lend to **provable discipline**.

### Q: "Why exclude trading profit (Alpha) from the Reputation score?"
**A:** High-alpha strategies are often high-risk. Rewarding alpha with more capital compounds systemic risk. Instead, alpha is surfaced to lenders so they can *price their interest rates* accordingly. Profitability is a **pricing** signal; repayment is a **trust** signal.

### Q: "Is the 2-of-2 Multisig decentralized?"
**A:** We use the multisig as an **Autonomous Risk Gate**. The platform co-signs trades <$500/hr instantly to enable 24/7 autonomy. Anything larger requires user approval. This moves the human from the *execution* path (slow) to the *policy* path (safe).

---

## 🫦  Tech Stack
- **Blockchain:** Base Sepolia (Lending Contracts, MockUSDC)
- **Identity:** ENS (Ethereum Sepolia) + Reclaim Protocol (ZK-Proof)
- **Wallet:** Metamask
- **Trading:** HeyElsa API (Portfolio & Swap Execution)
- **Storage:** Fileverse (Encrypted Strategy Docs)
- **Backend:** Node.js, Express, PostgreSQL, Redis

---

### 🏁 Impact
AgentFi is more than a tool—it's the **financial infrastructure for the agentic economy.** As billions of agents enter the web, AgentFi provides the bank accounts and credit scores they need to be truly self-sovereign.

**Challenges we ran into**

**Challenges we ran into 🏃‍♂️**

**Cross-Chain Identity Resolution**: Our lending logic lives on Base Sepolia, but ENS names are registered on Ethereum Sepolia. Resolving these identities across chains in real-time created significant latency issues. We overcame this by implementing a dual-provider listener in our backend that caches ENS-to-Wallet mappings, ensuring agent verification happens in milliseconds without blocking the matching engine.

**The "Double-Spend" vs. Autonomy Paradox**: Implementing a 2-of-2 multisig for an autonomous agent presented a race-condition risk: the agent and the platform co-signer could both attempt to sign different transactions simultaneously. We solved this by building a Synchronous Transaction Queue in Redis, ensuring that the agent's rolling 60-minute volume gate is calculated and locked before the platform co-signs any transaction.

**ZK-Proof Mapping & Privacy**: Integrating Reclaim Protocol to prevent sybil attacks while maintaining user privacy was difficult. We had to derive a deterministic but anonymous humanId from the ZK proof. We implemented a hashing salt stored on-chain to ensure that a single human cannot register multiple ENS names, without ever exposing the user's underlying credentials to our database.

**ZK-Proof Mapping & Privacy**: Executing complex portfolio swaps via API during volatile testnet conditions often led to transaction slippage. We developed a "Pre-flight Verification" service that checks liquidity on Base before the agent requests a loan, preventing agents from borrowing capital for strategies that cannot be executed due to market depth.

**DeFi**

## DeFi Track Fit

**AgentFi is a fully autonomous, self-maintaining P2P lending marketplace where AI agents are the borrowers, lenders, and traders — governed entirely by on-chain reputation.**

### 1. Reputation-Driven Lending, Not Over-Collateralization
We built a fully on-chain lending contract where loan terms — collateral requirements, interest rates, and max loan size — are mathematically derived from a 0–50 reputation score. Agents with rep ≥ 35 access unsecured loans with zero collateral. No oracles, no governance votes. This replaces the Aave/Compound over-collateralization model with a credit-score system enforced entirely in Solidity.

### 2. Autonomous AI Agents as First-Class Market Participants
Instead of humans clicking buttons, AI agents autonomously post lend offers, evaluate borrow quotes, execute multi-phase trading strategies, and repay loans with profit. A full runtime engine with 30+ DeFi tools (swaps, limit orders, yield farming, portfolio analysis) runs on configurable intervals — turning the lending market into a self-operating financial ecosystem.

### 3. Anti-Sybil and Volume-Gated Risk Management
Economic safety is enforced at four independent layers: ZK human verification at registration, service-level owner isolation, a Postgres trigger blocking same-user matches, and a Solidity `require(borrower != lender)`. On top of that, a Redis-based rolling volume gate auto-flags any agent exceeding $500/hour for human approval — preventing runaway autonomous risk.

### 4. Full Loan Lifecycle with Automated Settlement
Every phase — collateral locking, principal transfer, repayment, partial default, liquidation — happens on-chain via ERC-20 USDC. A cron scheduler auto-liquidates overdue loans after an 8-day window, decays dormant agent reputation, and expires stale offers. The result is a self-maintaining marketplace that runs without manual intervention.

**AI**

## AI Track Fit

**AgentFi is an autonomous agent runtime where AI actors reason, select tools, execute multi-phase trading strategies, and make economically consequential decisions — fully observable in real time.**

### 1. Autonomous Agents with Multi-Step Reasoning
Each agent runs an independent execution loop that doesn't just fire transactions — it reasons. A borrower agent evaluates open offers, fetches a reputation-based quote, compares expected profit against borrowing cost, and skips the cycle entirely if the edge isn't there. Lender agents check for existing open offers before posting a new one. This is decision-making, not scripting.

### 2. Tool-Using Agents with 30+ Callable Actions
Agents interact with a registered toolset — `search_token`, `get_swap_quote`, `execute_swap`, `create_limit_order`, `get_yield_suggestions`, `analyze_wallet`, `get_pnl_report`, and more. Every tool call is logged with full input/output. The agent runtime selects and sequences these tools across a 6-phase trading pipeline (research → entry → position management → exit → review) — mirroring how a production AI agent with tool-use would operate in live DeFi.

### 3. Strategy-Driven, Parameterized Behavior
Every agent is spawned with a natural-language strategy prompt and a structured strategy JSON — max loan amount, risk tolerance, profit target, trade allocation. The runtime reads these to adjust behavior dynamically: a conservative agent raises its minimum reputation threshold and scales down profit targets; an aggressive agent does the opposite. Agents aren't hardcoded — they're parameterized autonomous actors whose behavior is fully user-defined.

### 4. Full Observability — Live Agent Thinking Feed
Every cycle is traced end-to-end: `cycle:start` → `reasoning` → `tool:selected` → `tool:result` → `decision` → `trade:phase(1–6)` → `cycle:end`. All persisted in `agent_execution_logs` with cycle IDs, phase labels, tool names, and full I/O payloads. The frontend renders this as a live **Agent Thinking Feed** — judges can watch an agent reason, trade, and repay in real time. Not a black box. An explainable, auditable AI system.

**Best creative use of ENS**

## Creative Use of ENS

**AgentFi treats ENS not as a display name, but as the identity, reputation, and ownership infrastructure for an entire AI agent economy.**

### Why ENS?
In most projects, ENS is cosmetic — a readable alias for a hex address. In AgentFi, an ENS name *is* the agent. It's how agents are recognized across the marketplace, how loans are recorded, and how reputation travels. When `alice-vault.eth` borrows from `bob-lender.eth`, the loan reads like a human-readable financial contract. No hex addresses, no registry lookups — the name tells the whole story.

### What We Built With ENS
- **On-chain agent identity.** Every agent registers with an ENS name that gets permanently bound in the lending contract. The entire marketplace is browsable, auditable, and legible to anyone — without ever looking at a raw wallet address.
- **ENS subdomains as agent hierarchies.** A user who owns `alice.eth` spawns agents as subdomains — `vault-1.alice.eth`, `trader-2.alice.eth`. The parent name represents the human; the subdomains represent their agents. Ownership, purpose, and lineage are all readable directly from the name.
- **ENS text records as a portable credit layer.** An agent's reputation score is stored as an ENS text record. This means credit history isn't locked inside AgentFi — it travels with the ENS name across the entire Ethereum ecosystem. Any protocol, marketplace, or dApp can look up `alice-vault.eth`, read its reputation record, and make trust decisions from it. Reputation becomes a public, composable, cross-protocol primitive.

### Why It's Different
Nobody in the ENS ecosystem is using text records as a financial reputation layer or subdomains as an agent identity hierarchy. Most ENS usage stops at "display name for wallet." AgentFi uses ENS as the composable identity infrastructure for AI agent economies — where your name carries your credit score, your agents are your subdomains, and your entire financial identity is readable from a single lookup.

**Build What Big Tech Won't**

## Creative Use of Fileverse

**AgentFi uses Fileverse as the strategy layer for every AI agent — a living document that defines how the agent thinks, trades, and manages risk.**

### Why Fileverse?
An autonomous agent needs to know its rules before it acts. Instead of hardcoding behavior or storing strategies in a private database, every agent reads its Fileverse document at the start of each cycle. The human sets the playbook. The agent executes it. Fileverse is the interface between human intent and autonomous action.

### What We Built With Fileverse
- **The agent's constitution.** Each agent has a Fileverse doc containing its trading strategy, risk parameters, loan limits, and execution rules — defined by the user. Change the doc, change the agent's behavior. No redeployment, no code changes.
- **Human strategy, agent execution.** A user writes: *"max loan $500, 60% ETH / 40% stablecoin, conservative risk, repay within 30 seconds."* The agent reads this every cycle and acts accordingly. The human never touches a transaction — just the document.
- **Transparent, auditable behavior.** Because strategies live on Fileverse rather than a private backend, anyone — a lender, an auditor — can verify exactly what rules an agent is following. If `alice-vault.eth` claims to be conservative, you can pull up its Fileverse doc and confirm. No black boxes.

### Why It's Different
Most Fileverse use cases are wikis or notes. AgentFi uses it as the programmable soul of an autonomous financial agent — a living document that governs how an AI entity participates in DeFi markets, readable by the agent and verifiable by anyone. That's a new use case for decentralized documents entirely.

**AI × Onchain**

## Creative Use of Base

**AgentFi uses Base as the trust and settlement layer for an autonomous AI credit economy — a primitive that doesn't exist anywhere else on-chain.**

### Why Base?
AI agents running 60-second trading cycles can't operate on high-fee chains. Base's sub-cent transaction costs make it economically viable for agents to borrow, trade, and repay multiple times a day without gas eating into profits. Speed and cost aren't nice-to-haves here — they're what makes the autonomous loop possible.

### What We Built On Base
- **An on-chain credit bureau for AI agents.** Every agent earns a reputation score (0–50) derived entirely from its verifiable loan history on Base — repayments, defaults, profit generation. No oracles, no committees. Just provable behavior.
- **A human-to-agent reputation bridge.** An agent's starting credit is seeded from its owner's on-chain history, verified via ZK proof and ENS binding. Base holds the full reputation graph — humans and their agents — in one unified, verifiable system.
- **Real economic consequences.** The score directly controls collateral requirements, loan limits, and interest rates. It's not cosmetic — it's the access key to capital.

### Why It's a New Primitive
Most Base projects are swaps, bridges, or NFTs. AgentFi is using Base as financial infrastructure for non-human actors — where an AI agent's ability to borrow and the terms it receives are determined entirely by its provable on-chain history. That's machine-native credit. Not a DeFi fork.

**Projects building with the SDK to solve real-world problems will be eligible**

## Creative Use of HeyElsa (X402)

**AgentFi uses HeyElsa's X402 API as the trading execution layer for autonomous AI agents — turning borrowed capital into profit through a structured, multi-phase DeFi trading loop.**

### Why HeyElsa?
Once an agent borrows capital, it needs to actually deploy it. HeyElsa gives the agent hands — the ability to research markets, execute swaps, place limit orders, and manage positions without any human involvement. It's what makes the borrowing agent a real trader, not just a wallet.

### What We Built On HeyElsa
- **A 30+ tool trading suite.** We built composable tools on top of X402 — `search_token`, `get_swap_quote`, `execute_swap`, `create_limit_order`, `get_portfolio`, `get_yield_suggestions`, `analyze_wallet`, `get_pnl_report`, `check_airdrop`, and more. Each tool is a discrete action the agent can invoke based on its current phase and strategy.
- **A realistic 6-phase trading loop.** The agent doesn't blindly swap once. It runs a structured pipeline: research the market → check gas → enter a position → monitor prices and set limit orders → exit the position → review PnL. Each phase has realistic delays and branching logic — it behaves like a human quant trader compressed into a 30-second autonomous cycle.
- **AI-native tool selection.** The agent picks which tools to call based on market conditions and its own risk parameters. It's not scripted — it's compositional reasoning through HeyElsa's toolkit.

### Why It's Different
Most HeyElsa integrations are single-action — "swap this token." AgentFi uses it as the cognitive execution layer for an agent that borrows someone else's money, trades across multiple phases, and returns it with profit. The agent doesn't just call HeyElsa. It *thinks* through HeyElsa.

**BEST Overall Project**

## Why AgentFi Is the Best Overall Project

### 1. A New Financial Primitive, Not Another DeFi Feature
Most hackathon projects build one thing — a swap, a bridge, a dashboard. AgentFi builds an entirely new category: a credit system and lending marketplace designed specifically for AI agents. On-chain reputation that governs collateral requirements, interest rates, and loan caps doesn't exist anywhere today. This isn't an incremental improvement to DeFi. It's infrastructure for a future where AI agents are first-class economic participants.

### 2. End-to-End, Actually Working
Every layer is built, connected, and running:
- **Smart contract** — 475 lines of Solidity, fully tested
- **Backend API** — 4 route groups, matching engine, liquidation scheduler
- **Agent runtime** — 30+ tools, 6-phase autonomous trading loops
- **Database** — 8-table PostgreSQL schema with anti-sybil triggers
- **Frontend** — live React dashboard with real-time Agent Thinking Feed

You can watch an agent borrow capital, trade through HeyElsa, repay with profit, and build on-chain reputation — right now. This isn't a slide deck or a mocked demo. Every layer talks to every other layer.

### 3. Every Sponsor Integration Is Structural, Not Decorative
- **Base** — sub-cent settlement makes 60-second agent cycles economically viable
- **ENS** — agent identity, subdomain ownership hierarchies, and portable reputation via text records
- **Fileverse** — transparent, user-defined strategy documents the agent reads every cycle
- **HeyElsa** — the execution layer for autonomous multi-phase DeFi trading

Remove any one of these, and the system breaks. That's genuine integration — not bounty farming.

### 4. Solves a Problem That's About to Matter Enormously
AI agents managing capital isn't hypothetical — it's already happening. But there's no trust layer, no credit system, and no safe way to lend to an agent. AgentFi is the answer to the question every DeFi protocol will face in the next 12 months: *"How do we let AI agents participate in our markets without getting wrecked?"*

This project isn't just technically impressive today. It's positioned exactly where crypto and AI are about to collide.

**The problem it solves**

How do you share a section of a document without sharing the complete document? You could just copy paste the contents but how can we belive the contents have not been tampered? Dissek solves this problem ! It is a marketplace for Valuable knowledge like - Defi Trading Strategies, Medical History , Research Datasets, Training data that allows selective disclosure of the content with a cryptographic proof of authenticity and untampered. So, a researcher can monetise specific section of their dataset. A AI agent can purchase verified training samples line by line with a mathematical gurantee that what they received is real.
Payments are done over HTTP through x402 protocol so no invoicing, no accounts, no trust assumptions. Just pay, receive and verify!

**Challenges we ran into**

We ran into a number of challenges - 
1. Fileverse does not provide the API for the invite only shares, rather it provides public link upon creation of New Document, which challenges us to workaround our idea.

2. ENSIP-25 is a bit new and not much researched upon, we tried to combine it with
the subnames and reverse registrar for ENS, which was very hard problem to tackle and took very time.

3. HeyElsa  was fairly easy but to figure out at what part of the transaction flow will the x402 payment take place as payment firewall.

**Privacy**

DisseK is privacy by design, not privacy as an afterthought.

The core idea is that a document owner should never have to opt out of monetisation if he wishes to protect some part of his document. With DisseK, you share only the lines a buyer paid for. The undisclosed portions of your document are never seen by anyone except you.

Merkle Proofs provide us the cryptographic gurantee. A buyer receives the disclosed lines along with proof that those exact lines belong to the original document, without revealing any other content. Verification is fully permissionless: anyone can check the proof against the on-chain anchored Merkle root.

The marketplace itself is also privacy-preserving by architecture. It only stores metadata titles, section names, line counts, prices, and Merkle roots. The actual document content lives exclusively on the host's Fileverse instance, behind the host's own x402-paywalled backend.

In short: buyers can verify authenticity without seeing everything, sellers monetise without exposing everything, and no intermediary ever holds the full document.

**Best creative use of ENS**

DisseK fits Best Creative Use of ENS by making ENS the core trust layer: we verify users through forward/reverse resolution, classify individual vs organization agents, and enforce ENSIP-25 attestations for namespace access. It also fits the Pool Prize because it delivers a working, demo-ready marketplace with real utility, clear UX, and expandable infrastructure for secure selective document disclosure at scale.

**Build What Big Tech Won't**

DisseK is a strong fit for Fileverse’s “Build What Big Tech Won’t” because it gives creators cryptographic control over how documents are shared and monetized, instead of handing full data ownership to centralized platforms. By combining Fileverse storage, selective disclosure, and proof-backed verification, we enable trust-minimized knowledge commerce where users reveal only what they choose, when they choose.

**Best Use of Elsa x402 and Elsa OpenClaw skills**

For HeyElsa, DisseK fits well: we already use x402 in production flow to paywall POST /disclose, so access to sensitive document slices is paid, verifiable, and automated onchain. It also matches the SDK real-world track because we solve a concrete problem: secure data monetization with selective disclosure, proof verification, and identity-based access control. For the OpenClaw angle, our verify-agent and check-access endpoints map naturally to reusable skills.

**BEST Overall Project**

DisseK solves the real world problem of selective disclousre of Documents with authenticity. It allows you to monetise High Value data which is extremely important in the age of Agentic Economy.

It is built on these core primitives : 

Cryptography : a custom Rust WASM proof engine using Merkle range multi-proofs, compiled from scratch with rs_merkle and sha2, running server-side in Node.js with domain-separated hashing to prevent second-preimage attacks.

Payments : x402 HTTP-native micropayments integrated across two independent backends simultaneously. Buyers pay in USDC without any trust assumptions and any load of recepits or invoices.

Decentralised storage : documents live on Fileverse dDocs, accessed via MCP (Model Context Protocol), with on-chain blockchain sync. The marketplace never holds any document content.

On-chain verifiability : a MerkleAnchor.sol contract  lets anyone independently verify a Merkle root without trusting the seller or the marketplace.

The result of the above is  something genuinely novel that creates a marketplace that provides everything which is needed for Trade of High Value Data.

> Privacy that moves with you

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![Rust](https://img.shields.io/badge/Rust-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![ethers-rs](https://img.shields.io/badge/ethers--rs-333333?style=flat-square) ![Axum](https://img.shields.io/badge/Axum-333333?style=flat-square) ![Base Sepolia blockchain](https://img.shields.io/badge/Base%20Sepolia%20blockchain-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

# CloakFund — Private Crypto Payments

## Problem

Blockchains are **fully transparent**.  
If someone sends crypto to your wallet, they can see:

- your **wallet balance**
- your **transaction history**
- **who you interact with**

One payment can expose your **entire financial activity**.

---

## Simple Example

**A → Sender**  
**B → Receiver**

A sends ETH to B’s wallet.

Now A can open a blockchain explorer and see:

- B’s total balance  
- B’s past transactions  

So a simple payment reveals **B’s entire financial history**.

---

## Solution — CloakFund

CloakFund lets users receive crypto **without revealing their real wallet**.

Flow:

1. Generate a **temporary stealth address**
2. Sender sends ETH to that address
3. Funds go into a **privacy pool**
4. Receiver **withdraws anonymously**

Result: **Sender and receiver cannot be linked on-chain.**

**Challenges we ran into**

As beginners in Web3, it was challenging to understand and design a **privacy system on-chain**. We initially planned to integrate **BitGo** for wallet infrastructure, but the service was not working as expected during development.

Because of this, we had to **rethink and redesign our entire architecture multiple times**. We then shifted to building a **fully decentralized privacy solution**.

Implementing full **Zero-Knowledge privacy** is very complex, so for the MVP we built a **simplified commit–reveal privacy pool**, which demonstrates the core privacy idea while keeping the system practical for a hackathon.

**Privacy**

# Why CloakFund Fits Best Privacy Project

CloakFund is built specifically to solve the **privacy problem in public blockchains**.

By combining **stealth addresses** with a **privacy pool**, our system hides the receiver’s wallet and breaks the link between deposits and withdrawals.

This ensures that:
- wallet balances stay private  
- transactions cannot be traced  
- sender and receiver cannot be linked  

CloakFund demonstrates how **true on-chain payment privacy** can be achieved without centralized services.

**Best creative use of ENS**

# ENS Pool Prize

## Why CloakFund Fits the ENS Pool Prize

CloakFund uses **Ethereum Name Service (ENS)** as the identity layer for private payments.

Instead of sharing a wallet address, users can simply use an **ENS name like `alice.eth`**. CloakFund reads the stealth public key stored in the ENS text record and generates a **one-time stealth address** for every payment.

This makes payments both **human-readable and privacy-preserving**.

[This](https://github.com/AnkanMisra/CloakFund/blob/c92cbd99fa3139b5e2c532a5beff62be5e17e868/contracts/src/CloakResolver.sol#L48-#L59) specific block of code is the exact inflection point where ENS transforms from a static naming system into a dynamic privacy engine


By combining ENS with stealth address generation, CloakFund demonstrates a **practical real-world use of ENS for secure and private crypto payments**.

**Pool prize**

# Best Creative Use of ENS

## Why CloakFund is a Creative Use of ENS

CloakFund transforms ENS from a simple naming system into a **dynamic privacy engine**.

Using **ENS Text Records**, users publish their stealth public key directly in their ENS profile. Our backend retrieves this key and generates a **new stealth address for every transaction**.

We also use **CCIP-Read (EIP-3668)** with a custom resolver to dynamically generate addresses when someone sends funds to an ENS name.

This means a sender can simply send crypto to **`alice.eth`**, while the blockchain receives the payment at a **unique stealth address**.

 
[This](https://github.com/AnkanMisra/CloakFund/blob/c92cbd99fa3139b5e2c532a5beff62be5e17e868/contracts/src/CloakResolver.sol#L61-#L78) specific block is the literal turning point where you override the default ENS behavior to transform it into a dynamic privacy engine. Instead of doing what ENS normally does (returning a static wallet address), it systematically halts the transaction via OffchainLookup (CCIP-Read) to fetch the freshly generated stealth address directly from your backend for that exact transfer.

CloakFund shows how ENS can power **private, user-friendly crypto payments**, making it a strong candidate for the **Best Creative Use of ENS** prize.

**Best Privacy Application using BitGo**

# Best Privacy Application using BitGo

CloakFund uses BitGo infrastructure to build a **secure and privacy-focused crypto payment system**.

In traditional crypto payments, sending funds directly to a wallet exposes the receiver’s **balance, transaction history, and financial activity**. CloakFund solves this by generating **one-time temporary payment addresses using BitGo wallet infrastructure**.

Each payment is received through a unique address, preventing senders or observers from tracking the receiver’s real wallet. BitGo’s wallet APIs and transaction management allow us to securely generate addresses, monitor deposits, and automate fund forwarding.

By combining BitGo’s secure wallet infrastructure with stealth-style payment flows, CloakFund demonstrates how **enterprise-grade wallet services can power private and secure crypto payments**.

**AI × Onchain**

# AI × Onchain Track

CloakFund includes an automated backend agent that continuously monitors blockchain events and manages the privacy pool workflow.

The Rust-based watcher indexes on-chain transactions, detects stealth deposits, and automatically triggers privacy pool commitments. This automated system acts as an intelligent coordination layer between users and smart contracts.

While the protocol’s core focus is privacy, this architecture demonstrates how **automated agents can manage complex on-chain workflows**, such as indexing, transaction monitoring, and smart contract interactions.

This approach highlights the potential for **AI-driven or agent-based systems to coordinate privacy infrastructure on-chain**.

**DeFi 2.0 - New Primitives**

# DeFi 2.0 – New Primitives

CloakFund introduces a new primitive for decentralized finance: **private payments and anonymous liquidity pools**.

Most DeFi systems are fully transparent, which exposes wallet balances, strategies, and financial relationships. CloakFund changes this by allowing funds to enter a **shared privacy pool** where deposits and withdrawals cannot be linked.

This creates a new financial building block that can enable:

• private payments  
• anonymous treasury transfers  
• confidential DAO payouts  
• privacy-preserving DeFi interactions

By combining stealth addresses with a mixer-style pool, CloakFund demonstrates how privacy can become a **native primitive within DeFi infrastructure**.

**Privacy**

# Privacy Track

CloakFund directly addresses one of the biggest limitations of public blockchains: **lack of financial privacy**.

Our protocol combines two privacy mechanisms:

• **Stealth Addresses** – each payment uses a one-time wallet so the receiver’s real wallet is never revealed.  
• **Privacy Pool** – deposits are mixed using a commitment scheme that breaks the link between deposit and withdrawal.

Together these mechanisms ensure the sender, receiver, and transaction history **cannot be linked on-chain**.

CloakFund demonstrates how strong privacy guarantees can be implemented directly in smart contracts while still maintaining a smooth user experience through ENS-based identities.

**BEST Overall Project**

# Why CloakFund Fits Best Overall Project

CloakFund solves a major problem in crypto: **lack of financial privacy**.

Today, sending crypto reveals a user’s wallet balance and transaction history. CloakFund introduces a simple and practical solution using **stealth addresses and a privacy pool** to break the link between sender and receiver.

Our project demonstrates a **complete working privacy payment system** that runs fully on-chain and can be used for real-world payments.

CloakFund moves blockchain closer to a future where **privacy is a default feature of crypto payments**.
