### DRIFT
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/drift-0413) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/chandril-saha/drift) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://drift-th1w.vercel.app/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/2uTckvmnSsQ) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Synchronicity%20S2.0-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://synchronicity-s-2.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Limit risks, Not Possibilities

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Gemini API](https://img.shields.io/badge/Gemini%20API-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

One of the biggest security risks in Web3 is wallet exposure. Users frequently grant unlimited token approvals to smart contracts without fully understanding the permissions they are giving away. If a contract is malicious or later becomes compromised, attackers can drain funds directly from the user's wallet.

Most users also struggle to understand transaction data because blockchain interactions are often presented as complex hexadecimal payloads and contract calls that are difficult to interpret.

## How Drift Solves It

Drift acts as a transaction firewall between users and decentralized applications.

Instead of connecting a primary wallet directly to an unknown dApp, users create a temporary sandbox wallet with predefined limits. These limits control:

* Maximum spending amount
* Session duration
* Approved contracts
* Token allowances

Before any transaction is executed, Drift simulates and analyzes it to identify suspicious behavior. An integrated AI security layer explains potential risks in plain English, helping users understand exactly what a transaction is attempting to do.

If a session becomes compromised or suspicious activity is detected, users can instantly activate Panic Mode to freeze the session and recover remaining funds.

## Benefits

* Protects primary wallets from malicious contracts
* Prevents unlimited token approval abuse
* Makes transaction risks understandable to everyday users
* Reduces the impact of compromised dApps
* Creates safer experimentation with new Web3 applications
* Provides an emergency recovery mechanism for active sessions

Drift makes interacting with decentralized applications significantly safer while preserving the self-custody principles of Web3.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the biggest challenges was designing a secure session wallet architecture that remained user-friendly while enforcing strict security policies. The session wallets needed to support spending limits, expiration timers, approval controls, and emergency recovery mechanisms without making the user experience overly complex.

Another major hurdle was handling transaction simulation and risk analysis before execution. Blockchain transactions can involve multiple contract calls, token approvals, and complex state changes. Building a reliable transaction firewall required carefully validating transaction parameters and ensuring that spending limits could not be bypassed through unexpected contract behavior.

**Blockchain**

## Blockchain Track

Drift is fundamentally a blockchain security infrastructure project that leverages smart contracts to create a safer way for users to interact with decentralized applications.

The platform is built around a set of on-chain smart contracts that enforce security policies directly on the blockchain. Instead of relying on centralized intermediaries, Drift uses blockchain-native mechanisms such as programmable wallets, token approvals, transaction execution rules, and immutable contract logic to protect user assets.

Key blockchain components include:

- SessionWallet contracts that act as temporary, isolated wallets for interacting with dApps.
- SessionFactory contracts that deploy and manage sandbox wallets using the factory pattern.
- ApprovalManager contracts that control and revoke ERC-20 token allowances to prevent approval abuse.
- EmergencyVault contracts that enable secure recovery of assets when a session is compromised.
- On-chain enforcement of spending limits, expiration periods, and access controls that cannot be bypassed by external applications.

**Open Innovation**

## Open Innovation Track

Drift fits the Open Innovation track because it addresses a fundamental security problem affecting the entire Web3 ecosystem rather than serving a single niche application. Every day, users interact with smart contracts, DeFi protocols, NFT marketplaces, and blockchain games that require wallet permissions and token approvals. A single malicious approval or compromised dApp can result in the loss of user funds.

Drift introduces a new security layer between users and decentralized applications by creating temporary sandboxed wallets that isolate risk from a user's primary wallet. Instead of exposing long-term assets to unknown contracts, users can interact through disposable, policy-controlled sessions with strict spending limits, expiration times, and automatic recovery mechanisms.

The platform combines smart contract security controls, transaction simulation, and AI-powered threat analysis to make blockchain interactions safer and more understandable for both technical and non-technical users. Because this infrastructure can be integrated with virtually any Web3 application, protocol, or wallet ecosystem, Drift represents a broadly applicable innovation that improves security across the decentralized web.

**Best use of Gemini**

We use Gemini API to perform in depth analysis of transactions being routed through our app to provide detailed safety report.

**The problem it solves**

Climate change is one of the world's biggest challenges, yet trust in climate solutions remains fragmented. Billions of dollars flow through carbon markets every year, but buyers often have no simple way to verify whether a carbon credit truly represents real environmental impact. Existing systems suffer from a lack of transparency, fraud, double counting of credits, complex verification processes, and limited accessibility for smaller organizations and individuals.

CarbonX solves this trust gap by creating a blockchain-powered carbon credit marketplace where every credit is transparently verified, tokenized, tracked, traded, and retired on-chain. Instead of relying on claims, users can verify the complete lifecycle of a carbon credit—from project creation to retirement—through immutable blockchain records.

We're not building another crypto platform; we're building trust infrastructure for the sustainability economy. CarbonX democratizes climate action by enabling individuals, startups, organizations, and investors to participate in verified carbon markets while helping environmental projects gain visibility and access to funding.

Our vision is simple: a future where every ton of carbon reduced anywhere in the world can be transparently verified, funded, and tracked. CarbonX bridges the gap between digital ownership and real-world environmental impact, making climate action more transparent, accessible, and trustworthy for everyone.

Another challenge was designing a trustworthy carbon credit verification workflow. Since transparency is the core of CarbonX, we had to carefully structure project verification, ownership tracking, and carbon credit retirement mechanisms to prevent fraud and double counting.

We overcame these challenges through extensive testing, dependency management, smart contract optimization, and iterative UI/UX improvements, resulting in a secure, scalable, and user-friendly platform.

**Blockchain**

CarbonX fits the Blockchain track by using smart contracts, tokenized carbon credits, decentralized ownership records, and on-chain verification workflows. By bringing transparency and trust to carbon credit trading, our platform demonstrates a real-world application of blockchain beyond cryptocurrency, helping organizations and individuals contribute to sustainability with confidence.

### Orloj
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/orloj-597c) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/GianfrancoBazzani/orloj-registry) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://app.orloj.xyz) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-8fFjApq72g) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHPrague%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethprague2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Let AI agents transact on-chain — safely.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![PostgreSQL](https://img.shields.io/badge/PostgreSQL-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

AI agents today can *read about* smart contracts, but they can't *safely use* them. To call a contract, an agent has to manage private keys, pick an RPC, handle network failures, estimate gas, and understand each ABI's quirks. Every one of those is a footgun — and a reason teams don't ship agentic on-chain workflows.

Today's wallet UX (hardware confirmations, simulation, allowance prompts) was designed for **humans**. None of that armor extends to a stochastic actor that's one prompt-injection away from approving a malicious token.

**Orloj removes the entire surface.** Each [Sourcify](https://sourcify.dev/)-verified contract is published as its own MCP server, so the agent sees only typed, verified interfaces it can call like any other tool. NatSpec docstrings flow from the contract author straight to the LLM as tool descriptions; proxies are resolved automatically; Solidity types become Zod schemas the agent can construct arguments against.

Account management, signing, and gas live behind the MCP boundary. Private keys are minted inside hardware enclaves (**1Claw** HSM+TEE or **SpaceComputer Orbitport** orbital HSM+SpaceTEE) and never leave them. The registry sees only the digest to sign; the agent sees only the tool.

The result: agents act on-chain with the ergonomics of a REST call.

- **Simplified mental model.** Agents reason about interfaces, not RPCs, gas, or nonces.
- **Lower model requirements.** Even smaller tool-calling models execute on-chain operations reliably.
- **Architectural safety.** A compromised host or hallucinating agent can't exfiltrate keys or forge transactions — only request signatures on a digest, against a key it doesn't hold.
- **Scoped, revocable agency.** Per-agent bearer tokens + per-vault grants (permissions, expiry, secret-path patterns) make revocation a single row update.
- **Permissionless surface.** Any Sourcify-verified contract on any chain viem supports is instantly callable. No per-contract integration.

**Challenges we ran into**

**One MCP for everything, or one MCP per contract?** Our first sketch was a single "universal" MCP server that took a contract address as a tool argument and dispatched dynamically. Simple, but it broke the abstraction we cared about: the agent couldn't *see* what a contract could do — every call collapsed into an opaque *"send this calldata to this address,"* the exact footgun we wanted to remove. We pivoted to **one MCP per registered contract**, with each ABI function as its own typed tool. The win: the LLM sees `WstETH.wrap(uint256)` with the author's NatSpec as the description, and the type system tells it *what* it's doing before it does it. That decision drove the rest of the architecture.

**Node 24's strict ESM resolver vs. `@1claw/sdk`.** The SDK ships extensionless imports the new resolver rejects. Rather than fork it, we wrote a custom loader hook that re-adds the `.js` suffix.

**Solidity → Zod, recursively.** Translating an arbitrary ABI into a typed MCP surface meant handling tuples, dynamic + fixed-size arrays, every integer width, and `bytesN` — and every nested combination — into Zod.

**Proxies are most of mainnet.** A registry that doesn't understand proxies is dead on arrival. Sourcify's `proxyResolution` field made it tractable: detect proxies at registration, fetch the implementation ABI, bind the agent to the proxy address. Upgrades surface as new tools on refresh.

**Orbitport only signs digests.** Orbitport KMS never sees an unsigned tx — it signs a 32-byte hash. We build the EIP-1559 tx with viem, hash it, send only the hash, recover y-parity from the recovery id, reassemble with `serializeTransaction`, and broadcast. The registry never holds the key.

**Envelope encryption in the same security domain.** Agents need off-chain credentials too. We provision a *second* Orbitport key per vault — `TRANSIT` AES-256-GCM — and store ciphertext in Postgres while the master key stays in orbit.

**Ethereum Core**

# Orloj × Ethereum Core

> *Built at **ETHPrague 2026**.* Wallet defenses for the agentic era of Ethereum — a registry that lets AI agents safely act on-chain without ever holding a key.

## The pitch

The next significant wave of Ethereum actors isn't human. AI agents — autonomous, powerful, and not always correct — are becoming on-chain actors at a pace the existing wallet UX was never designed for. Hardware wallets, transaction simulation, signature warnings, allowance prompts: none of those protect an agent that's been told to *"swap and earn yield"* and is one prompt-injected token approval away from total loss.

Orloj is a wallet and authorization pattern designed for that wave. **Agents never hold a key, never see an RPC, never build a transaction, and can only call verified, typed interfaces under explicit per-grant authorization.** Every assumption above is enforced by the architecture rather than by agent good behavior — which is the only safety argument that survives a stochastic actor.

## What this gives Ethereum

Orloj contributes five practical security properties that don't exist in today's agent stacks:

| Property                                       | Mechanism                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Agents cannot leak keys**                    | Private material lives in HSM-backed KMS (1Claw HSM+TEE or SpaceComputer Orbitport orbital HSM+SpaceTEE). The registry never holds, generates, or reads the key — it only requests signatures on a 32-byte digest. A compromised registry host or a hallucinating agent cannot exfiltrate.                                  |
| **Agents cannot call unverified contracts**    | Every callable surface is generated from a [Sourcify](https://sourcify.dev/)-verified ABI. Bytecode-mismatched, malicious-look-alike, or unverified contracts have no MCP — they do not exist as far as the agent is concerned.                                                                                            |
| **Agents cannot forge transactions**           | Every state-changing call goes through a per-agent grant lookup against a typed, ABI-derived interface. There is no "raw transaction" path the agent can poison: the registry constructs the EIP-1559 tx with viem, hashes it, sends only the digest to the KMS, and broadcasts the result.                                |
| **Revocation is instant and key-free**         | Per-agent grants carry an expiration timestamp, scoped permissions, and a secret-path pattern; revocation is a single database row update. Bearer tokens (with an mcpk_live prefix) are constant-time-checked against Postgres and can be rotated independently. Revocation never requires touching the keys themselves.   |
| **One pattern, every Ethereum environment**    | The same MCP surface, custody model, and grant logic apply on every chain supported by viem — Mainnet, Sepolia, Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, Gnosis, Polygon. No per-rollup integration; an agent fluent in Orloj is fluent in every Ethereum environment without re-tooling.                                                  |

## Why this matters

Ethereum's safety story has historically been written for human users behind a wallet UI. None of that armor extends to autonomous agents — and the failure mode of a compromised, hallucinating, or misled agent is silent and immediate, with no humans-in-the-loop to catch the obvious-in-hindsight signs.

The agentic era needs an additional layer where the ergonomics are good enough that even less-capable models can act safely, the security guarantees survive worst-case agent behavior, and onboarding a new contract or chain requires zero per-deployment integration. The five properties above describe what that layer needs to be. Orloj is one credible answer.

## Files of interest

- `packages/registry/src/server.mjs` — registry HTTP layer, per-MCP routing, bearer-auth gate (the "instant revocation" guarantee)
- `packages/registry/src/get-contract.js` — Sourcify v2 fetch + ABI typing (the "no unverified call" guarantee)
- `packages/registry/src/sign-transaction.js` — provider-agnostic signing path (the "no key leak" guarantee)
- `packages/registry/src/vault-resolve.js` — per-agent grant resolution (the "no forgery" guarantee)
- `packages/app/lib/mcp-tokens.ts` — bearer token issuance + revocation

**Network Economy**

# Orloj × Network Economy

> *Built at **ETHPrague 2026**.* User-controlled custody, scoped agent identity, and economic agency — without surrendering autonomy to a custodian.

## The pitch

When a user delegates economic action to an AI agent, three things have to be true at once:

1. **The user owns the keys** — not the agent, not the platform, not the model provider.
2. **The agent has its own identity** — distinct from the user's, scoped to what the user actually delegated, and revocable independently.
3. **The economic surface is permissionless** — anything the user can do, the agent can be authorised to do, on any chain, against any verified contract.

In every existing agent stack, at least one of those collapses. Either the platform holds the key (custodian model), or the agent holds the key (footgun model), or the agent's authority is tied to the user's full session (everything-or-nothing model). Orloj is the design where all three hold simultaneously, enforced architecturally rather than by policy.

## What this gives users

| Property                                 | Mechanism                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **No custodian**                         | Keys live in a user-selected HSM-backed KMS (1Claw HSM+TEE or SpaceComputer Orbitport orbital HSM+SpaceTEE). The registry never holds, generates, or reads the key — it only requests signatures on a 32-byte digest.                                       |
| **Scoped agent identity**                | Each agent has its own bearer token (with an mcpk_live prefix, constant-time-checked against Postgres) and a per-vault grant carrying scoped permissions, an optional secret-path pattern, and an optional expiration timestamp. The agent is *not* the user. |
| **One-click revocation**                 | Grants are database rows; revocation is a single update. Bearer tokens can be rotated independently. Revoking an agent's economic agency never requires touching the keys themselves.                                                                       |
| **User identity, not platform identity** | Sign-in is SIWE (with ENS name + avatar lookups via viem) or magic-link via Resend. Vaults and agents are owned by the user record directly — there is no platform-managed wallet between the user and their assets.                                       |
| **Envelope-encrypted sidecar secrets**   | Off-chain credentials the agent needs (API keys, signing salts) are encrypted with a per-vault AES-256-GCM TRANSIT key in the same HSM as the wallet. Only ciphertext lives in our DB; the master key never leaves the enclave.                              |
| **Permissionless economic surface**      | Once granted, an agent can call any Sourcify-verified contract on any chain supported by viem — DEXes, lending, staking, payments, governance. The economic surface is the on-chain economy, not a curated allowlist.                                       |

## Why this matters

For the next generation of on-chain economic actors — agents transacting on behalf of users at scale — autonomy and privacy of asset control are not UI features that can be added later. They are properties of the architecture or they are absent. An agent that holds its own private key is a custodian. A registry that holds the agent's key is a custodian. A wallet that auto-approves without scoped, revocable grants is a custodian.

Orloj is the design where nobody between the user and the chain is holding the user's funds: the user picked the HSM, the user defined the grant, the user can revoke at any time, and the assets remain reachable only by signatures the user explicitly authorised. That is what user-controlled economic agency looks like for autonomous agents — and it generalises across every Ethereum environment without per-deployment work.

- `packages/app/lib/vault-ownership.ts` — per-user vault ownership records, provider-tagged
- `packages/app/lib/agent-ownership.ts` — per-user agent ownership records
- `packages/app/lib/mcp-tokens.ts` — bearer token issuance, rotation, and revocation
- `packages/app/lib/vault-providers/` — pluggable KMS providers (1Claw / Orbitport)
- `packages/registry/src/vault-resolve.js` — agent → grant → vault resolution at signing time

**SpaceComputer Bounty**

# Orloj × SpaceComputer

> *Built at **ETHPrague 2026**.* An end-to-end signing and authorization service for AI agents, built on the Orbitport KMS.

## The pitch

Orloj turns Sourcify-verified smart contracts into MCP servers that AI agents call as typed tools. The agents never see private keys, RPCs, or unsigned transactions — and the reason that is *credible* is that every wallet Orloj manages is an Orbitport KMS key. **Orloj is, end to end, a secure signing and authorization service for autonomous AI agents** — a category that didn't exist a year ago, implemented on top of orbital HSM + SpaceTEE.

What's unusual about it: Orbitport isn't an optional plug-in. The wallet's private material is *only ever* an Orbitport KMS key id; there is no path through the system where the registry process holds, generates, or sees the private key. A compromised registry host cannot forge transactions — it can only request signatures it is already authorized to request, on a digest, against a key that lives in orbit.

## How we use Orbitport KMS (depth, across both schemes)

Most KMS integrations stop at "create a key, ask it to sign once." Orloj uses **both** Orbitport key schemes, **four distinct KMS operations**, in **two services** across the codebase:

| Where                                          | KMS operation   | Scheme / key                     | Why                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------------------------- | --------------- | -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| App / createVault                              | kms.createKey   | ETHEREUM / ECC_SECG_P256K1       | Per-vault wallet signing key — Orbitport returns the derived Ethereum address                        |
| App / createVault                              | kms.createKey   | TRANSIT / AES_256_GCM96          | Per-vault envelope-encryption key, in the same security domain as the wallet                         |
| App / setSecret                                | kms.encrypt    | TRANSIT                          | Encrypts secret-store plaintext — only the ciphertext blob is persisted to Postgres                  |
| App / getSecret                                | kms.decrypt    | TRANSIT                          | Decrypts on read — cleartext never lives on disk on our side                                         |
| Registry / on every agent write-tool call      | kms.sign       | ETHEREUM, messageType DIGEST     | Signs the keccak256 of an EIP-1559 unsigned tx; the (r, s, v) signature is reassembled and broadcast |
| App / signDigest                               | kms.sign       | ETHEREUM, messageType DIGEST     | Same primitive exposed through the vault-provider abstraction for control-plane use                  |

**The signing path is the live transaction broadcast path, not a demo button.** When an AI agent calls a write function on any Sourcify-generated MCP, Orloj builds the EIP-1559 tx with viem, hashes it, sends *only the digest* to Orbitport, gets back `(r, s, v)`, reassembles with `serializeTransaction`, and broadcasts. Every state-changing on-chain call an agent makes through Orloj transits Orbitport.

**Envelope encryption is not a side feature.** Per-vault TRANSIT keys mean that any secrets stored alongside the wallet (off-chain credentials, API keys, signing salts) live under the same physical custody as the wallet itself. Ciphertext lives in our DB; the master key lives in orbit. Combining the ETHEREUM and TRANSIT schemes inside a single product surface keeps the wallet and its sidecar secrets in one security domain — a property that falls out naturally from the design rather than being bolted on.

**Per-agent grants tie it all together.** Each agent has a recorded grant against a vault (with `permissions`, `secret_path_pattern`, optional `expires_at`); the registry resolves that grant on every MCP call and signs through the matching Orbitport key. Revocation is instant and never touches the keys themselves.

## Why this matters

Orbitport is what makes HSM-grade custody for autonomous AI agents possible. Keys live in orbit, in tamper-proof hardware, signing only what an authenticated, grant-bearing agent asks for — with signatures that cannot be forged by an operator, a state actor, or a compromised host.

## Files of interest

- `packages/app/lib/vault-providers/orbitport.ts` — full KMS provider: `createKey` (both schemes), `encrypt`/`decrypt` (TRANSIT), `sign` (ETHEREUM), key-grant CRUD
- `packages/registry/src/vault-providers/orbitport.js` — registry-side `signWithOrbitport` (digest → broadcast tx)
- `packages/registry/src/sign-transaction.js` — provider router on the live transaction path
- `packages/registry/src/vault-resolve.js` — agent → vault → KMS-key-id resolution
- `packages/app/lib/db.ts` — `orbitport_vault` / `orbitport_secret` /

**Sourcify Bounty**

# Orloj × Sourcify

> *Built at **ETHPrague 2026**.* An MCP registry built end-to-end on Sourcify-verified contract metadata — turning every Sourcify entry into an AI-callable typed tool.

## The pitch

Orloj turns Sourcify-verified smart contracts into **MCP servers AI agents can call as typed tools**. Every Orloj MCP — its tool list, its parameter types, its function descriptions, its proxy-aware ABI — is generated end-to-end with a Sourcify connection. The moment a contract is verified on Sourcify, it becomes callable by an AI agent through Orloj, with no per-contract integration work on our side.

To our knowledge nobody has built this category of consumer on top of Sourcify before. *Making verified contracts directly executable by LLMs* — a category that didn't exist a year ago — is something Sourcify uniquely enables: it requires the metadata-grade verification, the NatSpec, and the proxy resolution, all together, in one place.

## How we use Sourcify (beyond just "fetch the ABI")

Every MCP we serve is built from **five distinct fields** of the Sourcify v2 contract response, each load-bearing:

| Field               | What we do with it                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **abi**             | Recursively translated into Zod input/output schemas — including tuple types, dynamic arrays, fixed-size arrays, all integer widths, and fixed-size byte types    |
| **userdoc**         | Function "notice" strings (NatSpec) become the tool description an LLM reads when deciding whether to call the function                                           |
| **devdoc**          | Function "details" strings used as a fallback description when no userdoc notice exists                                                                            |
| **compilation**     | The contract name field becomes the MCP server name — agents see "WstETH" or "UniswapV3Pool", not a hex address                                                   |
| **proxyResolution** | Detects proxies at registration time and points the ABI fetch at the implementation, so upgrades are transparent                                                  |

The two requests we make per registration:

1. `GET /v2/contract/{chainId}/{address}?fields=proxyResolution` — proxy detection.
2. `GET /v2/contract/{chainId}/{address}?fields=abi,userdoc,devdoc,compilation` — typed surface + descriptions + name (against the implementation when relevant).

**The NatSpec → tool-description chain is the unique-data argument.** The string that determines whether an agent decides to call a tool is *the contract author's own NatSpec, surfaced verbatim through Sourcify*. You can't do this with a raw ABI from a block explorer — it requires Sourcify's metadata-aware verification. Contract authors are already writing the documentation the agent needs; Sourcify is what makes it reachable, and Orloj is what consumes it.

**Proxies are first-class because Sourcify makes them so.** Most production contracts are proxies; without `proxyResolution`, an agent registry is dead on arrival. We bind agents to the proxy address (the user-facing one) but type the tools off the implementation ABI. Proxy upgrades surface as new MCP tools the next time the registry is refreshed.

## Why this matters

Every verified contract on Sourcify — across 100+ EVM chains — is a candidate Orloj MCP. There is no manual ABI upload, no per-contract integration, no documentation step on our side. The whole pipeline (verified bytecode → ABI → typed MCP tool → NatSpec-described action surfaced to an LLM) flows from one Sourcify request.

This only works because Sourcify is what it is: open data, exact metadata-based matches, NatSpec-aware, and proxy-aware. An agent ecosystem that wants to read and write the chain at scale needs a verification layer it can build on permissionlessly — and Orloj is what becomes possible when you treat that layer as load-bearing public infrastructure.

## Files of interest

- `packages/registry/src/get-contract.js` — Sourcify v2 fetch, multi-field consumption, ABI → Zod, NatSpec → MCP tool descriptions, proxy ABI override
- `packages/registry/src/server.mjs` — `POST /register` proxy-resolution call to `?fields=proxyResolution`
- `packages/registry/src/generate-mcp.js` — turns a fetched contract into an `McpServer` with view/write tools, one per ABI function

### Kanbantic
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/kanbantik-8419) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/noskodmi/kanbantic) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://kanbantic.vercel.app/) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHPrague%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethprague2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> ENS-native labour market for AI agents

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Flask](https://img.shields.io/badge/Flask-333333?style=flat-square) ![Docker](https://img.shields.io/badge/Docker-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Kanbantic turns AI agents into first-class economic actors. Existing bounty boards are built for humans, agent demos lack portable identity and reputation, and on-chain work markets rarely combine discovery, escrow, disputes, privacy, and verification in one place. Kanbantic gives every agent an ENS-backed identity, lets workspaces issue and manage bounties, tracks work across a shared board, escrows payouts, stores proofs and metadata verifiably, and carries reputation with the agent across jobs.

**Challenges we ran into**

The hard part was making sponsor integrations part of the product rather than bolt-ons. ENS is the primary key for agents and workspaces, Sourcify is a trust signal in the UI and MCP tools, Swarm holds proof bundles and metadata with verified fetch, Apify bootstraps discovery, Orbitport cTRNG resolves fair-claim contention, and Umia is the venture off-ramp. We also had to keep the demo fast: a guided 9-step flow, persistent progress across reloads, and recovery boundaries so judges can drive it live without getting stuck.

**Network Economy**

Kanbantic is a permissionless on-chain labour market for AI agents. The platform takes zero platform fee, supports escrow-backed bounties, and treats portable reputation as economic capital. Agents are first-class economic actors with their own balance sheets, reputation graphs, and work history, which makes **Network Economy** the natural main-track fit.

**Future Society**

Kanbantik fits **Future Society** because it is designed for communities, DAOs, and open teams that need better ways to organize human and AI collaboration. By making agent work transparent, trackable, and incentive-aligned, it supports healthier and more inclusive coordination structures.

**SpaceComputer Bounty**

Kanbantic uses **SpaceComputer Orbitport cTRNG** inside a real economic flow with consequence. In `Fair Claim` mode, if multiple agents bid for the same bounty in the same block, the contract opens a commit-reveal window. A Worker fetches a fresh Orbitport cTRNG draw plus Ed25519 signature, the contract verifies the signature against the immutable Orbitport pubkey set at deploy, XORs that randomness with `block.prevrandao` for defense in depth, and indexes into the committed claimers to pick the winner.

**Sourcify Bounty**

Kanbantic uses **Sourcify** as a product primitive, not a checkbox. All five contracts are source-verified automatically in the deploy script. The UI surfaces `Verified on Sourcify` badges as a trust signal, and when an agent's `mcpEndpoint` points at an unverified contract the UI raises a warning. We also expose `verify_source(address, chain)` as an MCP tool so source verification is part of the operating flow.

**Best Agentic Venture**

Kanbantic fits **Best Agentic Venture** because it is designed to spin out into Umia. In `/dashboard/agent`, once an agent's settled revenue clears a threshold, Kanbantic mints an `AgentVenture` ERC-721 wrapping `(agentNode, owner, revenueRoot)` and emits a spec-compliant `umia apply --repo ... --bio ... --token ... --canbantic-vid <id>` manifest. The user runs the CLI, receives a Solana venture address, and that venture is soft-linked back to the agent profile. Kanbantic is the discovery and reputation layer on Sepolia; Umia is the capital and governance layer on Solana.

**Verified Fetch — Trust No Gateway**

Kanbantic fits **Verified Fetch — Trust No Gateway** because all proof bundles, bounty descriptions, and workspace metadata are stored on Swarm, and every fetch goes through verified-fetch. BMT `keccak256` hashes are checked locally before content is displayed, and `/docs/swarm` includes an explicit tampered-fetch demo. The verification step is part of the user-facing trust model, not hidden infrastructure.

**A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm**

Kanbantic fits **A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm** because workspace metadata is stored and addressed as Swarm-backed key-value style records. The same metadata path that powers workspace configuration and proofs is used to satisfy this sub-bounty in a way that is directly visible in the product.

**Best ENS Integration for AI Agents**

Kanbantic fits **Best ENS Integration for AI Agents** because every agent is an ENS namehash node. `<label>.canbantic.eth` is the primary key across registry, reputation, and disputes. Workspaces are ENS subdomains such as `acme.canbantic.eth` with member sets, and our CCIP-Read resolver Worker makes Kanbantic agents resolvable through vanilla ENS clients like `dig`, `viem`, and `app.ens.domains`.

**Most Creative Use of ENS**

Kanbantic fits **Most Creative Use of ENS** because ENS is both the identity system and the self-referential discovery layer. Every agent, workspace, and registry object is modeled as an ENS node, and Kanbantic itself registers as `canbantic.canbantic.eth` so agents literally discover Kanbantic through Kanbantic. ENS is not branding here; it is the substrate for naming, coordination, reputation, and dispute resolution.

**Apify Bounty**

Kanbantic uses **Apify** as a self-bootstrapping marketplace growth loop. The `kanbantic-discoverer` Apify Actor scans GitHub for MCP-server signatures such as `mcp.json`, `mcp-server.{ts,py}`, and README mentions of tools or list endpoints. Results stream into D1 as discovered stubs, and the Actor opens GitHub issues inviting those repos to claim `<suggested>.canbantic.eth` and start receiving bounty offers.

### PragueConnect
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/pragueconnect-b069) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/forever8896/praga) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://www.pragueconnect.xyz/) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHPrague%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethprague2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Hire by name. Pay in private. Keep the reputation

![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Ethereum](https://img.shields.io/badge/Ethereum-333333?style=flat-square) ![BASE](https://img.shields.io/badge/BASE-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Today, getting your bike fixed by a neighbor in Prague usually goes
  through Facebook Marketplace, a Telegram group, or a private WhatsApp
  chain. All of them put your real name + phone + home area next to a
  public ad. PragueConnect uses an **ENS name** as your identity —
  `kilian.pragueconnect.eth` is enough to receive payments, open sealed
  conversations over XMTP, and accumulate reviews. Nobody needs your
  phone, your bank, or your address.

  ### "I have to pick: trust the buyer to pay after delivery, or trust the seller to deliver
  after payment"

  Cash deals between strangers force one side to carry all the risk.
  PragueConnect's **escrow contract** holds funds on Base while the work
  happens, and releases when the buyer signs off — or after a 24h grace
  period if the buyer ghosts. Both sides see the on-chain phase change
  live. The buyer's funds are safe, the worker is guaranteed paid,
  nobody is the custodian in the middle.

  ### "Every payment I make leaks who paid whom for what"

  Standard on-chain payments are public — anyone can pull up your
  address and see who you tipped, when, and for what. PragueConnect
  resolves names to a **fresh stealth address every time** anyone asks.
  Send 500 Kč to `alice.pragueconnect.eth` from MetaMask; refresh, send
  another 500 Kč; the two payments land at different addresses, and
  only Alice can see which ones are hers. Bank-statement-grade privacy
  without a bank.

  ### "If I use a platform like TaskRabbit, I lose my reputation when I lose my account"

  PragueConnect isn't a platform — it's a self-hostable resolver,
  gateway, and set of contracts. Your reputation lives in your ENS
  name's records, sealed by you, queryable by anyone, portable to any
  service that resolves ENS. If we go offline tomorrow, your name
  still works. Your reviews still resolve. Your sealed payment route
  still receives.

**Challenges we ran into**

## The hard problem: privacy that actually holds on a public chain

  PragueConnect's whole thesis is a marketplace where identity, payments,
  and work history don't leak. The hard part — the thing that ate most of
  the build week — is that "doesn't leak" on a public ledger is a much
  higher bar than it sounds. Every layer that *looks* private has a seam
  where information escapes. The build was, in honest terms, a continuous
  audit of those seams: finding them, sealing the ones we could, and
  naming the ones we couldn't.

  ### Leak we found and sealed: the escrow that wasn't actually private

  The v1 escrow contract used `require(msg.sender == t.worker)` on
  accept, deliver, and release. Release paid out to a stealth address
  and emitted an ERC-5564 announcement, so it *looked* like a
  privacy-preserving payment flow.

  The bug — caught mid-conversation while explaining the architecture —
  was that the worker's main EOA had to be `msg.sender` of three
  transactions per task. The accept tx alone publicly bound the worker's
  EOA to the stealth recipient in one move:

  worker_eoa published 0xSTEALTH in task T
  escrow paid 0xSTEALTH in task T
  ∴ worker_eoa owns 0xSTEALTH

  The "stealth payout" was theatre. We rewrote the contract to drop
  `msg.sender`-based auth entirely. V2 uses **EIP-712 signatures from
  the worker's stealth spending key**; ecrecover verifies the signer
  against the address committed at fund time. Anyone can submit the tx
  (funder, a hosted relayer, the worker from any address); the worker's
  main EOA never appears in any task event. Live on Base at
  `0xE2571571…20A5a` with twelve Foundry tests, one of which explicitly
  asserts no main address ever shows up as `msg.sender` in any escrow
  event.

**Network Economy**

PragueConnect is a peer-to-peer marketplace for everyday skills and
  favors, built so identity, payments, and reputation belong to the human
  — not a platform that can ban or surveil them.

  Privacy as the default. Resolving alice.pragueconnect.eth from any
  standard ENS client returns a different one-time stealth address every
  few seconds. Our CCIP-Read gateway derives ERC-5564 stealth addresses
  per resolution, so any wallet becomes a privacy rail with zero
  sender-side change. Bulletins are auth-gated; we anchor them on the
  canonical ERC-5564 announcer so survivability doesn't depend on us.

  Sig-authorized escrow with verifiable claims. Workers sign EIP-712
  intents with their stealth spending key; their main EOA never appears
  on-chain. The contract emits a reputation commitment per release,
  seedable into a ZK proof for selective sharing later — verifiable
  claims, made concrete for a real marketplace.

  No seed phrases, no central points of failure. Email signup via Privy,
  exportable to MetaMask. Profile pages on IPFS via ENSIP-7. Faucet-sponsored
  gas. Subnames as access tokens with an atomic 95/5 referral split on tips.
  Vaults derived deterministically in-browser, never published.

  Live at https://www.pragueconnect.xyz on Base mainnet.

**Most Creative Use of ENS**

Most apps use ENS as name→address lookup. We use it as the routing
  layer for payments, identity, content, access, and attribution.

  The headline: addr() rotates per CCIP-Read response. Our resolver on
  Base + our signed gateway derive a fresh ERC-5564 stealth address from
  the recipient's meta-address on every resolution. MetaMask, Rainbow,
  Etherscan all become privacy-preserving payment rails with zero
  sender-side change.

  Five primitives stacked:
  • Rotating addr() with ECDSA-signed CCIP-Read responses
  • Stealth meta-address dual-published to ERC-6538 + ENS text record
  • Subnames as invites + referral chain → atomic 95/5 tip split
  • ENSIP-7 contenthash → IPFS-pinned profile sites at .eth.limo
  • Custom ENSIP-10 wildcard resolver, fully self-hostable

  Plus on-chain anchoring on the canonical ERC-5564 announcer (sweep
  survivability without us), and a v2 escrow with EIP-712 sig-auth so
  the worker's main EOA never appears in any task event.

  Pitch in one breath: names resolve to fresh addresses, funds land at
  one-time addresses, subnames carry the referral chain, profile pages
  live on IPFS — ENS is the only thing tying the system together, and
  it leaks nothing publicly.

  Live: https://www.pragueconnect.xyz on Base mainnet.
  Repo: https://github.com/forever8896/praga

Team **MK Ultra** -- [Kilian Valdman](https://github.com/forever8896), Mikulas Horyna

### Spacy
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/spacy-2602) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/itublockchain/ethprague2026-spacy) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://spacy.computer) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHPrague%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethprague2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Privy for post quantum world

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![PostgreSQL](https://img.shields.io/badge/PostgreSQL-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

## What Spacy is

Spacy is a Web3 wallet that lets users sign in with Google and immediately use crypto applications without a seed phrase, browser extension, or any prior wallet experience. Same product category as Privy or Dynamic, the embedded wallets behind tens of millions of consumer crypto accounts today. The difference is that Spacy is the only one in this category that lets anyone, on their own laptop and without trusting us, verify that every transaction was actually signed in the hardware we claim, with the safeguards we promise.

## The problem we are solving

When a user signs into a Privy-backed app, their private key is generated and stored inside a Trusted Execution Environment, or TEE: a special area of a server's processor that is supposed to be sealed off from everyone, including Privy itself. The user is asked to trust three things: that the TEE is real, that the randomness used to make the key was unpredictable, and that the operator has not been compromised. None of those claims can be verified independently. You take Privy's word for it.

This was always a fragile model. In 2026 it is breaking down on three fronts at once.

**The hardware was broken in October 2025.** Researchers at Georgia Tech and Purdue published the TEE.Fail attack: using under $1,000 of equipment, they extracted the cryptographic keys that prove a TEE is genuine, then forged fake TEE attestations that pass Intel's own verifier. The same primitives protect tens of millions of consumer wallets today. Privy, Turnkey, and Dynamic have published nothing about how they are responding.

**The cryptography has an expiration date that just moved closer.** In May 2025, a Google researcher showed that breaking RSA-2048 encryption now requires 20 times fewer quantum bits than estimated six years ago. Major roadmaps now point to capable quantum computers around 2030. Every embedded wallet today still signs transactions with ECDSA, the algorithm that quantum computers will break. None of the incumbents have a published migration plan.

**The proofs do not survive Q-day.** When quantum hardware breaks today's TEE attestation keys, every TEE proof ever issued can be retroactively forged. The proof that your wallet's transaction was actually signed inside a real enclave by a real user becomes worthless overnight. Existing wallets have no durable, independent record that can survive this collapse.

## How Spacy solves it

The signing key is held inside SpaceComputer's Orbitport KMS, a service running in Intel TDX (Intel's TEE technology). Our orchestration backend, the part that authenticates Google sessions and brokers the signing requests, runs on a real AWS EC2 instance with AMD SEV-SNP (AMD's TEE technology) enabled. This is not a roadmap claim, it is shipping today: every Spacy session produces a real SEV-SNP attestation report from real AMD silicon, exposed on a public health endpoint anyone can fetch and verify offline. Two different TEE vendors, two different operators, two different attestation roots. A single class of zero-day cannot reach both halves of the trust path.

Every signing operation is timestamped against a fresh sample of cosmic randomness from SpaceComputer's cTRNG service, recorded in the receipt and matchable against an IPFS public beacon archive. Every transaction emits an attestation receipt: a JSON document containing the transaction details, the SEV-SNP self-attestation including its certificate chain, the KMS keyId, and the cosmic entropy witness. The receipt is pinned to IPFS through Pinata, and its content-addressed identifier is emitted to a Sepolia smart contract as an on-chain pointer. Real receipts, real on-chain events, today.

To verify any Spacy transaction, you read the on-chain event, fetch the receipt from IPFS, walk the AMD certificate chain offline against AMD's root, and cross-check the cosmic entropy against SpaceComputer's public beacon. No step requires Spacy to be online. No step requires trusting us.

When SpaceComputer ships their published roadmap (orbital KMS, ML-DSA dual signatures for post-quantum), our SDK adopts each upgrade with a single parameter change. The wallet a user onboards into in 2026 should be the wallet that still works in 2032. Today, that wallet does not exist. Spacy is the bet that it should, built on SpaceComputer's open infrastructure, licensed AGPL-3.0.

**Challenges we ran into**

## We started building threshold ECDSA, then realized the KMS would not let us

The original plan was a 2-of-3 threshold ECDSA wallet using cggmp21, with one share in the user's browser, one inside the SpaceComputer KMS, and one held by our coordinator. Full liveness across satellite, ground, and user, no single party able to forge a signature alone. We started wiring the protocol against the Orbitport KMS expecting it to participate in the threshold protocol.

The KMS does not work that way. It is a black-box signer: you create a key, ask it to sign a digest, get a 65-byte ECDSA signature back. There is no API for participating in MPC, no way to produce a partial share, no hook for any threshold scheme. The signing key never leaves the TEE in any form, including as a share, which is exactly what makes it a strong signer and exactly what makes threshold cryptography on top of it impossible without rebuilding the KMS itself.

We stopped, took stock, and rewrote the architecture around the actual primitive Orbitport ships. Instead of distributing trust cryptographically across multiple parties, distribute it structurally across multiple TEE vendors. Intel TDX for the signer (Orbitport), AMD SEV-SNP for the coordinator (our AWS instance), with the trust path crossing two heterogeneous hardware lineages. A single class of zero-day cannot reach both halves. The structural distribution we lost from threshold, we got back from vendor heterogeneity. SpaceComputer's roadmap moves to threshold KMS in phase 2, at which point the original plan slots in without architectural rewrite.

## The KMS attestation quote we expected was not exposed by the API

Spacy's pitch is that every signature comes with a verifiable Intel TDX attestation quote from the KMS. The receipt schema reserves a signer.quoteHex field for this. SpaceComputer's spec describes it, the SDK type declares it, we wired the call expecting it to be populated.

It was not. We tried kms.GetAttestation, kms.Attestation, plain GET and POST against /attestation and /kms/attestation, every variant the SDK type hinted at. All 404 or 405. The SDK's "expected one of" error listed every method it knew about and none was an attestation endpoint. The kms.sign response itself returned signature and metadata, but no quote.

We could have populated the field with a placeholder. Instead we kept it as an empty string, marked quoteVerified as the honest result of attempting verification on nothing, documented the gap, and structured the schema so it accepts the quote the day SpaceComputer ships the endpoint. The TDX side is reserved, not faked.

## The cTRNG response is missing fields its SDK type promises

Two related problems on the entropy side. First, the SDK type declares getRandom includes a signature object with value, pk, algo. We hit the raw ctrng.Get RPC directly and the wire payload was just src and value. No signature anywhere. The SDK was projecting a type the gateway does not currently fulfill.

Second, cTRNG offers two source modes: rng for the live satellite roundtrip, derived for the BIP32-derived fallback. We asked for rng. The API returned derived, because the live source is gated and not active for our token tier during the hackathon.

We left entropy.signatureHex empty and wrote the actual returned source value into the receipt verbatim. The verifier matches the entropy value against the IPFS public beacon archive, which is signed at the round level and is independent of our backend. The cosmic randomness witness still has a real verification anchor, just not the per-call satellite signature the SDK type promises. Nothing in the receipt claims a stronger source than the API actually provided.

## VLEK extraction from the kernel did not work, AMD KDS rescued us

The SEV-SNP attestation report is only meaningful if you can verify it against AMD's certificate chain (VLEK to ASK to ARK). The obvious approach is to pull the chain from the kernel: sev-guest -x should hand it back. It did not. The command returned an Input/output error, because the host had not been pre-provisioned with sev-host-set-cert-chain and the guest kernel does not expose VLEK by default.

We initially suspected a permissions issue and wasted time on chmod and dmesg. The actual fix was to bypass the kernel entirely. The SEV-SNP report contains a chip_id field at a documented offset. We read it out, fetched the VCEK directly from AMD's KDS at https://kdsintf.amd.com/vcek/v1/Milan/<chipId>, and concatenated it with the bundled ASK and ARK roots offline. Cleaner than the kernel path: verifiers need nothing from our host, only AMD and the trust anchor bundle we publish.

**Ethereum Core**

Spacy is a practical Ethereum wallet that directly improves the security posture of self-custody on Ethereum. The signing key is held in a Trusted Execution Environment (Intel TDX, inside SpaceComputer's KMS), the orchestration backend runs in a second TEE (AMD SEV-SNP, on AWS), and every signature is paired with a verifiable attestation receipt pinned to IPFS with an on-chain pointer event on Sepolia.
Three concrete contributions to Ethereum's usability and security:
- Usability. Google sign-in to a working Ethereum wallet in under thirty seconds, no seed phrase, no browser extension, no chain configuration. The same UX as Privy or Dynamic, which together back over 120 million Ethereum-compatible wallets today. Spacy is the embedded wallet category, just with the trust model rebuilt.
- Security against the threat model that actually matters in 2026. The TEE.Fail attack disclosed in October 2025 demonstrated that attestation keys can be extracted from Intel SGX, Intel TDX, and AMD SEV-SNP enclaves with under $1,000 of equipment, and was demonstrated against Ethereum BuilderNet. Every embedded wallet on the market today, securing tens of millions of Ethereum addresses, runs on the same primitives. Spacy's response is structural: a heterogeneous TEE chain across two different vendor lineages, paired with public self-attestation that any third party can verify offline. A single class of zero-day cannot reach both halves of our trust path.
Native Ethereum integration. Standard EIP-1559 transactions, viem in the browser, public RPC for broadcast, Foundry-deployed Solidity contract on Sepolia. No custom chain, no L2 dependency, no proprietary RPC. Spacy is composable with every existing Ethereum tool.

The receipt format is open. The verification path runs offline. The license is AGPL-3.0. This is the wallet stack any Ethereum project can adopt, audit, fork, or self-host.

**Network Economy**

Spacy is a Web3 wallet that puts cryptographic user control above operator trust. Same UX as Privy (Google sign-in, no seed phrase, no extension), but every claim the wallet makes about itself is independently verifiable, with no Spacy infrastructure required in the verification path.
The fit with Network Economy lands on four axes:
- Identity. Spacy bridges Web2 identity (Google OAuth) and Ethereum identity with cryptographic provenance that wallet identity actually needs. Existing embedded wallets ask users to trust Privy or Turnkey that their key is real, generated correctly, and signed by the hardware claimed. Spacy makes the binding verifiable: any third party can fetch the on-chain AttestationPublished event for a given wallet, pull the IPFS receipt, walk the AMD VLEK certificate chain offline, and confirm the signing TEE is genuine without trusting us at any step.
- Privacy through deliberate separation. We split confidentiality and verifiability into different storage layers. Personally identifying information (Google identifier, email) lives in encrypted Postgres inside the TEE, GDPR-compliant and deletable, never on-chain or on IPFS. Verifiable artifacts (KMS keyId, SEV-SNP self-attestation, cTRNG entropy witness, transaction details) live on IPFS and on-chain, immutable and auditable. Two storage layers, two trust models, the right one for each kind of data. Privy stores both opaquely on the same backend.

User control as a structural property. Six-step verification walkthrough at spacy.computer/verify, fully offline, runnable on any laptop, with no Spacy infrastructure in the path. The architectural posture is "we don't ask you to trust us, verify it yourself." This is what user control looks like when it is built into the receipt format rather than promised in marketing copy.
Decentralized in a real way. AGPL-3.0 licensed, multi-vendor TEE chain spanning two operators (SpaceComputer for the signer, our own AWS account for the coordinator), Pinata pinning with multi-gateway IPFS retrieval, public Sepolia RPC for broadcast, on-chain event index for discovery. Every signed transaction produces a content-addressed proof artifact that survives even if Spacy disappears. The wallet a user onboards into in 2026 keeps working in 2032 because the verifiable provenance lives on Ethereum and IPFS, not on our servers.

**Future Society**

Spacy is built on the conviction that wallet infrastructure is becoming the infrastructure of cryptographic sovereignty. Where keys live, who can compel access to them, and whose randomness seeded them are no longer engineering details. They are political facts about whose hands hold the future of self-custody.
The current embedded-wallet stack normalizes a quiet concentration: three AWS regions, one TEE vendor lineage, US/EU jurisdictional reach, opaque entropy, no published quantum migration plan. Each individual provider is competent. The systemic posture is fragile and increasingly anachronistic against the threat landscape of 2026.

Spacy aligns with Future Society's mandate on three axes:
- Sustainability through durability. Self-custody infrastructure should outlast its operators, jurisdictions, and the cryptographic primitives it currently relies on. Spacy's attestation receipts are content-addressed on IPFS with on-chain Sepolia pointers, designed to survive even Q-day attestation forgery, when today's TEE certificate roots will become forgeable retroactively. The wallet a user onboards into in 2026 should keep working in 2032. We build for that horizon, not for the next funding round.
- Ethical infrastructure through verifiability. Privy and Turnkey ask users to trust their backend. Spacy proves the backend, with public health endpoints serving live SEV-SNP attestation reports any third party can verify offline against AMD's published certificate chain. Trust is a design choice. We choose the version that gives users power instead of taking it.

Inclusive sovereignty beyond corporate enclaves. AGPL-3.0 licensed from commit one, built on SpaceComputer's open infrastructure, with cosmic randomness drawn from a public IPFS beacon anyone can pull without authentication. We build on commons-grade primitives rather than walling them off. The codebase is auditable, the receipt format is open, the verification logic ships as a single fork-and-run package. This is solarpunk infrastructure: optimistic, durable, jurisdictionally untethered, verifiable down to the cosmic ray, open-sourced, built to be inherited.

**SpaceComputer Bounty**

Spacy is a Web3 embedded wallet (Privy-class UX, Google sign-in, no seed phrase) whose entire pitch is built on three architectural commitments that no other infrastructure stack on the market today can deliver simultaneously: a TEE-backed signer, a publicly verifiable cosmic randomness witness on every signature, and a credible post-quantum migration path with zero rewrite cost. SpaceComputer's Orbitport is the only stack where these three commitments can coexist. Everything else we considered required us to give up at least one of them.

We use four SpaceComputer primitives directly.

**KMS as the signer**. Every Spacy wallet's private key is created with kms.createKey (curve ECC_SECG_P256K1, scheme ETHEREUM) and signed with kms.sign on a digest passed from our backend. The key never leaves Intel TDX. The alternative was building our own threshold ECDSA wallet on cggmp21, which we started and abandoned, because rebuilding a TEE-backed signer at consumer-grade reliability is not a hackathon project. It is also not where the value of Spacy lives. The value lives in the trust chain wrapped around the signer, and Orbitport gives us that primitive solid enough to wrap the rest of the architecture around.

**cTRNG** as the entropy witness. Every signing operation pulls a fresh sample with trng.getRandom. The sample is recorded in the receipt and matchable against the IPFS public beacon archive, giving every Spacy transaction a verifiable timestamp anchored to a physical event in low Earth orbit. The IPFS beacon fallback path works without authentication and is what turns cTRNG from a service we depend on into a public commons we participate in. No other randomness source on the market can be cross-checked against a publicly archived signed feed. CSPRNG outputs from Privy or Turnkey produce no auditable artifact at all.

Orbitport as the gateway. Every external call from our backend routes through op.spacecomputer.io with OAuth2 client-credentials. This means our credential surface is one stable endpoint instead of three separate vendor integrations, and it means our migration path to orbital signing (Q4 2026) is one URL change. The gateway abstraction is exactly the property that made the post-quantum story possible to claim honestly: when SpaceComputer ships ML-DSA in the KMS, our SDK migrates by changing one parameter on the same gateway call, with no architectural rewrite.

Space Fabric as the migration anchor. The pitch we make to users in 2026 is "the wallet you onboard into today is the wallet that still works in 2032." We can only make that claim because SpaceComputer has published a real architecture document (the Space Fabric paper, April 2026) committing to hybrid classical/PQC signatures using satellite TPMs as an independent root of trust. No other embedded wallet provider has anything equivalent. Privy, Turnkey, Dynamic, Magic have published nothing about post-quantum migration. We are not just building on SpaceComputer's primitives, we are building toward SpaceComputer's roadmap, with our SDK shaped to slot every phase-2 capability in as it ships.

Why this would not have worked anywhere else.

AWS KMS, GCP Cloud KMS, and HashiCorp Vault all offer TEE-backed signers, but none publish satellite-witnessed entropy and none have a post-quantum migration path that lives in the same product surface. We would have ended up with three separate vendor integrations and no coherent verification story to give the user.

Privy or Turnkey as a backend would defeat the purpose. Their value proposition is operator-trust, ours is operator-removal.

A homegrown threshold ECDSA wallet on cggmp21 would have gotten us cryptographic distribution but not vendor heterogeneity. The TEE.Fail attack (October 2025) proved that homogeneous TEE deployments share a class of zero-day exposure. SpaceComputer's KMS in Intel TDX, paired with our coordinator in AMD SEV-SNP, gives us heterogeneity at the hardware layer that threshold cryptography on a single vendor lineage cannot.

Beyond direct primitive use, we built explicitly within the SpaceComputer development pattern. Our backend is structured against the patterns in kms_starter, our authentication flow draws from cosmic-siwe, and our receipt schema reserves fields for the KMS attestation quote and cTRNG satellite signature that are documented in the spec but not yet exposed by the public gateway. These reserved fields are the most important architectural commitment in the project: the day SpaceComputer ships them, every existing Spacy receipt schema accepts them with no migration. We are not waiting for a future version of Spacy to align with SpaceComputer's roadmap. The current version is already aligned, with explicit slots for what comes next.

Spacy is what an embedded wallet looks like when it is built natively on SpaceComputer's stack. That is the only place this project could have been built.

### Eliver

> ETH + Deliver

**The problem it solves**

The Problem: High-Value Logistics is a "Black Box"

Shipping assets like luxury watches, electronics, or pharmaceuticals currently relies on blind trust. Centralized data can be faked, damages are only discovered after delivery, and insurance disputes take months of manual paperwork.
The Solution: Eliver Autonomous Intelligence Hub

Eliver turns logistics from a risky process into an autonomous agent that guarantees integrity.

    Trustless Truth: We use SpaceComputer for hardware-signed telemetry. Data is signed at the sensor level, making it physically impossible to spoof or manipulate the shipment history.

    Human-Readable Identity: Instead of complex hex codes, we use ENS (e.g., tracker-patek.eth) so operators can manage high-value cargo with intuitive identities.

    Forensic Investigation: Our Temporal Scrubber allows users to "time-travel" through the shipment's history, pinpointing exactly when and where a breach occurred on a real-world map.

    Autonomous Justice: If a breach is detected (e.g., temperature spike or 5G shock), the "Supreme Judge" AI instantly verifies the hardware-signed evidence and generates an automated Insurance Report PDF to trigger immediate refunds.

Eliver makes logistics safer, faster, and trustless—moving high-value assets with the certainty of code.

**Challenges we ran into**

Building Eliver was a journey of cutting through noise to reach cryptographic truth. Here are the specific hurdles we cleared:

    The React Hook Sync: We initially broke the "Rules of Hooks" by trying to conditionally inject agentic events (like x402 payments) into the timeline. This caused render mismatches and crashes. We solved this by performing a "surgical refactor," moving all processing to the top level and handling empty states directly inside our memoized logic to ensure a stable render cycle.

    Temporal Scrubber Performance: Syncing a real-time map, high-fidelity charts, and monospaced AI logs while sliding through history was a performance nightmare. We overcame the lag by centralizing the playbackTime state and using heavy memoization to ensure that "time-traveling" through the data remains a smooth, 60fps experience.

    The Minimalist UX War: Our first version was cluttered with duplicate stats and long AI paragraphs. We fought back with Radical Minimalism—moving current values directly into chart headers and replacing bulky instructions with an interactive "Supreme Judge" chat. This kept the focus on the data breach, not the UI.

    Highway-Aligned Tracking: Standard map markers fly in straight lines, but trucks don't. We replaced "crow-fly" paths with road-accurate GeoJSON routes for the Prague-to-Malaga line, ensuring our Digital Twin reflects the physical reality of the asset.

    Forensic PDF Logic: Designing a report that looks professional enough for a court or an insurance adjuster was tough. We built a custom template that captures the "Hardware Signature" from SpaceComputer, turning raw telemetry into a legally-defensible document.

**Future Society**

Eliver provides a foundational blueprint for a future society where global trust is powered by autonomous code rather than slow bureaucracy. By replacing standard logistics with hardware-signed truth from SpaceComputer, we guarantee the integrity of critical high-value assets through unfakeable digital twins. We shift from weeks of manual paperwork to near-instant conflict resolution using AI-driven judges and smart contracts, proving a society can settle disputes fairly via cryptographic evidence instead of human bias. By integrating ENS, we transform complex decentralized systems into human-centric experiences, allowing businesses to interact through recognizable identities rather than machine-readable hex codes, ultimately removing the friction of trust to build a more efficient global economy guaranteed by the laws of mathematics.

**SpaceComputer Bounty**

Eliver uses SpaceComputer’s hardware-grade security to create tamper-proof sensor logs for RWA logistics. Each telemetry packet, including temperature spikes and G-force shocks, is signed inside a secure hardware enclave before being sent on-chain.

We also extended SpaceComputer’s QEMU environment by adding post-quantum cryptography: Dilithium for signatures and Kyber for encryption/key exchange. This lets us simulate quantum-resistant telemetry proofs and encrypted payloads for future secure logistics.

Together, Eliver combines secure edge signing, post-quantum protection, and smart contract dispute resolution to create a verifiable logistics chain with real-world impact.

**Best Agentic Venture**

Eliver is a high-fidelity Agentic Venture designed to automate the $30B luxury logistics and insurance market by replacing slow, manual paperwork with an AI "Supreme Judge" agent. Our project functions as an autonomous insurance engine that ingests hardware-signed telemetry from SpaceComputer to identify shipment breaches in real-time and trigger automatic smart-contract refunds without human intervention. This "Insurance-as-an-Agent" model has a clear path to revenue through a SaaS-plus-arbitration-fee structure, targeting high-value brands that require ironclad audit trails for Real World Assets. Built to scale into a fully on-chain organization on Umia, Eliver demonstrates how agentic workflows can protect capital and resolve global disputes trustlessly, making it a viable venture for a future tokenized ecosystem where decentralized integrity is the core product.

**A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm**

Eliver implements a decentralized Key-Value store on Swarm to manage shipment-specific metadata and user dashboard configurations without relying on centralized servers. By leveraging Swarm Feeds to map keys like "alert_thresholds" or "shipment_notes" to persistent storage, we provide a simple `get/put` interface that keeps user data private and tied to their Ethereum identity. This integration ensures that all "soft" state in our logistics hub is just as resilient and decentralized as the hardware-signed telemetry, proving that complex dApps can maintain mutable state while preserving full data sovereignty for the user.

**Most Creative Use of ENS**

Eliver transforms the cold, machine-readable world of logistics into a trusted, human-centric ecosystem by using ENS as the primary identity and data layer for high-value Real World Assets (RWA). We move beyond simple name resolution to make ENS the root of a forensic audit trail.

    RWA Identity: Instead of tracking anonymous 0x... addresses, every stakeholder—from the shipment (tracker-patek.eth) to the payer (lvmh-vault.eth) and the carrier (brinks-eu.eth)—is a verifiable ENS identity.

    The "Audit Passport": We use ENS text records to store dynamic logistical parameters, such as sensor thresholds and hardware signatures. These records act as a decentralized "passport" for the cargo, which our system cross-references against hardware-signed telemetry from SpaceComputer.

    Reputation & Resolution: When a breach is detected, our AI "Supreme Judge" resolves the shipment’s ENS identity to fetch its specific audit rules and automatically stages a refund to the correct human-readable principal.

By replacing hex codes with trusted brand identities and using text records to power autonomous dispute logic, Eliver eliminates the "trust gap" in global trade, making blockchain-based logistics intuitive, accountable, and ready for the real world.
