### OPM
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/opm-c347) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/dhananjaypai08/opm) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://opm-sec.vercel.app/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://www.loom.com/share/9d3ded933558492fa7503d6fe26749b5) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHMumbai%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethmumbai2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-3-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> On-chain security layer for npm

![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![ink](https://img.shields.io/badge/ink-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

**OPM secures your npm workflow by running AI security scans, verifying package integrity on-chain, and analyzing dependency graphs before any code reaches your node_modules**

---

### What it solves

The npm ecosystem runs on trust that often goes unchecked. A single **npm install** can pull in hundreds or thousands of transitive dependencies. Developers usually have no clear way to know whether one of those packages contains malware, a typosquatted name, or a known vulnerability.

Recent supply chain incidents show how dangerous this model is. Wallet drainers, credential stealers, and prototype pollution exploits have all been distributed through packages that looked legitimate at first glance. These attacks have already caused millions in losses and continue to target both Web2 and Web3 developers.

OPM introduces a safety layer in front of the install process. Instead of trusting every dependency blindly, packages are analyzed and verified before they are allowed into a project.

---

### What you can use it for

* **opm install**
A drop-in replacement for npm install. Every package is scanned before installation using AI security agents, vulnerability databases, and blocklists such as ChainPatrol. If a version is unsafe, OPM recommends or installs the safest available alternative.

* **opm check**
Scans your entire dependency tree including transitive dependencies. Multiple AI agents analyze packages in parallel for typosquats, malicious code patterns, and known CVEs. Results are aggregated and anchored to a Merkle root so the analysis can be verified later.

* **opm fix**
Automatically updates vulnerable or suspicious dependencies in package.json. If a package has a safer version or trusted alternative, OPM suggests and applies the fix.

* **opm push**
Publishes your package to npm while also registering its checksum and metadata on-chain. The publish step includes a multi-agent security scan and optional ENS-linked identity so consumers can verify who published the package and what security checks it passed.

* **opm audit**
  Performs a deeper security audit of your project. Dependencies are checked against on-chain risk scores, ChainPatrol blocklists, and the OSV vulnerability database.

---

### How it makes things safer

| Without OPM                                                  | With OPM                                                                                |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `npm install` trusts packages by default                     | Packages are checked against vulnerability databases and security scores before install |
| Transitive dependencies are hard to inspect                  | Full dependency graph with risk propagation and verifiable Merkle roots                 |
| Supply chain attacks are often discovered after installation | AI agents and rule-based scanners detect threats before code enters the project         |
| Maintainer identity is only an npm username                  | Optional ENS-linked identities and signed metadata                                      |
| Security audits are static reports                           | Audit results stored on decentralized storage and linked to package records             |
| No verification of how scans were produced                   | Multi-agent analysis with cryptographic integrity for results                           |

---

### Who it's for

* **Developers using npm**
  `opm install` and `opm check` work with existing Node.js projects and require no blockchain knowledge.

* **Package maintainers**
  `opm push` provides verifiable package metadata, identity linking, and security attestations.

* **Security teams**
  Dependency graph scanning and risk propagation highlight vulnerabilities buried deep inside dependency trees.

* **Web3 builders**
  ENS-linked identities, on-chain package records, and verifiable dependency graphs help build more trustworthy software supply chains.

**Challenges we ran into**

Agent onboarding :
How do we onboard agents without verifying? Use labelled datasets without revealing the data itself

Reasoning Model API Constraints
OpenAI's reasoning models (o4-mini) reject temperature and response_format parameters that work fine with standard chat models. The scanner had to detect reasoning models at runtime and strip unsupported parameters from the request body, or every scan with a mixed model pool would fail.

**Privacy**

OPM addresses the #1 threat vector in modern software: npm supply chain attacks. It scans every dependency (direct and transitive) for typosquats, known CVEs, and malicious patterns using multiple AI agents. Packages are verified on-chain with signed checksums. The full dependency tree is cryptographically committed via a Merkle root. New scanning agents must pass **ZK-verified benchmarks** before they can participate. Every audit report is stored immutably on IPFS. The result: no package reaches node_modules without verifiable proof it's safe

**AI**

### 1. Multi-Agent Security Scanning

Every opm push, opm check, and opm fix command runs multiple AI agents in parallel. Each agent analyzes the package source code, version history, dependency list, and CVE data, then returns a structured report with a risk score (0–100), vulnerabilities, supply chain indicators (install scripts, eval usage, network calls, environment access), and a recommendation (SAFE, CAUTION, WARN, BLOCK).

Agents use different LLM models such as GPT-5.4, o4-mini, and community models to avoid single-model blind spots. Results are combined using intelligence-weighted scoring based on benchmark performance in coding and reasoning tasks.

---

### 2. Permissionless Agent Registration with ZK Verification

Anyone can register an AI agent using opm register-agent. Before registration, the agent must pass 10 labeled security test cases covering typosquats, CVEs, obfuscated malware, and safe packages, achieving 100 percent accuracy.

Accuracy is verified with a zero-knowledge proof built using Circom and snarkjs. The circuit computes the accuracy from the agent’s responses and expected labels and generates a proof that accuracy equals 100 percent without revealing the test data. The proof is verified on-chain during registration, and only verified agents can submit scores to the OPM contract.

---

### 3. AI-Powered Dependency Analysis in opm check

When opm check runs, a fast rule-based scan first queries OSV vulnerabilities, checks typosquats, and reads on-chain risk scores across all dependencies. AI agents then analyze the direct dependency list and full dependency tree.

Each agent returns flagged issues, severity levels, recommended replacements, and an overall risk assessment. If two or more agents flag the same package, opm fix can automatically update package.json with a safer version or replacement.

---

### 4. Structured Output and Response Normalization

Each AI agent returns JSON following a strict schema defined in CHECK_SYSTEM_PROMPT. Since LLM providers often return slightly different formats such as different field names or severity labels, OPM includes a normalization layer that validates and converts every response into a consistent AgentScanResult structure before scoring.

---

### 5. Intelligence-Weighted Consensus

Final risk scores are computed using intelligence-weighted consensus rather than simple averaging. Each agent’s contribution is weighted by its model’s benchmark performance from Artificial Analysis rankings. Stronger models therefore have greater influence on the final security score that is stored on-chain.

**Best creative use of ENS**

OPM uses ENS as the identity and metadata backbone for the entire package ecosystem.

**Author identity**: Package authors are identified by their ENS name, not just an npm username. When you run opm push, your ENS name is resolved from your signing key and attached to the on-chain package registration. Consumers can verify the author via opm view djpai.eth to see their on-chain reputation, published packages, and security scores.

**Package metadata as ENS text records**: Each push writes structured records to ENS:

opm.version - current package version
opm.checksum - tarball integrity hash
opm.risk_score - aggregate AI security score
opm.fileverse - link to the Fileverse audit report
opm.deptree - Merkle root of the dependency graph
opm.signature - author's cryptographic signature
**ENS subnames for packages**: Each package gets its own ENS subname (e.g., express.djpai.eth) with package-specific records, so a single author ENS name can host metadata for multiple packages without collision.

**ENS contenthash for IPFS**: The Fileverse audit report's IPFS content hash is read from the Fileverse Portal smart contract and written into the ENS contenthash field, making reports resolvable via ENS-native tooling.

**ENS as version resolver**: In package.json, you can use an ENS name as a version specifier ("express": "djpai.eth"). OPM resolves the ENS name, verifies the author is registered on-chain, and installs the safest available version:

// packages/cli/src/services/version.ts
if (isENSVersion(version)) {
  const authorAddr = await resolveAddress(ensName);
  const profile = await getAuthorByENS(ensName);
  // verify author is registered on-chain
  const safestVersion = await getSafestVersion(packageName);
  return { version: safestVersion, source: 'ens', ensName, authorAddress };
}
**Multicall batching**: All ENS record writes are batched into a single multicall transaction to minimize gas costs, writing 10-14 records in one tx instead of 14 separate transactions.

**Build What Big Tech Won't**

Hosted on cloud : https://opm-fileverse-4dc48255e118.herokuapp.com

Agent aggregated report sample : https://docs.fileverse.io/0x05EfCD46eC916cA68BF677968cc786E88135d70C/53#key=QQ7Dhuj4gANrs3BW-9nOwHP_qhnyp8jlr9tLUc7tdYx1sK4FScVb5_SVj6sqo7Ww

OPM uses Fileverse as the decentralized storage layer for security audit reports. When a package is scanned through opm push or opm check, the full report including AI agent findings, CVE data, risk scores, and dependency analysis is formatted as markdown and uploaded to Fileverse as a dDoc. The returned link is stored in the OPM registry contract and also written to an ENS text record called opm.fileverse.

OPM then reads the IPFS content hash from the Fileverse Portal contract by extracting the portal address and file ID from the dDoc URL and querying the files() function to obtain the metadataIPFSHash. This CID is written to the ENS contenthash field so the audit report can be resolved directly through ENS.

As a result, every OPM security audit is stored on IPFS through Fileverse, linked via ENS, and referenced on-chain, creating a permanent and verifiable audit trail.

**AI × Onchain**

OPM implements a permissionless multi-agent orchestration protocol anchored entirely on Base Sepolia. The **OPMRegistry** smart contract (deployed at **0x16684391fc9bf48246B08Afe16d1a57BFa181d48**) serves as the canonical source of truth for package integrity, agent authorization, and risk scoring. Every opm push registers a package version on-chain with a signed checksum, **triggers parallel AI agent scans across heterogeneous LLM providers, and writes intelligence-weighted aggregate risk scores** back to the contract via submitScore(). Agent registration itself is on-chain: any wallet can call registerAgent() to join the scanning pool, but only after passing a ZK-verified benchmark gate. The contract enforces authorizedAgents[msg.sender] checks so only verified agents can write scores. This creates a fully on-chain AI agent marketplace where model quality is cryptographically attested and scan results are immutably stored. The dependency graph Merkle root is also committed on-chain during publish, enabling consumers to verify that the entire transitive dependency tree has not degraded since the author's last audit. All of this runs on Base for low-cost, high-throughput settlement while **leveraging EIP-8004 patterns** for structured on-chain data attestation, making OPM a production example of AI inference results being settled and verified on a Layer 2

**Privacy**

OPM uses zero-knowledge proofs (Circom circuits + snarkjs) to verify AI agent quality without exposing the benchmark data or individual test results. When a new agent registers via opm register-agent, it is evaluated against 10 labeled security test cases covering typosquats, CVE exploitation, obfuscated malware, and clean packages. The **ZK circuit takes the agent's responses and the expected labels as private inputs**, computes accuracy internally, and produces a proof that accuracy equals 100% without revealing which test cases exist, what the expected outputs are, or how the agent performed on any individual case. The proof hash and system prompt hash are stored on-chain (proofHash and systemPromptHash in the RegisteredAgent struct), so anyone can verify that a registered agent passed the benchmark without the benchmark dataset ever being exposed. This prevents adversarial agents from gaming the test suite by memorizing answers, since the **labeled data remains a private input to the proof generation circuit**. The verification is fully on-chain: the contract checks the proof before authorizing the agent wallet, ensuring that privacy-preserving attestation is enforced at the protocol level rather than trusted off-chain

**BEST Overall Project**

OPM is a fully functional CLI tool that ships real security infrastructure: multi-agent AI scanning, on-chain package registry, ZK-verified agent onboarding, dependency graph analysis with Merkle proofs, ENS identity integration, and decentralized audit storage on IPFS. It works end-to-end as a drop-in npm replacement that any developer can install and use today on any Node.js project

**The problem it solves**

The Problem It Solves
Most crypto wallets are built for technical users, not everyday people.
Sending funds can be stressful due to long addresses, irreversible transactions, and unclear confirmation steps.
Security often depends on a single device and weak user habits.
Seed phrase handling is confusing, and mistakes can lead to permanent asset loss.
For merchants and small businesses, accepting crypto in person is still fragmented and hard to operationalize.
What People Can Use Startum For
Personal payments: Send and receive crypto with a guided flow that reduces mistakes.
In-person transactions: Accept payments via QR or NFC in retail/pop-up/storefront contexts.
Safer signing: Require both app interaction and NFC card presence for sensitive actions.
Daily wallet management: Track balances, recent activity, and transaction status in one place.
Fast payment requests: Create amount-based receive requests using built-in numpad + QR/NFC modes.
How It Makes Existing Tasks Easier
Converts complex crypto actions into step-by-step guided flows.
Reduces copy-paste/address errors with cleaner input and confirmation UX.
Shows clear states (pending, success, failure) so users know exactly what happened.
Improves merchant flow with immediate “payment received” feedback.
Lowers onboarding friction with structured setup and clear security prompts.
How It Makes Existing Tasks Safer
Adds a physical trust layer using NFC card interaction.
Uses confirmation checkpoints before final transaction submission.
Encourages stronger operational security through setup and verification steps.
Reduces accidental actions by separating selection, authorization, and confirmation.
Keeps a self-custody-first approach while making secure behavior more user-friendly.

**Challenges we ran into**

Challenges I Ran Into
1) Module import path breakages after moving to new onboarding structure
What happened:
When I split onboarding into dedicated screens and folders, some relative imports pointed to the wrong directories, which caused compile errors.

How I fixed it:

Corrected import paths for theme and shared UI components in onboarding screens.
Re-ran diagnostics on affected files to confirm no unresolved modules remained.
Outcome:
Build errors were removed and the onboarding flow compiled cleanly.

2) Clipboard API mismatch in React Native flow
What happened:
Copy/paste actions used the old React Native clipboard API, which is no longer the recommended approach in modern Expo setups.

How I fixed it:

Migrated copy/paste logic to Expo Clipboard.
Updated both reusable UI components and screen-level handlers using clipboard actions.
Outcome:
Copy address and paste recipient features worked consistently and passed type checks.

3) Missing icon dependency/type resolution
What happened:
Icon imports failed with type/module resolution errors during diagnostics.

How I fixed it:

Added the vector icons package explicitly to dependencies.
Installed related package updates through Expo-compatible install commands.
Outcome:
Icon-related compile/type issues were resolved across wallet, pay, receive, and settings screens.

4) Data shape mismatch in activity transaction list
What happened:
The activity screen passed props that did not match the transaction row component contract (field names and timestamp type mismatches).

How I fixed it:

Normalized mock data structure to match expected props.
Converted timestamps into compatible date string format.
Added an empty state for filtered results.
Outcome:
Activity screen rendered correctly and no longer threw prop/type errors.

5) APK build and artifact management
What happened:
Release build logs were noisy with Gradle warnings, and the generated APK was nested deep in Android output folders.

How I fixed it:

Completed a full release build using Gradle assembleRelease.
Verified build success and manually copied the APK to the repository root for easy access.
Outcome:
A production release APK was generated successfully and made easy to locate for sharing/testing.

Key Lesson
The biggest wins came from running diagnostics frequently, fixing integration issues in small batches, and validating each layer (dependencies, paths, component props, build output) before moving to the next feature.

**Privacy**

Startum is built for privacy-first crypto payments. Instead of exposing full wallet data to prove trust, we generate a selective disclosure proof for each payment that only reveals what is necessary: authorized amount, recipient, and timestamp. This lets users prove payment intent without revealing full balance history or unrelated transactions.

How Startum fits the Privacy track
Selective disclosure by design: Payment proofs share only minimal, transaction-specific data.
User-controlled custody: Keys are not centralized in a single provider-controlled wallet flow.
Physical second factor for signing: NFC card interaction adds an extra trust layer before sensitive actions.
Data minimization in UX: Users can complete send/receive flows without oversharing account context.
Practical privacy for real use: Works in both peer-to-peer and merchant flows (QR + NFC receive modes).
Why this matters
Most wallets force a tradeoff between usability and privacy. Startum closes that gap by giving users a smooth payment experience while preserving control over what they reveal and when they reveal it.

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![WebSockets](https://img.shields.io/badge/WebSockets-333333?style=flat-square) ![Docker](https://img.shields.io/badge/Docker-333333?style=flat-square) ![SQLite](https://img.shields.io/badge/SQLite-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![ESP32](https://img.shields.io/badge/ESP32-333333?style=flat-square) ![FastAPI](https://img.shields.io/badge/FastAPI-333333?style=flat-square)

**Software**

BioVolt is designed as a reusable, collaborative experiment platform rather than a one-off hardware prototype.

It uses a common telemetry format, modular backend, simulator, database, and dashboard so researchers and developers can:

- Connect different microbial-cell and sensor designs
- Reuse the same data-processing pipeline
- Add new biomass, OD680, carbon-fixation, or optimization models
- Test ideas through simulation before hardware is available
- Compare experiments using consistent data structures
- Extend the platform without redesigning the entire system

The goal is to make bioelectrochemical research more accessible, reproducible, and collaborative by allowing new hardware, algorithms, and datasets to plug into the same open system.

**Hardware**

The software is the measurement and visualization layer around the physical BioVolt hardware:

```text
BioVolt cell + sensors
        ↓
ESP32 firmware
        ↓ USB serial / COM5
ESP32 serial bridge
        ↓ WebSocket
Backend
        ↓
Dashboard
```

- The hardware produces the real signal: electrodes generate BPV voltage/current, ADS1115 reads BPV and BPW34, BH1750/GY-302 reads light, and DS18B20 reads temperature.
- The ESP32 firmware reads those sensors and sends raw values plus health status.
- The serial bridge transports the ESP32 frames to the backend.
- The backend validates data, applies calibration, calculates current, power, energy, OD680, biomass, and carbon fixation, then stores and broadcasts the results.
- The frontend displays live values and graphs.

The simulator is only a pre-hardware substitute. Its PWM-like spikes and load-sag model help test the dashboard before or between hardware runs; they are not evidence that the real cell is producing spikes.

For the hardware track, the remaining validation is physical:

- Verify wiring and sensor health.
- Connect and measure the real electrical load.
- Calibrate voltage/current against the multimeter.
- Capture proper BPW34 dark and blank references for OD680.
- Compare sustained ESP32 readings against the dashboard.
- Run the system for an extended period to check noise, drift, and connection stability.

A software load setting changes calculations; it cannot physically reduce the ESP32 circuit voltage. The real voltage drops only when the load is connected to the hardware circuit.

### LeakLens
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/leaklens-b832) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/AvProgramm/LeakLens) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://leaklens-69r1.onrender.com/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XiNgos17XCs) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-MUBA%20Blockchain%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://muba-hackathon.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Know what's exposed. Know what to do.

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![REST API](https://img.shields.io/badge/REST%20API-333333?style=flat-square) ![Gonka Router](https://img.shields.io/badge/Gonka%20Router-333333?style=flat-square) ![XposedOrNot](https://img.shields.io/badge/XposedOrNot-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

When your email shows up in a data leak, the existing tools tell you almost nothing useful. You get a list of company names and dates, no sense of how serious it actually is, no explanation of what was exposed, and no clear next step. Most people either panic over something minor or ignore something that actually matters.

There's also a trust problem most people don't think about: checking whether your own account was compromised means handing your email to whichever company runs the lookup, and trusting that they're not logging it themselves.

**LeakLens solves both problems.**

- Checks an email against known data leaks
- Runs the result through multiple independent AI models on Gonka Router, each one scores severity and explains in plain language what was actually exposed
- If the models disagree on how serious something is, that disagreement is shown rather than hidden, so you know when a verdict needs a second look
- Every inference step is backed by a visible Gonka Request ID, so the assessment can't be traced back to a centralised operator quietly logging your data

The result is a clear leak score, a plain-language explanation of what's actually at risk, and a prioritised checklist of what to secure first, instead of a bare list you have to interpret yourself.

**Challenges we ran into**

### **1. AI Rate-Limiting & Token Exhaustion**

While testing our multi-model consensus logic against the Gonka Router and XposedOrNot APIs, we quickly hit `429 Too Many Requests` errors. Spam-clicking the "Scan" button during UI testing was burning through our Gonka test network tokens and locking us out of the leak database.

* **How we got over it:** We implemented a strict client-side session cache (`SESSION_CACHE`) in our vanilla JavaScript frontend using Maps. If a user scans an email they've already checked during that session, the dashboard instantly serves the cached JSON payload instead of re-pinging the network. We paired this with strict UI debouncing, disabling the submit button and rendering a loading spinner while the dual-layer API pipeline resolves.

### **2. Decoupling the UI from Pending AI Logic**

Because we are a team of four, we couldn't afford to have the frontend developer sitting idle while the backend team engineered the Gonka API integration and cross-model prompt logic.

* **How we got over it:** We defined a strict JSON data contract on day one. We built the entire frontend using a hardcoded `MOCK_AI_VERDICT` object that mirrored the exact shape the Gonka Router would eventually return. We also engineered "graceful degradation" into the UI: if the AI consensus layer fails or the Gonka key isn't configured (returning a `503`), the dashboard doesn't crash. Instead, it gracefully displays an amber "Unavailable" badge for the AI score while still successfully rendering the underlying XposedOrNot breach data.

### **3. Late-Stage Git Merge Conflicts**

Working in a lightweight, zero-build-step environment (pure HTML/CSS/JS) meant multiple team members were frequently touching the same `app.js` and `style.css` files. Near the end of the build, pulling the backend API routes into the frontend branch resulted in a massive merge conflict that threatened to wipe out hours of UI styling.

* **How we got over it:** Rather than risking a broken file state by manually untangling Git conflict markers under a deadline, we executed a "clean clone" strategy. We cloned a fresh instance of the remote repository (`LeakLens-Clean`), manually injected our finalized UI files, and pushed the clean commit. We then had the whole team pull from `main`, resetting everyone to a unified, functional state.

**AI For Society**

LeakLens fits the AI For Society track by democratizing personal cybersecurity and bridging the digital literacy gap.
Currently, when everyday internet users discover their data was exposed in a breach, they are met with technical jargon and intimidating statistics (e.g., "244 million records exposed"). They know they are at risk, but they do not understand the specific threat level, nor do they know what immediate actions to take.
LeakLens uses AI to translate raw breach data into personalized, actionable security intelligence. By leveraging the Gonka Router's multi-model consensus, our tool analyzes the specific combination of leaked data (e.g., plain-text passwords vs. just usernames) and outputs a plain-language Leak Score, a transparent Reasoning Trace, and concrete next steps.
Instead of fear-mongering, our decentralized AI provides unbiased, verifiable guidance. LeakLens empowers the average digital citizen to understand their actual risk exposure and take back control of their privacy without needing an IT background.

**Challenges we ran into**

- Collecting  Dataset for the Project.

- To deploy

**The problem it solves**

ChainShield solves the problem of users accidentally interacting with fraudulent or risky Ethereum transactions and smart contracts.

Before a user signs a transaction, the system analyzes it for warning signs such as:

- Unlimited token/NFT approvals
- New or unverified smart contracts
- Known malicious wallet addresses
- Suspicious transaction functions
- Transactions far larger than the wallet’s normal activity
- Prior interactions with malicious contracts
- Behavioral anomalies

It combines machine learning, fixed security rules, and three focused analyzers to produce a simple risk score and decision:

- `SAFE` → safe to proceed
- `SUSPICIOUS` → review carefully
- `HIGH_RISK` / `CRITICAL` → do not sign

.

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Rust](https://img.shields.io/badge/Rust-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![move](https://img.shields.io/badge/move-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Cross-border payments in Southeast Asia are still slow, expensive, fragmented, and difficult to reconcile. Businesses and financial institutions often depend on multiple intermediaries, local payment partners, FX providers, and manual compliance processes just to move money across borders.

**Splash is building the settlement infrastructure for cross-border payments — designed for banks, businesses, and institutions, not for users to interact with crypto.**

* **Lower-cost settlement:** Stablecoin-based settlement can reduce intermediary costs. In Phase 1, Splash targets **free settlement**, with a long-term model starting from as low as **0.80%** depending on the corridor and off-ramp.
* **Faster cross-border payments:** USD/stablecoin settlement can move in near real time, while recipients can receive funds in their **local currency within minutes**, subject to the local payment rail.
* **SEA e-Invoicing & reconciliation:** Splash connects payment activity with invoice and transaction records, creating an **audit anchor** for cross-border business payments.
* **Non-speculative institutional treasury:** Instead of exposing businesses to DeFi yield or market speculation, Splash treats stablecoins as a **settlement asset** and provides an institutional treasury/omnibus layer focused on real-world payment flows.
* **Agentic Finance with human control:** AI can analyse transactions, learn business payment behaviour, and **propose** actions — but execution remains controlled by authorised users and institutional policies.
* **Built-in auditability:** Transaction and payment records can be anchored using **Walrus**, with **Seal** supporting encrypted data access and privacy.
* **Private, faster onboarding:** **zkLogin** enables a smoother onboarding experience without forcing users to manage traditional blockchain credentials.
* **Blockchain invisible to the user:** Blockchain operates as the **settlement layer underneath the infrastructure**. Businesses do not need to understand wallets, tokens, gas, or blockchain interactions.

**The goal is simple: make blockchain-powered settlement feel like normal financial infrastructure.**

**Challenges we ran into**

Building cross-border payment infrastructure is not only a technical challenge — it is also a **regulatory, operational, and corridor-specific challenge**.

* **Different corridor requirements:** Every country has different payment rails, FX requirements, settlement processes, and compliance expectations. A solution that works in one SEA corridor does not automatically work in another.
* **Regulatory complexity:** Cross-border payments involve licensing, KYC/AML, sanctions screening, stablecoin regulations, and local financial regulations. Designing Splash to work within regulated financial environments required us to separate the **technology layer from the regulated execution layer**.
* **Local remittance & off-ramp partners:** Stablecoin settlement is only one side of the transaction. The recipient still needs reliable access to local currency. Finding suitable, compliant remittance and off-ramp partners across Southeast Asia became a key challenge.
* **Balancing speed with compliance:** Our goal is near-instant settlement, but financial institutions cannot sacrifice compliance and auditability for speed. We had to design Splash so that faster settlement does not mean weaker controls.
* **Making blockchain invisible:** One of our biggest product challenges was hiding blockchain complexity from the end user. Businesses should experience Splash as a normal payment infrastructure layer — not as a crypto application.
* **Privacy vs. auditability:** Institutions need transaction records for reconciliation and compliance, while sensitive business information must remain private. This drove our exploration of **Walrus + Seal** for auditable yet encrypted data storage.

**PAYMENTS & STABLECOINS**

- Payments, Audit Anchor & Omnibus Treasury.
- USD/USDC/USDT In Local Currency out. 
- B2B focus before c2c 
- Stablecoin Treasury ( Non - Speculative )
- SEA Focus and design to scale globally.

**AI × SUI**

1. Agentic Finance
2. 0xWal is the AI Copilot :
- Propose but never executes
- Remeber user patterns using MemWall ( Memory Wall ) , never the Sensitive data
- Using Walrus to store invoice in Encrypted blob and Seal for who can access.
- In Phase 2+ AI can manage and send money and approval on Whatsapp or Splashz mobile app with 2-3 multi sig shared approval.

**Challenges we ran into**

# Challenges We Ran Into

- **Unstable AI provider responses:** Gonka models sometimes timed out, returned HTTP 400 errors, or produced invalid structured output. We added task-specific timeouts, bounded retries, output validation, graceful degradation, and different models for independent verification.

- **Slow verification pipeline:** Multiple sequential AI calls made results take too long. We reduced unnecessary calls, kept two independent verifiers plus one consensus judge, and added a resumable background-job API with frontend polling.

- **Progress disappeared after refresh:** Verification originally depended on one browser request. We stored the active job ID locally and resumed polling after refresh while backend processing continued.

- **Missing completed history records:** Gonka could route two verifier requests to the same served model, conflicting with a database uniqueness rule and rolling back persistence. We changed inference uniqueness to use Gonka request IDs and improved persistence error logging.

- **History showed only some records:** Frontend loaded paginated history but rendered only a small batch. We now fetch all user-owned pages and render every loaded record with search and verdict filters.

- **Evidence retrieval configuration:** Text claims required live public sources, but search was initially unavailable. We integrated Brave Search, added configuration health reporting, and retained safe fallback behavior when search fails.

- **OAuth redirect problems:** Google and GitHub authentication could return users to unreachable localhost URLs. We aligned provider callback URLs, Supabase Site/Redirect URLs, and frontend OAuth redirect configuration.

- **Frontend and backend authorization:** Requests returned HTTP 401 when browser sessions were not forwarded correctly. We attached Supabase Bearer tokens, refreshed expired sessions once, and kept backend ownership checks and Supabase RLS as security boundaries.

- **Multilingual results:** Translating only frontend labels left AI reports in English. We added English, Bahasa Melayu, and Simplified Chinese throughout the UI and passed the selected output language through the verification pipeline.

- **Container and AWS deployment:** ECR tags, IAM permissions, runtime environment files, and stale local image tags caused deployment confusion. We adopted exact immutable release tags, separate frontend/backend images, health checks, and documented rebuild, push, pull, and recreate steps.

- **Public HTTPS without a domain:** Direct EC2 ports were unsuitable for OAuth and public testing. We used separate Cloudflare Quick Tunnels for frontend and backend, then restricted EC2 inbound rules while documenting the temporary-URL limitation.

- **Trust and transparency:** AI results must not be presented as guaranteed truth. We exposed evidence sources, model disagreements, confidence, limitations, Gonka request IDs, and clearly labelled Evidence Support as a support indicator rather than a probability of truth.

**The problem it solves**

# TruthScope

TruthScope is an evidence-first claim-verification prototype built for Malaysian public-interest and political information.

## Problem statement

Public claims spread through speeches, news, social media posts, forwarded messages, and screenshots faster than most people can investigate them. Checking one claim often requires users to:

- find original sources among repeated or copied reporting;
- distinguish direct records from commentary;
- check dates, quotation context, units, and omitted qualifiers;
- compare sources that support and contradict the claim;
- judge whether an AI answer is evidence-based or merely confident; and
- understand why models disagree.

Political claims add another risk: source identity, party affiliation, office, race, religion, or popularity can become shortcuts for credibility. A system that produces one unexplained “true/false” label may hide uncertainty and reproduce those shortcuts.

## Proposed solution

TruthScope helps users investigate a claim instead of asking them to trust one model. It:

1. extracts atomic, verifiable claims;
2. gathers public source pages and preserves provenance;
3. checks date, quotation, and statistical context;
4. asks two distinct Gonka-hosted verifier models to assess the same evidence;
5. uses a third distinct model to compare agreement and disagreement;
6. audits judgment language for political-bias indicators;
7. calculates deterministic evidence and confidence scores; and
8. shows sources, limitations, failures, and Gonka request metadata to the user.

**AI For Society**

TruthScope uses Gonka Router as the inference layer for every AI reasoning stage in its public-interest claim-verification workflow. The system extracts checkable claims, plans evidence searches, compares multiple verifier assessments, produces a consensus judgment, and audits the final language for possible political-bias indicators.

Multiple verifier roles request different Gonka-hosted models so the result does not depend on one model's opinion. TruthScope records each requested model, served model, latency, Gonka Request ID, warnings, and disagreements. Users can therefore inspect how a result was produced instead of being asked to trust an unexplained AI verdict.

Gonka Router also allows the workflow to degrade safely when one model times out or returns invalid output Available evidence and successful analyses remain visible, while the result clearly reports its limitations rather than forcing a true-or-false answer.

### PharmaTrust
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/pharmatrust-5388) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/jianzhi86/Sui-Hackaton) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://sui-hackaton-one.vercel.app/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/AEYb1wMIF48) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-MUBA%20Blockchain%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://muba-hackathon.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> On-chain pharma custody, verified by AI on Sui

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![React.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/React.js-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Counterfeit and diverted pharmaceuticals are hard to catch with paper records or private databases. A paper trail can be forged, and a database can be silently edited by whoever controls it. Neither gives a patient, pharmacist, or regulator a way to independently verify a specific package's history before use.

PharmaTrust puts the entire custody chain on Sui instead, so it's public, tamper-evident, and permanently attributed to whoever signed each step. Manufacturers register a batch on-chain, optionally backing it with staked SUI as collateral, and print QR codes straight onto packaging. Distributors and pharmacies record every hand-off as a checkpoint, including cold-chain temperature readings, permanently tied to their wallet with no way to forge who touched it. Anyone can scan a package, with no wallet needed, and instantly see its full custody history, run an independent AI cross-check across two different models for tampering or timing anomalies, and check a public recall registry before dispensing or buying. Regulators or pharmacy staff can place a hold the moment something looks wrong, and it immediately blocks further sales and checkpoints rather than just flagging paperwork, with graduated financial penalties in the form of slashed stake scaled to how serious the finding is. Customers pay for medicine with a single-use QR plus a scratch code that's physically deleted from the blockchain the instant it's redeemed, so the same package can never be sold twice off one photo of the QR.

In short, it turns "trust me, this is genuine" into "verify it yourself, for free, in seconds."

**Challenges we ran into**

A stale environment variable silently broke every write transaction in production. After adding staking, suspicion reports, and single-use sale QRs to the Move contract, we discovered VITE_PACKAGE_ID on our Vercel deployment still pointed at a much older contract version published before any of those features existed, one that even gated place_hold behind a RegulatorCap we'd since removed. Every write transaction was failing with argument-count mismatches while every read still worked, which is exactly why it went unnoticed: the site looked fine until you tried to actually submit something. We caught it by disassembling the deployed package bytecode directly and diffing its function signatures against our current contract, which taught us never to trust "the site loads" as proof a deployment is actually current.

A hosted AI model silently substituted itself for another. Our two-model AI cross-check depends on genuinely independent verdicts, but we found that requests to one model, Kimi-K2.6, were being silently served by a completely different model on the router's side, with no error and no indication in the response, which defeated the whole point of cross-checking two models. We fixed it by adding an X-Gonka-No-Fallback header, which turned the silent substitution into an honest error revealing the model had zero capacity, and swapped in a model we verified was genuinely distinct.

Sui's public JSON-RPC endpoints deprecated the API our wallet-kit version depends on partway through the project, returning "Method not found" with no CORS headers, which broke every browser call outright. We solved it by pointing at a CORS-enabled public RPC provider instead of Mysten's own endpoint.

Move package upgrades quietly break event-based indexing. A minor contract change that only tightened a validation check, with no struct changes, looked like a safe sui client upgrade instead of a fresh publish, until we discovered every event's package ID switches to the new address after an upgrade, silently orphaning every dashboard that filters events by a fixed package ID. We now always publish fresh rather than upgrade, trading batch and unit continuity for a single reliable source of truth in the event log.

**AI × SUI**

PharmaTrust is built natively on Sui and leans on its object model as the actual mechanism, not as a bolt-on ledger sitting behind a normal backend. A Batch is a shared Sui object that every party in the supply chain (manufacturer, distributor, pharmacy) attaches a checkpoint to directly, giving the whole custody chain a single, permissionless, tamper-evident source of truth without needing a centralized database anywhere.

The single-use sale QR is the clearest example of thinking in Sui's terms rather than porting over a generic smart-contract pattern. Instead of an "already sold" boolean that a bug or race condition could bypass, the QR is backed by a Unit object that gets deleted outright the instant it's paid for. An object that no longer exists on-chain simply can't be referenced by a future transaction, so the single-use guarantee comes from the object model itself, not from application logic hoping nobody finds a way around a flag.

The AI side is genuinely wired into that on-chain state, not bolted onto a demo. Two independently-queried models reason directly over a batch's live checkpoint and hold history read straight from Sui, cross-checking for tampering or timing anomalies, and a second pass reasons across every batch from one manufacturer at once to catch patterns a single-batch check would never see. The point of the AI is specifically to notice things the on-chain record makes visible but that a person skimming it wouldn't catch.

There's also a real economic layer built on actual Coin<SUI> transfers, not a UI-only score: manufacturers post SUI as collateral when they register a batch, and a confirmed hold slashes a graduated share of it straight to whoever caught the problem, so reporting a counterfeit is directly rewarded instead of being unpaid diligence.

Building this also meant running into Sui's real constraints rather than staying on a happy path: chunking multiGetObjects calls under the 50-ID cap, paginating queryEvents thousands of events deep instead of quietly truncating at the first page, and learning the hard way that sui client upgrade changes an event's package ID, which would have silently broken every dashboard built on event history. And finally, there's no access control anywhere in the contract on purpose. Any wallet can register a batch, scan a checkpoint, place a hold, or buy, with no admin approval step standing between a first-time visitor and trying the whole flow immediately.

> #Network In Your Area -- BlackPinkChain

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Blockchain](https://img.shields.io/badge/Blockchain-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![AI/ML](https://img.shields.io/badge/AI/ML-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

**1. Network needs change by activity**
Normal connectivity may be enough for browsing, but gaming, livestreaming, video calls, or crowded events may require lower latency, better stability, or stronger uplink performance.

**2. Users do not know when premium network capabilities are useful**
Telecom providers may already have QoS or other programmable network capabilities, but users usually do not know when they need them or whether they will actually improve the experience.

**3. Premium network services are not context-aware**
Existing add-ons are often static. Our platform uses provider-supplied user and network context to generate a purchase offer only when the customer is likely to benefit.

**4. Multi-provider sessions are difficult to manage and settle**
If one provider can no longer meet the required service level, the session may need to continue through another provider while keeping one customer purchase and fairly splitting the payment.

**Challenges we ran into**

**1. Autonomous payment on Sui**
We initially wanted the AI agent to fully control payment, but non-custodial transactions still require user authorization. We had to redesign the flow so the user approves the purchase while the agent manages the session and settlement.

**2. Integrating off-chain network data with on-chain payment**
Network quality, session duration, and provider switching happen off-chain, while settlement happens on Sui. We needed a clear way to connect verified service results with smart-contract payment logic.

**3. Defining the business model**
We initially considered acting as a reseller of network capacity, but this created dependency on provider availability and weak margins. We later repositioned the platform as provider-facing infrastructure for selling premium network experiences.

**4. Handling one session across multiple providers**
We had to define how a user keeps the same paid session when Provider A becomes unsuitable, how Provider B takes over, and how one final payment is split based on each provider’s actual contribution.

**PAYMENTS & STABLECOINS**

- Customers pay for actual premium-network usage.
- One session can involve multiple providers.
- Customer receives one final charge.
- Payment is split according to verified provider contribution.
- Stablecoins support predictable settlement value.
- Smart contracts reduce manual reconciliation.

**AI × SUI**

- AI evaluates user activity, network quality, eligibility, and available capabilities.
- AI decides whether an upgrade is needed and which service is suitable.
- AI monitors the session and can trigger provider switching.
- Sui records session transactions and provider contributions.
- Smart contracts automate transparent multi-provider settlement.

**AI For Society**

- AI recommends upgrades only when users genuinely need them.
- Avoids unnecessary or generic upselling.
- Helps users access better performance for gaming, livestreaming, work, and events.
- Makes advanced network capabilities easier for normal users to access.
- Encourages more efficient use of provider network services.

[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/blocks-and-scissors-c165) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/ronxmi3/block-and-scissors) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/uM_TnW5ubX0) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-MUBA%20Blockchain%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://muba-hackathon.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Trust the cut not the promise

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Blocks & Scissors solves the trust problem that happens when a customer and a barber disagree over whether the final haircut actually matches the reference that was agreed on beforehand. Normally, the customer has to either pay despite being unhappy, or refuse payment and leave the barber with no guaranteed protection.

Our solution uses an AI-verified escrow system. The customer locks the payment in a Sui smart contract before the service. After the haircut, the reference image and final result are compared by our AI scoring pipeline. If the score meets the agreed threshold, the barber is paid automatically. If it does not, the customer is refunded.

This makes the process safer for both sides: customers get protection against clearly mismatched results, while barbers get protection against customers refusing to pay after an acceptable service. The same model could later be applied to other reference-based services such as tailoring, tattoos, detailing, repairs, and commissioned work.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the biggest challenges was getting the AI score to react to the haircut itself rather than differences in the photos. Raw image similarity was too sensitive to lighting, backgrounds, camera angle and styling. I improved this by adding hair-focused crops, grayscale and blurred shape comparisons, mirrored side-profile matching, and separate checks for haircut family, texture, back length and fade/taper structure. I also added confidence-aware penalties so uncertain classifications do not affect the score too aggressively.
Another challenge was connecting the off-chain AI result to an actual on-chain payment. The AI runs in the FastAPI backend, while the escrow lives on Sui. I built an oracle flow where the backend submits the final score through an authorized OracleCap, and the Move contract decides whether to pay the barber or refund the customer. I tested the flow using Sui dry-runs and live testnet transactions, and also handled issues such as network mismatches, gas configuration and preventing an escrow from being settled twice.
The final MVP works end-to-end, but the AI is still optimized mainly for side-profile fade and taper comparisons, so broader hairstyle support and multi-angle verification would be the next major improvement.

**AI × SUI**

Blocks & Scissors fits the AI × SUI track because the project combines AI-based verification with on-chain payment settlement. The AI backend compares a customer’s reference haircut with the completed haircut using OpenCLIP and custom haircut-specific scoring logic, including hairstyle structure, texture, back length, fade/taper characteristics, and confidence-aware penalties. This produces a similarity score from 0–100.

Sui is then used as the settlement layer. Before the service, the customer locks the payment inside a Move escrow object containing the customer, barber, funds, and agreed threshold. After the AI produces its score, an authorized backend oracle submits that score to the smart contract. If the score meets or exceeds the threshold, the contract releases the escrowed SUI to the barber; otherwise, it refunds the customer.

This means AI is responsible for evaluating the real-world result, while Sui provides neutral, transparent, and enforceable settlement. The project demonstrates a broader pattern of AI-verified service escrow, where AI can assess completion and Sui can automatically enforce the pre-agreed payment outcome.

Team **Blocks And Scissors** -- [Badr Naji](https://github.com/HelloWorld2006A), [Rayyan Babar](https://github.com/ronxmi3), [Hadia Bashir](https://github.com/hadia-bashir)

### NutShell
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/nutshell-8558) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/jianwen0414/NutShell) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/9R6w-uX2oNQ) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/9R6w-uX2oNQ) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-MUBA%20Blockchain%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://muba-hackathon.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Verified crisis detection that buys real downside

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![ethers.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/ethers.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![PostgreSQL](https://img.shields.io/badge/PostgreSQL-333333?style=flat-square) ![Three.JS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Three.JS-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Chainlink](https://img.shields.io/badge/Chainlink-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

### The evidence layer was confidently wrong before it was useful

Our biggest failure was not a crash. It was a correct measurement driving a wrong
conclusion.

A scripted claim said $40M had been drained from a Base bridge. Our oracle check
compared Base DEX spot against Chainlink, found them agreeing to within 0.14%,
and returned CONTRADICTS. Both models then scored the claim FAKE at 22 and 25,
both citing that exact reading, and the decision fell from HEDGE_SMALL to REJECT.

The measurement was right. The inference was garbage. $40M is roughly 0.014% of
ETH's market cap, so a drain that size need not move the price at all. Price
agreement is not evidence that no drain occurred, but the model had no way to
know that.

We fixed it by classifying what a claim actually asserts (price, custody, or
halt) and letting each check contradict only claims about the thing it measures.
Corroboration stays unrestricted, because finding real distress is always worth
surfacing, while wrongly ruling out a true report is the error that costs someone
a hedge. After the fix the same scenario returned zero contradicting checks and
MiniMax scored it 68 REAL.

A related one: we pointed a balance check at Aave v3's `Pool` contract and it
reported 114 USDC while DeFiLlama showed billions in TVL. Aave v3 holds reserves
in aTokens. We were measuring an address that never custodies anything and
reporting "no drain" with total confidence. Now an address below a custody floor
returns INCONCLUSIVE instead of a reassuring zero.

### Thetanuts: the order book has traps that only fail on-chain

**Spreads look like puts.** Filtering on `isCall === false` seemed obviously
right. Every longer dated order we selected that way reverted with
`Panic(17) OVERFLOW` inside the contract. Their calldata carries two or three
strikes: they are spreads, not vanilla puts. We now require exactly one strike
before an order is fillable.

**`previewFillOrder` echoes your own input back.** Its `totalCollateral` field
returns the budget you passed in, not a computed charge, so it can never reveal a
shortfall. We had been approving against it and were only accidentally correct,
because integer flooring means the real charge always lands just under the
budget. Worth knowing before it bites someone else.

**A fill reverted with "transfer amount exceeds allowance" against an allowance
that was sufficient.** We chased four wrong theories (unmined approval, wrong
variable, rounding, a referrer fee) before static calling the fill against every
candidate order and finding all of them would succeed. The approval had mined on
one node while our `eth_call` was served by another a block behind. A stale read,
not a logic bug. Retrying filled it.

**There is no early exit.** We tested it rather than assuming: `close()` reverts
unless one address holds both sides, `reclaimCollateral()` is seller only, and
nothing bids for puts. Recovery on abandoning a hedge is 0%. That single fact
reshaped the product, because if you cannot undo a purchase then the only place
you can save money is before you make it. It is why agreement gates spending.

### Gonka: the model catalogue can lie to you

`GET /models` listed `moonshotai/Kimi-K2.6`. Every `POST /chat` against it
returned `400 unsupported model`, naming in its own error body the two models it
would actually serve. A health check that trusts the catalogue reports a full
three model panel while live runs quietly fail quorum, which is exactly what
happened to us.

So we stopped asking the catalogue and started judging on outcomes. The call path
records success and failure per model in a rolling window, and a model that
resolves but has answered nothing is reported as unusable. The health endpoint
cannot be contradicted by the thing it is checking.

Two more, both measured: **streaming silently disables the SDK timeout**, because
the HTTP response opens immediately, so one queued call ran 600s past a 120s
budget. We stayed non-streaming. And **node selection happens upstream**, so the
same model answers in under a second or in 40 seconds depending which node takes
it. We send a duplicate request at 14s and take whichever lands first, which
turns a straggler into a fast vote instead of a lost one.

**The problem it solves**

**Crypto moves on news before it moves on price.**

When a bridge is drained or a lending market halts, the information is public
minutes before the oracle catches up. If you are asleep, at work, or just not
refreshing Twitter, you absorb the entire move.

The obvious defence is to hold put options all the time. Almost nobody does,
because permanent protection costs several percent of notional a year against a
yield of a few percent. It is negative carry by construction, so protection has
to be event driven. That moves the hard part somewhere else: an event driven
hedger is only as good as its trigger. Fire on rumour and you burn premium on
every false alarm. Wait for confirmation and you buy insurance after the crash.

**NutShell is the trigger.** It reads eight public newswires continuously,
measures each claim against Base mainnet itself, has three independent AI models
score it, and buys a real protective put on Thetanuts only when the evidence and
the models agree.

### Who it is for

- **Anyone holding ETH, BTC or SOL who cannot watch the news 24/7.** The agent
  watches instead, and it can only ever spend a capped premium budget.
- **Small DAO treasuries with no risk desk.** Automated, bounded downside cover
  with a written reason attached to every trade.
- **Anyone who just wants a claim checked.** The verification page is public and
  needs no wallet. Paste a headline, get three named models scoring it with their
  request ids.

### What it actually changes

| Before | With NutShell |
|---|---|
| You find out when the price already moved | The agent reads the wire and the chain in the same minute |
| Protection costs more than the position earns | One dollar of premium bought $912 of ETH downside cover, about 0.1% of notional |
| "The AI said so" | Every verdict names its model, shows its request id, and the id resolves on Gonka's chain |
| A hedge is a number in a spreadsheet | Every position traces back to the exact sentence that bought it, under one id |

Premiums come out of vault yield. Principal is never touched. The agent runs on a
policy bounded burner wallet that can do exactly one thing, buy a protective put,
against exactly one allowlisted contract, under a hard per trade ceiling.

**Live on Base mainnet.** Four real fills, real USDC, all verifiable on BaseScan.

**BEST PRODUCT BUILT ON THE THETANUTS SDK**

**Does it work?** Yes, and it is running, not described. Four options bought on
Base mainnet with real USDC, each one a deployed contract with an entry
transaction on BaseScan. One ETH put is open right now. An earlier position was
held to expiry and settled out of the money, recovering nothing, which is the
honest outcome for insurance that was not needed.

**Are the options load-bearing?** Stub out Thetanuts and there is no product
left. The entire thesis is that a trustworthy trigger makes event driven
protection affordable, and the put is the protection. We use the SDK for order
book reads, quote decoding, exact approvals and fills, and the selection funnel is
built around the venue's real constraints: single strike vanilla puts only, a
quote TTL near 60 seconds that the whole select, approve, sign and broadcast path
has to fit inside, a delta band, a minimum expiry horizon, and available depth.
Cash settled synthetics gave us BTC and SOL cover without those assets existing
on Base.

**Does it fit the market?** Protective puts are the most understood hedge in
finance and almost nobody in crypto holds them, for one reason: you cannot afford
to hold them permanently. That makes the trigger the product, not the option. We
built the trigger and used Thetanuts to act on it. The users are retail holders
and small treasuries who want a floor under a position without watching a feed
all night. What happens after the hackathon is that this needs a real yield
source plugged into the vault interface, which already accepts one unchanged.

**AI × OPTIONS**

**The bar is one real on-chain trade against live pricing, and we cleared it four
times.**

| Asset | Strike | Entry transaction |
|---|---|---|
| ETH | $2,340 | `0x9c4bb145…828f8c` (open) |
| BTC | $75,500 | `0xbbb8b74b…c06309` |
| SOL | $97 | `0xda94b0b8…c385a7` |
| ETH | $2,380 | `0xe2d5fcce…d62c1b2d` (settled OTM) |

This is an autonomous hedging agent in the sense the track describes. The AI is
not a natural language wrapper over a trade button. It is the thing that decides
whether money moves at all, and the decision is a real one that says no far more
often than yes.

The interesting part is the refusal. Three models score a claim, and consensus
produces two numbers: a truth score and an agreement score. Both have thresholds.
Two readings of the same event can share a truth score of 91 while agreement
falls from 86% to 31%, and the second buys nothing. You can drag that agreement
slider yourself on our landing page and watch the live policy engine flip
HEDGE_FULL to ESCALATE.

Size is then bound by whichever of five caps bites first: premium reserve, daily
cap, per trade hard ceiling, book depth, or the tier. The incident record names
which one bound it. In our worked example, policy cleared full size and the per
trade ceiling cut it to three dollars, and the page says so.

**AI For Society**

The challenge names an **AI Fact Checker** as the preferred application: a
decentralized truth engine using multi-model inference, producing a Truth Score
with a traceable reasoning trail. That is precisely what NutShell's verification
layer is, and we then did something no other fact checker does. We put money
behind the verdict.

Against the stated requirements:

| Requirement | How we meet it |
|---|---|
| All AI reasoning on Gonka via gonkarouter.io | Every inference in the product. No other provider appears anywhere in the verification path. |
| Multi-model consensus, at least two models | Three: MiniMax, Kimi and DeepSeek, called in parallel on an identical prompt, with model substitution disabled so the panel is genuinely three different models. |
| Claim extraction from a URL, tweet or text | Public paste box at `/`, no wallet and no signup. Also fed automatically by eight RSS newswires. |
| Truth Score 0 to 100 and a reasoning trace | Both, from a second layer synthesizer that explains but is never allowed to set the score. |
| Transparency UI showing Gonka Request IDs per step | Every verdict card shows its request id, copyable, with a link that resolves the shard on Gonka's own chain API. The chain record names the model, which independently confirms which model answered. |
| Neutrality prompting | Temperature 0, models instructed to cite specific evidence, and grounded in measured chain state rather than their own priors. |
| Consensus logic when models disagree (noted as a major plus) | Agreement is a first class metric with its own policy threshold, shown at equal visual weight to the score. When the panel splits, a challenge round runs, and disagreement alone can veto an action the truth score would have allowed. |

**Why this matters for society, in one line.** A fact checker that only prints a
score costs nothing to be wrong. Ours commits real money on the strength of its
verdict and refuses to commit when its own models disagree, which is the
strongest honesty guarantee a verification system can offer.

The same engine also degrades honestly. One of our three models left the router
mid build while still being advertised by its catalogue. The health panel reports
that from observed call outcomes rather than from the listing, and the UI says
"two of three answered" instead of quietly averaging what is left.

### Tali Treasury
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/tali-treasury-01f4) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/shuheng0330/Tali-Treasury) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/YUoc7b4GcGc) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-MUBA%20Blockchain%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://muba-hackathon.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> AI-Powered Payroll, Expenses & On-Chain Protection

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![PostgreSQL](https://img.shields.io/badge/PostgreSQL-333333?style=flat-square) ![Supabase](https://img.shields.io/badge/Supabase-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Payroll, employee requests, statutory contributions and expense reimbursement are often handled across separate systems. This creates repetitive data entry, slow approvals, limited visibility and a dangerous gap between approving a payment and actually completing it.

Tali brings these workflows together. Employees can submit overtime, leave and receipt claims through one mobile-friendly application. Employers can review each request, understand its payroll impact, run payroll and monitor team earnings. Treasurers can manage expense limits, review exceptions and track reimbursements.

For payroll, Tali calculates employee pay together with EPF, SOCSO and EIS allocations. Approved overtime and unpaid leave are incorporated into the payable period before the final calculation. Salary and statutory payments are then executed atomically through a Sui Move contract. If any required contribution is below the mandate’s minimum, the entire transaction is rejected and no USDC moves.

For expenses, Gemini extracts structured information from receipts and timesheets, reducing manual entry. Deterministic policy checks evaluate limits, categories, dates, duplicate receipts and approved recipients. Uncertain claims are sent to a human reviewer instead of allowing AI to control funds.
Tali also supports salary streams, allowing employees to see earnings accrue over time and withdraw vested pay using their own wallet. Every confirmed payment or refusal can be independently verified through its Sui transaction.

**Challenges we ran into**

Malaysian statutory payroll rules do not treat every payment component equally. EPF uses contribution schedules and excludes overtime from its wage basis, while SOCSO and EIS include overtime and apply wage ceilings. Unpaid leave must also reduce the wage before the statutory split is calculated. We separated each statutory calculation, encoded the correct calculation order and added extensive tests for wage bands, ceilings, overtime and leave adjustments.

Blockchain payment failures can be ambiguous. A network timeout does not necessarily mean that a transaction failed, and automatically retrying could create a duplicate payment. We solved this by deriving and storing the transaction digest before broadcasting, using atomic compare-and-set state transitions and reconciling the exact digest on demand. An uncertain payment is never automatically signed or submitted again.

Wallet connection alone was not secure enough for authentication. We implemented signed, single-use wallet challenges, one-hour HTTP-only sessions, exact-origin validation and account-switch invalidation. Receipt analyses are stored as private, short-lived drafts that can be consumed only once when creating a claim.

We also needed to make complex blockchain and payroll evidence understandable on mobile screens. Early versions contained dense calculations and long technical explanations. We redesigned the interface around clear outcomes, compact summaries and expandable evidence, allowing users to understand the result first while still giving judges access to policy checks, exchange-rate details and transaction proofs.

**PAYMENTS & STABLECOINS**

Tali directly addresses payroll, payouts and treasury management using USDC on Sui Testnet. Employers fund immutable payroll mandates, while separate expense mandates control reimbursements. Sui Move contracts enforce budgets, payment limits, approved recipients, expiry and statutory contribution floors. Payroll pays the employee, EPF, SOCSO and EIS atomically: either every payment succeeds together or the entire transaction is rejected. This demonstrates a real stablecoin workflow with working wallet authentication, payroll execution, expense reimbursement, salary streams and publicly verifiable transaction evidence.

**AI × SUI**

Tali combines AI-assisted document processing with on-chain payment execution. Gemini extracts structured information from receipt and timesheet images, reducing manual entry for employees. The extracted information is treated as untrusted input and passes through deterministic policy checks and human review where required. Once approved, a restricted backend agent can prepare payments, but Sui remains the final authority and enforces the mandate on-chain. This creates a practical AI-assisted workflow in which automation improves speed without giving the AI unrestricted control over money.
