### Infer134
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/infer-1d7c) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/savchart/infer134) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHPrague%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethprague2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Private AI inference

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

AI agents and companies increasingly need to buy small units of inference from external workers, but today this usually means opaque API billing, no clear per-job payment state, and poor auditability. Putting everything onchain is not a good answer either, because prompts, outputs, and model details can be private or commercially sensitive.

Infer134 solves this by creating a local-first pay-per-inference workflow with private offchain execution and transparent settlement metadata.

A buyer can choose a worker-published GPU/model offer, submit a prompt, receive an offchain result, verify a signed execution receipt, and release payment. The prompt and output stay offchain, while hashes, worker identity, receipt hash, and payment state provide a clear audit trail.

People can use Infer134 to:

  - let AI agents purchase inference jobs from independent compute workers;
  - make AI agents and companies increasingly need to buy small units of compute, such as LLM inference, from external workers. Today this usually means using opaque API billing, trusting a centralized provider, or exposing too much private data when trying to add blockchain payments.

Infer134 makes this workflow safer and clearer by separating the private work from the public settlement trail.

A buyer can submit an inference request, choose a worker-published GPU/model offer, keep the prompt and output offchain, receive a signed execution receipt, and release payment based on explicit job state. The system stores only minimal settlement metadata such as hashes, worker identity, receipt hash, and payment state.

People can use Infer134 to:

  - let AI agents pay for inference work per request;
  - let independent GPU workers publish local compute capacity;
  - give buyers a readable receipt for what was executed;
  - avoid putting prompts, outputs, or model data onchain;
  - make payment state transparent without turning private inference into public data;
  - demonstrate how x402-style pay-per-request flows could work for AI services.

The current MVP is local-first and intentionally narrow. It does not claim trustless proof-of-compute. Instead, it focuses on a practical buyer journey: discover a worker, create a job, run inference offchain, verify the signed receipt, and release payment.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the main challenges was keeping the demo honest while still making it understandable for the judges.

It would have been easy to show a fake GPU marketplace with static offers, but that would not reflect the behavior of the real system. Instead, we connected the buyer UI, provider UI, backend catalog, and local provider-node runtime so that offers only appear when the worker is actually online and the selected model/runtime is ready.

This created a few tricky edge cases:

* The backend could contain previously published offers while the provider node was offline.
* A worker could publish a vLLM model while the local runtime was only running in mock mode.
* The buyer page needed to hide stale offers without making the app look broken.
* The demo needed to clearly explain what is verified and what is still trusted.

We addressed this by adding runtime-readiness checks and filtering the buyer marketplace to show only live, compatible GPU/model bundles. If the provider node is unavailable or the runtime does not match, the UI now explains that stale offers are hidden instead of pretending they are usable.

Another challenge was defining the trust boundary. Infer134 does not prove that a model output is semantically correct. In the MVP, we verify hashes, payment state, and signed execution receipts. Making that distinction explicit helped keep the project focused and avoided overclaiming “trustless AI” or “proof of compute” before those pieces exist.

**Ethereum Core**

Infer134 uses Ethereum as the settlement and verification layer for offchain work.

The MVP keeps inference private and offchain, while Ethereum-style settlement metadata can track hashes,
worker identity, receipt hash, and payment state. This keeps the chain focused on what it is good at: transparent state, payment coordination, and auditable commitments.

The current prototype uses local Anvil and native ETH escrow for the demo path. It is intentionally local-first, but the architecture is designed so stablecoin settlement, x402-style payments, or stronger contract-based escrow can be added later.

**Network Economy**

Infer134 fits Network Economy because it creates a small market for useful work between buyers and independent compute workers.

AI agents or companies can request inference, workers can publish GPU/model capacity, and each job has explicit payment state. The project demonstrates a practical economic primitive: pay-per-inference without requiring the buyer to expose private prompts or outputs.

Instead of building another generic AI platform, Infer134 focuses on a network where local workers can sell compute as a service and buyers can choose offers based on worker identity, model, runtime readiness, and price.

**Future Society**

Infer134 fits Future Society because it explores how AI agents can buy compute while preserving privacy and accountability.

As agents become more autonomous, they will need to interact with external services, pay for work, and verify what happened. Infer134 shows one way to make that interaction safer: prompts and outputs stay offchain, while buyers still receive signed execution receipts and a clear payment trail.

The project is also honest about its trust model. It does not claim full proof-of-compute or trustless AI. Instead, it gives users a readable workflow for private inference, worker accountability, and transparent settlement, with clear upgrade paths toward reputation, TEEs, disputes, and stronger verification.

**Best Agentic Venture**

Infer134 fits Umia because it is built around agentic payments and a concrete AI-agent workflow.

The project shows an agent or buyer discovering available inference workers, choosing a model/GPU offer, creating a paid job, receiving an offchain result, verifying a signed execution receipt, and releasing payment. This is exactly the kind of flow autonomous agents will need when they buy services from external providers.

Infer134 also has a plausible venture direction: a marketplace where companies, agents, and independent GPU owners transact per inference request. The MVP is intentionally narrow, but the core business primitive is clear: workers publish compute capacity, buyers pay per job, and the platform coordinates receipt-based settlement.

Future versions could add real x402 payments, stablecoin billing, worker reputation, ENS-based discovery, and stronger verification for high-value agent workflows.

**Best ENS Integration for AI Agents**

Infer134 fits the ENS track because identity is central to the buyer and worker experience.

The MVP uses ENS-style names such as `research-agent.eth` for the buyer and `gpu-prague.eth` for the worker. These names make the compute marketplace easier to understand than raw wallet addresses: a buyer can see which worker is claiming the job, which identity signed the execution receipt, and where payment is being released.

In the current prototype, ENS resolution is mocked/local-first, but the product boundary is clear. Real ENS integration could replace the local identity layer with actual ENS names, text records, worker metadata, service endpoints, model capability records, and reputation links.

This makes ENS useful not just as a wallet label, but as a discovery and trust layer for AI agents buying compute from independent workers.

### Hallmark
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/hallmark-3bb7) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Aghostraa/resumify.eth) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://hallmark-beta-ivory.vercel.app/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://www.loom.com/share/ddd7f11cab0d4ebc8d3be5faf11b897c) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHPrague%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethprague2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Ever wanted to have resume of your work onchain?

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Ethereum](https://img.shields.io/badge/Ethereum-333333?style=flat-square) ![ENS](https://img.shields.io/badge/ENS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Viem](https://img.shields.io/badge/Viem-333333?style=flat-square) ![EAS](https://img.shields.io/badge/EAS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Blockscout](https://img.shields.io/badge/Blockscout-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Smart contracts are deployed anonymously — wallets, auditors, and agents have no standard way to judge if a contract is safe, verified, or trustworthy before interacting.

Hallmark solves this by giving every contract a structured **trust score** (0–100) built from five axes: source verification via Sourcify, pattern recognition, risk flags, ecosystem adoption, and static security checks. It also generates a **developer resume** — an aggregated view of all contracts a wallet has deployed across 10+ chains, with verification rates and risk summaries.

The **Agent tab** exposes an on-chain AI agent identity using ENS + ENSIP-26 text records, letting autonomous agents carry verifiable credentials on-chain rather than in a backend database.

Key integrations:
- **Sourcify**: full/partial match drives 0–20 of the verification score axis
- **ENS**: human-readable contract names + AI agent identity (ENSIP-26 subnames as agent credentials)
- **Blockscout**: multi-chain contract discovery across 10 EVM networks
- **OLI labels**: open labeling initiative data for contract classification

**Challenges we ran into**

Building a streaming analysis pipeline that fetches contract data from Blockscout, Sourcify, and ENS simultaneously without blocking the UI was the hardest part. We solved this with a server-sent events (SSE) stream from the API — each pipeline step fires a progress event so the UI updates in real time rather than waiting on a monolithic response.

Scoring normalization across five independent axes (each 0–20) required careful calibration so the total (0–100) feels meaningful: a contract with no Sourcify match but clean security still scores respectably, while a high-risk unverified contract bottoms out clearly.

The ENS agent identity layer (ENSIP-26) required writing a custom text record schema for agent metadata — there was no existing standard we could drop in, so we defined one compatible with EIP-7694 drafts and stored it on Sepolia ENS subnames.

**Ethereum Core**

Hallmark builds foundational trust infrastructure for Ethereum contracts. Every contract gets a deterministic ENS subname (`{addr6}.resume.{devLabel}.hallmarked.eth`) carrying a structured 0–100 trust score across five axes: source verification, pattern classification, static security analysis, risk flags, and ecosystem adoption. The result is written as ENS text records — permanently queryable by any wallet, agent, or tool with no backend dependency. Developer resumes aggregate all deployed contracts under a single namespace, making the contract layer of Ethereum navigable and auditable for the first time. This is core Ethereum usability work: making contracts safer to interact with, easier to evaluate, and harder to obfuscate.

**Network Economy**

Hallmark tackles on-chain identity at two levels. For developers: a portable resume lives entirely in ENS — `resume.{devLabel}.hallmarked.eth` — no centralized store, no API key, no trust in Hallmark's infrastructure. For AI agents: the analysis agent carries a full ENSIP-26 identity (`agent-context`, `agent-endpoint[sse]` text records on its ENS subname), so any caller can verify who scored a contract and how to reach the agent's SSE endpoint. Every contract name includes an `issued-by` text record pointing back to the agent ENS name, forming a verifiable provenance chain. Identity and economic reputation are fully on-chain, user-controlled, and censorship-resistant.

**Sourcify Bounty**

Sourcify verification is a first-class scoring axis in Hallmark — not a badge, but a scored signal. Full match contributes the full 20 points; partial match contributes 10; unverified contracts score 0 on this axis regardless of other signals. We call the Sourcify API live during every analysis pass and write the match type (`exact_match`, `partial_match`, `unverified`) as an ENS text record (`sourcify-verified`), making the result permanently on-chain and queryable without re-hitting Sourcify. This brings Sourcify's 27M+ contract dataset directly to end users and creates a strong incentive loop: verified contracts score higher, rank better in developer resumes, and are more trusted by agents — making verification economically rational.

**Best ENS Integration for AI Agents**

The Hallmark agent is an autonomous on-chain actor with a real ENSIP-26 identity — not a cosmetic ENS name. Its subname carries `agent-context` (JSON with model, version, capabilities, and URL to the security pattern.json living on our github), `agent-endpoint[sse]` (the live SSE analysis endpoint), `agent-endpoint[api]`, and `issued-by` records. Any client can discover the agent, verify its identity, and call it using only ENS — no hardcoded URLs, no centralized registry. The agent uses this identity functionally: it signs OLI attestations on Base under its ENS name, writes `issued-by` records on every contract it scores, and mints the entire developer resume namespace autonomously. ENS is the agent's credential system, service discovery layer, and trust anchor simultaneously.

**Most Creative Use of ENS**

Hallmark uses ENS in a way we haven't seen elsewhere: a four-level hierarchical subname tree as a portable identity and reputation system. The agent wallet owns `hallmarked.eth` and registers `{devLabel}.hallmarked.eth` → `resume.{devLabel}.hallmarked.eth` → `{addr6}.resume.{devLabel}.hallmarked.eth` for every contract a developer scores. The leaf name carries the full trust profile as text records. Reading back is done via direct `readContract` calls on the public resolver using `namehash` — same pattern as ENSIP-26 agent identity — bypassing the full ENS resolution chain entirely. The ENS namespace *is* the developer resume: enumerate all subnames under `resume.{devLabel}.hallmarked.eth` and you have their complete verified contract history, queryable by anyone, owned by the developer.

### PragueExplorer
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/pragueexplorer-7c79) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/ZafarNasimov/Prague-Explorer) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/6KIaVcsuPfI) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/6KIaVcsuPfI) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHPrague%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethprague2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Privacy-first ZK geocaching on Scroll

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![foundry](https://img.shields.io/badge/foundry-333333?style=flat-square) ![Zk proofs](https://img.shields.io/badge/Zk%20proofs-333333?style=flat-square) ![Scroll](https://img.shields.io/badge/Scroll-333333?style=flat-square) ![EAS](https://img.shields.io/badge/EAS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Account Abstraction](https://img.shields.io/badge/Account%20Abstraction-333333?style=flat-square) ![Semaphore](https://img.shields.io/badge/Semaphore-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Prague Explorer is a privacy-first geocaching game for EthPrague attendees and Prague tourists. Players find physical QR codes hidden at six real Prague landmarks, scan them in person, answer a Czech history quiz, and claim an on-chain EAS attestation — without the contract ever learning who they are.

**The privacy model is the core innovation.** Presence is proved by combining a per-cache QR secret (only obtainable on-site) with a Semaphore v4 ZK proof generated entirely in the browser (~3 seconds). The contract sees only an opaque nullifier and a display name — never a wallet address, email, or any externally-linked identity. Nullifiers are scoped per-cache (`scope = cacheId`), so claiming two different caches produces cryptographically uncorrelated nullifiers that cannot be linked on-chain.

**Zero friction for users.** Privy embedded wallets let anyone sign in with email or Google — no MetaMask, no seed phrase. A Pimlico ERC-4337 paymaster on Scroll Sepolia covers gas entirely. A successful claim produces an EAS attestation the user owns permanently: a composable, portable credential, not a custodied badge.

**Cultural layer.** Each cache is tied to a real Prague landmark. Cache beneficiary addresses point to Czech cultural institutions that receive optional ETH micro-donations on claim. The app ships in Czech and English.

**Challenges we ran into**

**In-browser ZK proving.** Integrating Semaphore v4 into a live Next.js frontend was non-trivial: the WASM circuit and proving key total ~6 MB. We preload the key on page mount and display a progress indicator so the ~3-second proving time feels intentional rather than broken.

**ERC-4337 on Scroll Sepolia.** Wiring Pimlico's paymaster with `permissionless` v0.3.5 required careful chain-ID configuration (534351) and handling the case where the paymaster rejects sponsorship. We built a fail-open fallback: if the paymaster declines, the user's EOA pays gas directly — the claim flow never breaks.

**Binding the display name to the proof.** To prevent front-running (changing the displayed name after proof generation), we embed the display name in the Semaphore message field: `message = uint256(keccak256(displayName)) >> 8`. The `>> 8` right-shift is required to fit within BN254's scalar field. Any post-generation name change produces an invalid proof, enforced at the circuit level.

**Semaphore anonymity-set trade-off.** The `joinCache()` call (group membership registration) is observable on-chain — an attacker can see that *someone* is joining cache X, but cannot determine who, because the identity commitment has no link to any external identifier. We mitigate this by funding user wallets from a separate deployer account so the gas-payer address is distinct from the Semaphore identity being registered.

**Ethereum Core**

Built entirely on Ethereum's core stack:

- **Scroll Sepolia** — zkEVM L2, full EVM equivalence, EthPrague-native
- **Semaphore v4** — Groth16 ZK proofs for anonymous group membership
- **EAS (Ethereum Attestation Service)** — composable on-chain credentials, one attestation per cache claim
- **ERC-4337 (Pimlico + permissionless v0.3.5)** — Kernel smart accounts, gasless UX
- **Foundry** — 15 passing tests, Deploy.s.sol, contract verified on Scroll Sepolia

All contracts are open-source. The Semaphore verifier and EAS contracts are deployed and reused from their canonical Scroll Sepolia addresses.

**Network Economy**

Prague Explorer puts user control first at the protocol level. Identity is derived entirely client-side from a QR secret + Privy user ID; the contract never sees a wallet address on claim. Nullifiers are scoped per-cache, making cross-cache linkability cryptographically impossible — even the contract cannot correlate two claims by the same person.

An optional ETH micro-donation on claim routes value directly to a Prague cultural institution's beneficiary address — a lightweight economic layer built into the claim flow with no intermediary and no custodian.

**Future Society**

Prague Explorer embeds Czech cultural heritage directly into Ethereum. Each of the six caches is tied to a real Prague landmark; quiz questions cover Czech history and local significance. Cache beneficiary addresses point to cultural institutions — museums, archives — that receive optional ETH donations on claim.

The app is fully translated into Czech and English and designed so any tourist with a phone and an email address can participate — no crypto background, no wallet app, no gas required. Privacy is not a feature toggle: it is the default, enforced at the circuit level.

Team **CrvenaZvezda** -- Vasily Sizykh, Alireza Sayahzadeh, Zafar Nasimov

### PocketChains
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/pocketchains-0544) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/vikzh/ethprague2026) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://pocketchain.vercel.app/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/bM6lsZgn1ps) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHPrague%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethprague2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Temporary sovereign chains for communities.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Swarm](https://img.shields.io/badge/Swarm-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

## Ethereum as an Operating System for temporary societies

No rollup deploy. No sequencer config. No bridge. No infra hell. A blockchain that comes into existence the way a group chat does.

**A new mental model.** Not one global ledger that everyone shares — *millions of small social chains*, each with its own:

- consensus (one-member-one-vote or stake-weighted PoS)
- economy (shared ETH pool, off-chain signed cheques)
- rules (invite policy, channel write policy, TTL)
- privacy (E2E encrypted chat, ECDH DMs, seed-in-fragment invites)
- reputation (membership, stake, voting history)

…but security and settlement *inherit from Ethereum*. One `ChainPool` contract holds the funds and verifies every signed transfer.

**Chains don't have to be permanent.** A chain can run for 2 hours. Or a festival. Or a hack night. Or a protest. Or a research team. Or this hackathon.

**You don't connect to a chain — you get invited.** The invite is a QR code carrying a shared secret. Joining is one wallet signature. Your identity inside is a fresh ephemeral key, scoped only to that chain. Stricter chains require a vouching signature from a member or the creator, enforced cryptographically by every honest client.

**Chains can physically overlap.** Right now at ETHPrague there could be 400 invisible PocketChains in this room. You bump into someone, scan a QR, unlock access. Part Pokémon GO, part BitTorrent, part secret society — all settled on Ethereum.

**Chains can die.** Inactive blockchains are eternal zombies. PocketChains aren't. When a community goes quiet, the chain dissolves — but its history compresses into an encrypted artifact you can keep, restore, or share.

PocketChains is what Ethereum looks like as infrastructure for ephemeral, sovereign social spaces.

**Challenges we ran into**

**Peer-to-peer state that survives.** Our messaging layer is a transport, not a database — messages gossip between peers and may not be cached anywhere reliable. But a chain needs history (chat, members, pending transfers). We made every member a temporary archive: they hold the raw envelope log and can export it as an encrypted backup. A fresh browser pulls history from peers when it can, and falls back to restored backups when it can't. The chain is peer-to-peer but rebuildable from any single member's state.

**Debugging an encrypted system.** Most traffic is opaque on the wire — chat is AES-GCM, DMs use ECDH between ephemeral keys. A "missing message" could be a peer issue, a key mismatch, a wrong recipient, or a member who hasn't republished. We added structured logging at every replay boundary that dumps signature recoveries and policy decisions but never plaintext, so we can trace failures without leaking anyone's chat.

**Setting up Swarm for encrypted backups.** We wanted users to lose their browser and still recover their chain. Swarm fit — decentralized, content-addressed — but getting it running took work: a local Bee light node, a funded Bee wallet on Gnosis Chain, and a usable postage batch (which needs xDAI, its own onboarding story). The payoff: a user saves an encrypted blob to Swarm, shares a 64-char reference, and rehydrates the whole chain in a new browser with one signature.

**Multiple consensus and invite policies.** Different groups want different rules: open invites with one-member-one-vote, creator-only with stake-weighted PoS, or member-approved with equal weight. Encoding that into the contract would have made it brittle, so policy lives in a creator-signed off-chain Settings envelope, and the replay engine enforces it. Tally logic and invite validation switch modes purely on what the latest Settings says.

**Ethereum Core**

PocketChains demonstrates a design pattern that scales without L2 infrastructure: one ChainPool contract hosts arbitrarily many independent payment pools, so creating a new 'pocket chain' costs one transaction instead of a rollup deploy. The transfer model is minimal: recovered signer must equal `from`, nonce strictly increases, balance must be sufficient, and anyone can submit a valid batch. The replay engine on the client shows how to build a trust-minimized app over an untrusted P2P layer (Waku): every signature, nonce, and policy is re-verified from raw materials on every state tick. No indexer, no relayer, no proof system — just a small contract and a strict client, scaling to as many parallel social chains as Ethereum block space can hold.

**Network Economy**

PocketChains gives every group its own micro-economy on Ethereum. Each chain is a shared ETH pool with off-chain signed cheques between members, optional stake-weighted governance, and on-chain batch settlement. No relayer, no custodian, no admin. The contract verifies every signature; withdrawals are a single Solidity function. The bigger thesis: instead of one global ledger that everyone shares, we get millions of small economies — for festivals, raids, research teams, or a single dinner — each with its own rules, but all anchored to Ethereum's security and settlement. Self-custodied group economy as a primitive, not a product.

**Future Society**

PocketChains is for communities that want their own sovereign space — temporarily. A chain can exist for two hours, a festival, a protest, or a research team. Inside it, group chat is end-to-end encrypted, DMs use ECDH between ephemeral keys, and invite policies (open / creator-only / member-approved) are enforced cryptographically. Polls handle group decisions, optionally weighted by stake. Encrypted backups to Swarm let the history survive even when the device dies. And when a community goes quiet, the chain dissolves — its history compresses into an artifact, instead of becoming another eternal zombie chain. This is the toolkit for ephemeral, sovereign, privacy-respecting communities on Ethereum.

Team **we must win** -- [Ilya Tsupryk](https://github.com/IlyaTsupryk), [viktor zhukovskiy](https://github.com/vikzh)

### fama
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/fama-5b40) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/JankaUhrinova/FAMA) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHPrague%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethprague2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> claims expire. credibility compounds.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

### Fama is Twitter with consequences.

Every post is a falsifiable claim with a deadline. When the deadline passes, the claim resolves, the author’s credibility updates, and future feed ranking changes. Instead of optimizing for engagement, Fama optimizes for being right.

### What do we solve

Let's be honest, your twitter timeline is full of thirst traps and rage baits. The more you engage with the post, the higher is it on your feed.
The most important tweets or the tweets that are carrying the value are often left behind

Fama solves this by turning posts into falsifiable claims with deadlines. Instead of likes or follower count deciding who gets seen, authors build a non-transferable credibility score from resolved claims.

People can use Fama to:

- Make public predictions with accountable outcomes
- Track who is consistently right over time
- Discover high-signal voices without relying on popularity
- Challenge claims by agreeing or disagreeing before the deadline
- Build a portable truth record
- Reduce misinformation incentives by making vague, viral posting less valuable

For users, Fama makes social discovery safer and more useful: the feed surfaces people with proven accuracy, not just people who are good at getting attention.

For communities, it creates a shared memory of who made which claims, when they made them, how the crowd voted, and what actually happened.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the main hurdles was wiring together several moving pieces without making the app feel fragile: authentication, wallet/KMS signing, generated media, and the social posting flow all had to agree on the same user and asset state.

### SpaceComputer

The trickiest bug was around key creation and signing with the OrbitPortSDK. Some requests looked correct from the frontend but failed because the backend payload shape did not match what the provider expected. I worked through it by isolating the flow with small server-side debug calls, comparing the raw API response against the SDK behavior, then tightening the request format and error logging so failures became obvious instead of silent.

### Swarm

We tried to implement swarm-based key-value storage. The problem was that the local node setup did not work, so we needed to use their hosted solution.

### Apify

The process of using Apify via x402 had two main issues.

First, the whole process is oriented around the `apify mcp cli`, which made raw HTTP requests harder to work with. We had to use some workarounds, especially since we use SpaceCoin KMS.

Second, even though some scrapers were marked as pay-per-request, we sometimes got an error saying they had to be paid per batch.

**Network Economy**

Fama fits the Future Society track because it explores how Ethereum can make online discourse more transparent, accountable, and fair.

Today’s social platforms reward engagement, which often favors outrage, misinformation, and popularity over accuracy. Fama proposes a different model: a social network where visibility is earned through a transparent record of resolved claims.

Every post is a falsifiable statement with a deadline. The claim, votes, and resolution are recorded through Ethereum-based infrastructure, while the author’s credibility score is non-transferable and earned over time. This creates a public accountability layer for social media without relying on a centralized platform to decide who is trustworthy.

Fama empowers communities by helping them identify high-signal contributors based on demonstrated accuracy rather than follower count, status, or paid amplification. It can be used by local communities, DAOs, research groups, journalists, public-good teams, and civic organizations to track predictions, commitments, and claims over time.

The project also supports fair and transparent governance. Communities can use Fama to evaluate proposals, public commitments, and decision-makers based on their historical truth record. Instead of reputation being subjective or platform-controlled, it becomes auditable, portable, and earned.

By combining Ethereum, soulbound credibility, and decentralized content storage, Fama aims to support a healthier information ecosystem where being accurate matters more than being loud.

**SpaceComputer Bounty**

Fama uses the **SpaceComputer Orbitport SDK / KMS** as the signing layer for user actions on-chain. Instead of asking users to connect a browser wallet, Fama provisions a dedicated Ethereum-compatible KMS key for each signed-in user through the Orbitport SDK.

When a user creates their account, the app calls `sdk.kms.createKey` with an Ethereum secp256k1 signing key configuration. We store the returned `keyId` and Ethereum address in our app database and bind it to that user account. That address becomes the user’s on-chain identity for posting claims and voting.

We then use Orbitport KMS to sign real Base Sepolia transactions. For example, when a user creates a Fama claim:

1. The claim text is uploaded to Swarm through SwarmKV.
2. The app encodes the `createPost(bytes32 swarmHash, uint64 deadline, uint64 voteLockWindow)` contract call.
3. The backend builds an EIP-1559 transaction.
4. The transaction digest is signed through `sdk.kms.sign` using `ETHEREUM_SECP256K1`.
5. The backend serializes and broadcasts the signed transaction.

The same KMS-backed flow is also used for voting: agreeing or disagreeing with claims calls the Fama contract from the user’s Orbitport-managed Ethereum address.

So Orbitport KMS is central to Fama’s UX: it lets Twitter-authenticated users interact with smart contracts without managing private keys manually, while still giving every user a real Ethereum signing address and verifiable on-chain activity.

**A Simple Key-Value Store on Swarm**

We have implemented our own KV storage on Swarm as a backbone of our application.  We built and use a local `@swarmkv/core` package that gives the app a simple key-value API over Swarm: `put`, `get`, `delete`, `keys`, `entries`, and `iterate`.

In Fama, every post is a falsifiable claim. Instead of storing the claim text directly on-chain, we write the claim text to Swarm through SwarmKV. Swarm returns a 32-byte content reference, and the `Fama` smart contract stores that reference together with the post metadata, deadline, author, vote window, and vote counters.

This gives us a clean split:

- Swarm stores the actual claim text as decentralized, content-addressed data.
- The smart contract stores the authoritative reference to that content.
- The indexer and frontend use the stored Swarm reference to hydrate the feed and display the original claim text.

We use SwarmKV to make Swarm feel like a normal developer database while still preserving Swarm’s decentralized storage model. For public Fama posts, the app uploads the post text, receives the Swarm reference, passes it into `createPost(bytes32 swarmHash, uint64 deadline, uint64 voteLockWindow)`, and later fetches the text back from Swarm when rendering the feed.

**Apify Bounty**

Fama uses APIFY for its claim-resolution workflow. Fama is a social prediction and credibility app where every post is a falsifiable claim with a deadline. After the deadline, the claim needs to be resolved against real-world evidence.

Our intended integration is to make that resolution step use **Apify Actors paid through X402**. When a claim reaches its deadline, a resolver can spawn an Apify scraper to gather external evidence from relevant public sources: X/Twitter posts, news pages, websites, market pages, product listings, or other real-time web data depending on the claim. The Apify Actor provides the evidence needed to decide whether the claim resolved as true or false.

The X402 part is important because the scraper is not just a free backend task. The resolver pays for the Apify service at the moment it is needed, using the X402 payment flow. This creates a concrete paid data workflow inside the app:

1. A user posts a claim on Fama.
2. The claim text is stored on Swarm and its reference is stored on-chain.
3. Other users vote before the deadline.
4. After the deadline, a resolver triggers an Apify Actor.
5. The Apify scraping job is paid for through X402.
6. The scraper returns evidence from real-world web sources.
7. The resolver uses that evidence to resolve the claim.
8. The Fama contract updates the claim outcome and user credibility.

This gives Fama a real use case for Apify in Web3: paid, on-demand real-world data collection for decentralized claim resolution. Instead of manually trusting a resolver with no supporting data, Fama can attach scraped evidence to the resolution process and make the cost of obtaining that evidence explicit through X402.

In future versions, this could evolve into an agent workflow: a Fama resolver agent pays an Apify scraper agent through X402, receives structured evidence, summarizes it, and submits the proposed resolution back to the Fama protocol.

**The problem it solves**

## The Problem It Solves

### Discovery Is Fragmented

AI tools are scattered across dozens of platforms — Hugging Face, OpenAI marketplace, Fiverr, Upwork. Finding the right agent for a specific task means searching multiple sites, comparing pricing, and hoping for API compatibility. There's no single place to browse, buy, and use AI agents.

### Payments Are a Bottleneck

Each AI service has its own billing system — Stripe, crypto wallets, API keys. For crypto payments specifically, users manage gas fees, network switching, and wallet connections. This terrible UX blocks mainstream adoption.

### No Unified Workspace

After buying an AI service, you get an API key or a login. There's no single place to actually *use* the agents you've purchased. You juggle multiple tabs, APIs, and SDKs.

### Agents Can't Buy for You

AI agents are powerful but can't autonomously discover and purchase services they need. A data analysis agent that needs a web scraping tool can't just go buy one — it requires human intervention at every step.

---

## What Cusygen Does

**One wallet connection. 18+ AI agents. Instant execution.**

| Feature | How It Works |
|---------|-------------|
| **Browse** | 18+ agents across 10 categories, each powered by a category-optimized NVIDIA LLM |
| **Purchase** | Single-click USDC payment via Locus on Base — no gas fees, no wallet switching |
| **Execute** | Chat workspace with streaming responses — ask anything, get real AI output immediately |
| **Autonomous** | Auto-buy mode: your agent discovers and purchases services based on your budget and interests |
| **Negotiate** | Make offers on any listing, subscribe monthly (60% off) or annually |
| **Review** | Multi-dimension ratings: quality, speed, communication |

---

## Why It's Different

| | Traditional | Cusygen |
|--|-----------|---------|
| **Cost** | $500+/project | $0.05 — $0.50 per agent |
| **Speed** | Days to onboard | Seconds to purchase and execute |
| **Models** | Generic chatbot for everything | Category-optimized: Qwen3 Coder 480B for code, Llama 4 Maverick for content, Nemotron 49B for research |
| **Trust** | Email invoices and reviews | On-chain transactions on Base, full audit trail |
| **Autonomy** | Human does everything | Agent buys and executes tasks while you sleep |
| **UX** | Multiple accounts and dashboards | One Locus wallet, one workspace, all agents |

**Challenges we ran into**

In-Memory Store Reset Between Routes (Dev Mode)
The webhook handler couldn't find purchases created by the checkout handler. purchases.find(p => p.id === purchaseId) always returned undefined.
Root cause: Next.js with Turbopack in dev mode hot-reloads modules independently. Each API route (/api/checkout and /api/webhooks/locus) got its own instance of the module-level purchases array. The store was effectively reset on every request.
Fix: Not fixable in dev mode — it's a fundamental limitation of in-memory stores with Turbopack HMR. Works correctly in production (npm run build && npm run start) where all routes share the same module instance. All end-to-end testing is done in production mode.

**Track: Checkout with Locus**

How Cusygen Fits: Checkout with Locus
The Track Is About Locus Checkout Integration
Checkout with Locus is a payment SDK — like Stripe, but for USDC on Base. Cusygen doesn't just add Locus Checkout as a payment option. Locus Checkout is the core payment rail that powers the entire marketplace.
---
Where Locus Checkout Lives in Cusygen
It's not bolted on — it's the foundation. Every dollar that flows through Cusygen goes through Locus Checkout:
User browses agent
       ↓
Clicks "Purchase via Locus"
       ↓
POST /api/checkout (creates Locus session)
       ↓
POST /api/checkout/agent/preflight/:sessionId  ← Locus SDK
       ↓
POST /api/checkout/agent/pay/:sessionId      ← Locus SDK
       ↓
GET /api/checkout/agent/payments/:txId        ← Locus SDK (poll)
       ↓
Webhook: checkout.session.paid               ← Locus confirms
       ↓
Service access token generated
       ↓
Agent is live in workspace

**The problem it solves**

Vaxa solves the problem of trustless, on-demand access to AI services.
Today, using AI APIs means committing to monthly subscriptions, sharing API keys, or trusting centralized platforms with your data and payments. There's no way to pay per-request without middlemen, and no verifiable track record of service quality.
Vaxa changes this by combining three things:
- x402 HTTP-native payments — Access AI agents with a single HTTP request. The server responds with 402 Payment Required, you send USDC on Avalanche, attach the tx proof, and get your result. No API keys. No subscriptions. No accounts. Standard REST that works with curl.
- ERC-8004 on-chain reputation — Every successful transaction builds an immutable reputation score (0-1000) on-chain. Users can objectively compare agents by reputation before paying. No fake reviews, no manipulation — just verifiable transaction history.
- Programmable PayAgent — A personal payment agent that enforces spending limits (daily/weekly/monthly), manages recurring subscriptions, sends conditional tips, and handles smart escrow — all within user-defined rules.
Real-world use cases:
1. A developer pastes code and gets instant security review for $0.05 — no account needed
2. A team sets up weekly auto-payments to a summarization agent via PayAgent rules
3. A user creates escrow for high-value AI tasks — funds only release when they approve the result
4. A Telegram bot accesses the same agents with bot-managed payments and daily limits
5. Agents call other agents (A2A) — a summarizer can trigger a translator in a single workflow
Why it matters: Vaxa proves that AI services can be monetized as micro-payments on-chain, with zero infrastructure overhead for consumers and instant, verifiable payment for providers — all built on Avalanche C-Chain.

**Challenges we ran into**

1. x402 in-band payment flow is counterintuitive to implement
The x402 standard requires a two-phase HTTP flow: server returns 402 Payment Required with payment details, client submits a blockchain tx, then re-sends the request with X-Payment-Proof. Getting this right in Next.js middleware — especially verifying the tx on-chain without blocking the response — took multiple iterations. I solved it by separating verification into the middleware and firing recordSuccessfulTx() as a fire-and-forget promise to avoid blocking the response.

**Agentic Payments on Avalanche**

Vaxa is built natively on Avalanche C-Chain (Fuji testnet) and would not exist without it:
- x402 payments settle on Avalanche — Every agent request triggers a USDC transfer on Fuji (Chain ID 43113). Payments are verified on-chain before results are delivered.
- ERC-8004 reputation lives on Avalanche — Agent reputation scores are stored in a Solidity contract deployed to Fuji. Every successful transaction calls recordSuccessfulTx(), updating an immutable, transparent score.
- PayAgent spend rules are Avalanche-native — Daily/weekly/monthly limits, whitelists, subscriptions, and conditional tips all execute as on-chain USDC transfers.
- Smart Escrow uses Avalanche for custody — Payment is held in escrow state and only released to the agent when the user approves the result, or refunded on rejection.
- Low fees + sub-second finality — Avalanche's C-Chain makes micro-payments (as low as $0.02) economically viable, which is critical for a pay-per-request AI marketplace.
The entire thesis of Vaxa — programmable money meets autonomous AI agents — is only possible because Avalanche provides the fast, cheap, EVM-compatible infrastructure that makes per-request payments practical.

> Trustless Labor Market for AI Agents

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Avalanche](https://img.shields.io/badge/Avalanche-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

## The Problem

Multi-agent AI systems have a coordination problem that no one has solved cleanly.

When Agent A needs to hire Agent B to do work, the deal is always one-sided:

- Agent A pays upfront and hopes the work arrives.
- Agent B does the work and hopes payment follows.

Neither is trustless. There is no escrow. There is no standard proof format. There is no shared reputation layer that travels between environments. The moment agents need to work together across systems, trust collapses back onto humans — which defeats the purpose of autonomous agents entirely.

The missing primitive is a trustless labor market: a place where agents can negotiate, commit, deliver, prove, and settle without any human in the loop.

AgentWork is that primitive.

## How It Works

The core mechanic is a three-party escrow loop:

```
Employer Agent  →  AgentEscrow.sol  →  Worker Agent
                        ↑
               ERC-8004 Validation Registry
```

**Step 1 — Post a Job**

An employer agent locks USDC into `AgentEscrow.sol` on Avalanche C-Chain. The job spec includes the task description, the capability required, the maximum payment, and a deadline. An ERC-8004 reputation threshold gates which worker agents are eligible to accept.

**Step 2 — Work & Verify**

A worker agent from the on-chain registry picks up the job. It completes the task and submits a result hash. A validator then records cryptographic proof of completion in the ERC-8004 Validation Registry — the first on-chain standard for verifiable agent task completion.

**Step 3 — Auto-Pay**

`AgentEscrow.sol` reads the validation confirmation directly from the registry and releases USDC to the worker. No human approves anything. No arbitration. No delay. Both agents' ERC-8004 reputation scores update automatically.

Settlement takes approximately 2 seconds on Avalanche C-Chain.

**Challenges we ran into**

# Challenges I ran into

### ERC-8004's reference implementation is Hardhat-only — incompatible with our Foundry workflow

ERC-8004 is the on-chain agent identity standard we built the whole protocol around. The reference contracts are genuinely well-built — they use UUPS upgradeable proxies, EIP-712 signatures, CREATE2 vanity address mining to get deterministic `0x8004...` addresses, and a five-step Hardhat deployment with pre-signed upgrade transactions. The problem is the entire deployment system is TypeScript + Hardhat (`hardhat.config.ts`, deployment scripts in `scripts/*.ts`) with no Foundry support. We couldn't use it from `forge script`.

We rewrote all three registries (`IdentityRegistry`, `ReputationRegistry`, `ValidationRegistry`) as standard non-upgradeable contracts using the regular OpenZeppelin library, preserving the full ERC-8004 interface surface. The key spec requirement we had to carry over manually: the `agentWallet` hotkey must clear on NFT transfer — wallet is tied to the registering party, not the token. This lives in the `_update` override and is easy to miss if you're not reading the spec carefully alongside the upgradeable source.

---

### ICM job dispatch without asset bridging

The cross-chain flow in the README sounds clean: employer on a Gaming L1 posts a job, worker picks it up, settlement on C-Chain. The hard part is **USDC lives on C-Chain but the employer only exists on the L1**.

Avalanche ICM (Teleporter) moves *messages*, not assets. `JobRelay.dispatchJob()` can relay a job intent cross-chain in one call, but it can't atomically pull USDC from an employer who has no presence on C-Chain. We landed on a clean separation: `postJob` creates the job record (callable by the relay on behalf of the employer), and USDC is handled as a pre-approval on C-Chain. The `trustedRelay` pattern on `AgentEscrow` makes `JobRelay` a first-class caller without giving it arbitrary contract access.

The contracts are fully deployed and wired on Fuji testnet — `AgentEscrow.setTrustedRelay(JobRelay)` is live on-chain. Full atomic bridging of USDC from L1 to C-Chain would be the next milestone.

---

### Teleporter interfaces aren't available as a Foundry library

The `ava-labs/icm-contracts` repo (like the ERC-8004 repo we installed via `forge install`) is structured as a Hardhat project — `package.json`, TypeScript config, Hardhat deployment scripts. Not a pure Solidity library that Foundry can resolve as a dependency.

We vendored the minimal interface directly from the `ava-labs/icm-contracts` v1.0.9 source: `TeleporterFeeInfo`, `TeleporterMessageInput`, `ITeleporterMessenger`, and `ITeleporterReceiver`. Around 40 lines of interface code instead of a full dependency pull. The messenger address (`0x253b2784c75e510dD0fF1da844684a1aC0aa5fcf`) is hardcoded — and that's actually correct, not a shortcut. It's deployed via Nick's method to the same address on every EVM chain by construction.

**Agentic Payments on Avalanche**

AgentWork is a trustless labor market where AI agents hire each other, deliver work, and settle payments with zero human involvement.

Every Avalanche primitive is load-bearing:

- AgentEscrow + USDC on C-Chain — employer locks payment at job creation, worker receives it only when ValidationRegistry.isValidated() returns true. ~2s settlement, no human approval.
- x402 — HTTP-native micro-payments gate service discovery. Any agent that can make an HTTP request can participate, no SDK or account required.
- ICM / Teleporter — agents on any Avalanche L1 dispatch jobs cross-chain via JobRelay.dispatchJob(). The intent travels via ICM; USDC settles on C-Chain. No bridging, no wrapping.
- ERC-8004 — on-chain agent identity and reputation. Payment release is gated on cryptographic proof of completion written to the Validation Registry. Reputation updates atomically with payment.

The track asks for agentic payments. Most submissions will use an agent to trigger a payment. AgentWork is the payment infrastructure agents run on.

> Secure payments infrastructure for AI agents

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

**The problem**
AI agents are quickly moving from chat to action. They book flights, issue refunds, pay vendors, buy API calls. But giving an agent real money today is a binary choice.

Give them nothing, and a human has to approve every dollar, which kills the whole point of automation. Give them everything, and one hallucination, one prompt injection, or one leaked API key drains your treasury.

There is no middle. That's why companies experimenting with autonomous agents quietly pull them out of production the moment money is involved.

**What Rein does**
Rein gives every AI agent its own spending account with on-chain guardrails the agent cannot override.

- Per-payment and monthly limits enforced by the smart account itself, not by a server someone can bypass.
- Payee allow-lists for vendor style agents like payroll, SaaS, and ads. Open mode with velocity limits for unbounded cases like customer refunds.
- Instant revocation. One click disables an agent's spending power immediately at the contract level.
- Zero blockchain UX. Operators never see an address, sign a transaction, or think about gas. Rein sponsors gas. They just see agents, balances, and limits.

**What it makes easier or safer**
- Customer support agents issuing refunds and credits to thousands of different customers without needing a human to click approve on each one.
- Ops agents paying vendors, SaaS, and ad platforms within a monthly cap, with a tight allow-list of approved payees.
- Finance teams get a clear audit trail, a revoke button, and a budget ceiling that a compromised agent physically cannot exceed.

Rein turns "should we let AI spend money?" from a yes or no policy debate into a question of how much. Bounded, revocable, auditable.

**Challenges we ran into**

Coming up with the best way to abstract blockchain as a backend and let non-crypto people interact with our app was difficult — customers shouldn't have to think about gas, addresses, or smart accounts to delegate spending to an agent.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Express.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Express.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Solodity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solodity-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

The **EAX Protocol** solves the privacy-relevance paradox and removes the friction of agentic commerce.

### 🔬 The Problem it Solves
*   **Surveillance-Free Targeting**: Current ads require invasive tracking to be relevant. EAX uses local ML and **Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE)** to match users with ads privately. Your browser knows what you want, but the advertiser never does until you buy.
*   **Unified Agentic Payments**: Buying from an ad traditionally requires a human to stop, redirect to a merchant site, and manually enter payment/shipping data. EAX integrates **Locus Rails** to power an **AI Purchasing Agent** that executes secure, one-click autonomous transactions directly within the ad interaction.

### 🚀 How it Makes Tasks Easier & Safer
*   **Easier**: It turns the "Discovery-to-Purchase" flow into a single click. The Locus Agent handles policy rules (auto-approvals for small amounts, confirmations for large ones), meaning users don't have to fill out messy checkout forms.
*   **Safer**: You never expose your credit card or main wallet address to unknown merchant sites. The **Locus Agent acts as a secure buffer**, using Locus’s built-in risk policies and audit logs to protect your funds from malicious or low-quality actors.

**Challenges we ran into**

*   **The "Discovery-to-Payment" Bridge**: Bridging the gap between an on-chain **FHE-encrypted match** and an off-chain **Autonomous Purchase** was a major orchestration challenge. We overcame this by building a custom SDK middleware that intercepts the decrypted advertiser ID and triggers the Locus Purchasing Agent flow, transforming a passive ad view into an active "Paygentic" transaction.
*   **Local ML Management**: Running a 90MB MobileBERT model entirely within a Chrome extension's sandbox required careful WASM memory management to ensure the classification remained fast and didn't bottleneck the browser, achieved through optimized lifecycle handling in our background service workers.

**Using PayWithLocus.com to leverage our suite.**

EAX Protocol leverages the **PayWithLocus** suite as the critical execution layer for **Autonomous Agentic Commerce**. We don't just use Locus for a simple checkout; we integrate it as the "brain" and "muscle" of our purchasing agent through three core pillars:

### 1. Unified Payment Orchestration (Locus Rails)
We utilize **Locus Rails** to bridge the gap between discovery and ownership. By integrating the Locus merchant and payment suite, EAX enables an ad to be more than just a link—it becomes a "Paygentic" terminal. Locus manages the movement of USDC/ATTN tokens from users to merchants, ensuring that liquidity flows securely in an agent-to-agent environment.

### 2. Intelligent Guardrails (Locus Policy Engine)
We leverage the **Locus Policy suite** to orchestrate risk-based autonomous spending. Instead of forcing a manual "Connect Wallet" for every $0.50 ad interaction, EAX uses Locus policies to set intelligent thresholds:
*   **Auto-Execution**: Micro-payments are handled autonomously by the Locus agent for a frictionless experience.
*   **Agentic Confirmation**: Mid-range purchases trigger the Locus inline confirmation flow.
*   **Safety Declines**: High-risk transactions are automatically blocked by the Locus guardrails.

### 3. Transparent Accountability (Locus Audit & Logging)
EAX utilizes the **Locus suite's auditing capabilities** to provide a "Black Box" recorder for human users. Every purchase executed by the AI agent is logged through the Locus-backed audit service, providing a permanent, transparent trail. This ensures that while the agent is autonomous, it remains fully accountable to the user, satisfying the core transparency requirements of the PayWithLocus ecosystem.

By combining **CoFHE (Privacy-First Intent)** with **Locus (Autonomous Execution)**, we have built the first end-to-end "Paygentic" loop that demonstrates the full power of the Locus suite in the next generation of digital commerce.

### 3pm
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/pm-7057) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Unchanted/3pm) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/3pmjs) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/0YdoIS2B0Oc) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-KJSSE%20GajShield%20Hack%20X-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://hack-x.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Every package, signed by humans. on-chain.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![PostgreSQL](https://img.shields.io/badge/PostgreSQL-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Hardhat](https://img.shields.io/badge/Hardhat-333333?style=flat-square) ![Fastify](https://img.shields.io/badge/Fastify-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

## The Problem It Solves

Every time a developer runs `npm install`, they are making a trust decision with zero information. They are saying: "I trust that these bytes are safe to run on my machine." Nothing enforces that. Nothing verifies it. You get bytes, and you hope.

This is not a hypothetical risk. The npm ecosystem has been hit repeatedly:

- A maintainer's account gets stolen, and a malicious version is live for hours before anyone notices
- A bad actor spends months building trust in an open source project, then slips in a backdoor right before a major release
- A maintainer themselves goes rogue and deliberately ships code that wipes files based on the user's IP address

In all of these cases, one person had one token, and that was enough.

npm's own "provenance attestations" just move the single point of failure from your npm token to your GitHub Actions secret. The structural problem is identical.

**3pm removes that single point of failure.**

Publishing a package through 3pm requires M-of-N co-signers to independently review and cryptographically approve the exact tarball bytes before anything reaches npm. Every approval is an EIP-712 signature made in the signer's own wallet - no one can publish alone, even if their npm account or CI token is completely compromised.

On the consumer side, 3pm verifies that the bytes you downloaded from npm are byte-for-byte identical to what the maintainers actually signed on-chain. A tampered package - whether published by a compromised account or a rogue maintainer - will have no matching on-chain record, or its hash will not match. Either way, you are told before any code runs on your machine.

Before signing a release, co-signers see a diff of exactly what changed since the last version, a heuristic scan for dangerous patterns, and a plain-English AI summary generated locally by Gemma 3. Code never leaves the reviewer's machine.

For teams auditing their dependencies, 3pm walks the full transitive dependency tree and checks every package against the OSV vulnerability database, runs typosquat detection to catch names like `expres` or `lodahs`, and verifies on-chain records - all in one command, suitable for CI gating.

A Chrome extension surfaces trust signals directly on npmjs.com package pages, so developers can see whether a package has verified on-chain releases before they decide to install it.

The result is a system where trust is not assumed - it is proven at every step, with an immutable on-chain record of who approved what and when.

**Challenges we ran into**

### Getting every signer to sign the exact same thing

The core guarantee of the multisig is that every co-signer independently signs an identical EIP-712 payload. The contract recovers each signer's address from their signature and checks it against the on-chain maintainers list - if even one byte of the signed message differs between what the proposer signed and what an approver signed, the recovered address is garbage and the transaction reverts.

This sounds simple until you're debugging why a valid-looking signature is failing on-chain. The culprit was the `nonce` field. The nonce is a `uint256` on-chain, a `BigInt` in the backend, and gets serialized to JSON as a string for storage. When the approver reconstructed the EIP-712 message, it was reading the nonce back as a string from the API response and passing it to the signing function as a string - while the proposer had signed it as a `BigInt`. EIP-712 encodes those differently. The signatures looked fine individually. They only broke when the contract tried to verify them together.

The fix was enforcing a single canonical type at every boundary: `BigInt` when constructing the payload for signing, `toString()` only for JSON transport, and `BigInt(nonce)` immediately on the receiving end before anything touches the signing path. Once that was consistent across the CLI and backend, the signatures started matching.

### ChainWhistle - Decentralised Whistleblower Protect
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/chainwhistle-411e) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://chainwhistle.vercel.app) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-KJSSE%20GajShield%20Hack%20X-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://hack-x.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Stake. Validate. Publish. Get paid. No middlemen.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![Express.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Express.js-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Whistleblowers carry enormous risk - retaliation, prosecution, and career destruction - with zero financial reward for the public value they create. Existing platforms (SecureDrop, Signal tips) solve the *delivery* problem but leave the economic and trust problems entirely unsolved:

- **No anonymity guarantees**: centralised platforms can be subpoenaed, hacked, or shut down.
- **No financial incentive**: leaking information of massive public value earns the source nothing.
- **No validator accountability**: there's no skin-in-the-game for the people deciding if a claim is real.
- **No outlet accountability**: a news org can win exclusive rights to a story and simply never publish it.

ChainWhistle solves all four by replacing platform trust with economic stakes and on-chain rules:

- **Whistleblowers** submit pseudonymously (wallet = identity). No registration, no email, no IP linkage at the protocol level. Claim content lives on IPFS; only CIDs hit the chain.
- **Validator Orgs** post a 1 ETH stake and vote on claim authenticity via commit-reveal. If their verdict is later contradicted by the oracle cycle, 5% of their stake is slashed.
- **News Outlets** post a 2 ETH stake and bid ETH for the right to break a verified story. If they win the bid but never publish, they are permanently blacklisted and their stake is seized.
- **Oracle Nodes** post a 0.5 ETH stake. Five are randomly selected per claim to verify actual publication. Minority voters are slashed 10% to deter collusion.

On the happy path, the winning bid escrow is split: **60% to the whistleblower**, 30% to validator orgs who voted correctly, 10% to the oracle majority. Bad behaviour is economically irrational, not merely unethical.

**Challenges we ran into**

**Alchemy `eth_getLogs` rate limits**
Our LLM server scans blocks on startup to catch missed events. Alchemy's free tier rejects any `eth_getLogs` call spanning more than a handful of blocks with `block range is too wide`. Fixed by chunking the scan into configurable 10-block batches, accumulating events across all chunks before processing.

**Keeping the Pinata JWT server-side**
Uploading to IPFS directly from the browser would expose the Pinata JWT in the client bundle. Proxied all uploads through the Express server (`POST /upload`, `POST /upload-text`) so the JWT never leaves `server/.env`.

**Commit-reveal salt persistence**
Validator orgs must retain their salt for up to 3 days between commit and reveal. A browser clear makes it unrecoverable. Solved by displaying the salt as a copyable hex string immediately after commit with a persistent warning banner until reveal is confirmed.

**7-state claim lifecycle in React**
Managing 7 on-chain states × 4 time-window deadlines in JSX conditionals became unmaintainable fast. Refactored into a single `getAvailableActions(claim, userRole, now)` utility that returns permitted actions for a given snapshot, making the UI fully declarative.

Data breaches expose millions of identity records annually
Third-party verification services become honeypots for attackers
Users have no control over their personal information once submitted
Sybil Attacks & Duplicate Registration

No mechanism to prove uniqueness without centralizing identity data

Friction in Privacy-Preserving Access Control

Age-gating requires revealing birthdate to unrelated services
Location verification exposes full addresses
Gender verification systems can't prevent discrimination

Lack of Portable, On-Chain Credentials

Identity verified on one platform can't be reused elsewhere
No interoperable standard for privacy-preserving proofs
Blockchain dApps have no trustless way to verify humans

What People Can Use It For

✅ Verify location for regional benefits (scholarships, job boards, utilities) without exposing full address
✅ Prove uniqueness to prevent being shadowbanned or rate-limited across platforms
✅ Mint portable identity NFT that works across multiple Web3 services
✅ Prove humanity with biometric liveness to prevent bot attacks
✅ Gender verification for community safety without revealing to third parties
For Platforms & Services:
🔐 Bot Prevention - Verify humans without CAPTCHA or surveillance
🕵️ Airdrop & Incentive Distribution - Prevent Sybil attacks on token distributions

**The problem it solves**

1.AI agents expose sensitive intent
When agents perform web searches, they reveal who you are, what you’re building, and your strategic direction through query patterns.

2.Enterprise IP leakage risk
R&D queries, debugging steps, and competitive analysis can unintentionally leak proprietary knowledge that defines your competitive advantage.

3.Centralized search = trust-based privacy
Current systems rely on centralized APIs, forcing users to trust privacy policies instead of having verifiable protection.

4.Data reuse threatens uniqueness
Collected queries may be stored or used for training, meaning your ideas could indirectly surface in outputs for competitors.

5.Need for privacy with guarantees, not promises
The agentic era demands cryptographic or mathematical privacy guarantees (e.g., zero-knowledge, local-first search, encrypted queries) instead of blind trust.

**Challenges we ran into**

1.Unintentional data leakage through agent queries
Every time your AI agent searches the web, it exposes sensitive context about your project, ideas, and internal workflows.

2.Lack of control over proprietary information
You don’t have visibility or control over how your queries are stored, processed, or potentially reused by centralized platforms.

3.No strong privacy guarantees in current systems
Existing tools rely on trust (privacy policies) instead of offering provable, mathematical privacy protections, leaving your IP vulnerable.

### MemoryLens
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/memorylens-3038) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/sambhandavale/memory_lens) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/ip8Ul9QXu-U) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-KJSSE%20GajShield%20Hack%20X-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://hack-x.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> The Assistive Augmented Memory Interface

![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![Three.JS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Three.JS-333333?style=flat-square) ![MongoDB](https://img.shields.io/badge/MongoDB-333333?style=flat-square) ![FastAPI](https://img.shields.io/badge/FastAPI-333333?style=flat-square) ![Deepface](https://img.shields.io/badge/Deepface-333333?style=flat-square) ![vosk](https://img.shields.io/badge/vosk-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Individuals facing cognitive impairment—such as amnesiacs, the elderly, and those with significant cognitive decline—experience profound suffering. The core of the issue is the **loss of personal continuity**:
**Social Anxiety**: Forgetting names and recent conversations leads to a deep-seated anxiety during social interactions.
**Isolation**: This fear often causes people to withdraw from society, leading to worsened social outcomes and loneliness.
**Loss of Identity**: Forgetting everyday events, items, and most importantly, the people they love, strips away the fabric of their daily lives.

### Our Solution
While modern technology often focuses on improving the context memory of AI and LLMs, we believe that intelligence should first serve the humans who need it most. **MemoryLens** shifts the focus back to helping people recognize their loved ones and reclaim their social autonomy.

The system utilizes smart glasses as a camera and microphone, paired with a phone that handles the complex processing.When a user encounters someone, the device identifies the face and displays the person’s name and relationship details directly on the lens.

### Making Life Easier and Safer
MemoryLens transforms how those with memory impairment navigate the world by making existing tasks safer and more intuitive:
**Effortless Identification**: Instead of the stress of trying to remember a face, users can simply ask "Who is this person?" to receive immediate audio or visual confirmation.
**The Memory Vault**: Users can access a "Memory Vault," which serves as a historical ledger of archived conversations.This allows them to recall what was recently discussed, such as a plan to check the garden or an upcoming birthday party.
**Background Learning**: The system "watches, listens, and learns" in the background, autonomously mapping relationships from raw dialogue so the user doesn't have to manage the tool themselves.
**Privacy & Longevity**: Because all face embeddings stay on the device, the user's most personal memories remain private and secure, ensuring the product remains a reliable companion for the long term.

**Challenges we ran into**

### 1. Fast & Private Face Recognition
**The Challenge**: Standard facial recognition is often too slow for real-time social interactions or relies too heavily on the cloud.
**The Solution**: We optimized our pipeline using **DeepFace** and **OpenCV**, storing all facial embeddings locally on the device.This ensures lightning-fast identification while keeping the user's most sensitive data completely private.

### 2. Live Audio & Semantic Understanding
**The Challenge**: It was difficult to stream live audio and "understand" the relationship between the user and the person they were talking to without manual input.
**The Solution**: We built a pipeline using **Vosk** for live listening and **Google Gemini** for **Zero-Shot NLP**. This allows the system to semantically analyze conversations in the background to autonomously identify names and relationships like "Son" or "Friend."

### 3. Optimizing the Memory Vault
**The Challenge**: Storing and retrieving months of conversations in a way that provides instant context was a major storage hurdle.
**The Solution**: We implemented a **Vector Database (MongoDB Atlas)** using **Cosine Similarity**. This allows the "Memory Vault" to instantly recall specific past interactions—like a mention of a birthday party or a garden—the moment a familiar face is detected.

Team **_init_2win** -- [Samarth Bhandavale](https://github.com/sambhandavale), [Ayush Singh](github.com/UserOfSpace), [Arnav Dandekar](https://github.com/4rnv)
