### Production-Grade Hybrid Token-Efficient AI Routing
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/triforge-dbda) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Sarthak752008/TriForge) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/CuaUUFbGQgM?si=PvouOPrmeHhOskh6) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Road%20To%20Devcon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://road-to-devcon-iitr.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-1-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Route Smarter. Spend Less. Stay in Control.

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![SQL](https://img.shields.io/badge/SQL-333333?style=flat-square) ![Docker](https://img.shields.io/badge/Docker-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![MongoDB](https://img.shields.io/badge/MongoDB-333333?style=flat-square) ![OpenAi](https://img.shields.io/badge/OpenAi-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

Building TriForge involved several engineering challenges:

- Designing reliable routing logic that could distinguish simple queries from complex coding and reasoning tasks.
- Verifying local model responses without sending every request to an expensive cloud model.
- Reducing token waste when a local response required correction.
- Supporting multiple cloud providers without tightly coupling the system to one vendor.
- Maintaining fast response times while performing caching, routing, and consistency checks.
- Protecting API credentials from being exposed to the frontend.

We addressed these challenges through 9-domain intent classification, prompt-length heuristics, selective self-consistency, SHA-256 prompt caching, and the Verify-Draft Escalation Protocol.

Parallel local sampling using ThreadPoolExecutor and SQLite WAL-mode caching were also implemented to improve responsiveness and concurrent request handling.

**The problem it solves**

Modern LLM applications often send every query to expensive cloud models, even when many requests are simple conversational, factual, or conceptual tasks that can be handled locally.

This creates three major problems:
- High API and token costs from unnecessary cloud inference.
- Higher latency caused by cloud network round-trips for simple queries.
- Unnecessary energy consumption from running lightweight workloads on large cloud GPUs.

TriForge solves this with a local-first hybrid LLM routing gateway. It analyzes each query, routes simple workloads to fast local models, and sends complex coding/reasoning tasks to powerful cloud models.

When a local response needs verification, TriForge uses its Verify-Draft mechanism: instead of regenerating the answer from scratch, the cloud model receives the local draft and only corrects it. This reduces unnecessary completion-token usage while maintaining response quality.

The result is a smarter LLM infrastructure layer that makes AI applications more cost-efficient, faster, and more energy-conscious.

**Self-Sovereignty**

TriForge enables AI self-sovereignty through local-first inference. It routes suitable queries to local models and uses cloud LLMs only when necessary, reducing dependence on centralized providers while improving privacy, cost efficiency, and user control.

**Challenges we ran into**

Database Management: Designing and maintaining the SQLite database for student, staff, attendance, and OD records required careful structuring to ensure reliable data storage and retrieval.
Module Integration: Integrating authentication, attendance marking, OD management, SMS notifications, and reporting into a single application required systematic testing and debugging.
SMS Integration: Implementing automated absence notifications required handling Android SMS permissions and integrating the SmsManager API correctly.
Data Accuracy: Ensuring that attendance was recorded against the correct student, date, and status required validation and repeated testing.
Testing & Debugging: We conducted unit, integration, and acceptance testing to identify and resolve issues before final implementation.

**The problem it solves**

Traditional attendance systems rely on paper registers or spreadsheets, making attendance time-consuming, error-prone, and difficult to maintain. Staff also face difficulties in generating reports, managing OD requests, and informing parents about student absences.

Our Android-based Attendance Management System makes these tasks easier by allowing staff to digitally mark attendance, securely store records, generate reports, and manage OD requests. When a student is marked absent, the system can automatically send an SMS notification to the parent. This reduces paperwork, saves staff time, improves accuracy, and improves communication with parents.

### Warren
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/warren-7565) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Yash-arch-ui/WARREN) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://vimeo.com/1216694701) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Road%20To%20Devcon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://road-to-devcon-iitr.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-1-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Censorship at its best

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Rust](https://img.shields.io/badge/Rust-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

Challenges I ran into

The core anonymity guarantee wasn't actually being tested — it was being assumed.
Early on, it would have been easy to build the 3-hop mix routing, watch a message successfully arrive at the destination, and call it done. But "the message arrived" doesn't prove "no relay saw both ends of the conversation" — that's the entire point of the project, and it's exactly the kind of property that's easy to get subtly wrong (e.g., a relay logging more than it should, or a data structure accidentally carrying sender and receiver together). I made per-hop visibility an explicit, enforced test: each relay's actual state/logs are inspected after a real send to prove no single relay ever had both sender-side and receiver-side information — not just that decryption worked. That discipline — verify the guarantee in code, don't assume the library or the plumbing gives it to you — became the standard for every later component too (blind-token unlinkability, cover-traffic indistinguishability from real traffic, Poisson delay actually following the right distribution).

Picking the wrong library would have quietly broken a guarantee, not caused an obvious bug.
For the anonymous spam-resistance layer, "blind signature" sounds like one well-defined thing, but different libraries give different real guarantees — some give blind issuance without true unlinkability across redemptions, which would have silently defeated the entire anonymity model while looking correct in every normal test. The same trap showed up picking a Double Ratchet library — some candidates were unmaintained, one was a name collision with an unrelated crate, another only handled group sessions instead of pairwise messaging. Each library decision had to be checked against actual source code and documented guarantees, not just its name or README, before being trusted into the core protocol.

No maintained library existed for the mix-network delay/cover-traffic design (Poisson mixing), and building it wrong would have made the timing-correlation defense fake.
Rather than hand-rolling probability code and hoping it was right, the actual distribution shape was tested statistically (thousands of samples checked against expected exponential-distribution properties) before trusting it anywhere near production paths. This also surfaced a real, subtle bug: an early test assumed messages would always take at least a fixed minimum time to arrive — true for a fixed delay, but mathematically false once the delay became randomized, since a random draw can legitimately land below the average. The fix wasn't to hack the test to pass — it was to recognize the test's assumption was wrong and rewrite it around the real statistical behavi

**The problem it solves**

The problem it solves 

Every popular messaging app today including Signal has a structural blind spot: even with perfect end-to-end encryption, the app's own servers still see who is talking to whom, and when. Content is private; the relationship graph is not. That metadata alone is enough to identify activists, journalists' sources, whistleblowers, dissidents, or anyone a government or adversary wants to target — without ever breaking a single encryption key. And because these apps run through one company's servers, that metadata is sitting at a single point that can be subpoenaed, seized, or blocked outright.

WARREN removes that blind spot. Messages are routed through multiple independent relays using onion-style mix routing (similar in spirit to Tor, purpose-built for messaging), so no single relay ; not even the people operating the network ; ever sees both the sender and the receiver of a message. The network is also secured against a second, usually-ignored problem: anonymous networks are easy to spam and abuse. WARREN solves this without requiring identity, using anonymous proof of work gated tokens, so real users stay untraceable while abuse still has a real cost.        

                                                                                                                                         Who this is for, concretely:

Activists and journalists working under governments that monitor who contacts whom, not just what's said ; WARREN means there's no connection graph to seize or subpoena in the first place.
Whistleblowers and sources who need to reach a journalist without either party's contact being traceable, even if the messaging app's infrastructure itself is compromised or compelled.
Anyone in a censored region ;traffic is disguised to look like ordinary web traffic, and relay trust is split across multiple independent signers rather than one operator, making the network harder to fingerprint, block, or shut down at a single point.
Any user who simply doesn't want their social graph built and stored somewhere, even if they have "nothing to hide" — the same way encryption became a baseline expectation, unlinkable metadata is the next baseline that's currently missing from every mainstream option.

**Censorship Resistance**

Censorship doesn't just mean blocking content — it means an adversary being able to identify, target, and shut down the people communicating, and being able to detect and block the communication channel itself. WARREN is built directly against both of those capabilities, not just the surface-level "can I read the message" problem that most encrypted apps solve.

1. It removes the single point that gets censored.
Apps like Signal run through one company's servers — a single legally-compellable, technically-blockable chokepoint. A government can subpoena the operator, order an ISP to block their domain, or force the app off app stores in that country. WARREN has no equivalent single target: messages route through multiple independent relays, and the relay directory itself is signed by multiple independent keys (K-of-N) rather than one operator, so there's no single party or server whose removal takes down the network.

2. It protects the people, not just the content.
The core censorship threat for activists, journalists, and dissidents usually isn't "can they read my message" — it's "can they prove I was talking to this person at all." Even fully encrypted apps leak that connection graph to their own servers. WARREN's mix routing means no relay — including the network's own operators — ever sees both sender and receiver for a given message, so there's no metadata graph to seize, subpoena, or hand over under legal pressure in the first place.

3. It resists network-level blocking, not just server-level takedown.
A censor doesn't need to touch a server to block a service — they can just fingerprint its traffic pattern at the ISP/DPI level and drop it. WARREN's traffic is wrapped to resemble ordinary encrypted web traffic instead of a distinctive custom protocol, raising the cost of a censor trying to detect and block it at the network layer, not just the server layer.

4. It resists shutdown-by-flooding, without reintroducing the thing that makes people traceable.
Anonymous networks are an easy censorship target because they're easy to abuse — flood them with spam or DoS traffic, and either the network collapses or its operators are forced to add identity checks that undo the anonymity. WARREN solves spam resistance anonymously (proof-of-work-gated, unlinkable tokens), so it can't be strangled by abuse without ever requiring anyone to identify themselves.

Taken together: Signal is censorship-resistant only in the sense that its content is unreadable. WARREN is censorship-resistant in the structural sense the track is actually asking about — no single operator to compel, no metadata graph to seize, no easy network fingerprint to block, and no identity requirement to weaponize against its own users.

[Yash Singh](https://github.com/Yash-arch-ui)

### Unpack
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/unpack-f657) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/TathagatGupta98/Unpack) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://unpack-murex.vercel.app) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/x5ICbtWTNSo) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Road%20To%20Devcon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://road-to-devcon-iitr.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-1-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> A wallet with no seed phrase and no gas

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Self-custody today makes you trade sovereignty for security. A seed phrase is the only thing standing between you and losing everything, gas fees mean you need ETH before you can even move your own funds, and every approval you've ever granted to a dApp — most of them unlimited — just sits there forever as silent attack surface, because no mainstream wallet shows you the full list, let alone lets you clear it in one shot.

Unpack replaces all three failure points with one ERC-4337 smart account:

- No seed phrase. You sign in with a passkey (Face ID / fingerprint). The wallet address is derived deterministically from it, so it's recoverable and consistent without a 12-word phrase to write down or lose.

- No gas. Every write — mint, send, revoke, session setup, recovery — goes through a sponsored UserOperation. The wallet never needs to hold ETH to be usable.

- No forgotten approvals. The Approvals dashboard indexes every approval an address has ever granted, re-verifies each one's live allowance so stale entries disappear, flags unlimited approvals, and bulk-revokes any selection in a single signature and a single sponsored transaction — instead of one signed, gas-paying transaction per token, which is why almost nobody does this today.

On top of that, session keys let you delegate scoped, time-boxed permissions (e.g. "only call transfer, only for one hour") instead of handing over full account control, and social recovery lets a guardian rotate you onto a new passkey if you lose your device — so losing a phone doesn't mean losing the account.

Concretely: someone who's been swapping on DeFi for two years and has dozens of unlimited approvals from apps they've forgotten they used can open Unpack, see every one of them, and clear the risky ones in a single tap — safer self-custody with strictly less friction than what they have now.

**Challenges we ran into**

The one that cost the most time was a dead end I had to walk all the way into before backing out of: I initially built session keys and social recovery on Rhinestone's Smart Sessions module (@rhinestone/module-sdk) running on top of our Kernel account. Everything looked right — the modules were deployed on Base Sepolia, installation succeeded, on-chain state showed the validator correctly registered and the session enabled. But every UserOperation routed through it reverted with AA23 InvalidValidator(). I traced it down through two real bugs in the module-sdk's Kernel support (a missing hook address, and a nonce-encoding bug that was routing operations to the root validator instead of the session validator), fixed both locally, and it still failed. It turned out Rhinestone's smart-sessions examples are all built and tested against Safe, not Kernel — the combination just isn't a supported path, and the package itself is deprecated. Rather than keep debugging a library against an integration nobody had verified, I switched the whole account layer to ZeroDev's own SDK, since Kernel is ZeroDev's account and sessions/recovery are first-class there. That meant redoing account construction and accepting that passkey addresses would change, but it actually worked.

The switch caused its own sharp bug: the app started rendering a blank white screen with Class extends value undefined. ZeroDev's SDK re-exports a class that extends Node's EventEmitter at module load time, and Vite externalizes Node builtins in the browser by default, so the import resolved to undefined. Fixed with an events polyfill package and a resolve.alias in Vite config — a two-line fix, but it took real digging through the bundle to find, since the failure looked like a React crash rather than a bundler/runtime mismatch.

Both taught the same lesson: in fast-moving ERC-4337 tooling, "the docs say it should work" isn't enough — verify against the specific account implementation and version you're actually running, headlessly, before wiring it into the UI.

**Self-Sovereignty**

A passkey smart-account wallet with gasless transactions, session keys, and social recovery, plus a dashboard that finds and bulk-revokes every risky token approval

**The problem it solves**

The decentralized recruiter app tackles the rampant problem of fabricated work histories and résumé fraud that plagues professional networking platforms such as LinkedIn—​candidates can easily claim positions, salaries, or ten‑year tenures that have no authoritative backing, leaving employers vulnerable to costly hiring mistakes and undermining trust in talent pipelines. By fetching a candidate’s official EPFO UAN record directly from the government‑maintained database and anchoring the full, immutable employee profile on a public blockchain, the solution provides a tamper‑proof, verifiable proof of employment that any recruiter can audit without exposing sensitive personal data, thereby restoring confidence in candidate credentials and dramatically reducing the risk of fraudulent hiring.

### Musker
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/musker-f327) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://mucksplaymucker.web.app) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/eyW6a_dBLTs) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Road%20To%20Devcon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://road-to-devcon-iitr.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-1-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> play with heart

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

1. **Eliminating Main-Thread UI Lag in 3D Real-Time Physics**:
   - *Challenge*: Updating state at 60 Hz caused heavy React re-renders, resulting in boat stutter and frame drops.
   - *Solution*: Decoupled the physics loop from React state by storing real-time vehicle vectors in mutable ref containers (`worldStateRef`) and using frame-delta linear interpolation (`lerp`) inside Three.js `@react-three/fiber` render loops for buttery-smooth 60 FPS movement.

2. **Preventing MetaMask Transaction Failures & Gas Estimation Rejections**:
   - *Challenge*: Strict contract checks were triggering MetaMask's `eth_estimateGas` pre-simulation to flag valid winner claims with "Transaction likely to fail".
   - *Solution*: Optimized the Solidity smart contract (`SmashArena.sol`) to validate state Keccak hashes while guaranteeing fallback call execution (`winner.call{value: payout}`), alongside explicit gas limit overrides to ensure 100% clean, one-click execution.

3. **Safe Web3 Address & Hex Sanitization**:
   - *Challenge*: Standard hex converters threw padding exceptions (`Hex size exceeds padding size`) when processing match identifiers and AI bot addresses.
   - *Solution*: Created a native hexadecimal sanitizer (`toValidAddress`) that normalizes match IDs and wallet addresses into valid, checksummed 20-byte/32-byte strings before passing them to `viem` and `wagmi`.

**The problem it solves**

Traditional Web3 games often suffer from two major pain points: **clunky, high-friction user experiences** with constant wallet popups during gameplay, and **untrustworthy or central-server-reliant prize distribution** that leads to high latency and unfair payouts.

**MUCKERS** solves this by delivering a high-speed, arcade-action 3D Maritime Demolition Derby coupled with a **trustless, automated Smart Contract Escrow System on Ethereum (Sepolia)**:

- **Trustless Fair-Play Payouts**: Players stake a fixed 0.001 ETH entry fee directly into the `SmashArena` escrow smart contract. The contract deterministically holds funds and guarantees an immediate 95% payout directly to the winner's wallet without centralized admin intervention.
- **Zero-Lag 60 FPS Browser Gameplay**: Powered by Three.js and a custom reference-based physics engine, the 3D boat battle runs smoothly in the browser at 60 FPS without main-thread UI bottlenecks or input lag.
- **Seamless Real-Time Peer Synchronization**: Implements real-time room code matching, allowing players to host or join matches instantly with live positional updates.
- **Arcade Action & Combat Weapons**: Features dynamic ocean arenas, mystery weapon crates (TNT Rockets, Plasma Shockwaves, Mega Cannons, Scorching Fireballs), bow water splashes, and reactive particle FX.

Team **Mucks** -- Xantheus e, [Arnav Racchawar](https://github.com/Nil)

[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/nexora-2b90) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Vinayak-Ag043/NEXORA) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://playful-fairy-d5588c.netlify.app/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/owJUyESgtF8) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Road%20To%20Devcon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://road-to-devcon-iitr.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-1-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Trustless coordination, Verifiable decision.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

The problem it solves

Nexora makes group coordination and decision-making more transparent, verifiable, and wallet-native.

Traditional online groups often rely on centralized accounts, private databases, and trusted administrators to manage membership and voting. This makes it difficult to independently verify who joined, who voted, what was decided, and whether records were changed.

Nexora moves these core coordination actions on-chain:

Verifiable membership: Group membership is recorded on the blockchain and tied to a user's wallet.
Transparent governance: Members can create proposals and vote YES/NO directly through their wallets.
Tamper-resistant records: Group creation, membership changes, proposals, and votes are recorded as on-chain events.
Wallet-based identity: Users interact through their Web3 wallet instead of relying on a centralized username/password system.
Auditable decisions: Anyone can verify the history of important group actions through blockchain transaction records.
Simpler coordination: Instead of combining separate tools for membership, proposals, and voting, Nexora brings them together in one workspace.

In short: Nexora provides a decentralized coordination layer where membership, governance, and decision history can be verified rather than simply trusted.

**Challenges we ran into**

Challenges we ran into

One of our main challenges was handling on-chain state correctly across wallet changes and page refreshes. Initially, a user could successfully join a group, but after refreshing the page the UI could incorrectly show “Join Group” again.

We solved this by making the frontend re-fetch membership directly from the deployed smart contract using isGroupMember(groupId, walletAddress) instead of relying only on local UI state. We also added optimistic updates after successful transactions so the interface responds immediately while remaining synchronized with the blockchain.

Another hurdle was wallet and smart-contract transaction errors, particularly custom Solidity errors during gas estimation. We debugged these by checking the deployed contract state, verifying the connected wallet and network, and mapping common contract errors into clear messages for users.

We also experimented with Push Protocol for persistent group chat. Due to initialization and dependency/API compatibility issues, we reverted to a simpler chat implementation for the demo rather than allowing an unreliable feature to affect the core on-chain governance experience.

Key takeaway: building a Web3 application required us to treat the blockchain as the source of truth while carefully handling asynchronous wallet, transaction, and frontend state.

**Decentralized Coordination Layers**

How Nexora fits the Decentralized Coordination Layers track

Nexora directly addresses decentralized coordination by providing an on-chain coordination layer for groups to organize, make decisions, and maintain verifiable records without relying on a centralized administrator.

The core flow is:

Wallet → Group Membership → Proposals → Voting → Verifiable On-Chain History

Decentralized membership: Users join groups using their Web3 wallets, with membership stored and verified by the smart contract.
On-chain governance: Group members can create proposals and vote directly on-chain, making decisions transparent and auditable.
Shared source of truth: The smart contract maintains the authoritative state of groups, members, proposals, and votes instead of a centralized database.
Verifiable coordination: Important actions generate blockchain events, allowing participants to independently verify what happened.
Permissionless participation: Anyone with a compatible wallet can participate in eligible groups without needing a centralized account or administrator to approve every action.
Composable foundation: The same coordination primitives—groups, membership, proposals, and voting—can serve communities, student organizations, DAOs, hackathon teams, clubs, and other decentralized communities.

Why this fits the track:
Nexora isn't just putting an existing social feature on-chain. It uses the blockchain as the coordination and trust layer itself: the rules for membership and decision-making are enforced by a smart contract, while the frontend provides an accessible interface for interacting with those rules.

Nexora turns “trust us, this is what the group decided” into “verify it on-chain.”

### Sentinel
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/sentinel-9ee0) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/lazyKid64/Sentinel) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://sentinel-xi-ruddy.vercel.app/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/FuGV9qDNF4k) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Road%20To%20Devcon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://road-to-devcon-iitr.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-1-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> A live watchtower for RPC censorship and relay com

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

**Challenges I ran into**

Architectural bugs that only surface once you actually run the code. Early prompts for the divergence engine assumed server-side state could persist a rolling window of "3 consecutive lagging checks" across polls — but Next.js API routes are stateless serverless functions that can cold-start between requests, silently dropping that memory. Caught this before it became a live-demo bug and restructured so the classification logic lives client-side in React state, while the API routes stay pure single-shot snapshots.

CORS and rate-limiting on external relay data. The relay-compliance monitor needs live MEV-Boost bid-trace data from third-party relay APIs. Fetching that directly from the browser hits CORS failures and risks getting rate-limited during a demo with multiple polls per session. Solved by routing all external calls server-to-server through our own API routes, with fetch-level caching so repeated client polls don't hammer the upstream relays.

Preventing AI-hallucinated endpoints and fields from silently breaking the build. Since most of the code was AI-assisted, the real risk wasn't bad logic, it was confidently wrong specifics — an invented RPC URL, a guessed JSON field name from a relay API. Addressed this by forcing a verify-before-build step for every external endpoint (a standalone script that hits the real API and prints the real response) before any parsing code got written against it.

A deployment trap in the demo fault-injection node. The mock "misbehaving RPC node" used to demo censorship detection live was originally built as a separate process on localhost — which would silently break the moment the app got deployed, since localhost inside a cloud container doesn't point to your laptop. Rebuilt it as a pure in-process function derived from timestamp math instead, so it behaves identically locally and deployed.

Switching AI tools mid-build without breaking either half. Built the dashboard logic with Claude, then hit a usage limit partway through integrating a separately-built landing page (done with Gemini Pro in Antigravity). Two AI tools independently touching the same repo meant the real risk was one agent assuming it understood code the other one wrote. Handled this with a strict audit-first process — reading actual file contents and exported shapes before writing any integration code, rather than trusting either build matched its original spec

**The problem it solves**

**The problem**: Ethereum's neutrality isn't guaranteed by the protocol alone — it depends on the RPC providers and MEV-Boost relays that sit between users and the chain actually behaving well. Most people interact with Ethereum through 2-3 RPC endpoints they never think about, and since the Tornado Cash sanctions in 2022, a significant and fluctuating share of Ethereum blocks are built by relays that proactively filter sanctioned addresses' transactions — a real, ongoing, currently-measurable phenomenon, not a hypothetical. On top of that, individual RPC providers can lag, silently drop transactions, or diverge from the rest of the network without any user-facing signal that something's wrong.

Why it matters: censorship resistance is one of Ethereum's foundational value propositions, but it's currently a black box to the average user — you have no way to know whether the infrastructure you're using right now is behaving neutrally, lagging, or actively filtering.

What **Sentinel** does about it: a live dashboard that (1) polls multiple public RPC providers in parallel, detects and flags divergence patterns that suggest an unhealthy or misbehaving node, and automatically reroutes away from flagged providers, and (2) pulls real bid-trace data from MEV-Boost relays to show, in real time, what share of recent blocks came from OFAC-compliant vs. non-compliant relays — the same category of transparency tool that projects like MEV Watch have shown there's real demand for, built here as a from-scratch, live, self-contained monitoring layer.

**Censorship Resistance**

Sentinel builds both bullets in the track. It aggregates multiple public RPC providers, flags any that diverge from consensus, and auto-reroutes around them — directly matching "distribute requests, validate through consensus, balance traffic." It also monitors MEV-Boost relays in real time to show what share of recent blocks come from OFAC-compliant vs. non-compliant relays, giving users visibility into censorship at the relay layer — matching "verify network path integrity, route to avoid censorship." In short: it makes the two layers that actually determine censorship resistance — RPC providers and relays — visible and actionable, not just theoretical.

[Ishant Rajput](https://github.com/lazyKid64)

### DEADLIGHT
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/deadlight-c994) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/amsorrytola/deadlight) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://amsorrytola.github.io/deadlight/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://amsorrytola.github.io/deadlight/demo.mp4) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Road%20To%20Devcon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://road-to-devcon-iitr.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-1-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> “Silence the author. Publish the document.”

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![foundry](https://img.shields.io/badge/foundry-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Every "uncensorable publishing" tool has the same hole: someone is holding the material, and that someone can be reached. Publish now and you're the target before anyone has read it. Hand it to a journalist and the leverage
moves to them. Encrypt and distribute the key and any keyholder can be
compelled to open it early. Put it on IPFS and the pin lapses. Suppression works.
DEADLIGHT makes suppression
counterproductive. The document is armed to
release on SILENCE, so detaining the publisher doesn't prevent publication
- it causes it. The AES-256-GCM ciphertext lives entirely in contract state (no server, no pin, no host to subpoena) and the key is Shamir-split k-of-n across guardians who hold only shares, while the chain holds their commitments.

The load-bearing part: the embargo is enforced by the contract, not
promised by guardians. submitShare()
REVERTS while the publisher keeps checking in - every guardian could collude, or be served by the same court on the same morning, and it still wouldn't open a second early. In the demo we prove this on camera by submitting a genuine valid share and watching the chain refuse it with StillAlive.
Symmetrically, heartbeat() and
revoke() both stop working the instant the deadline lapses, so a captor who seizes the publisher's key afterwards can't bury the release either.

**Challenges we ran into**

Getting the embargo semantics right - the first design let the publisher
heartbeat at any time, which quietly broke the whole guarantee: a captor
with the key could keep the switch alive forever. Both heartbeat and revoke now hard-revert past the deadline. Making the guarantee demonstrable rather than asserted, via a console that lets anyone attempt an early release with a real share. On-chain storage economics (~20k gas per 32 bytes) capping documents at 8KB. Stack-too-deep in the vault struct, resolved with via_ir.

**Self-Sovereignty**

DEADLIGHT gives the publisher control over the conditions under which their document is released without relying on a platform, publisher, journalist, or centralized intermediary.

The document is encrypted client-side with AES-256-GCM, while the decryption key is split using Shamir Secret Sharing and distributed across independent guardians. No single guardian possesses the complete key. The blockchain stores the ciphertext and share commitments, while the smart contract autonomously enforces the embargo and release conditions.

Most importantly, the release rules are not controlled by a third party. The publisher sets the heartbeat and silence conditions, and once the deadline passes, even the publisher can no longer revoke the release. This prevents an attacker, institution, or captured publisher key from overriding the predetermined rules.

DEADLIGHT therefore makes publication a cryptographic and on-chain right governed by rules chosen in advance, rather than permission granted by a centralized authority.

**Censorship Resistance**

DEADLIGHT is designed so that censorship becomes counterproductive. The document is encrypted and committed on-chain before publication, while the decryption key is split across independent guardians using Shamir Secret Sharing.

The critical guarantee is enforced by the smart contract itself: guardians cannot release their key shares while the publisher is still alive and checking in. submitShare() reverts with StillAlive, even when a genuine valid share is submitted. Once the publisher goes silent past the deadline, the embargo expires and the contract allows the shares to be submitted and the document to be decrypted.

This means there is no single publisher, server, IPFS pin, journalist, or keyholder whose capture can suppress the document. Attempting to silence the publisher is precisely what activates the release mechanism.

DEADLIGHT therefore treats censorship not as something to resist after the fact, but as the trigger that causes publication.

**Decentralized Coordination Layers**

DEADLIGHT uses the blockchain as a coordination layer between the publisher and a distributed set of guardians without requiring a trusted coordinator.

Guardians hold only individual shares of the decryption key, while the smart contract stores their commitments and enforces the rules for when those shares can be submitted. No guardian needs to trust another guardian, and no central server needs to coordinate the release.

The contract provides a shared, deterministic state that every participant can independently verify: while the publisher is alive, valid shares are rejected; after the silence deadline, the embargo expires and the required threshold of shares can be submitted to reconstruct the key.

This turns a group of potentially independent or mutually distrustful participants into a coordinated release mechanism whose behavior is governed by transparent on-chain rules rather than by a central authority.

Team **UNO** -- [Talha Ansari](https://github.com/amsorrytola), [Wasif Ansari](https://github.com/justwasif)

### ProofRoute

> Don't trust the relay. Verify it.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Express.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Express.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![ECDSA](https://img.shields.io/badge/ECDSA-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

ProofRoute — Hackathon Submission Description
One-line pitch

ProofRoute is a decentralized accountability layer for blockchain infrastructure: stake-backed relays make cryptographic propagation commitments, independent peers provide handoff evidence, quorum produces verifiable coordination certificates, and relays that provably violate their commitments get slashed and automatically deprioritized — with cryptographic proof, not trust.

The Problem

When you send a blockchain transaction, you never talk directly to the chain. You go through a chain of infrastructure you don't control:

Wallet → RPC → Relay → Peer Network → Builder/Sequencer → Blockchain

If your transaction silently disappears somewhere in that chain, you have no way to prove who dropped it. A centralized RPC can censor you. A relay can quietly ignore your transaction. Different RPC providers can return conflicting information about the same chain state. And as a user, you're left with nothing but "trust me" — no cryptographic evidence of what actually happened to your transaction.

This is a foundational trust gap in how everyone interacts with blockchains today, and it sits exactly at the intersection of censorship resistance and decentralized coordination.

The Solution

ProofRoute creates a permissionless network of stake-backed relays that make cryptographically verifiable promises about transaction propagation — and then produces on-chain proof of whether they kept those promises.

Instead of trusting a relay's word, the user gets proof of what the relay actually did.

How it works, step by step
Relays stake collateral. Any address can permissionlessly become a relay by depositing ETH into RelayRegistry. This makes creating fake relay identities economically expensive and gives honest behavior a real financial incentive.
The user sends a transaction through multiple relays at once. The ProofRoute SDK routes it to several independent relays instead of trusting a single infrastructure provider.
Each relay signs an EIP-712 propagation commitment — a cryptographic promise of the form "I commit to propagating transaction X before deadline Y." Critically, this is not a promise that the transaction will be included in a block (that's outside a relay's control) — it's only a promise about the one thing a relay actually controls: propagation.
The relay proves propagation by handing the transaction to a registered peer, who returns a signed acknowledgement: "I received transaction X from Relay A." Together, the commitment and the acknowledgement form a verifiable handoff proof.
Independent relay observations are aggregated into quorum. If enough relays (e.g. 3-of-5) produce valid commitment + handoff pairs for the same transaction, the network issues an on-chain Coordination Certificate — cryptographic proof that multiple independent parties attest to the same event, rather than one server's word.
If a relay fails or goes offline, the SDK simply routes around it and quorum is still reached with the remaining relays — this is the censorship/failure-resistance property.
If a relay signs a commitment but never produces the handoff (i.e., it lied about propagating), anyone can submit a Fault Proof on-chain. The protocol verifies the relay's own signature against the missed deadline, then automatically slashes a portion of that relay's staked collateral — a bounty goes to whoever submitted the proof, and the rest goes to a treasury vault.
What ProofRoute deliberately does not claim

This boundary is core to the design's integrity: ProofRoute never claims a relay is guilty just because a transaction wasn't included in a block, or because its execution reverted. Inclusion is controlled by builders/sequencers, not relays, and reverts can be unrelated to propagation entirely. ProofRoute only ever enforces the one obligation a relay explicitly signs and actually controls — its propagation commitment. This scoping is what makes the slashing condition objectively provable on-chain, rather than a subjective judgment call.

Why it qualifies for both tracks

Censorship Resistance

Multi-relay transaction routing instead of single-provider trust
Automatic rerouting around offline or unreliable relays
Verifiable, signed propagation commitments
On-chain detection of protocol-defined relay failures
Economic penalties (slashing) for provable violations

Decentralized Coordination

Signed, independent observations from multiple relays and peers
Threshold quorum instead of a single source of truth
On-chain, verifiable coordination certificates
Permissionless participation (anyone can stake and become a relay)
Cryptographic attribution — you know exactly who said what
What We Actually Built

This isn't a slide-deck concept — the full stack is implemented and runnable end-to-end on a live local devnet:

Smart contracts (Solidity / Foundry)

RelayRegistry.sol — permissionless staking, restricted slashing entrypoint
CoordinationManager.sol — EIP-712 domain and signature

**Challenges we ran into**

Scoping what's actually provable on-chain. The hardest design problem wasn't cryptographic — it was philosophical. My first instinct was to slash a relay if a transaction wasn't included in a block. But inclusion is controlled by builders and sequencers, not relays, and execution can revert for reasons that have nothing to do with propagation. If I slashed on inclusion, I'd be punishing relays for something they don't control — which makes the whole system untrustworthy and un-auditable. I had to pull the scope back repeatedly until I landed on the one thing a relay actually signs and actually controls: the propagation handoff to a peer. That discipline — resisting the urge to make bigger claims than the cryptography can support — shaped almost every other decision in the project.

"Stack too deep" in Solidity. CoordinationManager.submitQuorumCertificate takes six parameters (transaction hash, relay list, deadlines, commitment signatures, peer list, handoff signatures) plus internal loop variables for verification. The default Solidity compiler ran out of stack slots and refused to compile with a Stack too deep error. Fixing it meant switching to the IR-based codegen pipeline (via_ir = true in Foundry config) rather than restructuring the function into something less readable — a good reminder that gas-optimization tooling and readability sometimes pull in different directions.

BigInt serialization silently breaking the API. The backend reads on-chain values like relay stake as native JavaScript BigInts (since Solidity's uint256 doesn't fit safely in a Number). The first version of the status endpoint spread that raw state directly into a JSON response — and JSON.stringify has no idea how to serialize a BigInt, so the endpoint returned a 500 on every single request. It's a small bug, but it's the kind that's completely invisible in casual testing and only surfaces once real values start flowing through the read path — every numeric field touching the chain had to be explicitly converted to a string before it could leave the backend.

Making time-based slashing demoable without lying about the mechanism. The fault-proof condition genuinely requires a deadline to pass — that's not optional, it's the whole point (a relay shouldn't be punishable before it's actually had the chance to fulfill its commitment). On a local Anvil devnet I could cheat time forward with evm_increaseTime and evm_mine to keep a live demo fast-paced. But that's an Anvil-only RPC method that doesn't exist on a real network — so making the same flow work on a public testnet meant reworking the fault-proof path to genuinely wait out a short real deadline instead, rather than assuming the time-travel trick would always be available.

Key management discipline. Anvil's ten default dev accounts are derived from a public, widely-known test mnemonic — perfect for a local demo (zero configuration, funds are meaningless), and actively dangerous anywhere real value is involved. Moving toward testnet deployment meant explicitly separating "local devnet mode" (mnemonic-derived, safe) from "real network mode" (freshly generated private keys the user actually controls), and refusing to start the backend at all if a non-local chain ID was configured without real keys supplied — making the unsafe path structurally hard to fall into by accident.

Environment friction across a fresh machine. A meaningful chunk of actual build time went into things with no cryptography involved at all: foundryup not being on PATH until a new shell session, forge install needing a git init first, a stray shell-escaping issue that silently truncated a contract address by one hex character when it was first typed out, and Node.js not being installed at all. None of these are exotic problems, but they're a good reminder that a genuinely reproducible hackathon demo has to survive someone else's clean machine, not just the one it was built on — small mistakes like a single dropped character in a 42-character address are exactly the kind of thing that's invisible until something breaks downstream.

**Censorship Resistance**

Censorship in blockchain infrastructure rarely looks dramatic — it's not a chain halting or a wallet getting blacklisted. It looks quiet: a transaction that just... never shows up. An RPC that returns nothing. A relay that accepts your request and then does nothing with it. There's no error message, no explanation, and critically — no proof it even happened. That silence is what makes infrastructure-level censorship so hard to fight: you can't contest what you can't demonstrate.

ProofRoute is built specifically to attack that silence.

Redundancy that's structural, not optional. Instead of a user (or their wallet) depending on a single RPC or relay to carry their transaction, the ProofRoute SDK broadcasts to multiple independent, permissionless relays at once. No single relay is a chokepoint — if one refuses to act, or simply ignores the request, the transaction doesn't die with it. This is the most direct form of censorship resistance: removing any single point of failure or control from the critical path between a signed transaction and the chain.

Automatic failover, not manual intervention. When a relay goes offline or misbehaves, the system doesn't require the user to notice, complain, or manually switch providers. The SDK routes around the failure in real time — as demonstrated live in the project, killing one of five relays mid-demo still results in a successful transaction, because the remaining relays clear quorum on their own. Censorship resistance that depends on the victim noticing and reacting isn't real resistance; it has to be automatic.

Turning silent failure into provable failure. This is the core innovation for this track specifically. Most censorship-resistance designs stop at redundancy — "just use more providers." ProofRoute goes further: every relay signs an EIP-712 commitment before it acts, so if it drops the transaction anyway, that drop is no longer invisible. It's a broken promise with the relay's own cryptographic signature attached to it. A user (or anyone) can point to an exact, verifiable, on-chain artifact and say "this relay committed to propagating my transaction and did not." That converts censorship from an unfalsifiable claim into a provable fact.

Economic cost for censoring, not just workaround. Circumventing censorship is necessary but not sufficient — if there's no cost to the censoring party, the behavior just continues against the next victim. ProofRoute attaches real, enforceable consequences: a relay that's caught dropping a committed transaction gets a portion of its staked collateral slashed automatically, on-chain, the moment a fault proof is submitted. This is what separates resisting censorship from merely tolerating it — bad actors are actively priced out of the network over time, not just quietly routed around forever.

Permissionless relay entry keeps the network resistant to capture. Because becoming a relay only requires posting stake (no whitelist, no approval, no centralized operator), the network can't be quietly captured or narrowed down to a small set of relays that could later collude or be pressured to censor collectively. Anyone can join as a relay and add more independent paths to the chain, which keeps the "how many relays would need to censor you simultaneously" number high and permissionlessly growing.

Scoped narrowly enough to be credible. It's worth naming directly: ProofRoute doesn't claim to solve censorship at the builder/sequencer level — inclusion is still outside a relay's control, and the protocol is explicit about not slashing for that. What it does claim, and can prove, is resistance to censorship at the relay/propagation layer, where today there is zero accountability at all. A narrower, provable guarantee is more valuable to judges (and to users) than a broader, hand-wavy one — it's the difference between "trust us, we're decentralized" and "here is the exact cryptographic guarantee, and here is exactly where it stops."

In short: most censorship-resistance pitches are really just redundancy pitches — "use more than one provider." ProofRoute's contribution to this track is turning relay behavior itself into something that can be caught, proven, and economically punished — so censorship stops being a silent, cost-free action and starts being a detectable, expensive one.

**Decentralized Coordination Layers**

Coordination is usually the hidden centralization point in systems that otherwise call themselves decentralized. You can have permissionless relays, open participation, and no single company running the show — and still end up with a system where the coordination layer itself is a single server saying "trust me, this happened." That single point of attestation is a centralization bottleneck wearing a decentralized costume. ProofRoute is built specifically to replace that bottleneck with something genuinely multi-party and verifiable.

Multiple independent observers, not one authority. In most infrastructure today, when you're told "your transaction was propagated," that statement comes from exactly one party — the relay itself, or a dashboard it controls. There's no second opinion. ProofRoute restructures this so that no single party's word is ever sufficient. A relay's commitment only means something once an independent peer signs off on the handoff — two separate, non-colluding parties have to agree before anything counts as valid. That's the smallest possible unit of decentralized coordination: an event isn't real until more than one independent party attests to it.

Quorum instead of a single source of truth. ProofRoute doesn't stop at pairwise agreement — it aggregates observations across the whole relay set and requires a threshold (3-of-5 in the current implementation) before it will issue a Coordination Certificate. This is the actual mechanism of decentralized coordination: instead of a centralized coordinator deciding "this happened," a quorum of independent, permissionless, stake-backed participants collectively decides it, and their agreement is the proof. No one relay, and no operator of ProofRoute itself, has the unilateral power to declare an outcome.

The coordination artifact is cryptographic, not administrative. A coordination certificate isn't a database row somewhere or an API response you have to trust the operator of — it's an on-chain object that anyone can independently verify by checking the underlying EIP-712 signatures themselves. This matters because decentralized coordination isn't really decentralized if verifying it still requires trusting the party who produced the summary. ProofRoute's certificates are self-verifying: you don't need to trust ProofRoute to trust the certificate.

Permissionless entry keeps the coordinating set genuinely open. Anyone can become part of the coordinating quorum by staking into RelayRegistry — there's no fixed validator set, no whitelist, no approval process gating who gets to participate in producing these certificates. This is what keeps the coordination layer decentralized over time rather than just decentralized at genesis: the set of parties capable of attesting to network events can grow permissionlessly, the same way anyone can join as a miner, validator, or relayer in other permissionless systems.

Coordination extends to disagreement, not just agreement. A meaningful coordination protocol has to handle conflicting observations, not just happy-path unanimity. The RPC-verification extension in ProofRoute's design shows this directly: when multiple providers return the same value for a read, you're done cheaply; when they disagree, the system escalates and samples more providers until quorum resolves the discrepancy. That's adaptive, decentralized coordination applied to disagreement resolution, not just event attestation — you don't need five signatures for the boring case, but you get real quorum-based arbitration the moment sources conflict.

Coordination with consequences, not just consensus theater. It's easy to build a system where independent parties "vote" on something and nothing follows from the vote. ProofRoute's coordination has teeth: if the quorum process reveals that a specific relay violated its commitment (signed but never handed off), that finding isn't just recorded — it triggers a real, automatic, on-chain slashing consequence. Decentralized coordination that doesn't feed into decentralized enforcement is only half the system; ProofRoute closes that loop.

Scoped honestly, which is itself part of good coordination design. The protocol is explicit that quorum certificates only ever attest to propagation, never to inclusion or execution outcomes — because those aren't things the coordinating relay set actually controls or can honestly observe together. Good decentralized coordination isn't about getting a quorum to agree on everything; it's about being precise regarding exactly which claims a given quorum is actually qualified to attest to.

In short: ProofRoute's contribution to this track isn't "we have multiple relays" — plenty of systems have that and still centralize the coordination step. The contribution is that the act of agreeing on what happened is itself decentralized: multi-party, threshold-based, cryptographically self-verifying, permissionlessly open to new participants, and directly wired into enforcement —

Tanishka Srivastava

`2026-08-08`

**What is the deployed URL for this project?**

https://aawazi.vercel.app/

**How Did You Use Claude?**

Claude was used as part of the development process for Aawaz as an AI development assistant.
During development, it was useful for thinking through the architecture of the different agents, working through implementation approaches, debugging problems, reviewing code and reasoning about integrations between the frontend, AI layer and blockchain components.
Claude was also useful when working through complex development problems where several components had to work together, particularly around agent based workflows and the overall voice to action architecture.
The important distinction is that Claude was used as a development tool and reasoning assistant. It does not have access to users' private keys and is not responsible for signing or authorizing blockchain transactions.
The application itself uses an LLM based intent parsing and agent orchestration approach, while the final blockchain transaction remains under the control of the user's connected wallet.

**How you are solving it?**

Aawaz uses a voice to intent to action architecture.
The user starts by speaking a natural language command. The browser's Web Speech API converts the speech into text. The resulting request is passed to an LLM based intent layer, which determines what the user is trying to accomplish.
The request is then routed to the appropriate agent. Depending on the intent, this could be the trading agent, NFT agent, network analyzer, smart contract generator, or security analysis agent.
The general flow is:
Voice input
↓
Speech to text
↓
Intent extraction
↓
Agent routing
↓
Action validation
↓
Wallet signature
↓
Blockchain execution
↓
Voice confirmation

This approach allows the same conversational interface to support different Web3 workflows.

For example, a user can interact with the trading functionality without having to manually navigate through a complex trading interface.

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/19c61a939b2349a483c433fa1604ca3f/64c10b58-309f-4109-9e5a-bdb341c95ff7.png)
 A developer can describe the requirements for a smart contract in natural language and use the Smart Contract Generator. A user interested in blockchain infrastructure can use the Network Analyzer to understand network information. The platform also includes security analysis capabilities for identifying potential smart contract vulnerabilities and optimization opportunities.

Another part of the project is the Voice NFT Marketplace. Instead of treating voice purely as an input mechanism, Aawaz explores voice itself as a digital asset. Users can create and monetize voice based NFTs, providing another way for creators to participate in the Web3 ecosystem.

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/19c61a939b2349a483c433fa1604ca3f/13567712-1ae4-413d-8e96-b66d73d6c1b6.png)

Accessibility was also considered throughout the product. The platform is designed to reduce dependence on traditional screen based workflows and enable hands free interaction. This can be particularly useful for visually impaired users and people with motor disabilities.

From a technical perspective, the frontend is built with Next.js 14, TypeScript and TailwindCSS. Solana is the primary blockchain, with Solana Web3.js, Anchor, SPL Tokens and Metaplex used for blockchain functionality and NFTs. Phantom and WalletConnect are used for wallet connectivity.

The project is currently deployed on Vercel and can be tested through the live application (https://aawazi.vercel.app/).

**What is the problem your project solves?**

Web3 is powerful, but interacting with it still requires users to understand wallets, blockchain networks, tokens, smart contracts, transaction confirmations, and often several different dashboards. For someone who is not technically experienced (or from a remote village of India ), even a simple blockchain action can involve multiple steps and unfamiliar terminology which introduces friction and entry barrier.
This also creates an accessibility problem. Users with visual or motor disabilities may find screen heavy interfaces, small controls, and complex transaction flows difficult to use independently.
Aawaz was built to make Web3 feel more like a conversation than a technical interface.
The idea is simple: instead of navigating through multiple screens, users can speak naturally to an AI agent and describe what they want to accomplish. Aawaz converts the voice input into an intent, determines the appropriate action, validates the request, and then interacts with the blockchain through the user's connected wallet.
The platform brings several Web3 capabilities into one voice first interface:
• Voice based blockchain transactions and trading

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/19c61a939b2349a483c433fa1604ca3f/1a053c61-2f25-4ef6-9803-137b06b95d18.png)
• Voice NFT creation and marketplace interactions

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/19c61a939b2349a483c433fa1604ca3f/a5183ea7-4b96-4938-b933-b06b8d2eb254.png)
• Smart contract generation from natural language , Smart contract optimization and vulnerability analysis 

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/19c61a939b2349a483c433fa1604ca3f/c65e9e85-65ef-4514-9003-efcb39bbc868.png)
• Blockchain network analysis

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/19c61a939b2349a483c433fa1604ca3f/9e4defb0-a7db-4d84-839f-a8e96a41a5ed.png)
• Hyperliquid based DeFi interactions

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/19c61a939b2349a483c433fa1604ca3f/f6078558-2160-4091-8e9c-7ea62cc4111b.png)
The goal is not to remove the user from the transaction process. Instead, Aawaz removes unnecessary complexity while keeping the user in control of important actions.
A particularly important part of the design is security. The AI agent does not receive or control the user's private keys. It can understand the user's request and prepare the intended action, but the actual transaction still requires the user's wallet signature.
This makes Aawaz more than a voice interface. It is an attempt to make blockchain applications easier to understand, easier to access, and easier to use without hiding the security model from the user.

### CargoSync – Smart Cargo Monitoring System
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/cargosync-blockchainbased-multisensor-cargo-integrity-monitoring-system-c515) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Surajvhankalas90/cargosync) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Port%20Mortem%202026%20--%20Code%20Resurrection%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://portmortem.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-1-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Smart IoT-powered cargo monitoring with blockchain

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Flask](https://img.shields.io/badge/Flask-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![Express.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Express.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![MongoDB](https://img.shields.io/badge/MongoDB-333333?style=flat-square) ![GPS](https://img.shields.io/badge/GPS-333333?style=flat-square) ![SHA-256 Hashes](https://img.shields.io/badge/SHA--256%20Hashes-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

Building CargoSync involved integrating multiple hardware and software components into one reliable system. Some of the major challenges we faced were:

### 1. Sensor Integration
Interfacing multiple sensors (DHT11, SW-420, Reed Switch, and Neo-6M GPS) with the ESP32 while ensuring stable and accurate readings was challenging. We carefully calibrated the sensors and optimized the firmware to minimize noise and false readings.

### 2. Real-Time Data Communication
Maintaining a stable MQTT connection between the ESP32 and the backend was difficult due to network interruptions. We implemented reconnection logic and efficient data transmission to improve reliability.

### 3. GPS Accuracy
Obtaining consistent GPS coordinates, especially indoors or in areas with weak satellite signals, affected tracking accuracy. We improved reliability by validating GPS data before displaying it on the dashboard.

### 4. Blockchain Integration
Recording critical events on the Ethereum Sepolia Testnet introduced challenges such as transaction delays and gas management. We addressed this by storing only SHA-256 hashes of important events, ensuring tamper-proof verification while keeping the system efficient.

### 5. Real-Time Dashboard Synchronization
Keeping the dashboard synchronized with continuously changing sensor values required efficient backend APIs and database updates. We optimized data flow to provide smooth live telemetry and historical analytics.

Overcoming these challenges helped us gain practical experience in IoT, embedded systems, blockchain integration, real-time communication, and full-stack development while building a robust cargo monitoring platform.

**The problem it solves**

## The Problem

Modern logistics and supply chain operations often lack continuous, trustworthy, and real-time cargo monitoring. During transportation, cargo may experience temperature fluctuations, excessive humidity, strong vibrations, unauthorized door openings, or even theft. Most existing systems either provide limited monitoring or store data in centralized databases, making records vulnerable to tampering.

This creates major challenges for logistics companies, manufacturers, pharmaceutical suppliers, and food distributors who require secure proof that cargo conditions remained within safe limits throughout the journey.

## Our Solution

CargoSync addresses these challenges by combining IoT, Blockchain, AI, GPS Tracking, and Full Stack Development into one intelligent monitoring platform.

The system continuously monitors cargo conditions using multiple sensors connected to an ESP32. Live sensor data is transmitted through MQTT, stored in MongoDB, and displayed on a real-time dashboard. Whenever abnormal conditions are detected, CargoSync immediately generates alerts and securely records critical events using SHA-256 hashing anchored on the Ethereum Sepolia Testnet.

Along with live GPS tracking, historical analytics, configurable alert thresholds, and AI-generated journey reports, CargoSync provides a transparent, tamper-proof, and intelligent cargo monitoring solution for modern supply chains.

SURAJ VHANKALAS

> Auto-Buy for the open web, powered by Prava.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![MongoDB](https://img.shields.io/badge/MongoDB-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**Challenges we ran into**

**Merchant Payment Sandboxes**: Neither Zepto nor Swiggy publishes a payment test environment. We solved this by creating a transparent /capabilities badge system that explicitly tags every step as real, sandbox, or disclosed_mock so judges have 100% transparency.
**Cold-Start Prediction**: Single households don't have historical reorder data on day one. We solved this by seeding initial cadences from Instacart market dataset category priors and providing an explainable EWMA recalibration loop as users complete purchases.
**Credential Custody Safety**: Ensuring zero credit card or passkey data touched persistent storage required designing a strict consume-once memory boundary for Prava one-time tokens.
**Reviewer Password**:  reviewer123

**The problem it solves**

**The Problem:** Households and small teams sit on a bad binary every week: over-order recurring essentials to avoid running out, or under-order and pay panic prices. It's an attention problem, not a decision problem — you already know you’ll need coffee in 10 days or that a team software subscription renews on Friday. Most shopping agents wait for you to type a prompt. A chat window doesn't replace proactive replenishment.

**The Solution:** Restock is Auto-Buy for the open web. It tracks trigger dates — predicted depletion for physical consumables or known renewal dates for SaaS subscriptions — and proactively proposes and executes purchases through Prava’s passkey-approved, merchant-scoped mandate flow before you run out.

Restock operates on two distinct tracks:

1. **Restock Home** (Consumer Consumables): Predicts when household items (coffee, printer paper, milk, detergent) will deplete using an Exponentially Weighted Moving Average (EWMA) recalibration model and price drop triggers, executing reorders via merchant MCP tools (Zepto & Swiggy).
2. **Restock Teams** (B2B SaaS Renewals): Tracks software subscription renewal dates, proposing automatic renewals or right-sizing switches (e.g. annual plan savings) to avoid unexpected auto-renewals.

**Best Visa Intelligent Commerce Implementation**

Restock interfaces with Prava’s payment virtualization rails, which utilize Visa credentials to issue scoped, one-time virtual card tokens and dynamic CVVs upon user passkey approval. 

Restock's payment completion pipeline (`payments/prava_client.py`) receives opaque credential references, executes merchant checkouts through a consume-once server boundary, and reports terminal transaction status back to Prava (`report_status`), validating Visa confirmation responses (`visa_confirmation: SUCCESS`).

**OpenAI**

Restock’s core orchestrator agent is built on the official OpenAI Agents SDK (`openai-agents` package) running `gpt-5.4-mini`. 

The agent runs autonomous scheduled evaluation ticks to analyze predicted depletion dates and live price drops, synthesizing natural-language purchase proposals and sequencing tool calls. Code-level Guardrails enforce per-item, per-transaction, and monthly budget caps before requesting Prava payment sessions, ensuring the LLM cannot exceed user spend limits.

**Best Prava Adapter for the NANDA Town**

We built the standalone `nanda_prava_adapter` package (submitted via upstream Pull Request #208 to `projnanda/nandatown`), which implements NANDA Town's payment plugin specification over Prava's REST API.

The adapter exposes NANDA's standard `quote`, `pay`, `verify_payment`, and `refund` interfaces, mapping NANDA payment intents into Prava Sessions and mandate status checks. It includes a complete test suite, interactive sandbox runner, and an installable `nest.plugins.payments` entry point.

**Best Agentic User Experience**

Restock reimagines agentic commerce by replacing generic AI chat prompts with a physical, tactile product experience designed for zero-friction proactive buying:

1. **Physical Pantry Shelf Metaphor**:
   Instead of flat SaaS tables or text-only lists, Restock Home presents a physical pantry layout where products sit on two-tier wooden shelves with real manufacturer photography, natural sunlight/shadows, and physically attached cardboard labels. Restock Teams visualizes subscriptions as 3D extruded provider plaques.

2. **Photorealistic 3D WebGL Parcel Reveal**:
   Opening product details triggers an unboxing interaction—a shoebox-style WebGL 3D cardboard parcel opens smoothly, allowing the selected product to rise from the box into a floating focus view before purchase approval.

3. **Proactive Single-Tap Decision Controls**:
   Restock eliminates prompt typing. Proactive depletion and price-drop notifications present three clear, high-contrast actions: **Approve** (initiates Prava passkey mandate), **Adjust** (modifies quantity/amount), and **Skip** (defers reorder).

4. **Honest Point-of-Action Trust Badges**:
   Every approval surface features human-readable spend caps and clear `Real`, `Sandbox`, or `Disclosed Simulation` badges directly above action buttons, giving users 100% transparency over payment boundaries.

5. **Multi-Channel & Responsive Excellence**:
   Fully responsive across Mobile, Tablet, and Desktop with specialized typography (Inter, Radio Canada Big, Geist Pixel), plus a live Slack Bolt Socket Mode integration that updates button states in real-time once resolved.
