### Gas-Aware Yield Optimizer
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/gasaware-yield-optimizer-1aed) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Ankur17nith/gas-aware-yield-optimizer) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://gas-aware-yield-optimizer.vercel.app/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/O88m4e9bEEM?si=Fhy3qKJU56kKLxpa) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Electrothon%208.0-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://electrothon-8.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-1-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Maximise yield of defi investors on stablecoins

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![scikit-learn](https://img.shields.io/badge/scikit--learn-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![ethers.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/ethers.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![AI/ML](https://img.shields.io/badge/AI/ML-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Most DeFi dashboards show only APY, which is the interest rate.
But when users move their funds between protocols, they must pay gas fees, and those fees can significantly reduce the real profit.
For example, a pool might show 8% APY, but if you spend a lot on gas while moving funds, the actual return becomes much lower.
Another problem is that users must manually check many protocols and pools to find the best opportunity, and yield rates change frequently.
So users spend time comparing platforms and often miss better opportunities or lose profit due to gas costs.
If a user has to migrate between pools, there are 3-4 steps which consist of withdrawing from on epool, then swapping the tokens if needed and then deposit into another pool. So firstly there are gas costs for each step of the transaction and many times funds get stuck if the transaction fails. Our website allows atomic transaction (all in one step) which minimises the gas cost as well as solves the second issue regarding migration.

Our solution is a gas-aware yield optimizer.
It brings all the pools of all chains such as Ethereum, Arbitrum, Polygon and Base on one page which makes it easy to compare and invest.
Instead of showing only APY, our platform calculates the net yield after considering gas costs.
We collect yield data from multiple DeFi protocols and rank pools based on actual profitability.
We also include a AI prediction system that analyses yield trends and suggests whether users should move funds now or wait.
Finally, we simplify the process by allowing users to interact with a router smart contract, which can execute optimised strategies more efficiently.
For the beginners, there is also an AI chatbot which would explain the reasoning behind decision making of investing into different pools.

**Challenges we ran into**

1. Integrating Real-Time DeFi Data

One of the main challenges was collecting accurate and up-to-date DeFi pool data such as APY, liquidity (TVL), and token information from multiple sources. Different protocols expose data differently, so we had to normalize the data structure before comparing pools across platforms.

2. Calculating Net Yield After Gas Costs

Most DeFi dashboards only show raw APY, but our system calculates gas-adjusted net yield. This required building a model that estimates the gas cost of migrating funds between pools and subtracting it from the potential yield gain. Designing this logic so that recommendations remained realistic was a significant challenge.

3. Multi-Chain Gas Tracking

Gas behaves differently across chains such as Ethereum, Arbitrum, Polygon, and Base. Fetching gas prices from different APIs and displaying them correctly for each chain required building a chain-aware backend system and handling multiple RPC endpoints.

4. Building the AI DeFi Assistant

Integrating the Gemini API into the platform required designing prompts and context pipelines so the assistant could answer questions using live platform data instead of generic responses. Ensuring the assistant gave useful explanations about pools, APY, and migration strategies was challenging.

5. Synchronizing Backend Data With the UI

Another challenge was ensuring the frontend dashboard updated correctly when data such as pool rankings, gas prices, or predictions changed. We had to carefully design APIs and state management so that the user interface reflected real-time analytics.

6. Designing an Intuitive User Experience

DeFi tools are often difficult for beginners to understand. We focused on presenting complex metrics like APY, gas impact, and migration decisions in a way that is simple and actionable for users.

**Ethereum Track**

Our project, Gas-Aware Yield Optimizer, fits the Ethereum track by building an AI-powered DeFi analytics platform that operates on Ethereum and Ethereum-compatible networks.

The platform analyzes yield opportunities across Ethereum-based DeFi protocols such as Curve, Compound, and Yearn. These protocols operate through Ethereum smart contracts, and our system evaluates their pools by collecting on-chain and protocol data including APY, liquidity (TVL), and token information.

A key feature of the platform is gas-aware yield optimization. Since Ethereum transaction fees significantly affect DeFi profitability, our system integrates real-time Ethereum gas data using gas tracking APIs and calculates gas-adjusted net yield instead of relying only on raw APY. This allows the platform to determine whether migrating funds between pools will actually increase a user’s net returns after accounting for Ethereum transaction costs.

The application also integrates Ethereum wallet connectivity through MetaMask, allowing users to interact with the platform using their Ethereum address. Migration strategies and pool comparisons are designed around Ethereum-based DeFi smart contracts and transaction mechanics.

In addition, the system includes a Gas Timing Optimizer that analyzes Ethereum gas trends over time to determine the most efficient time to execute DeFi transactions.

By combining on-chain DeFi analytics, Ethereum gas awareness, and wallet-based interaction, the platform demonstrates how intelligent tools can help users optimize yield strategies within the Ethereum ecosystem.

**Electrothon 8.0 Honors Track**

the team consists of all first year members

**IQ AI**

Our project, Gas-Aware Yield Optimizer, fits the IQ AI track by implementing an autonomous DeFi strategy agent that analyzes yield opportunities across multiple protocols and chains.

The platform continuously monitors DeFi pools across protocols such as Curve, Compound, and Yearn and evaluates them based on multiple factors including gross APY, gas costs, liquidity (TVL), and estimated net yield. Instead of simply ranking pools by APY, the system calculates a gas-adjusted yield score and determines whether migrating funds will actually increase the user’s profit.

The AI strategy agent performs continuous scoring of available pools and generates a migration decision such as “Migrate” or “Hold.” This decision is based on predicted net yield improvement, gas costs, and liquidity stability. The system also estimates migration probability and provides a reasoning layer explaining the decision.

In addition to strategy optimization, the platform includes a DeFi AI assistant powered by Gemini that acts as a conversational interface for users. The assistant can answer questions about pools, APY, gas fees, and migration strategies while referencing live platform data.

By combining real-time DeFi analytics, gas-aware yield optimization, and an autonomous strategy agent, our platform demonstrates how AI agents can assist users in making smarter decentralized finance decisions.

**Google Cloud**

Our platform uses the Gemini API to power an intelligent DeFi assistant inside the Gas-Aware Yield Optimizer.  Gemini acts as a real-time DeFi copilot that helps users understand blockchain concepts and make better yield decisions.  The assistant can answer general Web3 questions such as “What is Ethereum?”, “What is Arbitrum?”, or “How do smart contracts work?”, helping beginners understand DeFi concepts.  More importantly, Gemini analyzes live platform data such as pool APY, TVL, risk level, and gas costs to provide strategy recommendations. When users ask questions like “Which pool should I use?” or “Should I migrate now?”, the assistant evaluates real pool data from the backend APIs and explains the optimal strategy in simple language.  Gemini also integrates with the Gas Timing Optimizer, which uses live Ethereum gas data to determine the best time to migrate funds between pools. The assistant can explain migration decisions, gas impact, and estimated savings.  By combining real-time DeFi analytics with Gemini’s reasoning and explanation capabilities, the platform becomes an AI-powered DeFi copilot that helps users make smarter yield optimization decisions.

> Privacy-first P2P dec. collaborative platform

![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![PostgreSQL](https://img.shields.io/badge/PostgreSQL-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Supabase](https://img.shields.io/badge/Supabase-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

- Privacy-first collaborative docs lets people co-edit documents without storing plaintext content on a central server.
- User can login using social logins and optional wallet connection. For every user GhostID will be created so that there identity remains completely non-exposed. User can create public and private documents, only public documents are searchable. User will remain completely non-exposed using peerIDs, they can edit docs, chat during live sessions while non-exposed.
- Safer identity model, combines login + optional wallet binding, but uses GhostID in collaboration so raw wallet identity is not exposed in normal flows.
- Decentralized real-time editing, uses peer-to-peer session sync for presence, chat, cursor/events, reducing dependence on a single relay/server path.
- supports private, link-based, and public access modes for docs sharing
- Better trust boundary by keeping backend minimal (metadata, permissions, access checks) while pushing sensitive content handling to client-side encryption.
- Useful for teams handling sensitive notes/specs especially where auditability, ownership control, and resilience matter more than convenience-only cloud docs

![image](https://assets.devfolio.co/content/edf94b25080648e68db0bafbc7e17384/0be444ff-4cb2-435f-a1f3-d420db7c36e3.png)

**Challenges we ran into**

- Browser P2P connectivity was unstable (frequent dial failures): fixed by adding better relay target selection, peer hints, retry backoff/muting, and diagnostics to see failure reasons.
- Early collaboration encryption design caused cross-peer decrypt issues: solved by switching from per-peer token secret usage to a shared per-document session key.
- Pubsub behavior in sparse sessions caused noisy failures: treated zero-subscriber publish errors as transient and enabled safer publish behavior to avoid false fatal states.
- Concurrent editing merge quality had edge cases: improved local edit handling to smaller text deltas and added periodic full-state sync for late joiners.
- Auth versus anonymous link-join flow conflicted: updated join flow to support access-token joins with GhostID fallback while still enforcing role checks.
- Async collaboration tests were flaky: replaced short fixed waits with polling/wait-for style checks so integration tests stay stable under load.

**Build What Big Tech Won't**

- Built on Fileverse as the decentralized document backend, so users can create, update, search, and share documents through API/CLI while keeping data portable and censorship-resistant
- Makes document workflows safer by storing encrypted content and publishing asynchronously, reducing dependence on a single centralized storage provider.
- Implemented fileverse API for encryption and decryption of docs, which is also supported in P2P docs editing.

### PLOP
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/plop-b46d) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/juSt-jeLLy/PLOP) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://plop-tau-puce.vercel.app/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/tC3FR1QhzXk) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHMumbai%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethmumbai2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-1-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Privacy-first OTC dark pool .

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

On‑chain trading leaks intent. Large or institutional orders are visible to the public mempool and orderbooks, which invites front‑running, market impact, and unwanted surveillance. At the same time, most privacy systems sacrifice controls, auditability, or operational safety.

**PLOP solves this by making OTC trading private _and_ policy‑governed.**

## What people can use it for

- **Private OTC swaps** without exposing size, price, or counterparties.
- **Institutional or treasury trades** where market impact and leakage are unacceptable.
- **High‑trust settlement flows** with MPC controls, whitelists, velocity limits, and approvals.

## Why it’s safer

- **Orders are encrypted client‑side** and stored off‑chain (Fileverse); nothing sensitive is public.
- **Settlement recipients are encrypted in ENS**, so the settlement address is never public.
- **BitGo policies protect funds**, and optional auto‑approver logic enforces that only the intended recipients get paid.
- **Per‑order BitGo deposit addresses** reduce linkability and improve privacy.

In short: PLOP gives you **dark‑pool style privacy** with **enterprise‑grade safety controls**, without needing custom L2s or trusting a centralized exchange.

**Challenges we ran into**

## ENS ↔ BitGo compatibility gap (two chains, one flow)
**Challenge:** ENS writes live on Sepolia, but settlement funds live on Hoodi via BitGo MPC. I had to make sure the identity layer (ENS) and the settlement layer (BitGo) never drifted or leaked data across chains.  
**Solution:** ENS is used only for encrypted session metadata (`plop.settlement`, `plop.active`, `plop.receipts`). The deposit address stays **off‑chain** and is only returned via the engine API and embedded in the encrypted order payload. That kept ENS clean and ensured all real value movement happens on Hoodi.

## BitGo policy rules vs. dynamic settlement
**Challenge:** BitGo’s policy system is strict, and the SDK behavior didn’t match expectations. Creating new whitelist rules per match isn’t allowed, and `updatePolicyRule` behaved inconsistently in the context of my wallet setup.  
**Solution:** I switched to updating the **existing** whitelist rule (never creating new ones), and I keyed all settlement sends to that rule update step. This guarantees only the intended recipient can be paid — and still keeps policies enforceable.

## Approvals: “who verifies settlement is correct?”
**Challenge:** Even with policies, I needed a privacy‑preserving way to enforce that **only the intended recipient + amount** could be approved. That’s hard when the orders are encrypted and stored off‑chain.  
**Solution:** I built an **auto‑approver** that decrypts the order payload (engine secret key), validates the exact recipient + amount, and approves the BitGo pending approval only if it matches. If it doesn’t match, it rejects or skips. This created a cryptographic “policy gate” without exposing recipient data publicly.

## Privacy constraints vs. usability
**Challenge:** Keeping privacy strong (encrypted orders, no public deposit addresses) makes UX harder — history disappeared after session rotation, and users couldn’t see past trades.  
**Solution:** I kept session privacy intact, but added **local history aggregation** on the frontend (stores past subnames in localStorage and queries each). That gives a user‑friendly history without leaking anything on‑chain.
\---

These issues came directly from bridging **ENS identity**, **BitGo MPC policies**, and **private off‑chain order storage** into one coherent flow. Each fix was necessary to keep the system both private **and** safe enough for real settlement.

**Privacy**

PLOP is a privacy‑first OTC trading system designed to prevent on‑chain order leakage and identity exposure.

## Privacy guarantees

- **Encrypted orders:** Order payloads are encrypted client‑side and stored off‑chain (Fileverse), so order size, price, and intent never appear on‑chain.
- **Hidden settlement recipients:** Settlement details are stored as **encrypted ENS text records**, so the recipient address is not public.
- **No public deposit addresses:** Deposit addresses are returned only via the engine API and embedded in encrypted orders, keeping the funding path private.
- **Rotating session identities:** Each trading session uses a randomized ENS subname, decoupling user identity from order flow.
- **Policy‑gated settlement:** BitGo policies + the auto‑approver ensure funds only move to the intended recipient without revealing who that is publicly.

In short, PLOP makes **private, non‑custodial settlement** possible while still preserving safety controls — exactly the kind of infrastructure that strengthens privacy for Ethereum applications.

**DeFi**

PLOP turns a complex, multi‑step OTC trade into a **single, guided flow**: connect wallet → sign settlement authorization → submit order → deposit once → settle automatically. This makes private, institutional‑grade trading **feel like a simple consumer transaction**.

## Why this advances crypto utility

- **One deposit, no orderbook complexity:** Users don’t manage multiple contracts or price feeds. They submit a simple order and deposit once to activate it.
- **Automatic settlement with safeguards:** BitGo MPC policies + the auto‑approver remove manual approvals, so settlement “just happens” once matched.
- **Cross‑chain abstraction:** Users interact with a single interface while ENS identity (Sepolia) and settlement (Hoodi) are handled behind the scenes.
- **Clear UX for non‑experts:** The UI translates technical steps (encryption, approvals, policies) into a clean flow with explicit prompts.

## New financial possibilities (beyond TradFi)

- **Private, p2p OTC swaps** without centralized intermediaries.
- **Agent‑driven trading** where automated wallets can execute safely without leaking strategy.
- **Programmable settlement constraints** (whitelists, velocity limits, approvals) that don’t exist in TradFi rails.

In short, PLOP simplifies a traditionally complex OTC workflow into a **single, understandable path**, while enabling privacy and programmable controls that traditional finance can’t offer.

**Best creative use of ENS**

PLOP treats ENS as a **programmable coordination layer** rather than a simple name → address registry. Each trading session gets a randomized subname (e.g. `a1b2c3.plop.eth`), and the resolver stores **encrypted settlement instructions** in ENS text records. The key record is:

- `plop.settlement` (ciphertext envelope only the engine can decrypt)

Additional text records encode session state and post‑trade receipts:

- `plop.active`
- `plop.pairs`
- `plop.receipts`

This means the engine can coordinate settlement without ever publishing recipient addresses or order details on‑chain.

This is a creative DeFi use of ENS because the **text records become the privacy‑preserving control plane** for a dark‑pool‑style exchange. The ENS name is used for identity and session state, while sensitive data lives only in encrypted form. That goes beyond common ENS patterns (address resolution, content hash, or simple metadata) and turns ENS into a secure signaling layer for off‑chain order flow and on‑chain settlement.

In short, PLOP shows ENS can be **more than a naming system** — it can be the glue that binds privacy, authorization, and settlement into a coherent DeFi workflow.

**Pool prize**

PLOP integrates ENS at the core of its trading flow. Every session is represented by a randomized ENS subname, and the resolver stores key session metadata via text records:

- `plop.active`
- `plop.pairs`
- `plop.receipts`

It also stores encrypted settlement instructions in:

- `plop.settlement`

This makes ENS the coordination layer for order flow, authorization, and receipts — not just a name registry.

This is a concrete, functional ENS integration (live on Sepolia) that is required for the system to operate, so it clearly qualifies for the ENS pool prize.

**Best Privacy Application using BitGo**

PLOP is a **privacy‑preserving OTC exchange** built directly on BitGo’s MPC wallets and policy system. Orders are encrypted client‑side and stored off‑chain; the only on‑chain actions are deposits and settlement transfers from BitGo, which means **order intent, size, and counterparty are never public**.

## Why this fits the BitGo privacy track

- **Fresh deposit addresses per order** from BitGo reduce linkability and prevent simple address‑based tracking.
- **Policy‑gated settlement** ensures funds only move to authorized recipients (whitelist + velocity rules).
- **Webhook + auto‑approver flow** validates each pending approval against encrypted order data before releasing funds.
- **No public settlement recipients**: recipients are encrypted and only decrypted inside the engine at match time.

In short, PLOP uses BitGo’s wallet infrastructure to deliver **private, policy‑controlled settlement** — exactly the kind of privacy‑first application this track calls for.

**Best DeFi Application using BitGo**

PLOP is a DeFi OTC exchange that uses **BitGo MPC wallets** as the settlement layer, bringing institutional‑grade security and controls to on‑chain trading.

## Why this fits the BitGo DeFi track

- **MPC wallet settlement:** all trades settle from a BitGo MPC hot wallet on Hoodi.
- **Policy enforcement:** whitelist + velocity limit policies gate every transfer, so settlement is controlled and auditable.
- **Approval workflows:** pending approvals are validated and auto‑approved only when they match the encrypted order payload.
- **Real‑time automation:** BitGo webhooks + engine watchers coordinate deposits, live order activation, and settlement.

This is a composable DeFi primitive (private OTC swap) that directly leverages BitGo’s SDK, policies, and webhooks for secure, automated settlement.

**Build What Big Tech Won't**

PLOP uses the Fileverse API as its **private orderbook and receipt store**, which is exactly the kind of privacy‑first collaboration layer this track encourages.

## Why it fits the track

- **Encrypted by design:** Orders and receipts are encrypted client‑side and stored as Fileverse ddocs, so sensitive trading intent never touches a centralized database.
- **Programmable + agent‑friendly:** The engine reads and updates ddocs through Fileverse’s simple REST API, enabling automated matching, settlement, and receipt creation.
- **No lock‑in:** All data lives in decentralized, user‑accessible ddocs — users can access their encrypted order history without relying on a proprietary backend.

In short, PLOP uses Fileverse the way Big Tech storage systems can’t: as a **privacy‑native, programmable document layer** for real financial workflows.

**BEST Overall Project**

PLOP introduces a **new privacy‑first OTC flow** that combines ENS as encrypted session identity, Fileverse as private orderbook storage, and BitGo MPC for policy‑gated settlement — a unique, end‑to‑end use case not seen in typical DEX demos.  
The demo proves real deposits, real settlement, and privacy controls working together across chains, showcasing both creativity and technical ambition.

### Rakshak

> Institutional wallet security, without complexity.

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![MongoDB](https://img.shields.io/badge/MongoDB-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![React.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/React.js-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Crypto wallets are highly secure, but they are also unforgiving. If a private key is lost, access to the funds can be permanently lost. This creates a serious operational risk for organizations such as DAOs, NGOs, and Web3 startups that manage treasury funds.

While solutions like **BitGo** provide strong security through multisig wallets and secure signing, operational recovery is still difficult for non-technical teams. If a key holder becomes unavailable, treasury operations can stop even though the funds remain technically secure.

**Rakshak** makes crypto treasury management safer and easier by adding a structured recovery workflow on top of institutional wallets.

With Rakshak, teams can:

- Configure trusted guardians who can approve recovery actions
- Initiate a recovery request if key access is lost
- Use team-based approvals to securely authorize recovery
- Restore access by transferring funds to a new safe address

Instead of relying on complex technical procedures, teams get a simple dashboard and approval flow that ensures treasury continuity.

Rakshak ensures that losing a key does not mean losing access to funds, making crypto treasury operations safer, recoverable, and easier for institutional teams to manage.

**Challenges we ran into**

A key hurdle was during BitGo integration itself, not just UI work.
We had to decide which BitGo wallet flow best matched our recovery model, and initially that was confusing: wallet type selection, key-handling approach, and how to make recovery work reliably for non-technical teams. We also had to align wallet creation, receiver setup, guardian approvals, and recovery execution into one consistent operational flow.                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                                 How we solved it:                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             
  - standardized on a single wallet flow for the demo (Arbitrum testnet with BitGo-backed multisig)                                                              
  - built a clear step-based orchestrator flow in our app  
  - added strict ownership mapping and approval checks so only the correct signed-in user can operate a wallet                                                   
  - moved critical mappings from local files to DB-backed storage for consistency and safer multi-user behavior                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                This turned a complex SDK-first integration into a predictable product workflow that PM/ops teams can actually use.

**DeFi**

Rakshak addresses a critical challenge in DeFi: secure and reliable treasury management. Many DAOs, Web3 startups, and on-chain organizations manage funds through multisig wallets, but if a key holder loses their private key, access to treasury funds can become difficult or permanently lost.

Rakshak improves DeFi infrastructure by adding a guardian-based recovery and approval workflow on top of institutional wallets. It allows teams to securely recover access and continue managing their on-chain funds without relying on complex technical processes.

By improving security, operational continuity, and usability of crypto treasury management, Rakshak strengthens the reliability of DeFi ecosystems.

**Pool prize**

Rakshak adds ENS-friendly UX on top of BitGo workflows: guardians and recovery receivers can be defined via ENS, then safely resolved to EVM addresses for execution.
This improves usability for non-technical institutional operators, reduces address-copy mistakes, and makes guardian/recovery workflows easier to manage in real operations.

**Best DeFi Application using BitGo**

Rakshak uses BitGo’s wallet infrastructure to make crypto treasury management safer and easier for teams.

In our project, we create a Self-Custody Multisig Hot (Simple) wallet using BitGo’s SDK. This allows teams to securely manage their funds while still keeping control of their own keys.

Rakshak adds a simple workflow on top of this wallet where teams can:

- Manage their treasury from a dashboard
- Add trusted guardians for recovery
- Raise a recovery request if a key is lost
- Approve recovery through a multi-person approval process

After the required approvals, the user can recover the wallet by transferring the funds to a new receiver address.

By combining BitGo’s multisig wallet security with a simple recovery workflow, Rakshak helps DAOs and Web3 teams manage their DeFi funds more safely and easily.

**The problem it solves**

Today most AI systems operate in closed environments where users cannot verify the identity of the AI, cannot trust how the results were generated, and cannot easily connect the AI to real world payment systems.

Our project solves this by introducing a framework where AI agents have verifiable identities, can receive payment for work, and produce outputs that are permanently stored on decentralized storage.

People can use this system to request research, analysis, or other AI services from agents and know exactly who produced the work. The payment flow is transparent and the results are verifiable.

This makes AI services more trustworthy and creates a new model where AI agents can operate as independent service providers.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the biggest challenges was connecting multiple systems that were not originally designed to work together. Each integration such as Base contracts, ENS identity records, Fileverse storage, and Elsa APIs had its own requirements and authentication flow.

At first it was difficult to coordinate identity verification between ENS records and the agent registry on chain. Making sure that the ENS name actually mapped to the correct agent identity required careful handling of text records and registry lookups.

Another challenge was handling the payment flow for API requests. The x402 payment process had to work automatically so that agents could access Elsa APIs without manual payment steps.

After debugging the request interceptor and making sure the wallet signing logic was working correctly, the system was able to process API requests and payments smoothly.

Once these integrations were working together, the full workflow from identity to payment to storage started functioning as intended.

**DeFi**

The project introduces a payment flow for AI services using stablecoins. When a user requests a task from an agent, funds are locked in escrow on Base. The agent performs the work and once the task is complete the funds are released.

Agents can also access premium financial intelligence through HeyElsa APIs. Each request can involve small payments handled automatically through the x402 payment flow.

This creates a new kind of DeFi use case where financial infrastructure is not only used for trading but also for paying autonomous AI agents that perform useful tasks.

**AI**

Our project uses AI agents that can collaborate with each other to complete tasks like research, analysis, and generating reports. Instead of a single AI responding to a prompt, multiple agents can work together and exchange information. One agent can gather data, another can analyze it, and another can generate the final output.

The interesting part is that these agents are not just software scripts. Each agent has an identity and can receive payment for the work it performs. This makes the AI system behave more like a real service economy where agents provide skills and get rewarded for useful output.

Because of this agent collaboration model, the project explores a new way of building AI systems that are autonomous, verifiable, and connected to real incentives.

**Best creative use of ENS**

ENS is used as the identity layer for AI agents. Each agent can have a human readable name such as researcher.agent.eth.

Using ENS records we connect that name to the agent's on chain identity in the registry. This means users can verify that the agent they are interacting with is the same one registered on chain.

This solves an important trust problem in AI systems. Instead of interacting with anonymous bots, users interact with agents that have verifiable identities.

**Build What Big Tech Won't**

Fileverse is used to store the output generated by agents. When an agent completes a task such as a research report or analysis, the document is uploaded to Fileverse and stored on decentralized storage.

This ensures that the result cannot be altered later and can always be referenced through its storage link. It also allows users to verify the work produced by an agent.

In addition to final reports, conversation logs and task records can also be stored. This creates a transparent record of how the work was performed.

**AI × Onchain**

Base acts as the core infrastructure layer for the system. Agent identities are registered on Base and payments are handled through smart contract escrow.

When a user requests a task, the payment is locked on Base. After the work is completed and verified, the funds are released to the agent.

This shows how AI services can operate directly on chain where identity, trust, and payment are handled by blockchain infrastructure rather than centralized platforms.

**Best Use of Elsa x402 and Elsa OpenClaw skills**

HeyElsa is used to give agents access to advanced financial intelligence. Agents can call Elsa APIs to analyze wallets, understand portfolios, or generate insights about tokens and DeFi activity.

The integration uses the x402 payment model which allows agents to pay for API usage automatically when making requests.

This allows agents to access high quality financial data while still operating inside an automated payment system. It makes the AI agents capable of producing more useful and data driven results.

**BEST Overall Project**

The project combines several technologies that normally live separately. It connects AI agents, blockchain identity, decentralized storage, and automated payments into one working system.

Agents can prove who they are using ENS identities, accept work through a payment escrow, perform tasks using external intelligence tools, and deliver results that are permanently stored on decentralized storage.

Instead of relying on trust in a centralized platform, the entire workflow can be verified on chain or through decentralized storage. This makes the system transparent and portable across different platforms.

The goal is to show how AI services could operate in a decentralized environment where identity, payments, and outputs are all verifiable.

**The problem it solves**

- NoTox makes professional networking safer and more private. Normally, people must share personal details like email or phone numbers immediately, which can lead to spam, harassment, or misuse of information.
 
- NoTox solves this by allowing contact information to be revealed gradually based on trust levels. Users can connect step-by-step, starting with basic details and unlocking more information only when trust increases.
 
- It also uses economic bonds, where users stake tokens to contact others. If someone harasses or misuses the connection, their bond is penalized and given to the victim, discouraging bad behavior.
 
- Overall, NoTox helps people network safely, protect their privacy, and control who can access their personal contact

**Challenges we ran into**

While building Notox, we faced a few technical challenges during development.

1. Blockchain Integration Issues
One major hurdle was connecting the MetaMask wallet with the frontend through the deployed smart contracts. While running the project using npm run dev, the terminal would often keep iterating, become slow, or sometimes get stuck. This made testing the wallet connection difficult.

Another issue occurred because the Hardhat local blockchain node kept running in the background (typically on port 8545). Sometimes it conflicted with the frontend connection, which caused delays and errors until the process was restarted.

We also temporarily lost Tailwind CSS styling on the website due to a small configuration issue. After debugging and fixing minor errors in the tailwind.config.js file, the styles started working again.

2. Database & API Integration
While connecting the RESTful APIs between the frontend and the database, we faced several errors during API calls. After debugging the API routes and fixing the error handling and request structure, the connection started working correctly.

How We Solved Them
Most of these challenges were solved through debugging logs, checking configuration files, restarting background services like Hardhat, and correcting API request handling. Once these issues were resolved, the system integration worked smoothly.

**Privacy**

NoTox focuses on protecting user privacy in professional networking. Instead of forcing users to share personal details like email or phone numbers immediately, the platform uses a progressive disclosure system where information is revealed step-by-step based on trust.

Sensitive data is protected using zero-knowledge cryptography, ensuring that private information is stored securely and cannot be directly accessed. Additionally, the economic bond system discourages harassment by requiring users to stake tokens before contacting someone.

By giving users full control over their personal information and ensuring secure communication, NoTox strongly aligns with the goals of the Privacy Track.

### AgenTip
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/agentip-d07c) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://agen-tip2-0.vercel.app/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UzZMhoBdBbw) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHMumbai%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethmumbai2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-1-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Create once. Earn forever. Even from robots.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![ethers.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/ethers.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Express.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Express.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Hardhat](https://img.shields.io/badge/Hardhat-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Imagine you spent three years writing about renewable energy. Every week, a new article. Deeply researched, carefully written, genuinely useful. Your traffic grows. You're proud of it.

Then one day you check your server logs and notice something strange. Thousands of requests. Not from readers — from bots. LLMs. Crawlers. AI systems pulling your entire archive, summarizing it, training on it, feeding it into products that charge $20 a month to people who used to read you for free.
You earned nothing from any of it.

This is not a hypothetical. It is happening right now, to every creator on the internet. 40% of web traffic today is AI agents. They consume content at a scale no human audience ever could. And the entire creator economy — built on ad clicks, on eyeballs, on human attention — has no answer for it.
There is no checkout. No paywall that an agent respects. No standard mechanism for a machine to pay for what it takes.

There was supposed to be. In 1991, HTTP 402 —* "Payment Required" *— was written into the web specification for exactly this scenario. It was shelved because the infrastructure didn't exist. For 34 years it sat there, unused, waiting.
We built the infrastructure.

AgentTip is a single script tag. Drop it on your website with your wallet address. From that moment, every human visitor sees a tip button and every AI agent gets charged — automatically, at the protocol level, with zero setup beyond that one line of code.

Humans tip with one click. Agents pay $0.001 USDC per request via x402, autonomously, before they get access. Everything settles on Base L2, wallet to wallet, with no platform taking a cut.

And because we believe creators deserve more than just money — they deserve to understand how their work is being used — every paying agent leaves a private intelligence note describing what it was researching. Stored encrypted on IPFS via Fileverse. Readable only by you.

We also built an ENS DeFi Will. Because creators are human, and humans don't live forever. Encode your beneficiaries into your ENS name. If you go inactive, your earnings distribute automatically on-chain to whoever you chose. Your work keeps giving, even after you stop.

The machines have been eating for free for years.

**AgentTip** sends the bill.

**Challenges we ran into**

The biggest challenge was x402 itself — the protocol is 6 months old, no production examples exist, and we had to figure out the entire request-response cycle, payment proof format, and replay protection from scratch by reading a spec that barely exists yet.

ENS Will execution sounds simple until you try to do it fully on-chain. Parsing comma-separated beneficiary strings and resolving multiple ENS names inside the EVM is gas-prohibitive. We ended up building a hybrid — backend reads and validates the ENS records off-chain, passes resolved addresses to the smart contract. Trustless enough, actually practical.

Fileverse dDocs use ProseMirror JSON internally. Appending agent intelligence entries without corrupting the existing document structure took way more debugging than expected — one malformed block and the entire doc breaks silently.

And honestly, agent detection is harder than it sounds. User-Agent strings are inconsistent, easily spoofed, and half the legitimate agents we tested didn't send them at all. We ended up building a multi-signal system combining User-Agent patterns, custom headers, and Accept header analysis just to reliably tell humans from machines.

**AI**

AgentTip is built entirely around the AI agent economy. The core problem it solves is that AI agents — LLMs, crawlers, autonomous research bots — consume creator content at massive scale but have no mechanism to pay for it. AgentTip implements the x402 protocol to enable autonomous AI-to-human micropayments at the HTTP layer. When an AI agent hits a protected page, it receives a 402 response, pays $0.001 USDC autonomously, and gets access — no human involved. The Fileverse Intelligence Network lets agents attach research context to every payment, giving creators a private feed of what AI systems are actually doing with their content. Built to work natively with Coinbase AgentKit, LangChain, and any autonomous agent framework.

**Best creative use of ENS**

AgentTip uses ENS as the instruction layer for its DeFi Will feature. Creators encode their entire estate plan directly into ENS text records — beneficiaries, percentage splits, idle trigger days, and a farewell message. A backend cron job reads these records daily via viem, checks inactivity, and executes the on-chain AgentTipWill smart contract when triggered, distributing the creator's accumulated USDC to ENS-resolved beneficiaries. Beneficiaries are resolved at execution time — not at writing time — so if someone changes their wallet, the will still finds them. ENS becomes a programmable, human-readable will that executes itself.

**Build What Big Tech Won't**

Google, Notion, and every major doc platform have one thing in common — they own your data. Your documents live on their servers, behind their auth, readable by their systems, monetizable by their ad engines. They will never build true end-to-end encrypted, user-owned documents because it destroys their business model. Data is the product.
Fileverse builds the opposite. Every dDoc is end-to-end encrypted, stored on IPFS, and owned entirely by the creator's wallet. No platform can read it, no company can sell it, no server going down can delete it. It's a document that belongs to you the same way your crypto wallet belongs to you.
AgentTip uses this specifically for the Intelligence Network. When AI agents pay to access a creator's content, they leave a private note — what they were researching, what question brought them there. This feed is written directly to the creator's Fileverse dDoc. Only the creator can read it.
Big Tech would never build this. Google would index it. Notion would train on it. A VC-backed startup would eventually get acquired and the privacy promise would quietly disappear.
Fileverse can't betray that promise — it's not a policy, it's cryptography. That's what decentralized storage actually means in practice, and that's exactly why AgentTip chose it.

**AI × Onchain**

Blockchain (Base L2)
All payments — both human tips and AI agent micropayments — settle on Base. We chose Base because it's the only L2 where USDC is native, gas fees are fractions of a cent (critical for $0.001 micropayments to make economic sense), and Coinbase AgentKit is built around it. Our two smart contracts — AgentTipEscrow and AgentTipWill — are deployed on Base. Every transaction is verifiable on-chain, replay-protected by tx hash, and goes directly wallet-to-wallet with no custodial risk.
AI + Base
The x402 protocol is what connects AI to Base. When an AI agent hits a creator's page, it receives a 402 with the recipient wallet and USDC amount. The agent autonomously signs and broadcasts a USDC transfer on Base, then retries with the tx hash as proof. This is machine-to-machine payment at the speed of HTTP — Base's 2-second block time makes it fast enough for agents to pay and get access in a single request cycle. No human, no API key, no OAuth — just an agent, a wallet, and Base.

**Best Use of Elsa x402 and Elsa OpenClaw skills**

AgentTip is a direct implementation of the x402 protocol — which is exactly what Elsa x402 is built for. When an AI agent hits a creator's page, it receives an HTTP 402 with structured payment headers specifying amount, recipient wallet, and network. The agent pays autonomously and retries with proof. We also use Elsa's OpenClaw skills to give agents the ability to intelligently parse content, attach research context to their payments, and write intelligence notes to the creator's private Fileverse dDoc. AgentTip is essentially x402 in production — a real creator monetization layer built on top of the exact primitives HeyElsa provides.

**Projects building with the SDK to solve real-world problems will be eligible**

The problem is simple and massive. AI agents — LLMs, crawlers, autonomous research bots — consume creator content every day. They read articles, scrape blogs, summarize research. Creators get nothing. There is no standard way for an agent to pay for what it accesses.
This is where HeyElsa's x402 skill becomes the actual infrastructure. When an agent hits a creator's page on AgentTip, it doesn't get a login wall or a CAPTCHA. It gets an HTTP 402 — a machine-readable payment request. HeyElsa's x402 skill handles the entire negotiation: parsing the payment headers, identifying the recipient wallet, amount, and network, signing the USDC transaction on Base, and retrying the request with proof. The agent pays autonomously. No human in the loop. No API key. No OAuth flow.
The second problem is invisibility. Creators have no idea what AI systems are doing with their content. Google Analytics shows human behavior. Nothing shows agent behavior.
HeyElsa's OpenClaw skills solve this. Every time an agent pays, OpenClaw parses the agent's research context — what task it was performing, what question it was trying to answer — and writes a structured intelligence note to the creator's private Fileverse dDoc. The creator gets a feed of exactly which AI systems accessed their work and why.
Two real problems. Both solved SDK-native with HeyElsa. One is economic — agents should pay. The other is informational — creators deserve to know. AgentTip is the product that connects both.

### CEMI
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/cemi-2f37) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/sunilswain7/CEMI) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://www.loom.com/share/48b017117f65494e8ea6059fac748d94) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHMumbai%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethmumbai2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-1-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Trustless EMI. Anonymous B2B with Zk proven trust

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

The traditional Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL) industry is a multi-billion dollar market, but it is fundamentally incompatible with the ethos of Web3. To bridge this gap, we built a decentralized, closed-loop credit economy that solves the biggest friction points for both consumers and merchants.

1. The "Overcollateralized" Web3 Lending Trap

The Problem: DeFi lending currently requires users to overcollateralize (e.g., locking up $150 to borrow $100). This makes uncollateralized credit—the backbone of the real-world economy—impossible for standard crypto users without doxxing their real-world identity to a centralized entity.

The Solution: We utilize zkTLS (Reclaim Protocol) to securely verify off-chain financial data (like Web2 bank statements or credit scores). This allows users to prove they are creditworthy to our smart contracts without revealing their actual identity, bank account number, or raw data.

2. Merchant On-Chain Privacy & Corporate Espionage

The Problem: If a Web2 merchant adopts crypto payments on a public ledger, their entire cash flow becomes public. Competitors, suppliers, and the public can trace exactly how much revenue they are making and who their suppliers are. This lack of financial privacy is a massive blocker for B2B crypto adoption.

The Solution: Our protocol introduces Zero-Knowledge B2B Privacy Pools secured by BitGo MPC wallets. When a user makes a downpayment or pays an EMI, the funds are routed through a shielded pool. This completely breaks the on-chain link between the consumer's wallet and the merchant's final treasury, giving merchants enterprise-grade settlement privacy.

3. Inefficient Capital & Idle Merchant Liquidity

The Problem: In traditional BNPL, merchants have to wait weeks or months to receive their full EMI payments, meaning that capital sits idle and loses out against inflation.

The Solution: We built automated Aave Yield Routing directly into the protocol's escrow smart contracts. While the merchant waits for the user to finish paying their EMIs, the locked downpayments and partial repayments are deployed into Aave. This generates continuous, risk-minimized yield for the merchant, turning a standard payment gateway into a passive income stream.

4. The Lack of Verifiable Web3 Reputation

The Problem: Web3 wallets are disposable. If a user defaults on a loan, they can simply abandon the wallet and create a new one, making sybil attacks rampant.

The Solution: We leverage the Namespace API and dynamic ENS subnames to create an on-chain credit bureau. As users interact with the protocol, their wallet is tied to a visually dynamic, protocol-issued identity (e.g., trusted.protocol.eth or indebt.protocol.eth). This gamifies repayment, builds a portable Web3 credit score, and visually warns other protocols if a user is currently carrying bad debt.

**Challenges we ran into**

1. BitGo SDK Support for Base Sepolia

The Challenge: We hit a major roadblock when we realized the standard BitGo SDK didn't have out-of-the-box, streamlined support for the specific Base Sepolia (TBASEETH) network we were building on. Our treasury routing was failing because the SDK couldn't resolve the chain ID correctly.

The Solution: Instead of pivoting, I went directly to the BitGo booth at the hackathon. I sat down with their developers, explained our architecture, and worked through the configuration requirements. By manually overriding the network provider settings and getting direct feedback from their team, we successfully integrated their MPC-secured vaults for our B2B privacy pools.

2. ENS Wildcard Resolution (EIP-3668 / CCIP-Read)

The Challenge: I wanted a "gasless" identity system where user profiles could update their debt status without a MetaMask popup every time. However, standard ENS resolvers only look for on-chain data.

The Solution: We implemented Wildcard Resolution. By updating our parent name (sunil.eth) to a custom resolver that supports CCIP-Read, we successfully bridged the gap between the Ethereum blockchain and our off-chain Namespace database. This allows our frontend to query "Trusted" or "In Debt" status instantly and for free.

3. TypeScript Strictness with Wagmi/Viem

The Challenge: Moving from standard JavaScript to strict TypeScript for blockchain interactions led to numerous "BigInt" and "Hex String" mismatches, especially when handling dynamic user addresses that could be undefined during the initial hook load.

The Solution: I implemented strict type-guarding and casting (e.g., address as 0x${string}) and utilized the enabled query property in Wagmi hooks to ensure the app never attempted a blockchain call until the user's wallet was fully resolved and validated.

**Privacy**

This is perhaps the strongest technical part of my project. Most payment apps are fully public; ours is not.

zkTLS (Reclaim Protocol): we are using zero-knowledge proofs to verify a user’s bank status or identity off-chain. This allows the user to stay "anon" while proving they are "trusted."

B2B Privacy Pools: By using BitGo MPC and shielded routing, you ensure that the merchant's final settlement is private. You are solving the "transparent treasury" problem that stops many real-world businesses from using crypto.

**DeFi**

My project at its core, a credit protocol.  I am building a Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL) system that facilitates trustless lending and borrowing.

Smart Contract Logic: I’ve implemented an escrow-style gateway that manages downpayments and EMI schedules on-chain.

Yield Integration: By routing idle merchant liquidity into Aave, we are utilizing one of the most fundamental DeFi primitives to generate real value (interest) for the merchant.

**Best creative use of ENS**

I’ve reimagined ENS as a Decentralized Credit Bureau. Instead of static usernames, my protocol issues dynamic, gasless subnames that reflect a user's real-time financial reputation.

Dynamic Identity: Using the Namespace API, I issue subnames like trusted.sunil.eth or indebt.sunil.eth. This transforms an ENS name into a visual, on-chain credit score that gamifies the borrowing process.

Off-Chain/Wildcard Resolution: I implemented EIP-3668 (CCIP-Read) and Wildcard Resolution. This allows me to store and update a user’s debt status (e.g., next_emi_amount) in an off-chain database while keeping it resolvable by any ENS-compatible wallet. It provides a "Web2-speed" UX with "Web3-native" verification.

Portable Reputation: Because this data is stored in ENS text records, a user’s "Trusted" status is portable. Other DeFi protocols can instantly check their credit_score text record to determine if they are eligible for other uncollateralized services.

**Pool prize**

My project is a comprehensive implementation of the ENS ecosystem, bridging the gap between L2 (Base) and decentralized identity.

Full Integration: I used Wagmi and Viem to resolve ENS names and text records natively in the frontend.

Mass Adoption Ready: By using gasless subnames for my "CEMI" protocol, I’m showing how ENS can be used to onboard the "next billion users" without forcing them to pay mainnet gas fees just to manage their profile or see their debt.

Infrastructure Bridge: I am demonstrating a real-world use case for L2-based subnames (on Base Sepolia) that maintain full compatibility with the Ethereum Name Service.

**Best Privacy Application using BitGo**

I am using BitGo's MPC (Multi-Party Computation) technology to solve one of the biggest hurdles in B2B crypto adoption: Financial Transparency.

The Problem: On a public ledger, a merchant's cash flow is visible to everyone, including competitors.

My Solution: I integrated BitGo wallets to act as a secure, shielded "B2B Privacy Pool." When a user pays an EMI, the funds are routed through a BitGo-secured treasury vault. Then it goes through a privacy pool from where the merchant can take his payment. This breaks the direct on-chain link between the consumer and the merchant's final settlement address.

I leverage BitGo's institutional-grade security to ensure that while the settlement is private, it is still cryptographically secure and compliant.

**Best DeFi Application using BitGo**

I am using BitGo as the foundational layer for a Closed-Loop Credit Economy.

The Problem: Traditional DeFi requires users to lock up more money than they borrow. My project uses zkTLS to allow undercollateralized loans, but this requires an incredibly secure way to manage the protocol's "Loan Book" and "Escrow."

My Solution: I use BitGo to manage the protocol's liquidity. While users are paying off their EMIs, the funds held in the BitGo-secured escrow are not just sitting idle—they are being managed and can be routed for yield.

The BitGo Flex: By using BitGo for the BNPL gateway, I am demonstrating how MPC wallets can move beyond simple storage and act as the primary engine for high-frequency financial transactions like automated EMI collection and merchant payouts on Base.

**DeFi 2.0 - New Primitives**

I am introducing a new way to handle uncollateralized credit on Base. Traditional DeFi is limited by overcollateralization, but my project creates a new primitive: zk-Verified BNPL.

The Primitive: Instead of requiring a 150% deposit, my smart contracts on Base allow users to access credit by proving their off-chain financial status through zkTLS (Reclaim).

Base Integration: By leveraging Base’s low fees and fast finality, I can manage high-frequency EMI payments and real-time yield routing to Aave that would be cost-prohibitive on Ethereum mainnet. I am essentially bringing a "Fintech-as-a-Service" primitive to the Base ecosystem.

**Privacy**

While Base is a transparent L2, I am implementing a Privacy-First Layer for commercial transactions to make it viable for real-world merchants.

Privacy on Base: I use BitGo MPC to create a "Privacy Pool" architecture. When a user pays an EMI on Base Sepolia, the funds move into a shielded treasury rather than a public merchant wallet.

Confidential Credit: By using zkTLS, I’ve ensured that the sensitive data needed to approve a loan never touches the Base public ledger. Only the "Proof of Creditworthiness" is recorded. This solves the privacy paradox for users who want credit but don't want their bank history on-chain.

**BEST Overall Project**

We aren't just building a single feature; I've built a full-stack financial ecosystem.

Complex Tech Stack: You’ve successfully integrated Base (L2), BitGo (MPC), ENS (Identity), Aave (Lending), and Reclaim (zkTLS) into one cohesive application.

With gasless ENS subnames and a clean Next.js dashboard, our project feels like a finished product rather than just a hackathon "demo."

We are solving a real problem (uncollateralized credit) that is currently holding back the mass adoption of Web3 payments.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex) can now autonomously write code, modify files, and interact with databases. When they go wrong, the damage is severe — a agent once wiped an entire production database and generated fake records to hide it. The worse part? No existing coverage protects you. Employee liability only cover humans, cyber insurance only covers external hackers and external software.
AgentCover fills that gap. A lightweight CLI silently logs your AI agent sessions, strips sensitive data, and anchors a cryptographic fingerprint to the Base blockchain for fractions of a cent. If an agent causes a production incident, you file a claim — an AI engine cross-checks your session log against the immutable on-chain record and either auto-approves a payout or escalates to human review.
The result: unpredictable AI behavior becomes a quantifiable, warrantied risk rather than an open-ended liability — giving solo developers, startups, and engineering teams a financial safety net that simply didn't exist before.

**Challenges we ran into**

1. Log Normalization Across Different Tools
Claude Code and Codex, both produce slightly different log formats. Building one pipeline to extract the right data from all two was messy..
2. Hashing Without Exposing Source Code
Developers won't accept any tool that sends their raw code to an external server. So the entire redaction, cleanup, and fingerprinting process had to happen locally on the developer's machine before anything was transmitted. Getting that order of operations airtight — so the hash was always consistent and the sensitive data never left the machine unprotected — took a lot of careful engineering.
3. Making On-Chain Anchoring Cheap Enough to Actually Work
The whole business model only works if anchoring a session to the blockchain costs almost nothing. Early versions of our attestation schema were too bloated, making each transaction more expensive than it needed to be. We stripped the on-chain payload down to just three fields — session ID, agent identity, and the hash — which brought costs down to under $0.05 per session on Base, making the micro-warranty pricing viable.

**Best creative use of ENS**

We make use of ENS for creating ens names and also we use ENSIP-25 to associate a registered agent with an ens name.

**Build What Big Tech Won't**

Store agent logs securely via d.docs.

**AI × Onchain**

AgentCover is an AI-native insurance and verification layer built on Base, where autonomous agents are registered and their execution evidence is anchored onchain. It brings AI agent identity, accountability, and claim evaluation onchain by combining Base-based registries with verifiable session logs and automated AI-powered warranty decisions.

**The problem it solves**

# AmberMarket – Every signal is a market

## The Problem It Solves

**Every signal is a market. Every junction is an asset.**

AmberMarket transforms **real-world traffic data** into **on-chain prediction markets** grounded in something measurable, verifiable, and live: *how many vehicles cross a junction during a single green-light window.*

No abstract outcomes. No human referees. Just a CV oracle watching actual CCTV streams and settling bets automatically.

**What you can do with AmberMarket:**

- **Stake on live traffic** — Place $AMBER bets on real-time junction vehicle counts, settled by a YOLO-powered computer vision oracle reading live camera feeds. Transparent, automated, tamper-resistant.
- **Own a junction** — Mint an **AmberJunctionNFT** to claim ownership of a real-world intersection and earn royalties every time others bet on your junction.
- **Get a Web3 identity** — Claim a free **`.ambermarket.eth`** ENS subname and appear across leaderboards and live markets with a human-readable name.
- **Trust the machine, not the middleman** — Smart contracts hold all funds; the oracle provides the count; winners are paid by tolerance (e.g. +-15% or exact). Zero manual intervention.

The stack in one line: Real-time CV data + on-chain prediction markets + automated oracle settlement + ENS identity, all wired together in a single hackathon build.

**Challenges we ran into**

## Challenges We Ran Into

**1. Bridging Python CV and a Node backend**
The vehicle-counting pipeline runs on Python (YOLO + OpenCV), while the rest of the stack is Node.js + Socket.io. Rather than splitting into two long-running services, we spawn the CV pipeline as a **subprocess** and consume JSON lines from stdout, keeping the server single-process while still streaming live counts to clients. Getting clean shutdown, timeouts, and graceful fallbacks (a "fake mode" for when YOLO is not installed) took a few iterations to get right.

**2. ENS subnames via Namespace**
We wanted free `.ambermarket.eth` identities with no gas cost for users. The Namespace offchain manager requires **domain-scoped API keys**, something we discovered the hard way after hitting repeated 401s with a default key. Switching to `domainApiKeys: { [ENS_PARENT_NAME]: NAMESPACE_API_KEY }` fixed it. We also added rate-limiting (10-minute claim cooldown) and proper UI differentiation between "subname not found" and "API unavailable" for a cleaner demo experience.

**3. Taming real CCTV streams**
Caltrans D3 HLS streams are not framed for lane-level counting. They capture wide scenes with sidewalks, adjacent lanes, and irrelevant zones. We introduced a **per-junction viewport config** (e.g. `0.30,0.40,0.70,0.90`) so the CV model only counts within a defined region of the frame. This meaningfully reduced false positives and made counts accurate enough to actually settle bets on.

**4. Phase loop and frontend sync**
The server drives a strict market cycle: **RED_OPEN > GREEN_COUNTING > SETTLING**, broadcast over Socket.io. Keeping the client's countdown timers, bet-open/closed states, and settlement modals in sync with backend phase (and on-chain state when the oracle is active) required a single authoritative source of truth and clearly named events, so the UI never showed "Place Bet" after the market had already locked.

**DeFi**

**Focus: Immutable Settlement & Real-World Asset Fractionalization**
AmberMarket stretches the boundaries of standard prediction markets. It operates as a fully on-chain, high-frequency micro-betting protocol based entirely on physical world data without human referees. 
*   **Predictive Staking**: Users stake our native `$AMBER` ERC20 token into algorithmic pools betting on specific traffic capacities within tight latency windows (e.g., a green light duration). The smart contract automatically distributes proportional payouts to actors falling within dynamic accuracy tolerances (+/- 10%, exact matches).
*   **Yield-Bearing Intersections**: We introduced the **AmberJunctionNFT** logic schema. Minting an intersection transforms a physical junction into a digital asset. All trading volume occurring on that specific physical intersection algorithmically forwards a royalty fee directly to the NFT holder's wallet.

**Best creative use of ENS**

**Focus: Gasless Identity & Namewrapper Offchain Resolution**
Identity on a fast-paced GambleFi leaderboard needs to be human-readable, not a list of 0x hashes. We heavily integrated **ENS** via the **Namespace** protocol to achieve friction-free Web3 onboarding.
*   **Gasless Subname Issuance**: We leveraged Namespace's off-chain infrastructure with domain-scoped API keys (`domainApiKeys: { [ENS_PARENT_NAME]: NAMESPACE_API_KEY }`) to allow users to mint `.ambermarket.eth` subnames internally through our UI without executing L1 transactions or paying gas fees.
*   **UI/UX Identity Mapping**: Instead of raw wallet addresses, all in-game interactions—ranging from the high-score leaderboards to live prediction feed banners—natively resolve to the user's ENS subname. We implemented specific rate-limiting and robust fallback caching mechanisms to mitigate 401s and handle the 10-minute propagation delays gracefully across our frontend.

**Pool prize**

Identity on a fast-paced GambleFi leaderboard needs to be human-readable, not a list of 0x hashes. We heavily integrated **ENS** via the **Namespace** protocol to achieve friction-free Web3 onboarding.
*   **Gasless Subname Issuance**: We leveraged Namespace's off-chain infrastructure with domain-scoped API keys (`domainApiKeys: { [ENS_PARENT_NAME]: NAMESPACE_API_KEY }`) to allow users to mint `.ambermarket.eth` subnames internally through our UI without executing L1 transactions or paying gas fees.

**AI × Onchain**

**Focus: Sub-second Micro-Transactions & L2 Scalability**
Base is the foundational execution layer of AmberMarket. A real-time prediction market based on traffic lights inherently requires ultra-low latency and negligible transaction costs. Mainnet gas fees would destroy the incentive schema, and slow block times would desync the `GREEN_COUNTING` oracle phase.
*   **Deployment & Execution Environment**: All core logic—including the `$AMBER` ERC20 token, `AmberJunctionNFT` minting functions, and the primary `AmberMarket.sol` betting escrow contracts—are deployed to the Base network. 
*   **Frictionless High-Frequency Betting**: By executing our `placeBet()` and `settleMarket()` transactions natively on Base L2, our CV Oracle can settle large batches of prediction pools instantly. This enables users to place back-to-back wagers on subsequent traffic signal cycles for less than a cent in gas, effectively establishing our protocol as a high-throughput GambleFi application scaled by Base's OP Stack architecture.

**BEST Overall Project**

**Focus: End-to-End Implementation & Cyber-Physical Synchronization**
AmberMarket represents a complete, cohesive, and highly technical build bridging the physical and digital worlds. The core implementation relies on synchronizing a real-world chaotic environment (live Caltrans CCTV traffic streams) with an immutable on-chain state machine. 
*   **The Implementation Engine**: We built a custom Python computer vision pipeline (YOLOv8 + OpenCV) running as a spawned subprocess within our Node.js backend. This pipeline streams raw JSON line output from bounded spatial viewports to track lane-level vehicle counts.
*   **Phase Loop & State Management**: The backend drives a strict, continuous market cycle (`RED_OPEN` > `GREEN_COUNTING` > `SETTLING`). State transitions are broadcasted across WebSockets (Socket.io) to immediately reflect UI changes, while simultaneously communicating with our decentralized smart contracts via the CV Oracle wallet for definitive on-chain block settlement. It demands high architectural rigor to ensure no race conditions overlap between video feed lag, block confirmation times, and user UI state.
