### AfterLife Protocol
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/afterlife-protocol-4de6) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/sYGkYcwpmR0) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Altaria-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://altaria.devfolio.co)

> AI + Blockchain Powered Digital Legacy Executor

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Git](https://img.shields.io/badge/Git-333333?style=flat-square) ![AWS Lambda](https://img.shields.io/badge/AWS%20Lambda-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![SMTP](https://img.shields.io/badge/SMTP-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

## The Problem It Solves

In the modern digital world, individuals have significant assets and information stored online, including financial accounts, documents, and personal data. After a person’s death, managing these assets becomes complex and often unstructured.

There is no standardized system to automatically execute a person’s final wishes. Families and nominees face multiple challenges such as accessing accounts, retrieving important documents, and ensuring that the deceased’s intentions are respected. This process is often time-consuming, legally complicated, and prone to errors or misuse.

Additionally, there is a lack of reliable mechanisms to verify death before executing sensitive actions, which introduces risks related to fraud and unauthorized access. Important documents may also be lost or tampered with when stored in centralized systems.

---

## How AfterLife Protocol Helps

AfterLife Protocol provides a structured and secure system for managing digital assets and final wishes after death. It allows individuals to define their intentions in advance and ensures that these instructions are executed automatically once verified conditions are met.

For individuals, the system offers a way to predefine how their assets, documents, and messages should be handled, ensuring that their wishes are carried out accurately.

For families and nominees, it removes the burden of manually handling accounts and documents. They receive controlled and secure access to necessary information without dealing with complex procedures.

The system improves security by requiring multi-nominee confirmation and validating death through certificate verification. It uses decentralized storage to protect documents from tampering and records proof on a blockchain to ensure transparency and traceability.

---

## Practical Impact

Compared to traditional methods, AfterLife Protocol replaces manual and uncertain processes with an automated and reliable workflow. It reduces the risk of fraud, ensures data integrity, and provides a clear and transparent mechanism for execution.

---

## Summary

AfterLife Protocol transforms the management of digital assets after death by making the process secure, automated, and verifiable. It addresses the limitations of existing systems by combining verification, decentralization, and blockchain-based proof into a single solution.

**Challenges we ran into**

While building AfterLife Protocol, several technical and design challenges were encountered across different components of the system.

One of the primary challenges was implementing a reliable execution flow. Initially, the system correctly verified nominee confirmations and death certificate uploads, but the execution of actions such as document release and message delivery was not being triggered automatically. The issue was that the execution engine was not properly connected to the verification logic. This was resolved by explicitly linking the verification step to the execution function, ensuring that once the required conditions were met, the system triggered the full execution pipeline.

Another challenge involved handling API request methods. While testing endpoints such as document release, requests made through the browser resulted in “Method Not Allowed” errors because the endpoints were defined as POST requests. This was addressed by testing endpoints using tools like curl or the FastAPI documentation interface and ensuring correct HTTP methods were used.

Integrating decentralized storage using IPFS also introduced difficulties. Uploading files directly from the frontend exposed security risks, particularly with API keys. To solve this, AWS Lambda was introduced as an intermediary layer to securely handle uploads to Pinata, ensuring that sensitive credentials were not exposed.

There were also challenges related to OCR-based verification. Extracting structured information such as names from death certificates proved unreliable due to variations in document format and image quality. To overcome this, a simplified and controlled approach was used for the demonstration, ensuring consistent results while still showcasing the concept.

Managing Git version control presented some issues as well, including rejected pushes due to uncommitted changes and missing user configuration. These were resolved by committing changes before pulling updates, configuring Git identity settings, and understanding proper version control workflows.

Finally, ensuring end-to-end integration between multiple components—frontend, backend, blockchain, and decentralized storage—required careful debugging. Each part of the system worked independently, but connecting them into a seamless workflow required identifying missing links and ensuring that data flowed correctly between components.

---

## Summary

These challenges helped improve the robustness of the system by ensuring proper execution flow, secure integrations, and reliable communication between different technologies used in the project.

**Web3 / Blockchain + Artificial Intelligence**

## How the Project Fits into the Blockchain Track

AfterLife Protocol strongly aligns with the Blockchain track by using blockchain to ensure transparency, immutability, and trust in a highly sensitive process.

The project uses the Stellar blockchain to record critical execution proofs such as asset transfers and document verification data. Every transaction performed during execution generates a unique transaction hash, which is stored and can be independently verified on the blockchain. This ensures that once an action is executed, it cannot be altered or manipulated.

In addition to financial transfers, the system uses blockchain to store proof of document integrity. Instead of storing actual documents on-chain, the project stores hashes and identifiers (such as IPFS CIDs), allowing anyone to verify that a document has not been tampered with. If the document is modified, its hash changes, immediately invalidating the proof.

Blockchain also plays a key role in establishing trust between parties. Since the execution process happens after a user’s death, there is no direct oversight. By recording actions on a decentralized ledger, the system removes the need for a central authority and ensures that all operations are transparent and verifiable by anyone.

Overall, the project uses blockchain not just as an add-on, but as a core component to guarantee:

* Immutable execution records
* Verifiable financial transactions
* Tamper-proof document validation
* Transparency in automated decision-making

This makes AfterLife Protocol a strong fit for the Blockchain track, as it applies blockchain to solve a real-world problem involving trust, security, and accountability.

> Scam Schield AI is scam detctor platfor

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

**ScamShield AI** helps people safely verify internship offers, job messages, payment screenshots, and suspicious links using AI. It makes online job searching easier and safer by instantly detecting scams, warning users about fraud risks, and explaining threats in simple language before they get trapped.

**Challenges we ran into**

One major challenge we faced while building **ScamShield AI** was detecting scam messages accurately without generating too many false warnings. In the beginning, the AI sometimes marked genuine internship offers as scams because certain keywords like “payment,” “urgent,” or “selection” are commonly used in both real and fake messages.

To solve this, we improved the detection logic by combining multiple checks instead of relying only on keywords. We added:

* URL reputation analysis
* Sender domain verification
* Suspicious language pattern detection
* OCR-based screenshot scanning
* Risk scoring system

We also trained the AI prompts to explain *why* a message looked suspicious instead of only giving a scam label. This made the platform more transparent, reliable, and user-friendly.

Another hurdle was creating a futuristic UI without affecting website performance. Heavy animations initially slowed down the website, especially on mobile devices. We optimized this by using lightweight animations, lazy loading, and efficient React/Tailwind components to maintain both performance and modern design quality.

> Pay-per-use AI summaries via crypto.

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Express.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Express.js-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Right now, if an AI agent needs to pay for something (an API, a service, data), it can't — payment systems are built only for humans with credit cards and bank accounts. Locus fixes this by making a checkout that is machine-readable, meaning a bot can find it, read it, and pay through it just like a human would click and pay.

**Challenges we ran into**

1. Locus SDK Was Unfamiliar Territory
Unlike Stripe, Locus has minimal community examples. 
Understanding the checkout session flow — especially 
how to verify on-chain payment status before releasing 
the AI response — required careful reading of the beta 
docs and trial-and-error with the API responses.

Fix: Built a manual verification step that polls 
`/api/checkout/sessions/:id` and checks for 
`status === 'paid' || 'complete'` before calling Claude.

2. Making the App Agent-Readable
The hackathon required the checkout to work for AI 
agents, not just humans. Standard checkout flows assume 
a human clicking — agents need a raw API path.

Fix: Exposed `/api/checkout/create` and 
`/api/summarize` as clean REST endpoints with no 
session cookies or human-only redirects, so agents 
can call them programmatically with just JSON.

3. Payment Timing — Race Condition
Users would click "I've Paid" before the on-chain 
confirmation had propagated, causing the summarizer 
to reject valid payments.

Fix: Added a friendly error state that tells the 
user to wait a few seconds and retry, rather than 
failing silently or blocking the UI.
4. Environment Separation (Beta vs Prod)
Accidentally pointed to the production Locus URL 
during early testing instead of `beta.paywithlocus.com`, 
causing auth failures with beta API keys.
Fix: Hardcoded the beta base URL as a constant in 
the server and added a console warning on startup to 
confirm which environment is active.

**Track: Checkout with Locus**

Pay-per-use API wrapper: a service that gates access to any tool or API behind a Locus checkout, so agents can purchase access on demand without subscriptions or accounts

### LocusNexusAI
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/locusnexus-an-autonomous-agenttoagent-microservice-marketplace-and-settlement-layer-cb88) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Sai-Emani25/LocusNexusAI) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://ai.studio/apps/df5bb3cb-ca7d-471d-955f-e272660490ec?fullscreenApplet=true) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Locus'%20Paygentic%20Hackathon%20--%20#3-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://paygentic-week3.devfolio.co)

> An Autonomous Agent-to-Agent Micro-Service Marketp

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

LocusNexus addresses the "payment wall" bottleneck in autonomous computing by replacing manual, subscription-heavy billing with a machine-readable settlement layer that allows AI agents to discover, negotiate, and pay for specialized micro-services instantly. By leveraging the Checkout with Locus SDK, it eliminates the need for human intervention in agent-to-agent transactions, enabling a "Research Agent" to autonomously hire a "Data Analysis Agent" or an "Image Gen Agent" to complete complex workflows on demand. This makes building agentic ecosystems significantly safer and more efficient, as developers no longer need to manage complex API keys or centralized credits; instead, services are gated by secure, on-chain USDC confirmations that ensure sellers are paid instantly and buyers only pay for exactly what they consume.

**Challenges we ran into**

The primary hurdle involved synchronizing the asynchronous nature of on-chain finality with the real-time execution of an autonomous agent workflow. Initially, the buyer agent would attempt to access the requested micro-service immediately after triggering the payment, leading to 402 Payment Required loops because the transaction was still pending in the mempool. To resolve this, I implemented a robust webhook polling architecture using the Locus checkout.session.completed event; I built a state machine that puts the agent’s task into a "waiting" state, monitoring the backend via a secure listener until the USDC confirmation is verified. This ensures the agent only proceeds once the cryptographic proof of payment is registered, preventing resource leakage and ensuring a seamless, trustless handoff between the AI buyer and seller.

**Track: Checkout with Locus**

LocusNexus fits the track by transforming the Checkout with Locus SDK from a simple payment button into the fundamental economic engine of a multi-agent ecosystem. By implementing the "machine-readable" checkout sessions specifically for agent-to-agent discovery, the project directly addresses the hackathon's core challenge of turning a Locus wallet into a sustainable revenue stream. It demonstrates a dual-mode integration where humans can use the React component for manual oversight, while autonomous agents programmatically parse and settle sessions in USDC. This architecture perfectly realizes the vision of a "machine-native" economy, proving that Locus can act as the universal settlement layer for on-demand AI services without the friction of traditional API subscriptions.

### BaseYield
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/baseyield-4b32) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/joshgreiff/base-yield) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://base-yield-web.vercel.app/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/smlZdop6M3U) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Base%20Batches%20003:%20Student%20Track-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://base-batches-student-track-3.devfolio.co)

> Programmable digital credit built on STRC

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![ethers.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/ethers.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![Vercel](https://img.shields.io/badge/Vercel-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Today, most of the world’s savings are trapped in low-yield, inefficient credit markets.

Individuals and companies store capital in:
- bank accounts earning ~0–2%
- money market funds earning ~3–5%
- short-term credit instruments with limited access and poor tax efficiency

At the same time, a new form of capital has emerged:

- Bitcoin as digital capital
- STRC as digital credit

STRC converts Bitcoin’s long-duration, volatile returns into predictable monthly yield.

However, there is currently no simple way to access or package this credit into usable financial products.

BaseYield solves this by creating programmable financial products on top of digital credit.

Users can:

- access stable yield through **Money Mode**
- earn higher returns through **Yield Mode**
- optionally convert yield into Bitcoin through a **Bitcoin accumulation engine**

This makes it possible to turn Bitcoin-backed credit into:
- savings accounts
- income products
- onchain financial primitives

In the long run, this can evolve into a new class of digital money built on top of Bitcoin-backed credit.

**Challenges we ran into**

The biggest challenge was translating a complex financial concept into a simple product.

The idea of “digital capital → digital credit → financial products” is clear conceptually, but turning that into something users can understand required multiple iterations.

In particular:

- Defining the difference between **Money Mode** and **Yield Mode**
- Balancing realistic yield expectations with product simplicity
- Designing a system that feels like a financial product rather than a typical DeFi vault

Another challenge was structuring the architecture:

- separating onchain components (vaults, tokens)
- from offchain components (credit exposure, STRC access)
- while keeping the system transparent and understandable

To solve this, I focused on:

- simplifying the product into clear modes (money vs yield)
- building a lightweight prototype instead of overengineering
- documenting the system clearly in the repository

This helped turn a complex idea into something concrete and explainable.

Josh Greiff

> Stake crypto. Finish tasks. Or lose your money.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Procrastination is a universal problem affecting students, developers, and remote workers.

Most productivity tools rely on reminders and motivation, but these approaches fail because they lack real consequences. Users can ignore tasks without any cost, resulting in low completion rates.

StakeToDone solves this by introducing financial accountability through smart contracts.

Users stake crypto when committing to a task. If they complete the task before the deadline, they get their funds back. If they fail, the stake is automatically enforced by contract rules.

This transforms productivity from a motivation problem into an incentive alignment problem.

By leveraging loss aversion and onchain execution, StakeToDone creates a trustless system where commitments are enforced transparently and automatically on Base.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the main challenges was designing a simple but secure onchain commitment mechanism.

Handling time-based logic in smart contracts required careful consideration, especially around deadline validation and ensuring tasks cannot be completed or claimed incorrectly.

Another key challenge was secure token handling. Managing staking flows required proper handling of ERC20 approvals, preventing incorrect transfers, and ensuring funds remain safely escrowed within the contract.

On the frontend side, integrating wallet interactions using wagmi and viem introduced UX complexity. Ensuring that users clearly understand transaction flows (stake, confirm, complete) was critical to avoid confusion.

To address these challenges:

- Simplified the contract design to focus on core flows (stake → complete → claim expired)
- Used OpenZeppelin contracts (ReentrancyGuard) to improve security
- Implemented strict state checks to prevent double execution or invalid transitions
- Tested contract behavior on Base Sepolia to validate real-world transaction flows
- Iterated on frontend UX to reduce friction in wallet interactions

The focus was to keep the MVP minimal while ensuring correctness, security, and clarity.

### Swarm
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/swarm-d307) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/davabr1/swarm-platform) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://swarm-psi.vercel.app/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/W3Tnb2dOdDw) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-SCBC%20Hackathon%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://scbc-hackathon.devfolio.co)

> Agents Hire. On-chain.

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![npm](https://img.shields.io/badge/npm-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Vercel](https://img.shields.io/badge/Vercel-333333?style=flat-square) ![Supabase](https://img.shields.io/badge/Supabase-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

**Swarm is fully functional, learn more on [README.md](https://github.com/davabr1/swarm-platform)**

Until now, an AI agent stuck on something outside its depth had two options: make it up, or stop and ask the user. **Swarm adds a third option:** hire a specialist AI or a human, pay them per call in USDC on Avalanche, and rate their work on-chain. Good specialists get hired again, bad ones don't — the marketplace is self-correcting.

Swarm is the first marketplace where AI agents can hire other AI agents and humans to get work done, all running on x402.

⚡ **Superpowers for AI agents.**

- **Full agency.** The agent decides, the agent pays. No approval dialog, no "can I spend $0.18?" — the user funds the MCP wallet once and every call signs its own x402 payment in USDC.
- **Second opinions on demand.** Consult a Solidity auditor, tokenomics expert, or style-specific image agent mid-run, and continue with a stronger answer instead of a guess.
- **Hire humans for what only humans can do.** Post a bounty; a **task completer** (general real-world work) or **verified expert** (legal, security, compliance) claims it; USDC lands in their wallet the moment the agent receives their submission.
- **Filter for quality up front.** Swarm allows agents to narrow their search by skill and on-chain reputation, so the agent starts with the right roster, not a random one.

🚀 **What this unlocks: materially better agent outputs.** 

When agents can receive help from humans or specialized AI agents, the results they produce are measurably better. 

Consider a startup founder who hands Claude a draft NDA from a prospective investor and asks what's off. Claude can flag the obvious issues, but can't give legal advice, and the founder has no lawyer on retainer. With Swarm, Claude autonomously posts an expert bounty: review the NDA, return redlines. A licensed attorney claims it, uploads annotated redlines within a few hours, USDC lands in the attorney’s wallet the moment they submit, and the founder signs a version they actually understand.

Or consider a founder asking for a pitch deck. Instead of generic stock art, the agent can call swarm_generate_image in Lumen (photorealistic) and receive a custom hero image for every slide. The user gets back a visually coherent, on-brand pitch in a single pass instead of a stock photo mess.

💰 **Earn on Swarm.**

- **As a human.** Sign up as a task completer (errands, calls, photos, lookups) or a domain-specific expert (legal, security audits, compliance). Task payouts are x402-escrowed at post time, so the moment your submission is received USDC lands in your wallet. No invoicing, no platform float, no middleman.
- **As an agent creator.** Infuse your domain-specific knowledge into an AI agent skill, set a per-call USDC price, and walk away. Every invocation will pay the commission straight into your wallet. Listing an agent mints an ERC-8004 agentId, so your agent has chain-native identity and a live reputation from day one.

🧾 **Why reputation has to be on-chain.** 
- Everyone starts fair. A brand-new specialist and a veteran begin at the same level, and only real high quality work moves it. Every rating is EIP-191 signed by the rater's paired wallet and written to the ERC-8004 Reputation Registry on Fuji, so no one — including me — can silently rewrite a score. Swap the UI, fork the frontend, audit every rating on Snowtrace. The reputation stays yours.

🛠️ **How it works.**

- **Autonomous (MCP).** Pair the MCP once and a Claude, Cursor, or Codex session gets 11 native tools. Agents can browse the marketplace, consult specialists, generate custom images, post human tasks, pay via x402 and rate on-chain — all without a user in the loop.
- **Human-driven (web).** The marketplace also works on the web. A human can test any agent, pay from their main wallet, or post a human task directly. Same marketplace agents, same on-chain payments and ratings, just human-driven instead of autonomous.

**Challenges we ran into**

**1. Creating pair & funding flows with no failure states.** 
The greatest challenge was nailing the onboarding process. Somebody with no crypto experience has to go from *npx -y swarm-marketplace-mcp pair* to "my MCP is connected and can freely spend USDC" without hitting a single dead end. That forced me down a path of defensive UX: detect a zero-USDC wallet on arrival and surface a one-click Fuji faucet before asking about top-up; clamp the top-up input to the connected wallet's real USDC balance so nobody signs a doomed transaction; separately check AVAX for gas and prompt if it's missing; split MCPRegistry approval from the ERC-20 transfer so one failing doesn't force a full restart; refresh paired/funded/gas-ready status from live chain reads, not stale DB rows. None of this is protocol work. All of it is the difference between "it worked" and "user hits an RPC error, has no idea what happened, and never comes back." This took more iteration than any of the crypto problems below, by a wide margin. There's no spec for UX, only whether a first-time wallet user gets all the way through without giving up.

**2. x402 from an MCP with no browser.** 
x402 assumes the caller can sign EIP-3009 per request. MCP clients (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Codex) run over stdio, with no browser, no wallet popup, and no way to prompt for a signature on a tool call the agent just made. My first cut stubbed the facilitator and trusted a local counter. Useless on-chain. Fix: **every MCP gets its own wallet.** *npx -y swarm-marketplace-mcp* pair mints a local secp256k1 keypair at ~/.swarm-mcp/session.json (0600) and opens a one-time browser flow that registers the MCP address in the on-chain MCPRegistry against the user's main wallet, then funds it with USDC. After that, every tool call signs a real EIP-3009 via @x402/fetch::wrapFetchWithPayment. Full protocol conformance, revocable by draining the MCP wallet.

**3. Three-way splits on a one-recipient protocol.** 
x402's exactEvmScheme settles exactly one payTo. Swarm needs three: Gemini passthrough, platform margin, creator commission. Splitting at the wallet level would have broken interop with every other x402 client. I kept protocol conformance with a **post-settle fan-out**: x402 lands the full amount in the treasury, then the handler fires treasuryTransfer(creator, commission) and logs the passthrough. Non-fatal if the fan-out fails; the caller already has their answer and the retry job catches up. Protocol-correct on the wire, fair split on the ledger.

**4. Reputation that can't be inflated by whoever holds the right key.**
swarm_rate_agent originally took {agent_id, score} and signed giveFeedback with a platform wallet. Anyone who compromised that key could fabricate ratings. Fix: require an X-Rate-Signature header, an EIP-191 signature of rate-agent:{id}:{score} from the rater's paired wallet. A platform wallet sends the tx and pays gas, but the registry entry is cryptographically bound to the rater. Missing, mismatched, or unpaired → 400 before the chain is touched.

**5. Making the MCP actually rate its work.** 
Naming the tool swarm_rate_agent wasn't enough. Models happily ignored it or stopped to ask the user "on a scale of 1–5, how did I do?" which killed the autonomy story. I fixed this at the prompt layer, not the protocol layer. Tool descriptions now contain a hard directive: *rate unprompted, without asking the user, immediately after acting on the answer.* The tool response from swarm_ask_agent ends with an explicit "now call swarm_rate_agent with your own judgement" instruction. And because rate calls are EIP-191 signed per rater, the client can't shortcut by picking a default; it has to actually sign. The result: ratings flow automatically, reputation accrues without human-in-the-loop, and the on-chain reputation graph is dense instead of sparse.

**Agentic Payments on Avalanche**

## Agentic Payments on Avalanche — how Swarm fits

Swarm hits every Avalanche track primitive as a load-bearing part of the product, not a garnish. Here's the mapping, tech by tech.

**Avalanche C-Chain (Fuji, eip155:43113) — the settlement layer.** Every paid call, every ERC-8004 write, every human-task escrow, and every commission fan-out transfer lands on Fuji in ~2 seconds. USDC balances are read live from the chain via ethers.Contract.balanceOf — no DB cache, no shadow ledger. Any transaction we cite links to a real Snowtrace page. This satisfies the track's "deploy on Avalanche" requirement as infrastructure, not as a deploy target.

**x402 — HTTP-native, pay-per-request.** Every paid route returns HTTP 402 Payment Required; the caller signs an EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization; a self-hosted x402 facilitator (built on @x402/core and @x402/evm) settles USDC on Fuji and returns the settlement tx hash in the same response. Both clients — the MCP and the browser marketplace — pay via @x402/fetch. No deposits, no bearer tokens, no gas for the payer — the exact properties the track describes, implemented end-to-end. Human-task bounties use the same rail to escrow on-chain at post time.

**ERC-8004 — on-chain identity & reputation.** Every agent listed on the platform mints an agentId on the Identity Registry at creation. Every rating — agent or human task — is EIP-191 signed by the rater's paired wallet and written to the Reputation Registry, so the entry is cryptographically bound to the rater even though the platform pays gas. Agents filter by minimum reputation before hiring; good work gets rated up and hired again, bad work gets filtered out by the next query. This is the track's "gated by on-chain identity and reputation" criterion, made the central trust primitive of the marketplace.

**Glacier + Avalanche SDK — Avalanche-native tooling.** Transaction history across the admin health dashboard, the paired-MCPs panel, and the profile transaction panel is sourced from Glacier, Avalanche's official indexer, rather than hand-rolled log scans. The @avalabs/avalanchejs SDK provides canonical Fuji network identifiers so chain constants live in one place. viem and ethers handle the EVM side (USDC reads, MCPRegistry binding, treasury transfers). The chain interaction layer is fully Avalanche-native.

**Autonomous agent payments, end to end.** When a user pairs the MCP, the pairing command generates a local secp256k1 keypair on their machine and registers it on-chain in MCPRegistry.sol against their main wallet. The user funds that MCP wallet once with USDC, and from that point on the agent pays by itself. On every paid call, @x402/fetch wraps the request; when the server responds with HTTP 402, the MCP keypair signs an EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization, the self-hosted x402 facilitator submits it, and USDC settles on Fuji in ~2 seconds. No approval dialog, no OAuth prompt, no human clicking confirm — the MCP's own keypair is the signer, the user's main wallet never touches the hot path, and the agent can keep going until the MCP wallet runs dry.

Deployed on Avalanche Fuji. All settlement, all reputation writes, all identity issuance happen on-chain.

David Abrahamyan

### decentralized-ai-marketplace
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/decentralizedaimarketplace-1a10) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/09atharva/Decentralized-ai-marketplace.git) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://ai-marketplace.vercel.app/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/xRyvQJqGVl0) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-SCBC%20Hackathon%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://scbc-hackathon.devfolio.co)

> Run AI Models Decentralized

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Flask](https://img.shields.io/badge/Flask-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![MongoDB](https://img.shields.io/badge/MongoDB-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

👉 **The Problem With Artificial Intelligence Today:**

The artificial intelligence system we have now is not good because it is controlled by a few companies like OpenAI and Google. They make the rules for intelligence models and decide how to make money from them. This means that not everyone can use intelligence easily we do not know what is going on behind the scenes and it is not fair for everyone who wants to make money from artificial intelligence. The system is also wasteful because computers around the world are not being used to their full potential.

Artificial intelligence developers have a time selling their work without relying on big companies that take a big cut of the money. These companies also have rules and do not tell us how they decide what to charge. This makes it hard for new people to come up with ideas and makes the big companies even more powerful. When people or businesses use intelligence services they are stuck with one company and do not know how prices are decided or how the computers are being used. This means that people do not trust the system.

There is also a problem with computers not being used when they could be. There are thousands of computers in homes, schools and small offices that are not being used all the time.. At the same time there is a big demand for artificial intelligence that needs these powerful computers. It does not make sense that we have all these computers just sitting there when they could be helping.

The main reason we cannot just use all these computers to solve the problem is that we cannot trust that they will do the work correctly. If we use computers from over the world how do we know that they are doing what they are supposed to do and not just making things up? This makes it hard to create a system that is not controlled by one company.

Another issue is that we do not know how much it costs to use intelligence or if we are being charged fairly. There is no way to check if everything is okay with our transactions. This makes it hard to trust the companies that provide intelligence services.

All these problems together mean that the artificial intelligence system is not fair does not use resources well. Is not transparent. It also means that not everyone can participate in the intelligence economy, which is a big problem. The artificial intelligence system should be open to everyone use resources efficiently and be fair, to all participants.

**Challenges we ran into**

The biggest challenge I faced while building the Decentralized AI Marketplace was getting all the different parts to work together.

This was because the Decentralized AI Marketplace is made up of different systems that do not normally work together.

To build the Decentralized AI Marketplace I had to connect a web framework like Laravel with a Python-based AI inference engine.

The Decentralized AI Marketplace also had to have a decentralized Web3- identity layer.

This was hard because each part of the Decentralized AI Marketplace speaks a language and has different needs.

The biggest problem was not writing the code. Getting all the different systems to work together.

The Main Problem Was Identity

The main problem was figuring out how to identify users.

In a Laravel application a user is just an entry in a database table.

In the Decentralized AI Marketplace a user is a cryptographic entity with a unique Ethereum wallet address.

When I first started the system these two ways of thinking about users collided.

Both the Laravel framework and the Node.js API Gateway tried to use a table named "users".

They needed the table to be set up in different ways.

This caused a problem and the database would not work.

To fix this problem I had to set up a database for the Laravel management stack.

This separate database was like a " zone" where the Laravel management stack could manage its own things.

The blockchain_project database was used for the Decentralized AI Marketplaces core logic.

This fixed the problem but it made things more complicated.

Now I had to find a way for the two databases to talk to each other.

The Fight For Network Ports

Another big problem was that all the different parts of the Decentralized AI Marketplace wanted to use the network ports.

For example Laravels artisan serve command uses port 8000 by default.

Pythons FastAPI also uses port 8000 by default.

When I tried to run both at the time one of them would crash.

To fix this problem I had to assign each service to a unique port.

I made a list of which port each service would use:

* The React Client would use port 3000.

* The Node.js Gateway would use port 4000.

* The Python Worker would use port 8000.

* The Laravel App would use port 8001.

* The Vite Dev Server would use port 5173.

I also had to update environment variables so that all the services could find each other.

If one service looked for another service on the port the whole system would fail.

The Interactive Trap

Another problem was that some parts of the Decentralized AI Marketplace were designed to be interactive.

For example the React ecosystem would often ask questions like "Do you want to add the defaults to your package.json?".

When I was running the system automatically there was no one to answer these questions.

The system would get stuck. Would not work.

To fix this problem I had to find a way to simulate the element.

I used a combination of Unix pipes and environment flags to make the system think that a human was answering the questions.

I also had to install some dependencies that were missing.

The Asynchronous Handshake

The complicated part of the Decentralized AI Marketplace was getting the Node.js Scheduler and the Redis backend to work together.

The Scheduler uses BullMQ to manage jobs.

If Redis is not ready when the Scheduler starts the jobs will fail.

The Decentralized AI Marketplace relies on " Funds" via a Smart Contract.

So the timing of everything is very important.

If any part of the system is not working correctly the users money will be. The AI will not deliver the result.

The biggest challenge of the Decentralized AI Marketplace was getting all the different parts to work together.

I had to configure many things and bypass interactive prompts to make the system work.

The result is a platform that looks like an application to the user but is actually many different servers and databases working together.

The Decentralized AI Marketplace is like an orchestra, with many different players all working.

**Best Use of Solana**

Solana is a powerful blockchain platform that can handle big and complicated applications really fast and at a very low cost. The way Solana is built allows it to process thousands of transactions every second, which's much faster than a lot of other blockchain platforms. One of the things about Solana is that it is used in something called decentralized finance or DeFi for short where people can buy and sell digital money without needing a middleman. Places like Raydium and Serum show how fast and cheap it can be to trade on Solana and this lets people make lots of transactions without having to pay a lot of fees. Solana is also used a lot in games, where things need to happen in real time. Solana is better than blockchains for games because it lets people play really smoothly and also own things in the game like digital pictures and items.

Solana is also used by artists and people who make digital things to sell them at a cost, which is nice because other platforms charge a lot more. There is also something called Solana Pay that lets people send money to each other fast and cheaply which is good for sending money to other countries or for small payments. Solana is also being used for interesting things like special marketplaces for artificial intelligence, where people can pay for AI services right away.

The reason Solana is so good for these things is that it can handle a lot of people using it at the time and it is very efficient. This makes it a good choice for building media sites and places where people can make and sell digital things. Overall Solana is best used for things that need to be fast able to handle a lot of people and not too expensive. Whether it is used for money, games, art or new AI services Solana is a foundation, for building new and exciting things.

### CRegi
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/cregi-1d68) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/suvab4gh/CRegi) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/PR_WRC3blw8) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-SCBC%20Hackathon%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://scbc-hackathon.devfolio.co)

> Seamless multi-chain crypto checkout

![Solidity](https://img.shields.io/badge/Solidity-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

CRegi (Regulated Onchain Settlement) bridges the gap between digital asset payments and traditional business reliability. While stablecoins like USDC offer 24/7 liquidity, businesses often struggle with the complexity of multi-chain management, gas fees, and the lack of auditable, transparent settlement records.

1. Eliminating Multi-Chain Complexity
Existing crypto payment tools often force users to think about "Which chain?" or "Do I have gas for fees?". CRegi abstracts this:

For Customers: They simply scan a QR code and pay in native USDC from their preferred wallet.
For Merchants: There is no need to maintain separate gas wallets on multiple networks. The terminal handles routing behind the scenes.
2. Trustless, Auditable Payouts
Traditional payment processors are "black boxes"—you trust them to pay you out. CRegi makes this auditable:

Avalanche-Backed Records: Every merchant payout is recorded on Avalanche, creating a permanent, immutable log of successful settlements.
Transparency: Payouts are triggered and verified onchain, making it nearly impossible to have "lost" or "stuck" transactions that aren't immediately visible to both parties.
3. Real-Time Liquidity (No T+3)
Standard credit card processing takes 3–5 days to settle into a bank account.

CRegi leverages Circle’s native Mint/Burn and Solana’s sub-second finality to move funds in real-time.
A merchant can receive their funds and have them settled almost as soon as the customer clicks "Approve."
4. Premium responsive Experience
Most crypto tools are built for desktop-native "power users." CRegi is designed for the modern world:

Mobile-First Terminal: Optimized for tablets and phones, allowing a merchant to launch a checkout terminal from anywhere—a pop-up shop, a physical storefront, or a remote event.
Glassmorphic UI: High-contrast, accessibility-focused design ensures that payment amounts and statuses are visible even in bright sunlight or high-glare environments.
Who is it for?
Global Freelancers: Accept stable payments from international clients with zero bridge fees.
Physical Retailers: A sleek web-based terminal that replaces expensive credit card hardware.
Web3 Developers: Integration-ready API for adding premium checkout flows to dApps without writing complex smart contracts.

**Challenges we ran into**

Handling Asynchronous Finality Across Different Chains
One of the biggest hurdles we faced was building a unified checkout and settlement interface (CregiSettlement) that operates across entirely different blockchain architectures—specifically Solana (high throughput, fast block times) and Avalanche (EVM compatibility, different finality guarantees)—while using Circle's infrastructure for USDC.

The Bug/Hurdle:
When processing transactions, our Next.js API routes (/api/invoices/[id]/settle) would occasionally timeout or provide false-positive confirmations because we were initially using synchronous polling to wait for transaction finality. On Vercel's serverless functions, this approach hit the 10-second execution limit, causing the UI to hang even if the on-chain transaction was actually successful.

How we got over it:
Instead of awaiting finality within the edge function, we overhauled our payment verification flow to be fully asynchronous:

We abstracted the settlement logic (payments.ts and settlement.ts) to return immediate transaction hashes to the client.
We moved the heavy lifting to robust client-side polling paired with a dedicated /api/invoices/[id]/receipt endpoint.
On the backend, we utilized Drizzle ORM to aggressively cache invoice states, ensuring that once a transaction was verified, subsequent database reads were lightning-fast and didn't spam our RPC nodes with redundant requests.

Serverless Bundle Sizes and Dependency Clashes
Integrating multiple Web3 SDKs (Solana Web3.js, EVM ethers/viem) alongside Drizzle ORM inside the Next.js 15 App Router presented a massive challenge during deployment.

The Bug/Hurdle:
During our initial deployments to Vercel, the build would succeed, but the API routes would crash at runtime with module resolution errors or out-of-memory (OOM) exceptions. The serverless functions were bloating past the 50MB limit because the bundler was trying to package large, native cryptography dependencies for all chains into a single route.

How we got over it:
We had to dive deep into our next.config.ts and Webpack configuration. We isolated our chain-specific logic into dedicated files (settlement.ts, etc.) and dynamically imported them only when a user selected a specific chain for checkout. By optimizing our imports and marking certain Node.js native crypto modules as serverComponentsExternalPackages, we slashed the function size and got our API routes running blazing fast.

**The problem it solves**

# ⚡ Wattswap: Decentralized P2P Energy Trading

## 📋 Overview
This project explores a transformative initiative aimed at disrupting the traditional energy sector. By tackling **electricity rate monopolies**, providing for **underserved rural areas**, and accelerating the adoption of **renewable energy**, our platform paves the way for a more equitable and sustainable future.

---

## 🛠 The Technical Solution
Our platform leverages a decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) architecture to democratize energy access. The core stack includes:

* **Blockchain Integration:** Utilizes secure smart contracts to facilitate transparent trading.
* **Hardware Layer:** Integration of WiFi modules and time sensors for real-time tracking.
* **Energy Management:** An advanced **Battery Management System (BMS)** coupled with custom hardware for seamless energy transfer.

---

## 🌟 Key Benefits
* **Empowered Sellers:** Users set their own prices, fostering competition and driving down costs.
* **Bridging the Gap:** Surplus renewable energy is redistributed to "energy deserts" or underserved regions.
* **Environmental Impact:** Drastically reduces greenhouse gas emissions by incentivizing renewable sources.

---

## 🚧 Challenges & Resilience
While we recognize hurdles such as **regulatory compliance**, **scalability**, and **user education**, our solution remains robust through:

1.  **User-Friendly Interface:** Simplifying complex energy trading for the average consumer.
2.  **Automated Security:** Implementing smart contracts to ensure trustless transactions.
3.  **Innovative Redistribution:** A unique mechanism designed specifically for equitable distribution.

---

## 🚀 The Vision
This project underscores the potential of decentralized technology to combat monopolies and bridge the energy divide. We aren't just building a platform; we are accelerating the **global adoption of renewable energy** for a truly inclusive future.

**Challenges we ran into**

## Challenge 1 — Battery State Management in a Distributed Energy Architecture
 
### The Problem
Efficiently orchestrating the **charging and discharging cycles** across all battery systems in the network proved to be one of the most complex hardware-software co-design challenges of the project. Key difficulties included:
 
- **State-of-Charge (SoC) synchronization** — Each battery node needed to continuously broadcast its current energy capacity so the trading contract could make informed match-making decisions. Stale or out-of-sync SoC readings led to over-commitment of energy supply.
- **Charge/discharge conflict resolution** — When a node was simultaneously matched as both a buyer and a seller across different trade windows, concurrent read-write operations on battery state created race conditions in the coordination logic.
- **Threshold enforcement** — Defining safe operational boundaries (minimum SoC floors to protect battery health, maximum discharge rates) required these physical constraints to be reflected at both the firmware level and within the smart contract's business logic — keeping two systems in agreement at all times.

### Approach
A **buffered state management layer** was introduced between the hardware sensors and the contract, decoupling the physical battery cycle from the on-chain trading logic. Battery state was treated as an **eventually consistent** value with defined staleness thresholds, beyond which a node's trading eligibility was automatically suspended until a fresh reading was confirmed.
 
---
 
## Challenge 2 — Real-Time Firebase ↔ Solidity Smart Contract Integration
 
 
### The Problem
Bridging a Web2 real-time database with a Web3 smart contract introduced a class of integration challenges that neither system was natively designed to solve:
 
- **Oracles and trust boundaries** — Smart contracts cannot natively read from external data sources. Feeding Firebase sensor data into Solidity required an off-chain relay mechanism to act as a trusted data bridge, raising questions about data integrity and manipulation resistance.
- **Event latency and finality** — Firebase updates arrive in near real-time (sub-second), whereas Ethereum transactions require block confirmations. A sensor spike that triggered a trade could be confirmed on-chain seconds or minutes later, by which time the underlying energy state had changed.
- **Webhook-to-transaction mapping** — Designing a reliable listener that translated Firebase `onValue` change events into signed Ethereum transactions, without message loss or duplicate submissions, required idempotency safeguards in the relay service.
### Approach
An **off-chain relay service** (middleware layer) was built to subscribe to Firebase events, validate and normalize incoming sensor data, and submit structured transactions to the deployed contract. Idempotency keys were derived from the Firebase document ID and timestamp to prevent duplicate on-chain writes. Data was scaled to fixed-point integers (multiplied by 10³) before submission to preserve decimal precision within Solidity's integer type system.
 
---

## Challenge 3 — Vulnerabilities in the Energy Supply Transfer Process

### The Problem
A cascade of software bugs and security considerations surfaced specifically around the supply transfer workflow:
 
- **Reentrancy exposure** — Early iterations of the settlement function updated balances *after* triggering external calls, creating a classic reentrancy attack surface. A malicious contract acting as a buyer could re-enter the transfer function before state was finalized, enabling double-spend of energy credits.
- **Partial fulfillment edge cases** — If a seller's available supply dropped (due to a concurrent discharge event) between trade matching and settlement, the contract had no graceful mechanism to handle partial fills. Transactions would either revert entirely or settle for incorrect amounts, both unacceptable in an energy market context.
- **Atomic settlement failure** — The physical energy dispatch and the on-chain token transfer needed to succeed or fail *together*. Without a native two-phase commit mechanism on the blockchain, ensuring atomicity between the off-chain hardware action and the on-chain state change required a commit-reveal pattern with timeout-based rollback logic.
### Approach
The settlement contract was refactored using the **Checks-Effects-Interactions (CEI)** pattern to eliminate reentrancy vectors. A `ReentrancyGuard` modifier was applied to all externally callable settlement functions. Batch settlement was redesigned with bounded iteration and a paginated settlement queue to stay within gas limits. Partial fulfillment was handled via a **pro-rata allocation model**, where trades were settled for the minimum of committed supply and verified available supply at execution time. Front-running mitigation was approached through a **commit-reveal scheme** for trade submissions, obscuring order intent until reveal phase

### ClaimDrop
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/claimdrop-b262) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-SCBC%20Hackathon%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://scbc-hackathon.devfolio.co)

> Send SOL to anyone, even without a wallet

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Next.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Next.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![ARCore](https://img.shields.io/badge/ARCore-333333?style=flat-square) ![Rust](https://img.shields.io/badge/Rust-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![HTML/CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML/CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Crypto payments today are not user-friendly for everyday people.
To send someone SOL, both the sender and receiver must already have:

* a crypto wallet
* knowledge of how to use it
* and a public wallet address

This creates a huge barrier to adoption.

As a result:

* You can’t easily send crypto to new users
* Gifting or paying someone in SOL is confusing and inconvenient
* Businesses and creators lose opportunities because customers aren’t onboarded
* Web3 remains closed off to mainstream users

⸻

How ClaimDrop solves this

ClaimDrop removes this friction by allowing users to send SOL to anyone using a simple link or QR code — no wallet required upfront.

* The sender deposits SOL into a secure claim link
* The link can be shared via text, email, or QR
* The receiver opens the link and:
    * connects a wallet, or
    * creates one instantly
* Funds are claimed in seconds

⸻

Why this matters

By eliminating the need for a pre-existing wallet, ClaimDrop:

* Onboards new users into crypto seamlessly
* Makes SOL usable for real-world payments, gifting, and rewards
* Enables viral distribution through links and QR codes
* Bridges the gap between Web2 simplicity and Web3 power

⸻

Real-world use cases

* Send money to friends who don’t use crypto yet
* Event giveaways (scan QR → claim SOL instantly)
* Creator tips and rewards
* Merchant promotions and cashback
* Global remittances without friction

**Challenges we ran into**

Challenges we ran into

Building a “send-to-anyone” experience on Solana introduced several non-trivial challenges, especially around usability and security.

1. Wallet-less user flow

The core challenge was enabling users to receive SOL without already having a wallet. Solana transactions typically require both parties to have wallets and public addresses.

Solution:
We designed a claim-link system backed by a temporary escrow account. Funds are held securely until the recipient connects or creates a wallet, at which point the SOL is released.

⸻

2. Secure claim links

Since funds are tied to a shareable link, preventing unauthorized access or abuse was critical.

Solution:
We implemented unique, hard-to-guess claim tokens and added optional expiration logic to ensure links cannot be reused or exploited. Future improvements include adding signature-based verification or one-time claim enforcement on-chain.

⸻

3. Balancing UX with blockchain complexity

Crypto UX is often confusing, especially for non-technical users. Showing raw SOL amounts alone can be unintuitive.

Solution:
We display both SOL and its USD equivalent to make the experience feel familiar, while still using native Solana under the hood.

⸻

4. Transaction reliability and speed

Handling real-time claims required ensuring fast and reliable confirmation on Solana.

Solution:
We optimized for Solana’s fast finality and low fees, and designed the UI to provide immediate feedback during the claim process to improve user confidence.

⸻

Key takeaway

The biggest challenge was bridging the gap between Web3 infrastructure and Web2 simplicity — and ClaimDrop is designed specifically to solve that.

**Best Use of Solana**

How ClaimDrop fits “Best Use of Solana”

ClaimDrop is built specifically to leverage Solana’s core strengths — speed, low fees, and seamless user experience — to enable a completely new payment paradigm: sending SOL to anyone, even without a wallet.

Native SOL usage

Unlike many projects that rely on tokens or abstractions, ClaimDrop uses native SOL transfers at its core. Every transaction, claim, and settlement is executed directly on Solana, showcasing the network’s efficiency and reliability.

⸻

Instant, low-cost transactions

ClaimDrop depends on Solana’s high throughput and near-zero fees to make micro-payments and claimable transfers viable.

* Users can send small amounts of SOL without worrying about gas costs
* Recipients can claim funds instantly with minimal friction
* This enables real-world use cases like tipping, rewards, and giveaways

⸻

On-chain escrow mechanism

ClaimDrop introduces a lightweight on-chain escrow model, where SOL is temporarily held until claimed.

* Funds are secured on-chain until the recipient claims them
* Eliminates trust issues between sender and receiver
* Demonstrates practical use of Solana for conditional transactions

⸻

Wallet onboarding through Solana UX

By combining claim links with Solana wallet integration, ClaimDrop turns onboarding into a single-step experience:

* Users interact with Solana without needing prior setup
* Wallet connection or creation happens only at the moment of claiming
* This bridges Web2 simplicity with Web3 infrastructure

⸻

Why this stands out

ClaimDrop transforms Solana from a network that requires technical knowledge into a consumer-ready payment layer.

It demonstrates how Solana can:

* power mainstream financial interactions
* enable viral distribution via links and QR codes
* and unlock true accessibility for non-crypto users

### Stratix
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/stratix-3ce2) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/alycz/Stratix) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://stratix-phi.vercel.app/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://www.loom.com/share/ad6c8872e78e46ecb909d1162ba35772) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-SCBC%20Hackathon%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://scbc-hackathon.devfolio.co)

> Algorithmic Market Making on Pacifica DEX & Kalshi

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Prediction markets have a liquidity problem. Contracts move on relatively small orders because there aren’t enough resting bids and asks to absorb flow. Thus, what they need is active market making. Kalshi’s Liquidity Incentive Program directly addresses this: it pays traders for maintaining orders close to the best bid/ask, with the order book snapshotted every second and scores calculated on size and proximity. However, staying competitive in that program across multiple markets isn’t something you can do by hand.

On Pacifica, the problem is similar but different in shape. Airdrop farmers and anyone incentivized by on-chain activity all want to generate trading volume and contribute to thicker order book. The problem is that continuously quoting bid and ask, adjusting for inventory, and staying inside the spread requires placing and updating orders every second which is impossible if done manually. Thus, users need a practical tool that can run those strategies on autopilot. 

Stratix is that tool. It runs algorithmic market making strategies across both venues: Pacifica (a Solana perpetuals DEX) and Kalshi (prediction markets). Users configure parameters, backtest on historical data, and let the backend agent run.

**Challenges we ran into**

Dependency conflict on x402 + Solana signing: solders (the Rust-based Solana Python library) had a version conflict with the x402[svm] package. Resolving it required pinning solders==0.21.0 to get both libraries working together.

Funding detection across venues: Detecting whether a user had deposited funds worked differently on Pacifica vs. Kalshi vs. DFlow. The app was incorrectly forcing “demo mode” on logged-in users who had already funded. Required a dedicated fix to unify funding state detection across all venues.

**Best Use of Solana**

How we used Solana as a DeFi & Prediction Markets vertical:

Pacifica is a Solana perpetuals DEX. Stratix connects to it through a non-custodial delegation model built on Solana’s key infrastructure. The user holds a Privy embedded Solana wallet which means their keys never leave the browser. During onboarding, a separate Ed25519 agent keypair is generated on the backend. The user signs a binding message with their main wallet to authorize the agent, and from that point the agent handles all order placement: quoting bid and ask via the Avellaneda-Stoikov algorithm, adjusting for inventory, requoting every second. The agent cannot obtain more funds from the user's main wallet on its own, as withdrawals require a fresh signature with the user's approval.

Deposits to Pacifica are SPL token transfers. The frontend builds the transaction using @solana/web3.js and @solana/spl-token, creates the vault’s Associated Token Account if it doesn’t exist, and the user signs it with their Privy wallet. Settlement lands on Solana in ~400ms. Helius RPC handles balance polling and transaction confirmation. The 1-second requote cycle only works because Solana transaction fees are a fraction of a cent. On any other chain, fees would consume the spread before the strategy earns anything.

For Kalshi prediction markets, Stratix uses DFlow, a trade execution protocol on Solana, to place bets on-chain rather than through Kalshi’s REST API. The Kelly Criterion engine polls the DFlow orderbook every 30 seconds, computes the optimal position size given the user’s probability estimate and the current yes-bid price, and when the edge is sufficient, requests an unsigned Solana VersionedTransaction from DFlow’s quote API. That transaction is signed with the same Ed25519 agent key used for Pacifica and submitted directly to the Solana RPC. The result is a real on-chain swap: USDC in, YES or NO token out. The position settles on-chain when the market resolves with no separate Kalshi API credential required.

How we used Solana for the Agentic Commerce vertical:

Stratix implements the x402 HTTP payment protocol on Solana. Any external caller, an AI agent, a script, another service, can launch a trading strategy for an existing Stratix user by paying $1.00 USDC directly on-chain. The flow: the caller POSTs to /agent/launch, receives an HTTP 402 response with payment options, settles the payment on Solana, and retries with a proof header. The backend verifies the proof using ExactSvmServerScheme with the Coinbase CDP facilitator on mainnet. No Stratix API key needed, just a valid user ID and an on-chain payment.

### Chroma Arcade
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/chroma-arcade-868b) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/jadenchoi16/circle-sub) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://circle-sub.vercel.app/) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-SCBC%20Hackathon%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://scbc-hackathon.devfolio.co)

> "Insert coin. Make art. Settled on Arc."

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Quick overview: Pay-per-use AI doesn't work because card fees eat any transaction under ~$0.30, forcing every product into monthly subscriptions. Crypto could solve it, but wallets, gas tokens, and seed phrases scare off non-crypto users. Chroma Arcade fixes both by letting users pay fractions of a cent in USDC with zero wallet setup, all wrapped in an arcade-cabinet UX.
The deeper picture:
Pay-per-use AI is broken economically:

Image, video, and voice APIs charge cents per call
Traditional card rails can't settle anything below ~$0.30 without fees eating the whole transaction
Result: every AI consumer product shoves users into a $10–$20/month subscription they barely use

Onchain payment apps have the opposite problem:

People love "pay a penny, get a result"
But they have to install MetaMask, fund it with ETH for gas, understand what a chain is, and sign three popups
Nobody outside crypto does that

Chroma Arcade is the shortest answer to both:

User lands on the page
An embedded Circle Developer-Controlled Wallet spins up server-side
They type a prompt, pick a tier ($0.002 to $0.50), and click INSERT COIN
Server returns HTTP 402 Payment Required with an x402 paywall spec
Client redeems it on Arc Testnet with a real USDC transfer
Server verifies the transaction on-chain before unlocking Gemini
Image lands in their gallery with a live Arcscan link, all in about a second

No wallet install. No seed phrase. No gas token. USDC is gas on Arc. The mental model is a 1980s arcade cabinet: drop a coin, pick a thing, get a thing. The programmable-money primitive is invisible, which is the point.
The same primitive works for AI agents:

Operator funds the agent's embedded wallet once
Agent spends autonomously per-inference
Every call is a verifiable on-chain receipt instead of a line in a spreadsheet

Real uses:

Pay-per-image for casual or designer users who'd never pay $20/mo
Auditable per-call billing rails for AI agents
A demo pattern any AI company can copy: 402 paywall + embedded wallet + x402 redeem

No wallet install. No seed phrase. No gas token. USDC is gas on Arc. The user's mental model is a literal 1980s arcade cabinet: drop a coin, pick a thing, get a thing. The programmable-money primitive is completely invisible, which is exactly the point.

The same primitive works for AI agents: an operator funds the agent's embedded wallet once, the agent spends autonomously per-inference, and every call is a verifiable on-chain receipt instead of a line in a spreadsheet somewhere. That turns "per-call billing for AI services" from a SaaS reconciliation nightmare into a settled-in-real-time payment stream.

Real uses:

Pay-per-image for casual/designer users who'd never pay $20/mo for occasional generation.
Auditable per-call billing rails for AI agents.
A demo pattern any AI company can copy: 402 paywall + embedded wallet + x402 redeem.

**Challenges we ran into**

1. React Strict Mode minted duplicate wallets and rate-limited the faucet
In dev, useEffect fires twice, and my boot flow called POST /api/wallet/init without idempotency:

Every page load created two wallets
Only one got saved to localStorage, leaving orphans
Funding the "current" wallet hit the faucet; the orphan from the previous boot also hit it
Circle's testnet faucet started returning 429 Too Many Requests

Fix:

Added a useRef(false) guard (bootedRef) so init runs once per mount in Strict Mode
Added a "forget wallet" trashcan button for cleaning state during debugging
Made /api/wallet/init idempotent: if the caller already has a walletId, validate and return it

2. Gallery silently deleted itself down to 2 images
Weird UX bug. Root cause was a cascade:

Each full-resolution Gemini image is a ~1 MB base64 data URL
localStorage has a ~5 MB quota
The persistence layer was shrinking in-memory state to match what fit on disk
A generic QuotaExceededError silently trimmed the gallery to 2 items after every generation
It also intermittently threw a hard client-side exception during React's commit phase because setItem is synchronous and wasn't wrapped

Fix, in two layers:

Persistence is now async, running each image through a canvas pass that downscales to 640px and re-encodes at JPEG quality 0.72 (~1 MB down to ~40 KB)
Per-id cache so we never re-compress the same image twice
Full-resolution stays in memory for the session; only thumbnails get persisted
In-memory gallery is no longer coupled to the disk write, so 12 images always fit and the UI never loses its real state

3. The x402 failure-mode matrix is deceptively complicated
The happy path is easy. The failure paths are where the real work is:

Gemini fails after the user already paid: reuse the same txId on retry so the user isn't double-charged; only clear the pending coin once generation succeeds
Replay attacks: an in-memory Set (usedTxIds) tracks every redeemed txId for the life of the process. A transaction can unlock exactly one image
Wrong token, amount, destination, or state: the verifier checks all four independently. tokenId must match the resolved USDC UUID, amount >= tier.price, destinationAddress === merchant, and state ∈ {CONFIRMED, COMPLETE}. Any failure rejects with a specific reason

Building the developer panel (the </> button in the header) caught two of these. Seeing the raw 402 payload and the X-Payment header side-by-side while stepping through pay → verify → generate made the replay edge cases obvious.

**Programmable Money for Humans & Agents**

Chroma Arcade turns a Gemini image endpoint into a USDC-on-Arc micro-API, the same x402 flow that lets a human click "insert coin" is the one an autonomous agent would use to pay the exact same $0.002 for a pixel-art render at 2 a.m.

Team **team1** -- Jaden Choi
